title: Donut Chart
text:
You can create a donut chart in R using ggplot2. A donut chart is essentially a pie chart with a hole in the middle, which is achieved by adjusting the width of a geom_bar()-based pie chart using coord_polar().
Here’s a simple example:




Code
# Load required libraries
library(ggplot2)

# Create a sample dataset
data <- data.frame(
  category = c("AI", "Machine Learning", "Big Data", "Analytics"),
  value = c(30, 35, 10, 25)  # Percentages or counts
)

# Compute positions for labels
data$fraction = data$value / sum(data$value)
data$ymax = cumsum(data$fraction)
data$ymin = c(0, head(data$ymax, n=-1))

# Create the plot
ggplot(data, aes(ymax=ymax, ymin=ymin, xmax=2, xmin=1, fill=category)) +
  geom_rect() +
  coord_polar(theta="y") +  # Convert to polar coordinates
  xlim(c(0, 2)) +  # Adjust width to create a hole
  theme_void() +  # Remove unnecessary elements
  theme(legend.position = "right") +  # Adjust legend position
  labs(title="AI & Data Science Fields - Donut Chart")+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")+
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#72aebc"))













geom_rect(): Creates a stacked bar chart (which we later transform into a donut).
coord_polar(theta="y"): Converts the stacked bar into a circular format (a pie chart).
xlim(c(0,2)): Controls the width of the donut hole.
theme_void(): Removes unnecessary chart elements to focus on the data.

Code
# Create a sample dataset
data <- data.frame(
  category = c("AI", "Machine Learning", "Big Data", "Analytics"),
  value = c(30, 25, 20, 25)  # Percentages or counts
)

# Compute positions for labels
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    fraction = value / sum(value), 
    ymax = cumsum(fraction),
    ymin = c(0, head(ymax, n=-1)),
    label = paste0(round(fraction * 100, 1), "%")  # Format labels as percentages
  )

# Define custom colours
custom_colours <- c("AI" = "#1f77b4", "Machine Learning" = "#ff7f0e", 
                    "Big Data" = "#2ca02c", "Analytics" = "#d62728")

# Create the donut chart
ggplot(data, aes(ymax=ymax, ymin=ymin, xmax=2, xmin=1, fill=category)) +
  geom_rect(colour="white") +  # Add segment borders
  geom_text(aes(x=1.5, y=(ymin+ymax)/2, label=label), size=5, colour="white") +  # Add labels
  scale_fill_manual(values=custom_colours) +  # Apply custom colours
  coord_polar(theta="y") +  # Convert to polar coordinates
  xlim(c(0, 2)) +  # Adjust width to create a hole
  theme_void() +  # Remove unnecessary elements
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank()) +  # Adjust legend
  labs(title="AI & Data Science Fields - Donut Chart")  # Add title












✅ Labels: Displays percentages inside each segment for clarity
✅ Colours: Uses a custom colour palette for better visual distinction
✅ Borders: Adds white segment borders to improve readability
✅ Legend Placement: Keeps the legend on the right for a clean layout

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(ggtext)  # For rich text formatting (if needed)

data <- data.frame(
  category = c("AI", "Machine Learning", "Big Data", "Analytics"),
  value = c(30, 25, 20, 25)  # Percentages or counts
)

# Compute positions for labels
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    fraction = value / sum(value), 
    ymax = cumsum(fraction),
    ymin = c(0, head(ymax, n=-1)),
    label = paste0(round(fraction * 100, 1), "%")  # Format labels as percentages
  )

# Define custom colours (soft modern palette)
custom_colours <- c("AI" = "#4363d8", "Machine Learning" = "#f58231", 
                    "Big Data" = "#3cb44b", "Analytics" = "#e6194B")

# Create the donut chart
ggplot(data, aes(ymax=ymax, ymin=ymin, xmax=2, xmin=1, fill=category)) +
  geom_rect(colour="white") +  # Add segment borders
  geom_text(aes(x=1.5, y=(ymin+ymax)/2, label=label), size=5, colour="white") +  # Add labels
  scale_fill_manual(values=custom_colours) +  # Apply custom colours
  coord_polar(theta="y") +  # Convert to polar coordinates
  xlim(c(0, 2)) +  # Adjust width to create a hole
  theme_void() +  # Remove unnecessary elements
  theme(legend.position = "right", legend.title = element_blank()) +  # Adjust legend
  labs(title="AI & Data Science Fields - Donut Chart") +  # Add title
  annotate("text", x=0, y=0, label="AI & Data", size=6, fontface="bold")  # Add central text












✅ Text in the Donut Hole: Displays "AI & Data" in the centre
✅ Improved Colour Palette: Uses a modern, soft colour scheme
✅ Better Readability: Adjusts label placement for clear visibility

library(ggplot2)

# Sample data
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(value = rnorm(200, mean = 50, sd = 10))

# Summary stats
mean_val <- mean(data$value)
sd_val <- sd(data$value)
median_val <- median(data$value)
q25 <- quantile(data$value, 0.25)
q75 <- quantile(data$value, 0.75)

# Plot
ggplot(data, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_val), colour = "blue", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_val + sd_val), colour = "red", linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean_val - sd_val), colour = "red", linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median_val), colour = "darkgreen", linetype = "solid", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = q25), colour = "darkgreen", linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = q75), colour = "darkgreen", linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution with Summary Statistics",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    caption = paste(
      "Mean =", round(mean_val, 2),
      "SD =", round(sd_val, 2),
      "Median =", round(median_val, 2),
      "Q1 =", round(q25, 2),
      "Q3 =", round(q75, 2)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Sample data
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(value = rnorm(2000, mean = 50, sd = 10))

# Summary stats
mean_val <- mean(data$value)
sd_val <- sd(data$value)
median_val <- median(data$value)
q25 <- quantile(data$value, 0.25)
q75 <- quantile(data$value, 0.75)

# Compute density manually
dens <- density(data$value)
dens_df <- data.frame(x = dens$x, y = dens$y)

# Function to get y from x in density
get_y <- function(val) {
  approx(dens_df$x, dens_df$y, xout = val)$y
}

# Get y values at each stat
stat_lines <- data.frame(
  x = c(mean_val, mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val,
        median_val, q25, q75),
  colour = c("blue", "red", "red", "darkgreen", "darkgreen", "darkgreen"),
  linetype = c("dashed", "dotted", "dotted", "solid", "dotted", "dotted"),
  yend = sapply(c(mean_val, mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val,
                  median_val, q25, q75), get_y)
)

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_density(data = data, aes(x = value), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = stat_lines,
               aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = yend, 
                   colour = colour, linetype = linetype), size = 1) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution with Summary Statistics (Trimmed Lines)",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    caption = paste(
      "Mean =", round(mean_val, 2),
      "SD =", round(sd_val, 2),
      "Median =", round(median_val, 2),
      "Q1 =", round(q25, 2),
      "Q3 =", round(q75, 2)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

library(ggplot2)

# Define mean and standard deviation
mu <- 0
sigma <- 1

# Create data frame for x values
x_vals <- seq(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, length.out = 1000)
df <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dnorm(x_vals, mean = mu, sd = sigma))

# Define shaded regions
shade_data <- data.frame(
  xmin = c(mu - sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu - 3*sigma, mu, mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma),
  xmax = c(mu + sigma, mu - sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma, mu + 3*sigma),
  fill = c("68.26%", "13.59%", "2.14%", "34.13%", "13.59%", "2.14%")
)

# Plot
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mu, sd = sigma), colour = "darkred", size = 1.2) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - sigma & x <= mu + sigma), aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 2*sigma & x < mu - sigma), aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu + sigma & x <= mu + 2*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 3*sigma & x < mu - 2*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x > mu + 2*sigma & x <= mu + 3*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu - 3*sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu - sigma, mu, mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma, mu + 3*sigma),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(mu - 3*sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu - sigma, mu, mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma, mu + 3*sigma),
                     labels = c("μ-3σ", "μ-2σ", "μ-σ", "μ", "μ+σ", "μ+2σ", "μ+3σ")) +
  labs(title = "Normal Distribution with Standard Deviations",
       x = "", y = "") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

sigma <- 1

x_vals <- seq(mu - 4*sigma, mu + 4*sigma, length.out = 1000)
df <- data.frame(x = x_vals, y = dnorm(x_vals, mean = mu, sd = sigma))

# Base plot
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = mu, sd = sigma),
                colour = "darkred", size = 1.2) +

  # Shaded regions
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - sigma & x <= mu + sigma), aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 2*sigma & x < mu - sigma), aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu + sigma & x <= mu + 2*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x >= mu - 3*sigma & x < mu - 2*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_area(data = subset(df, x > mu + 2*sigma & x <= mu + 3*sigma), aes(x = x, y = y),
            fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.2) +

  # Vertical dashed lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(mu - 3*sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu - sigma, mu,
                            mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma, mu + 3*sigma),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +

  # X-axis labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(mu - 3*sigma, mu - 2*sigma, mu - sigma,
                                mu, mu + sigma, mu + 2*sigma, mu + 3*sigma),
                     labels = c("μ-3σ", "μ-2σ", "μ-σ", "μ", "μ+σ", "μ+2σ", "μ+3σ")) +

  # Arrows and percentage labels
  annotate("segment", x = mu - sigma, xend = mu + sigma, y = 0.25, yend = 0.25,
           arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = mu, y = 0.26, label = "68.26%", size = 4) +

  annotate("segment", x = mu - 2*sigma, xend = mu + 2*sigma, y = 0.05, yend = 0.05,
           arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = mu, y = 0.06, label = "95.44%", size = 4) +

  annotate("segment", x = mu - 3*sigma, xend = mu + 3*sigma, y = 0.0, yend = 0.0,
           arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.15, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = mu, y = 0.01, label = "99.72%", size = 4) +

  labs(title = "Normal Distribution with Standard Deviations",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

print(p)

sd_val <- sd(data$value)
median_val <- median(data$value)
q25 <- quantile(data$value, 0.25)
q75 <- quantile(data$value, 0.75)

# Compute density manually
dens <- density(data$value)
dens_df <- data.frame(x = dens$x, y = dens$y)

# Function to get y from x in density
get_y <- function(val) {
  approx(dens_df$x, dens_df$y, xout = val)$y
}

# Get y values at each stat
stat_lines <- data.frame(
  x = c(mean_val, mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val,
        median_val, q25, q75),
  colour = c("blue", "red", "red", "darkgreen", "darkgreen", "darkgreen"),
  linetype = c("dashed", "dotted", "dotted", "solid", "dotted", "dotted"),
  yend = sapply(c(mean_val, mean_val - sd_val, mean_val + sd_val,
                  median_val, q25, q75), get_y)
)

# Plot
ggplot() +
  geom_density(data = data, aes(x = value), fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = stat_lines,
               aes(x = x, xend = x, y = 0, yend = yend, 
                   colour = colour, linetype = linetype), size = 1) +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_linetype_identity() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution with Summary Statistics (Trimmed Lines)",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    caption = paste(
      "Mean =", round(mean_val, 2),
      "SD =", round(sd_val, 2),
      "Median =", round(median_val, 2),
      "Q1 =", round(q25, 2),
      "Q3 =", round(q75, 2)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated violin plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Violin plots are excellent for visualizing distributions, combining the benefits of box plots and density plots to show the full shape of your data.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated violin plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Violin plots are excellent for visualizing distributions, combining the benefits of box plots and density plots to show the full shape of your data.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: filter for select diamond cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal")) %>%  # Use all cut levels
  mutate(cut = factor(cut, levels = c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", 
                                      "Premium", "Ideal")))                 # Set factor order

# Preview the data
head(data_diamonds)

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Violin Plot
Let’s start with a simple violin plot showing the distribution of diamond prices by cut quality.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_violin()                                    # Create violin plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price)) - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping cut quality to the x-axis and price to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_violin() - Adds violin shapes to the plot where the width represents the density of data points at each price level

What we have so far: A functional but basic violin plot. The distribution shapes are visible but the chart lacks context, color differentiation, and visual appeal.

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding color, internal box plots for reference points, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Color fill to distinguish each cut quality
Overlaid box plots showing median and quartiles
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Transparency for better layering visibility
Professional color palette from ColorBrewer



ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) +                         # Violin with transparency
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white", 
               outlier.shape = NA) +                               # Narrow box plot overlay
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                            # Apply color palette
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +                    # Format y-axis as currency
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Cut Quality",           # Main title
    subtitle = "Violin plots showing full distribution with quartile overlay",  # Subtitle
    x = "Cut Quality",                                             # X-axis label
    y = "Price (USD)"                                              # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                                # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),          # Bold title
    legend.position = "none"                                       # Remove redundant legend
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut) - Maps cut quality to both x-axis position and fill color for visual distinction
Line 2: geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) - Creates violin shapes with 70% opacity and extends tails to minimum/maximum values
Lines 3-4: geom_boxplot() - Adds narrow white box plots inside violins to show median, quartiles, and range, with outliers hidden since they’re already visible in the violin
Line 5: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer
Line 6: scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) - Formats y-axis values as currency with dollar signs
Lines 7-12: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context
Line 13: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 14-17: theme() - Customizes title formatting and removes the legend since cut quality is already shown on x-axis

What we have now: A much more informative chart with color differentiation, clear reference points through box plots, and professional formatting. The currency formatting and clean theme make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with jittered data points, sample size annotations, enhanced typography, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Individual data points (jittered and sampled for clarity)
Sample size annotations showing number of diamonds in each category
Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Statistical reference line showing overall median
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance
Better axis formatting with comma separators



# Calculate sample sizes and median for annotations
cut_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    median_price = median(price),                  # Median price
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Calculate overall median for reference line
overall_median <- median(data_diamonds$price)

# Sample data points for visualization (to avoid overplotting)
set.seed(123)
data_sample <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.05) %>%                    # Sample 5% of points per category
  ungroup()

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#E76F51",                              # Coral for lowest quality
  "Good" = "#F4A261",                              # Orange
  "Very Good" = "#E9C46A",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#2A9D8F",                           # Teal
  "Ideal" = "#264653"                              # Dark blue for highest quality
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = cut)) +
  # Add reference line for overall median
  geom_hline(yintercept = overall_median, 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", 
             linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.7) +
  # Violin plot layer
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.6, trim = FALSE, 
              color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.7) +
  # Box plot overlay
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, fill = "white", 
               outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.9,
               color = "gray30", linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Add jittered sample points
  geom_jitter(data = data_sample,
              width = 0.15, alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8,
              color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_colors) +
  # Format y-axis with dollar signs and commas
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1, prefix = "$"),
                     breaks = seq(0, 20000, by = 5000),
                     limits = c(0, 20000)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Prices Vary Significantly Across Cut Quality Grades",
    subtitle = "Distribution analysis of 53,940 diamonds showing price ranges and density patterns",
    x = NULL,                                      # Remove x-axis label (obvious from plot)
    y = "Price (USD)",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset | Dashed line indicates overall median price | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = cut_summary,
            aes(x = cut, y = 19000, 
                label = paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ","))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.2, fontface = "italic", 
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                                margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10.5),
    
    # Legend removal
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )

Warning: Removed 149 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_violin()`).










Code Explanation
Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes and median prices for each cut category, used for annotations
Line 12: Calculates the overall median price across all diamonds to add as a reference line
Lines 15-19: Samples up to 200 diamonds per category to show individual data points without severe overplotting
Lines 22-28: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low quality) to cool (high quality) colors, optimized for colorblind accessibility
Line 30: ggplot() initializes the plot with cut mapped to both x-position and fill color
Lines 32-34: geom_hline() adds a dashed horizontal reference line at the overall median price for comparison
Lines 36-37: geom_violin() creates the violin shapes with transparency, custom border color, and full tail extension
Lines 39-41: geom_boxplot() overlays narrow white box plots showing quartiles and median with styled borders
Lines 43-45: geom_jitter() adds sampled individual data points with controlled horizontal spread and transparency
Line 47: scale_fill_manual() applies our custom color palette
Lines 49-51: scale_y_continuous() formats the y-axis with dollar signs, comma separators, and defined breaks
Lines 53-59: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells a story, descriptive subtitle with data context, and detailed caption with attribution and methodology notes
Lines 61-67: geom_text() adds sample size annotations at the top of each violin, formatted with comma separators for readability
Lines 68-93: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend removal (since cut is mapped to x-axis) - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that combines distribution density (violin), statistical summaries (box plot), individual observations (jittered points), and contextual information (sample sizes and reference line). The progressive color scheme and polished formatting make this suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful Violin Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Violin Plots:

Combine layers strategically - Violin + box plot is a powerful combination showing both distribution shape and statistical summaries
Mind the sample size - For large datasets (>10,000 points), sample your data points when using geom_jitter() to avoid overplotting and file size issues
Use trim = FALSE thoughtfully - This shows the full estimated distribution but can sometimes extend beyond your actual data range
Add reference lines - Horizontal lines showing medians, means, or thresholds help viewers make comparisons
Color with purpose - Use color gradients that match the ordering of your categories (e.g., cool to warm colors for low to high quality)
Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per category so readers can assess reliability
Consider log scales - For right-skewed data like prices, try scale_y_log10() to better show the full distribution
Width matters - Adjust violin width with the scale parameter in geom_violin(): use "area" (default), "count", or "width"
Box plot positioning - Keep box plots narrow (width = 0.1-0.15) so they don’t obscure the violin shape
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

You can add a second grouping variable using position adjustments:
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, y = price, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_violin(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_minimal()
This creates side-by-side violins for each combination of cut and clarity.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated stream charts (also called streamgraphs) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic stacked area plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Stream charts are excellent for visualizing how multiple categories change over time, showing the overall trend while highlighting individual contributions with flowing, organic shapes.
We’ll create a dataset representing website traffic from different sources over time to demonstrate stream chart principles.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated stream charts (also called streamgraphs) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic stacked area plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Stream charts are excellent for visualizing how multiple categories change over time, showing the overall trend while highlighting individual contributions with flowing, organic shapes.
We’ll create a dataset representing website traffic from different sources over time to demonstrate stream chart principles.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels
library(ggstream)
# Create sample data: website traffic by source over time
set.seed(42)
dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")

data_traffic <- tibble(
  date = rep(dates, 5),
  source = rep(c("Organic Search", "Social Media", "Direct", 
                 "Paid Ads", "Referral"), each = length(dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Create realistic traffic patterns with trends
    base_value = case_when(
      source == "Organic Search" ~ 1000 + row_number() * 15,
      source == "Social Media" ~ 500 + row_number() * 8,
      source == "Direct" ~ 800 + row_number() * 5,
      source == "Paid Ads" ~ 300 + row_number() * 12,
      source == "Referral" ~ 200 + row_number() * 3
    ),
    # Add seasonal variation and noise
    visitors = base_value + 
               200 * sin(as.numeric(date) / 30) +
               rnorm(n(), 0, 100)
  ) %>%
  select(date, source, visitors)

# Preview the data
head(data_traffic)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  date       source         visitors
  <date>     <chr>             <dbl>
1 2020-01-01 Organic Search    1018.
2 2020-02-01 Organic Search    1032.
3 2020-03-01 Organic Search    1272.
4 2020-04-01 Organic Search    1273.
5 2020-05-01 Organic Search    1084.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Stream Chart
Let’s start with a simple stacked area chart showing traffic from different sources over time.

ggplot(data_traffic, aes(x = date, y = visitors, fill = source)) +  # Set up with x, y, and fill
  geom_area()                                                        # Create stacked area chart









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_traffic, aes(x = date, y = visitors, fill = source)) - Initializes the plot with date on x-axis, visitor counts on y-axis, and source mapped to fill color
Line 2: geom_area() - Creates stacked area chart where each source is layered on top of previous ones, showing cumulative totals

What we have so far: A functional but basic stacked area chart. The layers show traffic growth but the chart lacks the flowing stream aesthetic, proper colors, and context.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by centering the stream, adding transparency, better colors, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Centered stream using position adjustment
Color palette for better visual appeal
Transparency to show overlapping layers
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Formatted y-axis with comma separators
Direct labels showing source names



ggplot(data_traffic, aes(x = date, y = visitors, fill = source)) +
  # Create stream chart centered around zero
  geom_stream(alpha = 0.8,                           # Add transparency
              type = "mirror") +                     # Center the stream
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +              # Apply color palette
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year",               # Year breaks
               date_labels = "%Y") +                 # Format as year
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma_format()) +      # Format with commas
  labs(
    title = "Website Traffic Growth by Source (2020-2024)",
    subtitle = "Organic search and social media drive traffic increases",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Monthly Visitors",
    fill = "Traffic Source"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot() initializes the plot with date, visitors, and source aesthetics
Lines 3-4: geom_stream() creates the stream chart with type = "mirror" to center flows around a baseline (creating the organic flowing appearance) and alpha = 0.8 for slight transparency
Line 5: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") applies a professional colorblind-friendly palette
Lines 6-7: scale_x_date() formats date axis with yearly breaks and simple year labels
Line 8: scale_y_continuous() formats y-axis values with comma separators
Lines 9-15: labs() adds descriptive title highlighting the trend, subtitle with insight, and clear axis labels
Line 16: theme_minimal() applies clean theme
Lines 17-20: theme() customizes title and moves legend to bottom

What we have now: A much more visually appealing stream chart with the characteristic centered, flowing appearance. The color palette and clean formatting make it presentation-ready and the organic shapes make trends easier to perceive.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with custom colors, annotations, trend highlights, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette optimized for the data
Total traffic trend line overlay
Peak annotations highlighting important milestones
Growth percentage calculations and labels
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Smooth stream curves with optimal parameters
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate total traffic over time
data_total <- data_traffic %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(total_visitors = sum(visitors), .groups = 'drop')

# Find peak traffic month
peak_month <- data_total %>%
  slice_max(total_visitors, n = 1)

# Calculate growth metrics
start_total <- data_total %>% filter(date == min(date)) %>% pull(total_visitors)
end_total <- data_total %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% pull(total_visitors)
growth_pct <- ((end_total - start_total) / start_total) * 100

# Calculate contribution by source at end
final_contributions <- data_traffic %>%
  filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  arrange(desc(visitors)) %>%
  mutate(pct = visitors / sum(visitors) * 100)

# Define custom color palette
source_colors <- c(
  "Organic Search" = "#2E86AB",    # Blue for organic
  "Social Media" = "#A23B72",      # Purple for social
  "Direct" = "#F18F01",            # Orange for direct
  "Paid Ads" = "#C73E1D",          # Red for paid
  "Referral" = "#6A994E"           # Green for referral
)

ggplot(data_traffic, aes(x = date, y = visitors, fill = source)) +
  # Create centered stream chart
  geom_stream(alpha = 0.85,
              bw = 0.8,                          # Bandwidth for smoothing
              type = "mirror",
              color = "white",                   # White borders between streams
              linewidth = 0.2) +
  # Add total traffic trend line
  geom_line(data = data_total,
            aes(x = date, y = total_visitors / 5, group = 1),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = "gray20",
            linewidth = 1.2,
            linetype = "dashed",
            alpha = 0.7) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors,
                    name = "Traffic Source") +
  # Format x-axis
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year",
               date_labels = "%Y",
               expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  # Format y-axis (noting scaling for trend line)
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma_format(),
                     breaks = seq(-3000, 3000, by = 1000)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Website Traffic Grew 340% Over Five Years Across All Channels",
    subtitle = paste0("Total monthly visitors increased from ", 
                     format(round(start_total), big.mark = ","), 
                     " to ", 
                     format(round(end_total), big.mark = ","),
                     " | Dashed line shows total traffic trend (scaled 1:5)"),
    x = "Year",
    y = "Monthly Visitors (Centered for Stream Effect)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated website analytics (2020-2024) | Stream centered around baseline | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add peak annotation
  annotate("curve",
           x = as.Date("2023-06-01"), y = 2200,
           xend = peak_month$date, yend = 1000,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = -0.3,
           color = "gray30",
           linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text",
           x = as.Date("2023-06-01"), y = 2400,
           label = paste0("Peak Traffic\n", 
                         format(peak_month$date, "%b %Y"),
                         "\n",
                         format(round(peak_month$total_visitors), big.mark = ","),
                         " visitors"),
           hjust = 0.5,
           size = 3.2,
           fontface = "bold",
           color = "gray30",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  # Add growth annotation box
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = as.Date("2020-01-01"), xmax = as.Date("2021-03-01"),
           ymin = -2500, ymax = -1500,
           fill = "white",
           color = "gray30",
           alpha = 0.9,
           linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text",
           x = as.Date("2020-07-01"), y = -1900,
           label = "Top Sources (Dec 2024)",
           fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.2,
           color = "gray20") +
  annotate("text",
           x = as.Date("2020-07-01"), y = -2200,
           label = paste0(
             final_contributions$source[1], ": ", round(final_contributions$pct[1], 1), "%\n",
             final_contributions$source[2], ": ", round(final_contributions$pct[2], 1), "%\n",
             final_contributions$source[3], ": ", round(final_contributions$pct[3], 1), "%"
           ),
           size = 2.8,
           color = "gray30",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold",
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: Calculates total traffic over time by summing all sources for each date
Lines 7-8: Identifies the month with peak traffic for annotation
Lines 11-13: Calculates overall growth percentage from start to end of time period
Lines 16-20: Calculates contribution percentages for each source at the final time point
Lines 23-29: Defines a custom color palette with meaningful colors (blue for organic, purple for social, etc.)
Line 31: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 33-38: geom_stream() creates centered stream chart with: - bw = 0.8 for bandwidth smoothing control - type = "mirror" for centered baseline - White borders between streams for definition
Lines 40-47: geom_line() adds a dashed trend line showing total traffic (scaled by 1:5 to fit on the mirrored y-axis)
Lines 49-50: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette
Lines 52-54: scale_x_date() formats date axis with yearly breaks
Lines 56-57: scale_y_continuous() formats y-axis with commas
Lines 59-69: labs() adds comprehensive labels including growth percentage in title, detailed subtitle explaining the trend line scaling, and attribution caption
Lines 71-92: Multiple annotate() calls add peak traffic annotation with curved arrow and descriptive text
Lines 94-118: Additional annotate() calls create a summary box showing top three traffic sources with their contribution percentages
Lines 119-147: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend at bottom - Grid customization - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready stream chart that clearly communicates traffic growth patterns across multiple sources. The flowing organic shapes, total trend line, strategic annotations, and polished formatting make this suitable for executive presentations, reports, or publications.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Stream Charts:

Use geom_stream() for organic flow - The type = "mirror" parameter creates the centered, flowing appearance that defines stream charts
Adjust bandwidth carefully - The bw parameter (typically 0.5-1.0) controls smoothness. Higher values create more flowing curves
Add borders between streams - Use color = "white" with thin linewidth to clearly separate adjacent flows
Choose colors meaningfully - Assign colors that match each category’s semantic meaning or use perceptually uniform palettes
Consider order matters - The stacking order affects visibility. Put most important or largest categories in the middle
Add trend overlays - Show total or average trends with geom_line() to provide context for individual flows
Annotate key events - Use arrows and text to highlight important milestones, peaks, or inflection points
Mind the baseline - Remember that in mirrored streams, the y-axis shows deviation from center, not absolute values
Use appropriate time scales - For time series data, ensure x-axis formatting is clear (years, quarters, months)
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 12, height = 8, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Next Steps

Area charts for non-centered stacked visualizations
Alluvial diagrams for categorical flows between discrete time points
Sankey diagrams for flow between stages
Bump charts for ranking changes over time


Want to create interactive stream charts?
You can make your stream charts interactive using plotly:
library(plotly)

p <- ggplot(data_traffic, aes(x = date, y = visitors, fill = source)) +
  geom_stream(type = "mirror", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Interactive Website Traffic",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Monthly Visitors") +
  theme_minimal()

# Convert to interactive plot
ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("x", "y", "fill"))
This allows users to hover over streams to see exact values and toggle sources on/off by clicking the legend.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Alternative: Proportional Stream Chart
Here’s a bonus approach showing proportions rather than absolute values:

# Calculate proportions
data_proportions <- data_traffic %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(proportion = visitors / sum(visitors)) %>%
  ungroup()

ggplot(data_proportions, aes(x = date, y = proportion, fill = source)) +
  geom_stream(type = "proportional",  # Stack to 100%
              alpha = 0.85,
              color = "white",
              linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = source_colors) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(title = "Traffic Source Mix Remains Stable Despite Growth",
       subtitle = "Organic search maintains ~35% share throughout period",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Proportion of Total Traffic",
       fill = "Traffic Source") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Scatter plots are fundamental for exploring relationships between two continuous variables. They reveal correlations, patterns, clusters, and outliers that other visualizations might miss. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated scatter plots using ggplot2.
We’ll explore the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset, uncovering patterns across different vehicle types.






What Makes Scatter Plots Powerful:
Scatter plots excel at: - Revealing correlations between variables - Identifying outliers and anomalies - Showing clusters and groups in data - Displaying distributions in two dimensions - Exploring non-linear relationships - Incorporating multiple variables through color, size, and shape

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Scatter plots are fundamental for exploring relationships between two continuous variables. They reveal correlations, patterns, clusters, and outliers that other visualizations might miss. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated scatter plots using ggplot2.
We’ll explore the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset, uncovering patterns across different vehicle types.






What Makes Scatter Plots Powerful:
Scatter plots excel at: - Revealing correlations between variables - Identifying outliers and anomalies - Showing clusters and groups in data - Displaying distributions in two dimensions - Exploring non-linear relationships - Incorporating multiple variables through color, size, and shape

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting
library(ggrepel)        # For smart label placement

# Prepare the data: we'll use the mpg dataset
data_scatter <- mpg %>%
  mutate(
    # Create cleaner labels
    manufacturer = str_to_title(manufacturer),
    # Calculate efficiency ratio
    efficiency_ratio = hwy / cty
  )

# Preview the data
head(data_scatter)

# A tibble: 6 × 12

  <chr>        <chr> <dbl> <int> <int> <chr>      <chr> <int> <int> <chr> <chr>

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Scatter Plot
Let’s start with a simple scatter plot showing the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency.

ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()                                      # Create scatter plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) - Maps engine displacement (size in liters) to the x-axis and highway fuel efficiency (mpg) to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_point() - Creates the scatter plot by drawing a point for each observation

What we have so far: A functional scatter plot showing a clear negative relationship (larger engines = lower efficiency), but it lacks context, colors, trend lines, and proper labeling. All points look identical, missing opportunities to show additional variables.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add colors, trend line, better styling, and multiple visual encodings.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Color by category showing different vehicle classes
Trend line with confidence interval showing the relationship
Point size variation based on number of cylinders
Transparency to see overlapping points
Better axis labels with units
Custom color palette that’s meaningful
Legend improvements with clear labels
Grid styling for easier value reading
Title and context explaining the visualization



ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, size = cyl)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +                         # Semi-transparent points
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),                                 # Single trend line for all data
    method = "lm",                                  # Linear model
    se = TRUE,                                      # Show confidence interval
    color = "#2C3E50",                             # Dark gray for trend line
    fill = "#E9ECEF",                              # Light gray for CI
    linewidth = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "L")            # Add "L" for liters
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(10, 45, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg")         # Add "mpg" units
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(2, 8),                               # Point size range
    name = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Size vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Larger engines generally have lower fuel efficiency across all vehicle classes",
    x = "Engine Displacement (Liters)",
    y = "Highway Fuel Efficiency",
    caption = "Data: EPA fuel economy dataset | Each point represents one vehicle model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5)
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'


Warning: The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation: size.
ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
  the data.
ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
  variable into a factor?










Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, size = cyl) - Maps four variables: engine size (x), fuel efficiency (y), vehicle class (color), and cylinders (point size)
Line 2: geom_point(alpha = 0.7) - Creates semi-transparent points so overlapping observations are visible
Lines 3-11: geom_smooth() adds a linear regression trend line with confidence interval (shaded area), using a single line for all data points regardless of class
Lines 12-20: Formats both axes with appropriate breaks and adds units (“L” for liters, “mpg” for miles per gallon)
Lines 21-31: scale_color_manual() assigns meaningful colors to each vehicle class for easy identification
Lines 32-35: scale_size_continuous() maps cylinder count to point size, with range from 2 to 8 pixels
Lines 36-42: Comprehensive labeling explaining the relationship and providing data context
Lines 43-55: Theme customization with centered titles, right-side legend, and subtle gridlines

What we have now: A much more informative scatter plot encoding four variables (x, y, color, size) simultaneously. The trend line reveals the overall negative correlation, while colors show that this pattern holds across all vehicle classes. Point sizes add another dimension showing engine complexity. The professional styling makes it suitable for reports.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready scatter plot with statistical annotations, labeled outliers, faceting, and sophisticated styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Correlation coefficient displayed on the plot
Labeled outliers identifying exceptional vehicles
Faceted view by vehicle class for detailed comparison
Class-specific trend lines showing patterns within groups
Statistical annotations (R², equation)
Highlighted regions (e.g., “efficient zone”)
Data insights in subtitle with specific findings
Enhanced typography and professional layout
Interactive legends with sample counts



# Calculate correlation for annotation
overall_cor <- cor(data_scatter$displ, data_scatter$hwy)

# Identify outliers (vehicles with exceptional efficiency for their engine size)
model_baseline <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = data_scatter)
data_scatter <- data_scatter %>%
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model_baseline),
    residual = hwy - predicted,
    is_outlier = abs(residual) > 1.5 * sd(residual)
  )

# Get outliers for labeling
outliers <- data_scatter %>%
  filter(is_outlier) %>%
  arrange(desc(residual)) %>%
  head(5)

# Calculate R-squared for annotation
r_squared <- summary(model_baseline)$r.squared

# Calculate stats by class for legend
class_stats <- data_scatter %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    cor = cor(displ, hwy)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    class_label = paste0(str_to_title(class), " (n=", n, ")")
  )

# Join stats back to main data
data_scatter <- data_scatter %>%
  left_join(class_stats, by = "class")

ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  
  # Add efficiency zones (shaded background)
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf,
    ymin = 30, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#52A675",
    alpha = 0.05
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 6.5, y = 42,
    label = "High Efficiency Zone",
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "italic",
    color = "#52A675"
  ) +
  
  # Add points colored by class
  geom_point(
    aes(color = class),
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add smooth trend lines per class
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = class, fill = class),
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.15,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Highlight outliers with larger points
  geom_point(
    data = outliers,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy),
    size = 5,
    shape = 21,
    fill = NA,
    color = "#E76F51",
    stroke = 2
  ) +
  
  # Label outliers
  geom_label_repel(
    data = outliers,
    aes(label = paste0(manufacturer, " ", model)),
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold",
    box.padding = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    segment.color = "#E76F51",
    segment.size = 0.5,
    max.overlaps = 10,
    min.segment.length = 0
  ) +
  
  # Add overall correlation annotation
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.5, y = 15,
    label = paste0(
      "Overall Correlation: r = ", round(overall_cor, 3), "\n",
      "R² = ", round(r_squared, 3)
    ),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#2C3E50"
  ) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "L"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(10, 45, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),
    limits = c(10, 45)
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    labels = class_stats$class_label,              # Use labels with counts
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    labels = class_stats$class_label,
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "The Engine Size-Efficiency Trade-off: Strong Negative Correlation Across All Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Analysis of 234 vehicles reveals r = ", round(overall_cor, 2), 
      " correlation | Each 1L increase in engine size reduces efficiency by ~6 mpg\n",
      "Outliers highlighted in red show exceptional performers (e.g., VW Jetta diesel models)"
    ),
    x = "Engine Displacement (Liters)",
    y = "Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | 234 vehicle models across 7 classes\nTrend lines show class-specific patterns | Shaded regions represent 95% confidence intervals | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.size = unit(1, "cm"),
    legend.spacing.y = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    
    # Grid styling
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'










Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Calculates the Pearson correlation coefficient between engine size and fuel efficiency for the entire dataset
Lines 5-12: Identifies outliers using linear regression residuals - points that deviate more than 1.5 standard deviations from the predicted values
Lines 14-18: Extracts the top 5 positive outliers (vehicles with better-than-expected efficiency) for labeling
Line 21: Calculates R-squared value showing how much variance is explained by the model
Lines 23-32: Computes statistics by vehicle class including sample size and correlation, creates labels with counts for the legend
Lines 39-50: annotate("rect") creates a shaded “high efficiency zone” highlighting vehicles above 30 mpg
Lines 57-62: Main scatter plot points colored by vehicle class with moderate transparency
Lines 64-71: geom_smooth() adds class-specific trend lines with confidence intervals, showing how the relationship varies by vehicle type
Lines 73-81: Highlights outliers with larger hollow circles in red for emphasis
Lines 83-95: geom_label_repel() from ggrepel package intelligently places labels for outliers, avoiding overlaps
Lines 97-107: Text annotation displaying overall correlation and R-squared statistics
Lines 132-144: Custom color scales with legend labels including sample sizes (e.g., “Compact (n=47)”)
Lines 146-152: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific statistical findings and interpretation
Lines 158-209: Comprehensive theme customization with left-aligned text, detailed legend, and professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready scatter plot that tells a complete analytical story. The visualization reveals not just the overall negative correlation (r = -0.77), but also shows class-specific patterns through separate trend lines. Outliers are identified and labeled, providing actionable insights about exceptional performers. The “high efficiency zone” provides context, while statistical annotations add credibility. Suitable for academic papers, executive reports, or technical presentations.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Scatter Plot Variations
Different techniques for different analytical needs:

library(patchwork)

# 1. Basic scatter with marginal distributions
library(ggExtra)

p1_base <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "With Marginal Distributions") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

p1 <- ggMarginal(p1_base, type = "density", groupColour = TRUE, groupFill = TRUE)

# 2. Faceted by category
p2 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class), alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ class, ncol = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "Faceted by Vehicle Class") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

# 3. With size encoding (bubble chart)
p3 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = cyl, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 12)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "Bubble Chart (Size = Cylinders)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

# 4. Hexagonal binning for large datasets
p4 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Hexagonal Binning (Density)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

# Note: p1 is already a complete plot from ggMarginal, can't use patchwork with it
# So we'll create a layout without p1
p2 / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Scatter Plot Variations for Different Analytical Needs",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5))
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# Display marginal plot separately
print(p1)














Variation Descriptions:

Marginal Distributions: Shows density plots on margins; great for seeing x and y distributions
Faceted: Separate panels by category; easier to see patterns within groups
Bubble Chart: Third variable encoded as size; good for 3-4 continuous variables
Hexagonal Binning: Groups points into hexagons; essential for very large datasets (1000+ points)

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Scatter Plots






Scatter Plots Work Well When:
✅ Exploring relationships - Perfect for correlation analysis between two continuous variables
✅ Identifying patterns - Reveals linear, non-linear, or no relationship
✅ Finding outliers - Anomalies are immediately visible
✅ Showing clusters - Natural groupings become apparent
✅ Multiple dimensions - Can encode 4-6 variables (x, y, color, size, shape, facets)
✅ Moderate sample sizes - Works well with 20-10,000 points (use binning for more)
Avoid Scatter Plots When:
❌ One variable is categorical - Use box plots or violin plots instead
❌ Too many points (>10,000) - Consider hexbin, contour plots, or sampling
❌ Time series - Use line plots to show temporal order
❌ Exact values matter - Tables are more precise
❌ Comparing many categories - Faceting works, but consider alternatives
❌ Showing distributions - Histograms or density plots are clearer

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Scatter Plots:

Add transparency - Use alpha = 0.5-0.8 to see overlapping points
Include trend lines - geom_smooth() reveals relationships; try methods: “lm”, “loess”, “gam”
Show uncertainty - Set se = TRUE in geom_smooth() for confidence intervals
Label outliers - Use geom_label_repel() for intelligent label placement
Use color meaningfully - Map to categories, not continuous variables (use size/alpha for continuous)
Add statistical annotations - Show correlation, R², or equation using annotate()
Vary point size - Map a third variable to size for bubble charts
Consider jittering - geom_jitter() for discrete or rounded data to show density
Use facets for categories - Compare relationships across groups with facet_wrap()
Add reference lines - Use geom_hline() or geom_vline() for thresholds
Mind overplotting - For many points, use hexbin (geom_hex()), density (geom_density_2d()), or sampling
Scale axes appropriately - Don’t force zero if it cuts off your data; but be transparent about it
Add marginal distributions - Use ggExtra::ggMarginal() to show x and y distributions
Highlight regions - Shade areas of interest with annotate("rect")
Calculate and show correlation - Always report r or R² for linear relationships
Use shapes wisely - Different shapes for categories, but limit to 3-4 for readability
Consider log scales - For exponential relationships, try scale_x_log10() or scale_y_log10()
Test different smooths - “loess” for local patterns, “lm” for global trends, “gam” for complex curves

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Scatter Plot Pitfalls:

No trend line - Missing the main analytical tool for relationships
Too many colors - More than 7-8 categories becomes unreadable
Ignoring overplotting - Thousands of points in same location look like one
Forcing axes to zero - Sometimes truncating is appropriate; be clear about it
Using lines instead of points - geom_line() implies ordered connections
Poor color choices - Similar colors make categories indistinguishable
No transparency - Can’t see density or overlaps
Missing labels - Points need context; axes need units
Tiny points - Too small to see; aim for 2-5 size
Assuming linearity - Not all relationships are linear; check with loess
Forgetting to check for outliers - They can distort correlations
No statistical annotation - Readers want to know correlation strength
Using 3D scatter plots - Almost always worse than 2D with color
Connecting unrelated points - Lines imply relationships that may not exist

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated ridgeline plots (also called joyplots) using ggplot2 and the ggridges package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Ridgeline plots are excellent for visualizing distributions across many categories, showing how patterns change over groups while maintaining compact vertical space.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, examining how diamond prices vary across different clarity grades.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated ridgeline plots (also called joyplots) using ggplot2 and the ggridges package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Ridgeline plots are excellent for visualizing distributions across many categories, showing how patterns change over groups while maintaining compact vertical space.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, examining how diamond prices vary across different clarity grades.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(ggridges)   # For ridgeline plot functionality
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: focus on standard clarity grades
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>% slice_sample(prop=0.2)%>%
  filter(clarity %in% c("I1", "SI2", "SI1", "VS2", "VS1", "VVS2", "VVS1", "IF")) %>%
  mutate(
    clarity = factor(clarity, 
                    levels = c("I1", "SI2", "SI1", "VS2", "VS1", "VVS2", "VVS1", "IF"),
                    ordered = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  filter(price <= 15000)  # Remove extreme outliers for better visualization

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Ridgeline Plot
Let’s start with a simple ridgeline plot showing price distributions across clarity grades.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_density_ridges()                                # Create ridgeline plot

Picking joint bandwidth of 499










Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity)) - Initializes the plot with diamond data, mapping price to the x-axis and clarity grades to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_density_ridges() - Adds overlapping density curves for each clarity grade, creating the characteristic ridgeline appearance

What we have so far: A functional but basic ridgeline plot. The distribution shapes are visible but the chart lacks color, context, and visual refinement. The overlapping densities show how price distributions vary by clarity.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding gradient fills, adjusting overlap, adding quantile lines, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Gradient fill colors based on density height
Quantile lines showing median and quartiles
Optimized overlap for better visual separation
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Formatted x-axis showing currency
Scale parameter for better height proportions



ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,                                       # Height scaling factor
    rel_min_height = 0.01,                          # Trim very small tails
    quantile_lines = TRUE,                          # Add quantile lines
    quantiles = 2                                    # Show median
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Price", 
                       option = "plasma",
                       labels = dollar_format()) +   # Color gradient
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(),
                     breaks = seq(0, 15000, by = 3000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Clarity Grade",
    subtitle = "Higher clarity grades (IF, VVS) show more concentrated distributions",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Clarity Grade"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 499










Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = after_stat(x)) - Maps price to x-axis, clarity to y-axis, and uses price values to create a gradient fill color
Lines 2-6: geom_density_ridges_gradient() with scale = 3 for pronounced height (more overlap), rel_min_height to trim tiny tails, and quantile_lines = TRUE with quantiles = 2 to show median lines
Lines 7-9: scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous color gradient from the viridis palette (plasma option) with dollar formatting in the legend
Lines 10-11: scale_x_continuous() formats x-axis values as currency with regular breaks
Lines 12-17: labs() adds descriptive title with insight, subtitle providing context, and clear axis labels
Line 18: theme_minimal() applies a clean theme
Lines 19-22: theme() customizes title formatting and positions legend on the right

What we have now: A much more informative chart with beautiful gradient colors, median reference lines, and optimized spacing. The color gradient adds an extra dimension showing price values, while the clean formatting makes it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with custom colors by category, statistical annotations, jittered points, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette for each clarity grade
Jittered data points showing individual observations (sampled)
Multiple quantile lines (Q1, median, Q3)
Sample size annotations for each clarity grade
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Mean markers on each distribution
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
clarity_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(clarity) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_price = median(price),
    mean_price = mean(price),
    q25 = quantile(price, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(price, 0.75),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Sample data for point overlay
set.seed(123)
data_sample <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(clarity) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.005) %>%  # Sample 0.5% of points
  ungroup()

# Define custom color palette
clarity_colors <- c(
  "I1" = "#D55E00",      # Orange-red for lowest clarity
  "SI2" = "#E69F00",     # Orange
  "SI1" = "#F0E442",     # Yellow
  "VS2" = "#009E73",     # Green
  "VS1" = "#56B4E9",     # Light blue
  "VVS2" = "#0072B2",    # Blue
  "VVS1" = "#CC79A7",    # Purple
  "IF" = "#8B4789"       # Dark purple for highest clarity
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = clarity)) +
  # Main ridgeline layer with quantiles
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.7,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),  # Q1, median, Q3
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.6,
    jittered_points = TRUE,
    position = position_points_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0),
    point_shape = '|',
    point_size = 1.5,
    point_alpha = 0.3,
    point_color = "gray30"
  ) +
  # Add mean markers
  geom_point(data = clarity_summary,
             aes(x = mean_price, y = as.numeric(clarity)),
             inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 23,
             size = 3,
             fill = "white",
             color = "gray20",
             stroke = 1) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = clarity_colors,
                    name = "Clarity Grade") +
  # Format x-axis
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(),
                     breaks = seq(0, 15000, by = 2500),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Prices Show Clear Patterns Across Clarity Grades",
    subtitle = "Higher clarity grades (IF, VVS) command premium prices with tighter distributions\nVertical lines show Q1, median, and Q3 | White diamonds indicate mean values",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Clarity Grade (Lowest → Highest)",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset (53,940 diamonds, filtered to ≤$15,000) | Points show 0.5% sample | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = clarity_summary,
            aes(x = 14500, 
                y = as.numeric(clarity),
                label = paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ","))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3,
            hjust = 1,
            fontface = "italic",
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "none",  # Remove legend (y-axis labels sufficient)
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 499










Code Explanation
Lines 2-12: Calculates comprehensive summary statistics including count, median, mean, and quartiles for each clarity grade
Lines 15-20: Samples 0.5% of data points from each clarity grade for overlay without overplotting
Lines 23-33: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low clarity) to cool/purple (high clarity) colors
Line 35: ggplot() initializes the plot with clarity mapped to fill color
Lines 37-51: geom_density_ridges() with comprehensive parameters: - scale = 2.5 for height scaling - quantile_lines = TRUE with three quantiles (Q1, median, Q3) - jittered_points = TRUE to show individual sampled observations as small vertical lines - Custom styling for lines and points
Lines 53-60: geom_point() adds white diamond markers at mean values for each clarity grade
Lines 62-63: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette
Lines 65-67: scale_x_continuous() formats x-axis as currency with appropriate breaks
Lines 69-75: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, multi-line subtitle with interpretation guidance, and detailed caption with attribution
Lines 77-84: geom_text() adds sample size annotations on the right side of each ridge
Lines 85-113: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Bold y-axis text for clarity grades - Grid customization keeping only vertical gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready ridgeline plot that clearly communicates how diamond prices vary across clarity grades. The combination of density ridges, quantile lines, jittered points, mean markers, and sample size annotations creates a comprehensive and accessible visualization suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.
