title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, edge filtering, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Separate hierarchy and communication edges with different styling
Edge width based on communication volume
Custom color palette with better contrast
Sector labels showing departments
Communication statistics annotations
Enhanced node styling with borders
Gradient edge coloring by weight
Professional typography and spacing



# Create full graph with all edges for visualization
full_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(d = all_edges, vertices = all_nodes, directed = TRUE)

# Add edge attributes
E(full_graph)$edge_type <- all_edges$type
E(full_graph)$edge_weight <- all_edges$weight

# Add node attributes
V(full_graph)$dept <- all_nodes$department[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]
V(full_graph)$node_level <- all_nodes$level[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]

# Define custom color palette
dept_colors <- c(
  "Executive" = "#8B4789",
  "Sales" = "#E76F51",
  "Technology" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Operations" = "#52A675"
)

# Create layout
set.seed(42)

ggraph(full_graph, layout = "fr") +
  # Draw edges with different styles by type
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = edge_type, 
                     alpha = edge_type,
                     width = ifelse(edge_type == "communication", edge_weight/10, 0.5)),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')),
                 end_cap = circle(3, 'mm')) +
  # Color edges by type
  scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = "gray70", 
                                      "communication" = "#a50f15"),
                          name = "Connection Type") +
  scale_edge_alpha_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = 0.3,
                                     "communication" = 0.7),
                         guide = "none") +
  scale_edge_width_identity() +
  # Draw nodes with enhanced styling
  geom_node_point(aes(size = (4 - node_level) * 4, 
                      fill = dept),
                  shape = 21,
                  color = "gray20",
                  stroke = 1,
                  alpha = 0.9) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name,
                     fontface = ifelse(node_level == 1, "bold", "plain")),
                 repel = TRUE,
                 size = 3.5,
                 max.overlaps = 20) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = dept_colors,
                    name = "Department") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Organizational Network: Hierarchical Structure and Cross-Department Communications",
    subtitle = "Force-directed layout showing both reporting lines (gray) and communication flows (red)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated organizational data | Edge width indicates communication volume | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for communication stats
  annotate("text",
           x = -2, 
           y = 2,
           label = paste0("Communication Flows:\n",
                         "Total Links: ", sum(all_edges$type == "communication"), "\n",
                         "Departments: ", n_distinct(all_nodes$department) - 1, "\n",
                         "Avg Weight: ", round(mean(communications$weight), 1)),
           hjust = 0,
           vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray30",
           fontface = "italic",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_graph(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Final result: A publication-ready edge bundling visualization that clearly separates hierarchical structure from communication patterns. The bundled edges reduce clutter while making it easy to see which departments communicate most frequently. The combination of size coding, color coding, and dual edge types creates a comprehensive visualization suitable for executive presentations, reports, or publications.

text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Edge Bundling Charts:

Choose appropriate layouts - Circular dendrogram works best for edge bundling; ensure your data has hierarchical structure
Adjust tension carefully - The tension parameter (0-1) controls bundling tightness; 0.8-0.9 usually works well
Separate edge types - Use different styling for hierarchical vs. data edges to maintain clarity
Use transparency wisely - Set alpha 0.3-0.6 for bundled edges to show density without obscuring nodes
Color meaningfully - Use color gradients to show edge properties like weight or frequency
Size nodes by importance - Make higher-level nodes larger for visual hierarchy
Rotate labels appropriately - Use node_angle() to rotate labels following the circular layout
Consider audience - Edge bundling works best when viewers need to see overall patterns, not trace individual connections
Limit edge count - Edge bundling is most effective with 20-200 edges; too few doesn’t show benefit, too many becomes messy
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("bundling.png", width = 12, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

library(r2d3)

  mutate(id = name) %>%

# Create interactive visualization (requires custom D3 script)

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated 2D density plots (contour plots) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
2D density plots are excellent for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables, showing concentration patterns and revealing clusters or correlations in bivariate data.
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, examining the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time for the Old Faithful geyser.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated 2D density plots (contour plots) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
2D density plots are excellent for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables, showing concentration patterns and revealing clusters or correlations in bivariate data.
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, examining the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time for the Old Faithful geyser.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels
library(viridis)    # For color palettes

# Prepare the data: use the faithful geyser dataset
data_faithful <- faithful %>%

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic 2D Density Plot
Let’s start with a simple 2D density contour plot showing the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time.

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +  # Set up with x and y
  geom_density_2d()                                                 # Create 2D density contours









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) - Initializes the plot with geyser data, mapping eruption duration to x-axis and waiting time to y-axis
Line 2: geom_density_2d() - Adds contour lines showing areas of high and low density in the 2D space, revealing two distinct clusters

What we have so far: A functional but basic 2D density plot. The contour lines reveal two clusters but the chart lacks color fill, data points, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding filled contours, data points, better colors, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Filled contours showing density levels with color
Data points overlay showing actual observations
Viridis color palette for better perception
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Contour labels showing density levels
Alpha transparency for layering



ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +
  # Filled density contours
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.8,                    # Filled contours with transparency
                         contour_var = "density") +      # Color by density
  # Overlay contour lines for definition
  geom_density_2d(color = "white",                       # White contour lines
                  linewidth = 0.3,
                  alpha = 0.5) +
  # Add data points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3,                                # Semi-transparent points
             size = 1.5,
             color = "gray20") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +              # Color palette
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful: Eruption Duration vs Waiting Time",
    subtitle = "Two distinct clusters reveal bimodal eruption patterns",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Waiting Time to Next Eruption (minutes)",
    fill = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot() initializes the plot with both x and y continuous variables
Lines 3-4: geom_density_2d_filled() creates filled contour regions colored by density, with alpha = 0.8 for slight transparency
Lines 6-8: geom_density_2d() adds white contour lines on top for clear boundary definition
Lines 10-12: geom_point() overlays the actual data points with transparency to show raw data alongside density estimate
Line 13: scale_fill_viridis_d() applies a discrete viridis color palette (plasma option) optimized for perception
Lines 14-20: labs() adds descriptive title highlighting the bimodal pattern, subtitle with context, and clear axis labels
Line 21: theme_minimal() applies a clean theme
Lines 22-25: theme() customizes title formatting and legend position

What we have now: A much more informative chart with filled density regions, clear contour boundaries, and visible data points. The color gradient and clean formatting make patterns easy to identify and the chart presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with continuous color gradient, statistical annotations, cluster identification, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Continuous color fill (filled polygons) for smooth gradients
Cluster centroids marked on the plot
Statistical ellipses showing 95% confidence regions
Correlation annotation with statistics
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Hex bins as alternative representation
Data source caption for proper attribution
Custom color palette optimized for the data



# Identify clusters using k-means
set.seed(123)
clusters <- kmeans(data_faithful, centers = 2)

# Calculate cluster centroids
centroids <- as_tibble(clusters$centers) %>%
  mutate(cluster = c("Short/Short", "Long/Long"))

# Add cluster labels to data
data_with_clusters <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(clusters$cluster))

# Calculate correlation
cor_value <- cor(data_faithful$eruption_time, data_faithful$waiting_time)

# Calculate summary statistics for annotation
stats_text <- paste0(
  "Correlation: r = ", round(cor_value, 3), "\n",
  "n = ", nrow(data_faithful), " observations\n",
  "Two clusters identified"
)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +
  # Filled 2D density with continuous scale
  stat_density_2d(aes(fill = after_stat(level)),
                  geom = "polygon",
                  alpha = 0.8,
                  color = NA,
                  contour_var = "density",
                  bins = 15) +
  # Add contour lines for reference
  geom_density_2d(color = "white",
                  linewidth = 0.4,
                  alpha = 0.6,
                  bins = 15) +
  # Add confidence ellipses for clusters
  stat_ellipse(data = data_with_clusters,
               aes(color = cluster),
               level = 0.95,
               linewidth = 1,
               linetype = "dashed") +
  # Add individual points colored by cluster
  geom_point(data = data_with_clusters,
             aes(color = cluster),
             alpha = 0.4,
             size = 1.8) +
  # Add cluster centroids
  geom_point(data = centroids,
             aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time),
             shape = 23,
             size = 5,
             fill = "white",
             color = "gray20",
             stroke = 1.5) +
  # Add centroid labels
  geom_text(data = centroids,
            aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time + 3,
                label = cluster),
            fontface = "bold",
            size = 3.5,
            color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom color scales
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma",
                       name = "Density\nLevel",
                       alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E76F51", "#2C5F8D"),
                     name = "Cluster",
                     labels = c("Cluster 1: Short", "Cluster 2: Long")) +
  # Format axes
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.5),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(40, 100, by = 10),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Shows Two Distinct Eruption-Waiting Patterns",
    subtitle = "Strong positive correlation (r = 0.901) with clear bimodal clustering\nDashed ellipses show 95% confidence regions | White diamonds mark cluster centers",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Waiting Time to Next Eruption (minutes)",
    caption = "Data source: Azzalini & Bowman (1990) | 272 eruptions | K-means clustering (k=2) | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add statistics annotation box
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = 1.6, xmax = 2.8,
           ymin = 85, ymax = 98,
           fill = "white",
           color = "gray30",
           alpha = 0.9,
           linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1.65, y = 95,
           label = "Statistics",
           hjust = 0,
           fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray20") +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1.65, y = 91,
           label = stats_text,
           hjust = 0,
           size = 3,
           color = "gray30",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold",
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.box = "vertical",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Performs k-means clustering with 2 centers to identify the two distinct groups in the data
Lines 6-7: Extracts cluster centroids and labels them descriptively
Lines 10-11: Adds cluster assignments to the original data
Line 14: Calculates Pearson correlation coefficient between eruption time and waiting time
Lines 17-21: Creates a formatted text string with key statistics for annotation
Line 23: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 25-31: stat_density_2d() with geom = "polygon" creates smooth filled density regions using a continuous color scale (15 bins for smooth gradients)
Lines 33-37: geom_density_2d() adds white contour lines for clear boundary definition
Lines 39-43: stat_ellipse() adds dashed ellipses showing 95% confidence regions around each cluster
Lines 45-48: geom_point() overlays data points colored by cluster membership
Lines 50-56: geom_point() adds white diamond markers at cluster centroids
Lines 58-63: geom_text() labels the cluster centroids with descriptive names
Lines 65-67: scale_fill_viridis_c() applies continuous magma color palette for density levels
Lines 68-70: scale_color_manual() applies custom colors to distinguish clusters
Lines 72-76: scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() format axes with appropriate breaks and expansion
Lines 78-84: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title, multi-line subtitle with interpretation, and detailed caption
Lines 86-108: Multiple annotate() calls create a statistics summary box showing correlation, sample size, and clustering information
Lines 109-137: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend positioned on right with vertical box layout - Grid customization - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready 2D density plot that clearly communicates the bivariate relationship between eruption duration and waiting time. The combination of continuous density gradient, confidence ellipses, cluster centroids, and statistical annotations creates a comprehensive visualization suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 2D Density Plots:

Choose between discrete and continuous fills - Use geom_density_2d_filled() for discrete levels or stat_density_2d() with geom = "polygon" for continuous gradients
Adjust the number of bins - Use bins parameter (typically 10-20) to control contour smoothness. More bins = more detail but can be cluttered
Always show the data - Overlay actual points with geom_point() to show data density and identify outliers
Use appropriate color palettes - Viridis palettes are perceptually uniform and colorblind-friendly. Consider option = "magma", "plasma", or "viridis"
Add white contour lines - When using filled densities, overlay thin white contour lines for clear boundary definition
Consider hexbin alternatives - For very large datasets (>10,000 points), geom_hex() may perform better than density estimation
Annotate key statistics - Include correlation coefficients, sample sizes, or cluster information directly on the plot
Use statistical overlays - Add stat_ellipse() for confidence regions or linear models with geom_smooth() to show trends
Mind the bandwidth - Adjust smoothing with h parameter in geom_density_2d() if default produces too much or too little smoothing
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

library(hexbin)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma",
                       name = "Count",
                       trans = "log10") +

       x = "Carat Weight",
       y = "Price (USD)") +

This creates hexagonal bins showing counts in log scale, ideal for 50,000+ data points.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)   # For data manipulation
library(circlize)    # For chord diagrams
library(scales)      # For formatting

# Create sample data: student migration between regions
regions <- c("Northeast", "Southeast", "Midwest", "Southwest", "West")

# Create a migration matrix
set.seed(42)
migration_matrix <- matrix(
  c(
    5000, 800, 600, 400, 1200,   # From Northeast
    900, 4500, 500, 800, 700,    # From Southeast
    700, 600, 3500, 500, 900,    # From Midwest
    500, 900, 400, 3000, 1100,   # From Southwest
    1300, 800, 1000, 1200, 4000  # From West
  ),
  nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(migration_matrix) <- regions
colnames(migration_matrix) <- regions

# Convert to data frame for easier viewing
migration_df <- as.data.frame(migration_matrix)
rownames(migration_df) <- regions

# Preview the data
head(migration_df)

          Northeast Southeast Midwest Southwest West
Northeast      5000       800     600       400 1200
Southeast       900      4500     500       800  700
Midwest         700       600    3500       500  900
Southwest       500       900     400      3000 1100
West           1300       800    1000      1200 4000

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 1: Basic Chord Diagram
Let’s start with a simple chord diagram showing student migration flows between regions.

# Create basic chord diagram
chordDiagram(migration_matrix)  # Create chord diagram from matrix









Code Explanation
Line 2: chordDiagram(migration_matrix) - Creates a chord diagram from the migration matrix where rows represent origin regions and columns represent destination regions

What we have so far: A functional but basic chord diagram. The connections are visible but the chart lacks custom colors, clear labels, and visual refinement. The default settings make it difficult to interpret flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding custom colors, adjusting gaps, adding a title, and improving the visual hierarchy.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Custom color palette for each region
Adjusted gaps between sectors for clarity
Transparency on chord connections
Grid colors matching region colors
Directional emphasis with color coding
Better spacing and layout
Title and annotations for context



# Define color palette for regions
region_colors <- c(
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#52A675", 
  "Midwest" = "#E76F51",
  "Southwest" = "#F4A261",
  "West" = "#8B4789"
)

# Set circlize parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,              # Start at top
  gap.degree = 3                  # Gap between sectors
)

# Create chord diagram with custom colors
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  grid.col = region_colors,       # Sector colors
  transparency = 0.5,             # Make chords semi-transparent
  annotationTrack = "grid",
  preAllocateTracks = list(
    track.height = 0.3            # Height for labels
  )
)

# Add region labels
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    circos.text(
      CELL_META$xcenter, 
      CELL_META$ylim[1],
      CELL_META$sector.index,
      facing = "clockwise",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      adj = c(0, 0.5),
      cex = 1
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

# Add title with proper margins
par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))  # Increase top margin for title
title("Student Migration Between Regions\n(Origin → Destination)", 
      cex.main = 1.3, font.main = 2, line = -1)







# Clear the plot
circos.clear()


Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Defines a custom color palette assigning specific colors to each region
Line 11: circos.clear() - Clears any previous circular plots
Lines 12-15: circos.par() sets global parameters including starting position (90 degrees = top) and gaps between sectors
Lines 18-25: chordDiagram() creates the diagram with: - grid.col applying custom region colors - transparency = 0.5 for semi-transparent chords - preAllocateTracks reserving space for labels
Lines 28-42: circos.track() adds custom text labels with optimal positioning and rotation
Lines 45-46: Adds a descriptive title
Line 49: circos.clear() - Essential cleanup to reset parameters

What we have now: A much more readable chord diagram with custom colors, better spacing, and clear labels. The transparency and color coding make it easier to trace individual flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, directional indicators, flow highlights, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Gradient chord colors showing direction of flow
Link border styling for definition
Sector annotations showing total in/out flows
Highlighted major flows with emphasis
Enhanced labels with values
Legend explaining the visualization
Professional color scheme optimized for accessibility
Order optimization for better layout



# Calculate flow statistics
total_out <- rowSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
total_in <- colSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
net_migration <- total_in - total_out

# Reorder regions by net migration
region_order <- names(sort(net_migration, decreasing = TRUE))

# Define enhanced color palette
region_colors_adv <- c(
  "West" = "#0072B2",
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#009E73",
  "Midwest" = "#E69F00",
  "Southwest" = "#D55E00"
)

# Clear and set parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,
  gap.degree = 5,                          # Increase gap for clarity
  track.margin = c(0.01, 0.01),
  cell.padding = c(0.02, 1, 0.02, 1)
)

# Set plot margins for title and legend space
par(mar = c(6, 1, 4, 1))  # Increased bottom margin

# Create chord diagram with enhanced styling
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  order = region_order,                    # Order by net migration
  grid.col = region_colors_adv,
  transparency = 0.4,
  directional = 1,                         # Show direction
  direction.type = c("diffHeight", "arrows"),
  diffHeight = mm_h(2),                    # Height difference for direction
  link.arr.type = "big.arrow",             # Arrow style
  link.arr.length = 0.2,
  annotationTrack = "grid",                # Only grid track
  annotationTrackHeight = mm_h(8),         # Increased track height
  link.border = "gray30",                  # Border around chords
  link.lwd = 0.5,                          # Border width
  link.sort = TRUE,                        # Sort links
  link.largest.ontop = TRUE                # Put largest on top
)

# Add sector names and statistics in one track
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    sector_name <- CELL_META$sector.index
    xcenter <- CELL_META$xcenter
    
    # Get inflow and outflow
    outflow <- format(round(total_out[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    inflow <- format(round(total_in[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    
    # Add region name
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(4),
      labels = sector_name,
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 1,
      font = 2,
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
    
    # Add statistics on same line, smaller
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(1),
      labels = paste0("↑", outflow, " ↓", inflow),
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 0.6,
      col = "gray40",
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

  side = 3,
  line = 0.3,
  cex = 0.8,
  col = "gray40"
)

# Add summary statistics
mtext(
  paste0(
    "Total: ", 
    format(sum(migration_matrix) - sum(diag(migration_matrix)), big.mark = ","),
    " students | Largest: Northeast → West (",
    format(migration_matrix["Northeast", "West"], big.mark = ","),
    ")"
  ),
  side = 1,

# Add caption

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Chord Diagrams:

Use circos.clear() religiously - Always call before and after creating chord diagrams to prevent parameter carryover issues
Order sectors meaningfully - Arrange regions by total flow, alphabetically, or by a meaningful metric using the order parameter
Add directional indicators - Use directional = 1 with arrows or height differences to show flow direction clearly
Adjust gaps strategically - Use gap.degree between 2-5 to balance compactness with readability
Color with purpose - Assign colors that match regional or categorical meanings, ensuring sufficient contrast
Show the data - Add annotations with actual flow values, totals, or percentages to provide concrete numbers
Mind the matrix diagonal - Self-loops (diagonal elements) can clutter the visualization; consider setting them to zero
Use transparency wisely - Set transparency between 0.3-0.6 to show overlapping flows without losing definition
Sort links for clarity - Use link.sort = TRUE and link.largest.ontop = TRUE to bring important flows forward
Export with care - Save as PDF or high-res PNG: pdf("chord.pdf", width = 10, height = 10) then run code, then dev.off()

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated bar charts using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
We’ll use the built-in mpg dataset from ggplot2, which contains fuel economy data from 1999 to 2008 for 38 popular car models.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated bar charts using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
We’ll use the built-in mpg dataset from ggplot2, which contains fuel economy data from 1999 to 2008 for 38 popular car models.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: calculate average highway mpg by car class
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%                           # Group data by vehicle class
  summarise(
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                        # Calculate mean highway mpg
    count = n()                                 # Count number of cars in each class
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_hwy))                        # Sort by mpg (highest to lowest)

# Preview the data
head(data_summary)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  class      avg_hwy count
  <chr>        <dbl> <int>
1 compact       28.3    47
2 subcompact    28.1    35
3 midsize       27.3    41
4 2seater       24.8     5
5 minivan       22.4    11
6 suv           18.1    62

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Bar Chart
Let’s start with a simple bar chart showing average highway fuel efficiency by vehicle class.

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = class, y = avg_hwy)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_col()                                          # Create bar chart (columns)









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = class, y = avg_hwy)) - Initializes the plot with our summarized data, mapping vehicle class to the x-axis and average highway mpg to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_col() - Adds bars to the plot where bar heights represent the actual values in the data

What we have so far: A functional but basic bar chart. The data is visible but the chart lacks context, proper ordering, and visual appeal.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by reordering bars, adding better labels, and applying a clean theme.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Reordered bars for better readability (highest to lowest)
Custom colors to make the chart more engaging
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Value labels on bars for precise data reading



ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy)) +  # Reorder bars by mpg
  geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") +                                          # Solid color fill
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_hwy, 1)),                           # Add value labels
            hjust = -0.2,                                              # Position labels to the right
            size = 3.5) +                                              # Set text size
  coord_flip() +                                                       # Flip to horizontal bars
  labs(
    title = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency by Vehicle Class",       # Main title
    subtitle = "Based on EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008)",           # Subtitle for context
    x = "Vehicle Class",                                               # X-axis label
    y = "Miles Per Gallon (Highway)"                                   # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                                    # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),              # Bold title
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()                               # Remove horizontal gridlines
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy) - Reorders the bars from highest to lowest fuel efficiency for easier comparison
Line 2: geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") - Creates bars with a custom blue color instead of default gray
Lines 3-5: geom_text() - Adds numeric labels to each bar, rounded to one decimal place and positioned slightly to the right
Line 6: coord_flip() - Flips the chart to horizontal orientation, making class names easier to read
Lines 7-12: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context
Line 13: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 14-17: theme() - Customizes specific theme elements like title formatting and removes horizontal gridlines for cleaner appearance

What we have now: A much more readable chart with proper ordering, context through labels, and a professional appearance. The horizontal orientation makes class names easier to read.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with color coding, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication or presentation.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Color-coded bars based on efficiency levels (high/medium/low)
Expanded y-axis to accommodate labels without overlap
Formatted axis labels with proper spacing
Custom color palette that’s colorblind-friendly
Enhanced typography for better readability
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Create efficiency categories for color coding
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  mutate(
    efficiency_level = case_when(                    # Create categorical variable
      avg_hwy >= 28 ~ "High (≥28 mpg)",             # High efficiency
      avg_hwy >= 22 ~ "Medium (22-27 mpg)",         # Medium efficiency
      TRUE ~ "Low (<22 mpg)"                        # Low efficiency
    )
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
efficiency_colors <- c(
  "High (≥28 mpg)" = "#52A675",                     # Green for high efficiency
  "Medium (22-27 mpg)" = "#F4A261",                 # Orange for medium
  "Low (<22 mpg)" = "#E76F51"                       # Red for low efficiency
)

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy, fill = efficiency_level)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +                                              # Slightly narrower bars
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(avg_hwy, 1), " mpg")),          # Labels with units
            hjust = -0.1,                                              # Position outside bars
            size = 3.5,
            color = "#2C3E50",                                         # Dark gray text
            fontface = "bold") +                                       # Bold font
  scale_fill_manual(values = efficiency_colors,                        # Apply custom colors
                    name = "Efficiency Level") +                       # Legend title
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)),           # Expand right side for labels
                     breaks = seq(0, 35, by = 5)) +                    # Set axis breaks
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway Fuel Efficiency Varies Significantly Across Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = "Two-seaters and subcompact cars lead in fuel economy, while pickups lag behind",
    x = NULL,                                                          # Remove x-axis label (obvious)
    y = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +                                      # Base font size
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),                              # Remove horizontal grid
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),                                # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)                              # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Creates a new categorical variable efficiency_level using case_when() to classify vehicles into high/medium/low efficiency groups
Lines 11-15: Defines a colorblind-friendly color palette with meaningful colors (green for high, orange for medium, red for low efficiency)
Line 17: aes(..., fill = efficiency_level) - Maps the efficiency level to bar colors
Line 18: geom_col(width = 0.7) - Creates slightly narrower bars for a more refined appearance
Lines 19-23: Adds formatted labels with “mpg” units, positioned outside bars with bold dark gray text
Lines 24-25: scale_fill_manual() - Applies our custom color palette and sets the legend title
Lines 26-27: scale_y_continuous() - Expands the right side of the plot to prevent label cutoff and sets regular axis breaks
Lines 30-34: Enhanced labels with a descriptive title, informative subtitle, and proper data attribution in the caption
Lines 36-59: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Typography adjustments (sizes, weights, colors) - Legend positioning at the bottom - Refined gridlines (keeping only major x-gridlines) - Proper margins for breathing room

Final result: A publication-ready visualization with clear data communication, professional styling, and accessibility considerations. The color coding adds an extra layer of information, while the polished formatting makes the chart suitable for reports, presentations, or blog posts.

text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Charts:

Always reorder categorical data - Use reorder() or fct_reorder() to sort bars by value for easier comparison
Choose colors purposefully - Use color to convey meaning (like efficiency levels), not just decoration. Check colorblind-friendliness with tools like ColorBrewer
Add context through text - Titles should tell a story, subtitles add detail, and captions credit data sources
Label your data directly - When possible, add value labels to reduce the need for axis reading
Use coord_flip() for long category names - Horizontal bars make text more readable than rotated labels
Embrace white space - Don’t overcrowd your plot. Remove unnecessary gridlines and add margins
Consider your audience - Internal reports might need basic charts, but presentations and publications deserve the advanced treatment
Test different themes - Start with theme_minimal() or theme_classic() and customize from there
Maintain consistency - If creating multiple charts, use the same color palette and styling across all visualizations
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave() with dpi = 300 for print-quality images

Want to save your custom theme?
You can create a custom theme function to reuse across all your plots:
theme_yourstyle <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#5A6C7D"),
    # ... add all your custom theme elements
  )
}

# Then use it like:
ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_col() +
  theme_yourstyle()

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Treemaps are excellent for visualizing hierarchical data and proportions. They display data as nested rectangles, where the size of each rectangle represents a quantitative value. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated treemaps using ggplot2 and the treemapify package.
We’ll analyze the distribution of car manufacturers and their fuel efficiency using the built-in mpg dataset.

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Treemaps are excellent for visualizing hierarchical data and proportions. They display data as nested rectangles, where the size of each rectangle represents a quantitative value. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated treemaps using ggplot2 and the treemapify package.
We’ll analyze the distribution of car manufacturers and their fuel efficiency using the built-in mpg dataset.

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(treemapify)     # For creating treemaps with ggplot2
library(scales)         # For formatting labels

# Prepare the data: summarize by manufacturer
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(manufacturer) %>%                        # Group by car manufacturer
  summarise(
    count = n(),                                    # Count number of models
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                           # Average highway mpg
    avg_cty = mean(cty)                            # Average city mpg
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))                              # Sort by count (highest to lowest)

# Preview the data
head(data_summary, 10)

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Treemap
Let’s start with a simple treemap showing the number of car models per manufacturer.

ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer)) +  # Set area size and fill color
  geom_treemap()                                                  # Create treemap









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer)) - Initializes the treemap with area representing the number of models (rectangle size) and fill assigning different colors to each manufacturer
Line 2: geom_treemap() - Creates the treemap layout, automatically calculating rectangle positions and sizes based on the area values

What we have so far: A functional treemap showing proportions, but it’s hard to identify which rectangle represents which manufacturer. The colors are randomly assigned and there’s no context.

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add labels, improve the color scheme, and provide context through titles and better formatting.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Manufacturer labels inside each rectangle for identification
Model count labels to show exact values
Custom color palette for better visual appeal
Title and subtitle to provide context
Cleaner theme with better spacing
Label sizing based on rectangle area for readability



ggplot(data_summary, aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer)) +
  geom_treemap() +                                                # Create treemap rectangles
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                             # White text for contrast
    place = "centre",                                             # Center the text
    size = 12,                                                    # Base text size
    grow = TRUE                                                   # Auto-size text to fit rectangles
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0("n=", count)),                            # Add count labels
    colour = "white",                                             # White text
    place = "bottom",                                             # Position at bottom of rectangle
    size = 10,                                                    # Slightly smaller text
    alpha = 0.8                                                   # Slight transparency
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +                      # Use viridis color palette
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Car Models by Manufacturer",         # Main title
    subtitle = "Based on EPA fuel economy dataset (1999-2008)",   # Context subtitle
    caption = "Rectangle size represents number of car models"    # Explain the visual encoding
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                               # Clean theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    legend.position = "none",                                     # Remove legend (redundant with labels)
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)                         # Add margins around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(area = count, fill = manufacturer, label = manufacturer) - Added label aesthetic to prepare for text labels
Line 2: geom_treemap() - Creates the base treemap rectangles
Lines 3-8: First geom_treemap_text() layer - Adds manufacturer names in white, centered, with grow = TRUE which automatically scales text to fit within each rectangle
Lines 9-15: Second geom_treemap_text() layer - Adds model counts at the bottom of each rectangle with “n=” prefix for clarity
Line 16: scale_fill_viridis_d() - Applies a colorblind-friendly viridis palette (discrete version) for better accessibility and visual appeal
Lines 17-21: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing context, and caption explaining what rectangle size represents
Lines 22-28: Theme customization - Removes the legend (since labels identify each manufacturer), styles the title and subtitle, and adds proper margins

What we have now: A much more informative treemap with clear labels identifying each manufacturer and showing exact counts. The color palette is visually appealing and accessible, and the context is provided through proper labeling.

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a sophisticated treemap that shows both quantity and quality (fuel efficiency) through size and color, with enhanced styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Color mapping to fuel efficiency - Rectangle color now represents average highway MPG (dual encoding)
Custom gradient color scale - Low efficiency (red) to high efficiency (green)
Borders around rectangles - Better visual separation
Enhanced label formatting - Shows both manufacturer and efficiency
Legend with custom formatting - Clear explanation of color meaning
Professional styling - Publication-ready appearance
Data insight annotation - Highlights key findings in subtitle



# Add efficiency categories for better interpretation
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  mutate(
    efficiency_category = case_when(                   # Create categorical labels
      avg_hwy >= 25 ~ "High Efficiency",              # High performers
      avg_hwy >= 20 ~ "Medium Efficiency",            # Average performers
      TRUE ~ "Lower Efficiency"                       # Below average
    )
  )

ggplot(data_summary, aes(
  area = count, 
  fill = avg_hwy,                                     # Color by fuel efficiency
  label = manufacturer, 
  subgroup = efficiency_category                      # Group by efficiency level
)) +
  geom_treemap(
    colour = "white",                                 # White borders between rectangles
    size = 2                                          # Border thickness
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    colour = "white",                                 # White text for visibility
    place = "centre",                                 # Center manufacturer name
    size = 14,                                        # Larger base size
    grow = TRUE,                                      # Auto-scale to fit
    fontface = "bold",                                # Bold text for emphasis
    alpha = 0.9                                       # Slight transparency
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(
    aes(label = paste0(count, " models\n", 
                       round(avg_hwy, 1), " mpg")),   # Multi-line label with count and efficiency
    colour = "white",                                 # White text
    place = "bottom",                                 # Position at bottom
    size = 10,                                        # Smaller for secondary info
    alpha = 0.7,                                      # More transparent
    lineheight = 0.9                                  # Tighter line spacing
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                  # Red for low efficiency
    mid = "#F4A261",                                  # Orange for medium
    high = "#52A675",                                 # Green for high efficiency
    midpoint = 22,                                    # Set midpoint of scale
    name = "Average Highway\nFuel Efficiency",        # Legend title
    breaks = seq(15, 30, by = 5),                     # Legend breaks
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),           # Add units to legend
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      barwidth = 15,                                  # Wider color bar
      barheight = 0.8,                                # Thinner bar
      title.position = "top",                         # Title above bar
      title.hjust = 0.5                               # Center the title
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Manufacturers: Market Presence vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Dodge leads in model count (37 models) but lags in fuel efficiency (17.9 mpg)\nVolkswagen and Honda balance quantity with quality (29.2 and 28.8 mpg respectively)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Rectangle size = number of models | Color = average highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +                     # Clean base theme with larger font
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 18, 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center the title
      margin = margin(b = 10)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11, 
      color = "#5A6C7D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center subtitle
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2                                # Better line spacing for multi-line
    ),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9, 
      color = "#6C757D", 
      hjust = 0.5,                                    # Center caption
      margin = margin(t = 20)
    ),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",                       # Place legend at bottom
    legend.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 15),                   # Space between plot and legend
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "white", 
      colour = NA
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20),            # Generous margins
    
    # Remove grid (not needed for treemap)
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-10: Creates an efficiency_category variable to group manufacturers into high/medium/lower efficiency brackets for potential subgrouping
Lines 12-17: Enhanced aes() mapping: - area = count - Rectangle size by model count - fill = avg_hwy - Color by fuel efficiency (continuous scale) - label = manufacturer - Manufacturer names - subgroup = efficiency_category - Groups for potential hierarchical organization
Lines 18-21: geom_treemap() with white borders (2px width) to clearly separate rectangles and improve readability
Lines 22-29: First text layer with bold, white manufacturer names that automatically scale to fit rectangles
Lines 30-38: Second text layer showing both model count and fuel efficiency in a compact two-line format at the bottom of each rectangle
Lines 39-52: scale_fill_gradient2() - Creates a diverging color scale: - Red for poor efficiency, green for good efficiency - Midpoint set at 22 mpg (approximate average) - Custom legend with formatted labels including “mpg” units - Horizontal color bar for better space usage
Lines 53-57: Comprehensive labels with: - Clear title explaining both dimensions (size and color) - Data-driven subtitle highlighting key insights - Detailed caption explaining all encodings
Lines 58-95: Extensive theme customization: - Centered titles and captions for balanced layout - Larger base font size for better readability - Professional spacing and margins - Customized legend placement and styling - Removed grid (unnecessary for treemaps)

Final result: A publication-ready treemap that tells a complete story. Viewers can instantly see both market presence (size) and fuel efficiency performance (color), with clear labels and professional styling. The dual encoding reveals patterns like Dodge’s high model count but poor efficiency, while Honda balances both aspects well.

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Treemaps

Treemaps work best for:
✅ Showing proportions - Quickly compare relative sizes of categories
✅ Hierarchical data - Display parent-child relationships (we can add subgroups)
✅ Part-to-whole relationships - See how individual parts make up a total
✅ Limited categories - Work best with 10-20 categories (more becomes cluttered)
✅ Dual encoding - Show two variables simultaneously (size + color)
Avoid treemaps when:
❌ Precise value comparison is critical (use bar charts)
❌ Data changes over time (use line charts)
❌ Too many small categories (creates tiny, unreadable rectangles)
❌ Negative values are present (treemaps require positive values)

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Treemaps:

Always add labels - Use geom_treemap_text() to identify rectangles. Unlabeled treemaps are nearly useless
Use color meaningfully - Don’t just use color for distinction; map it to a second variable (like efficiency, growth rate, or category)
Consider borders - White borders between rectangles improve clarity and prevent colors from bleeding together
Limit your categories - If you have too many categories, group smaller ones into “Other” to maintain readability
Use grow = TRUE - This makes text automatically resize to fit rectangles, ensuring readability for all sizes
Choose appropriate color scales:

Sequential (light to dark) for continuous positive values
Diverging (red-white-green) when there’s a meaningful midpoint
Categorical for distinct groups

Add multiple text layers - Use separate layers for main labels and supporting information (like our count + efficiency example)
Test text contrast - Ensure text is readable against all background colors. White text with slight transparency often works well
Include a legend - When color encodes data, always include a properly labeled legend explaining what it represents
Provide context in subtitles - Don’t just show the data; highlight key insights or patterns in your subtitle
Sort your data - Arrange categories by size (descending) before creating the treemap for better visual organization
Consider hierarchical treemaps - Use the subgroup parameter to create nested treemaps for multi-level hierarchies

title: Creating Informative Treemaps with ggplot2
text:
Advanced: Hierarchical Treemap Example
Want to show multiple levels of hierarchy? Here’s a bonus example with manufacturers grouped by country:

# Add country information (simplified example)
data_hierarchical <- mpg %>%
  mutate(
    country = case_when(
      manufacturer %in% c("audi", "volkswagen") ~ "Germany",
      manufacturer %in% c("toyota", "honda", "nissan", "subaru") ~ "Japan",
      manufacturer %in% c("hyundai") ~ "South Korea",
      TRUE ~ "USA"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(country, manufacturer) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(data_hierarchical, aes(
  area = count,
  fill = avg_hwy,
  label = manufacturer,
  subgroup = country                      # Group by country first
)) +
  geom_treemap() +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_border(          # Add borders around country groups
    colour = "white",
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_treemap_subgroup_text(            # Add country labels
    place = "centre",
    colour = "white",
    alpha = 0.7,
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 16
  ) +
  geom_treemap_text(                     # Add manufacturer labels
    colour = "white",
    place = "centre",
    size = 10,
    grow = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 22,
    name = "Avg Highway MPG"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Car Models by Country and Manufacturer",
    subtitle = "Hierarchical view showing country-level groupings"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5)
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated spider charts (also called radar charts) using the fmsb package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Spider charts are excellent for visualizing multivariate data, comparing multiple entities across several dimensions, and showing strengths and weaknesses in a circular format.
We’ll create a dataset representing performance metrics for different smartphone models across various categories.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated spider charts (also called radar charts) using the fmsb package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Spider charts are excellent for visualizing multivariate data, comparing multiple entities across several dimensions, and showing strengths and weaknesses in a circular format.
We’ll create a dataset representing performance metrics for different smartphone models across various categories.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)   # For data manipulation
library(fmsb)        # For spider/radar charts
library(scales)      # For formatting

# Create sample data: smartphone performance metrics (0-100 scale)
smartphones <- data.frame(
  Battery = c(85, 70, 90, 75, 80),
  Camera = c(90, 85, 75, 95, 80),
  Performance = c(95, 90, 80, 85, 92),
  Display = c(88, 92, 85, 80, 86),
  Price = c(70, 80, 95, 65, 75),
  Design = c(92, 88, 82, 90, 85)
)

rownames(smartphones) <- c("Model A", "Model B", "Model C", "Model D", "Model E")

# Add max and min rows (required by fmsb)
smartphones <- rbind(
  rep(100, 6),  # Max values
  rep(0, 6),    # Min values
  smartphones
)

# Preview the data
head(smartphones)

        Battery Camera Performance Display Price Design
1           100    100         100     100   100    100
2             0      0           0       0     0      0
Model A      85     90          95      88    70     92
Model B      70     85          90      92    80     88
Model C      90     75          80      85    95     82
Model D      75     95          85      80    65     90

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Chart 1: Basic Spider Chart
Let’s start with a simple spider chart showing performance metrics for one smartphone model.

# Select first phone (Model A) - rows 1-2 are max/min
radarchart(smartphones[c(1, 2, 3), ])  # Max, Min, Model A









Code Explanation
Line 2: radarchart(smartphones[c(1, 2, 3), ]) - Creates a radar chart using rows 1 (max values), 2 (min values), and 3 (Model A data). The first two rows define the scale range.

What we have so far: A functional but basic spider chart. The shape shows Model A’s profile but the chart lacks color, proper labels, and visual refinement. The default settings make it difficult to read.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by comparing multiple models, adding custom colors, adjusting grid lines, and improving labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Multiple models for comparison
Custom colors with transparency
Grid customization for better readability
Axis labels for each dimension
Legend identifying each model
Line styling for differentiation
Title for context



# Define colors for each model
colors_border <- c("#2C5F8D", "#52A675", "#E76F51")
colors_fill <- c(
  rgb(44, 95, 141, alpha = 50, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(82, 166, 117, alpha = 50, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(231, 111, 81, alpha = 50, maxColorValue = 255)
)

# Create radar chart with three models
radarchart(
  smartphones[c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), ],  # Max, Min, Models A, B, C
  axistype = 1,                      # Axis type (0-4)
  pcol = colors_border,              # Line colors
  pfcol = colors_fill,               # Fill colors
  plwd = 2,                          # Line width
  plty = 1,                          # Line type (solid)
  cglcol = "grey",                   # Grid line color
  cglty = 1,                         # Grid line type
  cglwd = 0.8,                       # Grid line width
  axislabcol = "grey30",             # Axis label color
  vlcex = 1.0,                       # Variable label size
  title = "Smartphone Performance Comparison\n(Models A, B, C)"
)

# Add legend
legend(
  x = "topright",
  legend = c("Model A", "Model B", "Model C"),
  bty = "n",
  pch = 20,
  col = colors_border,
  text.col = "gray20",
  cex = 1,
  pt.cex = 2
)









Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Defines custom colors for borders and fills with transparency using rgb() function
Lines 11-24: radarchart() with multiple parameters: - Includes three models (rows 3, 4, 5) plus max/min (rows 1, 2) - pcol and pfcol for line and fill colors - plwd = 2 for thicker lines - cglcol, cglty, cglwd for grid styling - axislabcol and vlcex for label styling
Lines 27-36: legend() adds a legend identifying each model with colored points

What we have now: A much more informative chart comparing three smartphone models. The custom colors, transparency, and legend make it easy to distinguish models and compare performance across dimensions.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with all models, enhanced styling, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

All five models displayed simultaneously
Enhanced color palette optimized for accessibility
Custom grid levels showing score ranges
Thicker grid lines at key thresholds
Larger variable labels for readability
Descriptive title and subtitle
Score annotations showing exact values
Enhanced legend with detailed information
Professional layout with proper spacing



# Define enhanced color palette (5 models)
colors_border_adv <- c("#0072B2", "#009E73", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7", "#F0E442")
colors_fill_adv <- c(
  rgb(0, 114, 178, alpha = 40, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(0, 158, 115, alpha = 40, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(213, 94, 0, alpha = 40, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(204, 121, 167, alpha = 40, maxColorValue = 255),
  rgb(240, 228, 66, alpha = 40, maxColorValue = 255)
)

# Calculate average scores for each model
avg_scores <- colMeans(smartphones[3:7, ])
overall_avg <- round(mean(avg_scores), 1)

# Set up plot area with margins
par(mar = c(2, 2, 4, 2))

# Create enhanced radar chart
radarchart(
  smartphones,  # All models with max/min
  axistype = 2,                      # Show axis values
  seg = 5,                           # Number of segments (grid circles)
  pcol = colors_border_adv,          # Line colors
  pfcol = colors_fill_adv,           # Fill colors
  plwd = 3,                          # Thicker lines
  plty = 1,                          # Solid lines
  cglcol = "grey70",                 # Grid line color
  cglty = 1,                         # Grid line type
  cglwd = 1,                         # Grid line width
  axislabcol = "grey30",             # Axis label color
  vlcex = 1.2,                       # Larger variable labels
  vlabels = colnames(smartphones),   # Variable names
  caxislabels = seq(0, 100, 20),     # Axis labels (0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100)
  calcex = 0.9,                      # Axis label size
  title = ""                         # No title here (add separately)
)

# Add custom title and subtitle
mtext(
  "Comprehensive Smartphone Performance Analysis Across Six Dimensions",
  side = 3,
  line = 2,
  cex = 1.4,
  font = 2,
  col = "gray20"
)

mtext(
  paste0("Comparing 5 flagship models | Overall average score: ", overall_avg, "/100"),
  side = 3,
  line = 0.8,
  cex = 1,
  col = "gray40"
)

# Add enhanced legend with statistics
legend_labels <- c(
  paste0("Model A (Avg: ", round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[3, ])), 1), ")"),
  paste0("Model B (Avg: ", round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[4, ])), 1), ")"),
  paste0("Model C (Avg: ", round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[5, ])), 1), ")"),
  paste0("Model D (Avg: ", round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[6, ])), 1), ")"),
  paste0("Model E (Avg: ", round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[7, ])), 1), ")")
)

legend(
  x = 0.9,
  y = 1.3,
  legend = legend_labels,
  bty = "n",
  pch = 15,
  col = colors_border_adv,
  text.col = "gray20",
  cex = 0.9,
  pt.cex = 1.5,
  title = "Models (with avg scores)",
  title.col = "gray20"
)

# Add caption
mtext(
  "Data source: Simulated smartphone performance metrics (0-100 scale) | Visualization: Your Name",
  side = 1,
  line = 0.5,
  cex = 0.75,
  col = "gray50"
)

# Add interpretation box
legend(
  x = -1.4,
  y = -0.9,
  legend = c(
    "Best Battery: Model C (90)",
    "Best Camera: Model D (95)",
    "Best Performance: Model A (95)",
    "Best Display: Model B (92)",
    "Best Price: Model C (95)",
    "Best Design: Model A (92)"
  ),
  bty = "o",
  box.col = "gray70",
  bg = "white",
  cex = 0.75,
  text.col = "gray30",
  title = "Category Leaders",
  title.col = "gray20"
)









Code Explanation
Lines 2-10: Defines enhanced color palette for five models using colorblind-friendly colors with reduced alpha for transparency
Lines 13-14: Calculates average scores across all dimensions for each model and overall average
Line 17: Sets plot margins with par(mar = c(2, 2, 4, 2))
Lines 20-38: radarchart() with comprehensive styling: - axistype = 2 shows actual numeric values on axes - seg = 5 creates 5 concentric circles - plwd = 3 for prominent lines - caxislabels sets custom axis labels (0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100) - vlcex = 1.2 for larger dimension labels
Lines 41-53: Adds two-line title using mtext() - main title and subtitle with overall statistics
Lines 56-73: Creates enhanced legend with average scores for each model included in parentheses
Lines 76-82: Adds caption with data source attribution at the bottom
Lines 85-101: Adds interpretation box showing which model leads in each category with exact scores

Final result: A publication-ready spider chart that clearly communicates performance comparisons across five smartphone models and six dimensions. The combination of colors, annotations, category leaders box, and comprehensive legend creates an accessible visualization suitable for reports, presentations, or marketing materials.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better fmsb Spider Charts:

Always include max/min rows first - The fmsb package requires the first two rows to be maximum and minimum values for proper scaling
Limit the number of overlays - Showing more than 5 entities becomes cluttered. Consider small multiples or filtering for clarity
Use transparency wisely - Set alpha between 30-50 in rgb() to show overlapping areas without losing definition
Choose appropriate dimensions - Use 4-8 variables; too few lacks insight, too many becomes unreadable
Ensure equal scales - All dimensions should use the same scale (e.g., 0-100) for fair comparison
Color with purpose - Use colorblind-friendly palettes and sufficient contrast between overlapping shapes
Label clearly - Increase vlcex parameter (1.0-1.3) to make dimension labels readable
Show the scale - Use axistype = 1 or 2 to display numeric values on axes
Consider alternatives - For time-series or many entities, parallel coordinates plots may be more appropriate
Export carefully - Spider charts work best as square plots: png("spider.png", width = 800, height = 800)

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other multivariate visualizations:

Parallel coordinates plots for comparing many entities
Heatmaps for matrix-style comparisons
Star plots (similar to spider charts but with lines from center)
Profile plots for showing patterns over categories


Want to create interactive spider charts?
You can make your spider charts interactive using plotly:
library(plotly)

# Reshape data for plotly
plot_data <- smartphones[3:7, ] %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("Model") %>%
  pivot_longer(-Model, names_to = "Dimension", values_to = "Score")

# Create interactive radar chart
plot_ly(
  data = plot_data,
  type = 'scatterpolar',
  r = ~Score,
  theta = ~Dimension,
  fill = 'toself',
  color = ~Model,
  colors = colors_border_adv
) %>%
  layout(
    polar = list(
      radialaxis = list(
        visible = TRUE,
        range = c(0, 100)
      )
    ),
    title = "Interactive Smartphone Comparison"
  )
This creates an interactive chart where users can hover for exact values and toggle models on/off.

title: Creating Beautiful Spider Charts with fmsb
text:
Alternative: Small Multiples Approach
Here’s a bonus approach showing each model separately:

# Set up layout for 5 plots
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 2))

# Colors for individual charts
model_colors <- colors_border_adv
model_names <- rownames(smartphones)[3:7]

# Create individual radar charts
for (i in 1:5) {
  radarchart(
    smartphones[c(1, 2, i + 2), ],  # Max, Min, Model i
    axistype = 1,
    seg = 5,
    pcol = model_colors[i],
    pfcol = rgb(col2rgb(model_colors[i])[1], 
                col2rgb(model_colors[i])[2], 
                col2rgb(model_colors[i])[3], 
                alpha = 50, maxColorValue = 255),
    plwd = 3,
    cglcol = "grey70",
    cglty = 1,
    cglwd = 1,
    axislabcol = "grey30",
    vlcex = 0.9,
    title = paste0(model_names[i], "\n(Avg: ", 
                   round(mean(as.numeric(smartphones[i + 2, ])), 1), ")")
  )
}

# Reset layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated Sankey diagrams using ggplot2 and the ggsankey package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Sankey diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows between categories, showing how quantities split, merge, and transition through different stages or groups.
We’ll create a fictional dataset representing student enrollment flows through different college majors and their career outcomes.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated Sankey diagrams using ggplot2 and the ggsankey package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Sankey diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows between categories, showing how quantities split, merge, and transition through different stages or groups.
We’ll create a fictional dataset representing student enrollment flows through different college majors and their career outcomes.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(ggsankey)   # For Sankey diagram functionality
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Create sample data: student flow from major to career
data_flow <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:300,
  major = sample(c("Engineering", "Business", "Liberal Arts"), 300, 
                 replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3)),
  year = "2020"
) %>%
  # Add career outcomes based on major with some realistic patterns
  mutate(
    career = case_when(
      major == "Engineering" ~ sample(c("Tech", "Consulting", "Other"), 
                                     n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                     prob = c(0.6, 0.3, 0.1)),
      major == "Business" ~ sample(c("Finance", "Consulting", "Tech", "Other"), 
                                  n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                  prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)),
      major == "Liberal Arts" ~ sample(c("Education", "Consulting", "Other"), 
                                      n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                      prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3))
    )
  )

# Transform data to long format for Sankey diagram
data_sankey <- data_flow %>%
  make_long(major, career)

# Preview the data
head(data_sankey)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  x      node        next_x next_node 
  <fct>  <chr>       <fct>  <chr>     
1 major  Business    career Consulting
2 career Consulting  <NA>   <NA>      
3 major  Engineering career Consulting
4 career Consulting  <NA>   <NA>
