title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)   # For data manipulation
library(circlize)    # For chord diagrams
library(scales)      # For formatting

# Create sample data: student migration between regions
regions <- c("Northeast", "Southeast", "Midwest", "Southwest", "West")

# Create a migration matrix
set.seed(42)
migration_matrix <- matrix(
  c(
    5000, 800, 600, 400, 1200,   # From Northeast
    900, 4500, 500, 800, 700,    # From Southeast
    700, 600, 3500, 500, 900,    # From Midwest
    500, 900, 400, 3000, 1100,   # From Southwest
    1300, 800, 1000, 1200, 4000  # From West
  ),
  nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(migration_matrix) <- regions
colnames(migration_matrix) <- regions

# Convert to data frame for easier viewing
migration_df <- as.data.frame(migration_matrix)
rownames(migration_df) <- regions

# Preview the data
head(migration_df)

          Northeast Southeast Midwest Southwest West
Northeast      5000       800     600       400 1200
Southeast       900      4500     500       800  700
Midwest         700       600    3500       500  900
Southwest       500       900     400      3000 1100
West           1300       800    1000      1200 4000

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 1: Basic Chord Diagram
Let’s start with a simple chord diagram showing student migration flows between regions.

# Create basic chord diagram
chordDiagram(migration_matrix)  # Create chord diagram from matrix









Code Explanation
Line 2: chordDiagram(migration_matrix) - Creates a chord diagram from the migration matrix where rows represent origin regions and columns represent destination regions

What we have so far: A functional but basic chord diagram. The connections are visible but the chart lacks custom colors, clear labels, and visual refinement. The default settings make it difficult to interpret flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding custom colors, adjusting gaps, adding a title, and improving the visual hierarchy.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Custom color palette for each region
Adjusted gaps between sectors for clarity
Transparency on chord connections
Grid colors matching region colors
Directional emphasis with color coding
Better spacing and layout
Title and annotations for context



# Define color palette for regions
region_colors <- c(
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#52A675", 
  "Midwest" = "#E76F51",
  "Southwest" = "#F4A261",
  "West" = "#8B4789"
)

# Set circlize parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,              # Start at top
  gap.degree = 3                  # Gap between sectors
)

# Create chord diagram with custom colors
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  grid.col = region_colors,       # Sector colors
  transparency = 0.5,             # Make chords semi-transparent
  annotationTrack = "grid",
  preAllocateTracks = list(
    track.height = 0.3            # Height for labels
  )
)

# Add region labels
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    circos.text(
      CELL_META$xcenter, 
      CELL_META$ylim[1],
      CELL_META$sector.index,
      facing = "clockwise",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      adj = c(0, 0.5),
      cex = 1
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

# Add title with proper margins
par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))  # Increase top margin for title
title("Student Migration Between Regions\n(Origin → Destination)", 
      cex.main = 1.3, font.main = 2, line = -1)







# Clear the plot
circos.clear()


Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Defines a custom color palette assigning specific colors to each region
Line 11: circos.clear() - Clears any previous circular plots
Lines 12-15: circos.par() sets global parameters including starting position (90 degrees = top) and gaps between sectors
Lines 18-25: chordDiagram() creates the diagram with: - grid.col applying custom region colors - transparency = 0.5 for semi-transparent chords - preAllocateTracks reserving space for labels
Lines 28-42: circos.track() adds custom text labels with optimal positioning and rotation
Lines 45-46: Adds a descriptive title
Line 49: circos.clear() - Essential cleanup to reset parameters

What we have now: A much more readable chord diagram with custom colors, better spacing, and clear labels. The transparency and color coding make it easier to trace individual flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, directional indicators, flow highlights, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Gradient chord colors showing direction of flow
Link border styling for definition
Sector annotations showing total in/out flows
Highlighted major flows with emphasis
Enhanced labels with values
Legend explaining the visualization
Professional color scheme optimized for accessibility
Order optimization for better layout



# Calculate flow statistics
total_out <- rowSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
total_in <- colSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
net_migration <- total_in - total_out

# Reorder regions by net migration
region_order <- names(sort(net_migration, decreasing = TRUE))

# Define enhanced color palette
region_colors_adv <- c(
  "West" = "#0072B2",
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#009E73",
  "Midwest" = "#E69F00",
  "Southwest" = "#D55E00"
)

# Clear and set parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,
  gap.degree = 5,                          # Increase gap for clarity
  track.margin = c(0.01, 0.01),
  cell.padding = c(0.02, 1, 0.02, 1)
)

# Set plot margins for title and legend space
par(mar = c(6, 1, 4, 1))  # Increased bottom margin

# Create chord diagram with enhanced styling
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  order = region_order,                    # Order by net migration
  grid.col = region_colors_adv,
  transparency = 0.4,
  directional = 1,                         # Show direction
  direction.type = c("diffHeight", "arrows"),
  diffHeight = mm_h(2),                    # Height difference for direction
  link.arr.type = "big.arrow",             # Arrow style
  link.arr.length = 0.2,
  annotationTrack = "grid",                # Only grid track
  annotationTrackHeight = mm_h(8),         # Increased track height
  link.border = "gray30",                  # Border around chords
  link.lwd = 0.5,                          # Border width
  link.sort = TRUE,                        # Sort links
  link.largest.ontop = TRUE                # Put largest on top
)

# Add sector names and statistics in one track
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    sector_name <- CELL_META$sector.index
    xcenter <- CELL_META$xcenter
    
    # Get inflow and outflow
    outflow <- format(round(total_out[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    inflow <- format(round(total_in[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    
    # Add region name
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(4),
      labels = sector_name,
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 1,
      font = 2,
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
    
    # Add statistics on same line, smaller
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(1),
      labels = paste0("↑", outflow, " ↓", inflow),
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 0.6,
      col = "gray40",
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

# Add title and subtitle
title(
  main = "Regional Student Migration Patterns Show Net Flow to West Coast",
  cex.main = 1.3,
  font.main = 2,
  col.main = "gray20",
  line = 1.5
)

# Add subtitle separately
mtext(
  "Arrows indicate direction | ↑ = Outflow, ↓ = Inflow",
  side = 3,
  line = 0.3,
  cex = 0.8,
  col = "gray40"
)

# Add summary statistics
mtext(
  paste0(
    "Total: ", 
    format(sum(migration_matrix) - sum(diag(migration_matrix)), big.mark = ","),
    " students | Largest: Northeast → West (",
    format(migration_matrix["Northeast", "West"], big.mark = ","),
    ")"
  ),
  side = 1,
  line = 2,
  cex = 0.75,
  col = "gray30"
)

mtext(
  "Net Winners: West, Southeast | Net Losers: Southwest, Midwest",
  side = 1,
  line = 3,
  cex = 0.75,
  col = "gray30"
)

# Add caption
mtext(
  "Data source: Simulated student migration data | Visualization: Your Name",
  side = 1,
  line = 4.5,
  cex = 0.7,
  col = "gray50"
)







# Clear
circos.clear()


Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: Calculates total outflow and inflow for each region (excluding self-loops on diagonal)
Line 7: Reorders regions by net migration for better visual layout
Lines 10-16: Defines enhanced color palette sorted by migration patterns
Lines 19-26: circos.par() sets comprehensive parameters including track margins and cell padding
Lines 29-47: chordDiagram() with advanced features: - order to arrange regions optimally - directional = 1 to show flow direction - direction.type using height difference and arrows - link.border and link.lwd for chord borders - link.sort and link.largest.ontop for visual hierarchy
Lines 50-84: circos.track() adds detailed annotations including region names and in/out flow statistics
Lines 87-96: Adds comprehensive title and subtitle explaining the visualization
Lines 99-109: Adds legend with key statistics and insights
Lines 112-117: Adds caption with data source attribution
Line 120: Essential cleanup with circos.clear()

Final result: A publication-ready chord diagram that clearly communicates migration patterns with directional indicators, flow statistics, and professional styling. The combination of arrows, colors, annotations, and legend creates a comprehensive visualization suitable for reports, presentations, or academic papers.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Chord Diagrams:

Use circos.clear() religiously - Always call before and after creating chord diagrams to prevent parameter carryover issues
Order sectors meaningfully - Arrange regions by total flow, alphabetically, or by a meaningful metric using the order parameter
Add directional indicators - Use directional = 1 with arrows or height differences to show flow direction clearly
Adjust gaps strategically - Use gap.degree between 2-5 to balance compactness with readability
Color with purpose - Assign colors that match regional or categorical meanings, ensuring sufficient contrast
Show the data - Add annotations with actual flow values, totals, or percentages to provide concrete numbers
Mind the matrix diagonal - Self-loops (diagonal elements) can clutter the visualization; consider setting them to zero
Use transparency wisely - Set transparency between 0.3-0.6 to show overlapping flows without losing definition
Sort links for clarity - Use link.sort = TRUE and link.largest.ontop = TRUE to bring important flows forward
Export with care - Save as PDF or high-res PNG: pdf("chord.pdf", width = 10, height = 10) then run code, then dev.off()

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other circular relationship visualizations:

Sankey diagrams for linear flow representations
Network graphs for complex interconnections
Arc diagrams for simpler connection displays
Circular dendrograms for hierarchical relationships

You can make your chord diagrams interactive using chorddiag:
# Install if needed

# Create interactive chord diagram

  migration_matrix,
  groupColors = region_colors_adv,
  groupnamePadding = 20,
  groupThickness = 0.1,
  chordedgeColor = "gray30",
  showTicks = FALSE,
  margin = 120
)
This creates an interactive HTML widget where users can hover over chords to see exact values and highlight specific flows.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated 2D density plots (contour plots) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
2D density plots are excellent for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables, showing concentration patterns and revealing clusters or correlations in bivariate data.
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, examining the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time for the Old Faithful geyser.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated 2D density plots (contour plots) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
2D density plots are excellent for visualizing the relationship between two continuous variables, showing concentration patterns and revealing clusters or correlations in bivariate data.
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, examining the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time for the Old Faithful geyser.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: use the faithful geyser dataset

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic 2D Density Plot
Let’s start with a simple 2D density contour plot showing the relationship between eruption duration and waiting time.

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +  # Set up with x and y
  geom_density_2d()                                                 # Create 2D density contours









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) - Initializes the plot with geyser data, mapping eruption duration to x-axis and waiting time to y-axis
Line 2: geom_density_2d() - Adds contour lines showing areas of high and low density in the 2D space, revealing two distinct clusters

What we have so far: A functional but basic 2D density plot. The contour lines reveal two clusters but the chart lacks color fill, data points, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding filled contours, data points, better colors, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Filled contours showing density levels with color
Data points overlay showing actual observations
Viridis color palette for better perception
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Contour labels showing density levels
Alpha transparency for layering



ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +
  # Filled density contours
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.8,                    # Filled contours with transparency
                         contour_var = "density") +      # Color by density
  # Overlay contour lines for definition
  geom_density_2d(color = "white",                       # White contour lines
                  linewidth = 0.3,
                  alpha = 0.5) +
  # Add data points
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3,                                # Semi-transparent points
             size = 1.5,
             color = "gray20") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +              # Color palette
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful: Eruption Duration vs Waiting Time",
    subtitle = "Two distinct clusters reveal bimodal eruption patterns",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Waiting Time to Next Eruption (minutes)",
    fill = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot() initializes the plot with both x and y continuous variables
Lines 3-4: geom_density_2d_filled() creates filled contour regions colored by density, with alpha = 0.8 for slight transparency
Lines 6-8: geom_density_2d() adds white contour lines on top for clear boundary definition
Lines 10-12: geom_point() overlays the actual data points with transparency to show raw data alongside density estimate
Line 13: scale_fill_viridis_d() applies a discrete viridis color palette (plasma option) optimized for perception
Lines 14-20: labs() adds descriptive title highlighting the bimodal pattern, subtitle with context, and clear axis labels
Line 21: theme_minimal() applies a clean theme
Lines 22-25: theme() customizes title formatting and legend position

What we have now: A much more informative chart with filled density regions, clear contour boundaries, and visible data points. The color gradient and clean formatting make patterns easy to identify and the chart presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with continuous color gradient, statistical annotations, cluster identification, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Continuous color fill (filled polygons) for smooth gradients
Cluster centroids marked on the plot
Statistical ellipses showing 95% confidence regions
Correlation annotation with statistics
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Hex bins as alternative representation
Data source caption for proper attribution
Custom color palette optimized for the data



# Identify clusters using k-means
set.seed(123)
clusters <- kmeans(data_faithful, centers = 2)

# Calculate cluster centroids
centroids <- as_tibble(clusters$centers) %>%
  mutate(cluster = c("Short/Short", "Long/Long"))

# Add cluster labels to data
data_with_clusters <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(clusters$cluster))

# Calculate correlation
cor_value <- cor(data_faithful$eruption_time, data_faithful$waiting_time)

# Calculate summary statistics for annotation
stats_text <- paste0(
  "Correlation: r = ", round(cor_value, 3), "\n",
  "n = ", nrow(data_faithful), " observations\n",
  "Two clusters identified"
)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time)) +
  # Filled 2D density with continuous scale
  stat_density_2d(aes(fill = after_stat(level)),
                  geom = "polygon",
                  alpha = 0.8,
                  color = NA,
                  contour_var = "density",
                  bins = 15) +
  # Add contour lines for reference
  geom_density_2d(color = "white",
                  linewidth = 0.4,
                  alpha = 0.6,
                  bins = 15) +
  # Add confidence ellipses for clusters
  stat_ellipse(data = data_with_clusters,
               aes(color = cluster),
               level = 0.95,
               linewidth = 1,
               linetype = "dashed") +
  # Add individual points colored by cluster
  geom_point(data = data_with_clusters,
             aes(color = cluster),
             alpha = 0.4,
             size = 1.8) +
  # Add cluster centroids
  geom_point(data = centroids,
             aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time),
             shape = 23,
             size = 5,
             fill = "white",
             color = "gray20",
             stroke = 1.5) +
  # Add centroid labels
  geom_text(data = centroids,
            aes(x = eruption_time, y = waiting_time + 3,
                label = cluster),
            fontface = "bold",
            size = 3.5,
            color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom color scales
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma",
                       name = "Density\nLevel",
                       alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E76F51", "#2C5F8D"),
                     name = "Cluster",
                     labels = c("Cluster 1: Short", "Cluster 2: Long")) +
  # Format axes
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.5),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(40, 100, by = 10),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Shows Two Distinct Eruption-Waiting Patterns",
    subtitle = "Strong positive correlation (r = 0.901) with clear bimodal clustering\nDashed ellipses show 95% confidence regions | White diamonds mark cluster centers",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Waiting Time to Next Eruption (minutes)",
    caption = "Data source: Azzalini & Bowman (1990) | 272 eruptions | K-means clustering (k=2) | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add statistics annotation box
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = 1.6, xmax = 2.8,
           ymin = 85, ymax = 98,
           fill = "white",
           color = "gray30",
           alpha = 0.9,
           linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1.65, y = 95,
           label = "Statistics",
           hjust = 0,
           fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray20") +
  annotate("text",
           x = 1.65, y = 91,
           label = stats_text,
           hjust = 0,
           size = 3,
           color = "gray30",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold",
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.box = "vertical",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Performs k-means clustering with 2 centers to identify the two distinct groups in the data
Lines 6-7: Extracts cluster centroids and labels them descriptively
Lines 10-11: Adds cluster assignments to the original data
Line 14: Calculates Pearson correlation coefficient between eruption time and waiting time
Lines 17-21: Creates a formatted text string with key statistics for annotation
Line 23: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 25-31: stat_density_2d() with geom = "polygon" creates smooth filled density regions using a continuous color scale (15 bins for smooth gradients)
Lines 33-37: geom_density_2d() adds white contour lines for clear boundary definition
Lines 39-43: stat_ellipse() adds dashed ellipses showing 95% confidence regions around each cluster
Lines 45-48: geom_point() overlays data points colored by cluster membership
Lines 50-56: geom_point() adds white diamond markers at cluster centroids
Lines 58-63: geom_text() labels the cluster centroids with descriptive names
Lines 65-67: scale_fill_viridis_c() applies continuous magma color palette for density levels
Lines 68-70: scale_color_manual() applies custom colors to distinguish clusters
Lines 72-76: scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() format axes with appropriate breaks and expansion
Lines 78-84: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title, multi-line subtitle with interpretation, and detailed caption
Lines 86-108: Multiple annotate() calls create a statistics summary box showing correlation, sample size, and clustering information
Lines 109-137: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend positioned on right with vertical box layout - Grid customization - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready 2D density plot that clearly communicates the bivariate relationship between eruption duration and waiting time. The combination of continuous density gradient, confidence ellipses, cluster centroids, and statistical annotations creates a comprehensive visualization suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful 2D Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 2D Density Plots:

Choose between discrete and continuous fills - Use geom_density_2d_filled() for discrete levels or stat_density_2d() with geom = "polygon" for continuous gradients
Adjust the number of bins - Use bins parameter (typically 10-20) to control contour smoothness. More bins = more detail but can be cluttered
Always show the data - Overlay actual points with geom_point() to show data density and identify outliers
Use appropriate color palettes - Viridis palettes are perceptually uniform and colorblind-friendly. Consider option = "magma", "plasma", or "viridis"
Add white contour lines - When using filled densities, overlay thin white contour lines for clear boundary definition
Consider hexbin alternatives - For very large datasets (>10,000 points), geom_hex() may perform better than density estimation
Annotate key statistics - Include correlation coefficients, sample sizes, or cluster information directly on the plot
Use statistical overlays - Add stat_ellipse() for confidence regions or linear models with geom_smooth() to show trends
Mind the bandwidth - Adjust smoothing with h parameter in geom_density_2d() if default produces too much or too little smoothing
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Want to create hexbin plots for large data?
For datasets with many thousands of points, hexagonal binning is more efficient:
library(hexbin)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 30) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma",
                       name = "Count",
                       trans = "log10") +
  labs(title = "Diamond Carat vs Price (Hexbin)",
       x = "Carat Weight",
       y = "Price (USD)") +
  theme_minimal()
This creates hexagonal bins showing counts in log scale, ideal for 50,000+ data points.

title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated edge bundling charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic hierarchical plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Edge bundling is an excellent technique for reducing visual clutter in network visualizations by bundling edges that follow similar paths. This creates a cleaner, more organized appearance especially useful for hierarchical data or networks with many connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing organizational relationships and communication patterns within a company.

title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated edge bundling charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic hierarchical plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Edge bundling is an excellent technique for reducing visual clutter in network visualizations by bundling edges that follow similar paths. This creates a cleaner, more organized appearance especially useful for hierarchical data or networks with many connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing organizational relationships and communication patterns within a company.

title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # For data manipulation
library(igraph)     # For network data structures
library(ggraph)     # For network visualization
library(scales)     # For formatting

# Create hierarchical structure (organizational chart)
hierarchy <- data.frame(
  from = c("CEO", "CEO", "CEO",
           "VP Sales", "VP Sales", "VP Sales",
           "VP Tech", "VP Tech", "VP Tech", "VP Tech",
           "VP Ops", "VP Ops"),
  to = c("VP Sales", "VP Tech", "VP Ops",
         "Sales East", "Sales West", "Sales Int'l",
         "Dev Team", "QA Team", "Design", "Data Science",
         "Logistics", "Customer Service")
)

# Create edges for cross-department communication
communications <- data.frame(
  from = c("Sales East", "Sales West", "Dev Team", "QA Team", 
           "Design", "Data Science", "Logistics", "Customer Service",
           "Sales Int'l", "Dev Team", "Sales East"),
  to = c("Dev Team", "Design", "QA Team", "Dev Team",
         "Dev Team", "Dev Team", "Sales East", "Sales West",
         "Data Science", "Data Science", "Logistics"),
  weight = c(15, 12, 25, 30, 18, 22, 10, 14, 16, 20, 8)
)

# Combine hierarchy and communications
all_edges <- bind_rows(
  hierarchy %>% mutate(type = "hierarchy", weight = 1),
  communications %>% mutate(type = "communication")
)

# Get all unique nodes
all_nodes <- data.frame(
  name = unique(c(all_edges$from, all_edges$to))
) %>%
  mutate(
    level = case_when(
      name == "CEO" ~ 1,
      name %in% c("VP Sales", "VP Tech", "VP Ops") ~ 2,
      TRUE ~ 3
    ),
    department = case_when(
      name == "CEO" ~ "Executive",
      grepl("Sales|Sales East|Sales West|Sales Int'l", name) ~ "Sales",
      grepl("Tech|Dev|QA|Design|Data", name) ~ "Technology",
      grepl("Ops|Logistics|Customer", name) ~ "Operations",
      TRUE ~ "Executive"
    )
  )

# Create graph from HIERARCHY ONLY for proper tree structure
hierarchy_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(d = hierarchy, vertices = all_nodes, directed = TRUE)

# Add all edges as attributes for later use
E(hierarchy_graph)$type <- "hierarchy"
V(hierarchy_graph)$dept <- all_nodes$department[match(V(hierarchy_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]

# Preview the data
head(all_edges)

      from          to      type weight
1      CEO    VP Sales hierarchy      1
2      CEO     VP Tech hierarchy      1
3      CEO      VP Ops hierarchy      1
4 VP Sales  Sales East hierarchy      1
5 VP Sales  Sales West hierarchy      1
6 VP Sales Sales Int'l hierarchy      1

head(all_nodes)

        name level department
1        CEO     1  Executive
2   VP Sales     2      Sales
3    VP Tech     2 Technology
4     VP Ops     2 Operations
5 Sales East     3      Sales
6 Sales West     3      Sales

text:
Chart 1: Basic Hierarchical Layout
Let’s start with a simple hierarchical tree showing the organizational structure.

ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "tree") +
  geom_edge_link() +                    # Draw edges
  geom_node_point(size = 5) +           # Draw nodes
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),     # Add labels
                 repel = TRUE, 
                 size = 3)









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "tree") - Initializes the plot using a tree layout which arranges nodes hierarchically
Line 2: geom_edge_link() - Draws straight lines representing connections
Line 3: geom_node_point() - Draws circles for each node
Lines 4-6: geom_node_text() - Adds labels with repel to avoid overlaps

What we have so far: A functional but basic tree layout. The hierarchy is visible but with many cross-connections, the chart becomes cluttered and hard to read.

title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
section: Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement with Edge Bundling
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement with Edge Bundling
Now we’ll improve the chart by applying edge bundling, adding colors, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Dendrogram layout for hierarchical display
Color coding by department
Node sizes by hierarchical level
Diagonal edges for tree structure
Improved labels with better positioning
Clean theme removing axes
Title and legend for context



# Use linear dendrogram layout first
ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "dendrogram", circular = FALSE) +
  # Draw edges
  geom_edge_diagonal(alpha = 0.4, color = "gray50") +
  # Draw nodes colored by department
  geom_node_point(aes(size = (4 - level) * 3, color = dept),
                  alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 hjust = 1.1,
                 size = 3) +
  # Apply color palette
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2",
                     name = "Department") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Organizational Hierarchy (Dendrogram Layout)",
    subtitle = "Hierarchical structure showing reporting relationships",
    caption = "Dendrogram layout organizes nodes by hierarchical level"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, edge filtering, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Separate hierarchy and communication edges with different styling
Edge width based on communication volume

Professional typography and spacing



# Create full graph with all edges for visualization
full_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(d = all_edges, vertices = all_nodes, directed = TRUE)

# Add edge attributes
E(full_graph)$edge_type <- all_edges$type
E(full_graph)$edge_weight <- all_edges$weight

# Add node attributes
V(full_graph)$dept <- all_nodes$department[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]
V(full_graph)$node_level <- all_nodes$level[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]

# Define custom color palette
dept_colors <- c(
  "Executive" = "#8B4789",
  "Sales" = "#E76F51",
  "Technology" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Operations" = "#52A675"
)

# Create layout
set.seed(42)

ggraph(full_graph, layout = "fr") +
  # Draw edges with different styles by type
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = edge_type, 
                     alpha = edge_type,
                     width = ifelse(edge_type == "communication", edge_weight/10, 0.5)),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')),
                 end_cap = circle(3, 'mm')) +
  # Color edges by type
  scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = "gray70", 
                                      "communication" = "#a50f15"),
                          name = "Connection Type") +
  scale_edge_alpha_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = 0.3,
                                     "communication" = 0.7),
                         guide = "none") +
  scale_edge_width_identity() +
  # Draw nodes with enhanced styling
  geom_node_point(aes(size = (4 - node_level) * 4, 
                      fill = dept),
                  shape = 21,
                  color = "gray20",
                  stroke = 1,
                  alpha = 0.9) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name,
                     fontface = ifelse(node_level == 1, "bold", "plain")),
                 repel = TRUE,
                 size = 3.5,
                 max.overlaps = 20) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = dept_colors,
                    name = "Department") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Organizational Network: Hierarchical Structure and Cross-Department Communications",
    subtitle = "Force-directed layout showing both reporting lines (gray) and communication flows (red)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated organizational data | Edge width indicates communication volume | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for communication stats
  annotate("text",
           x = -2, 
           y = 2,
           label = paste0("Communication Flows:\n",
                         "Total Links: ", sum(all_edges$type == "communication"), "\n",
                         "Departments: ", n_distinct(all_nodes$department) - 1, "\n",
                         "Avg Weight: ", round(mean(communications$weight), 1)),
           hjust = 0,
           vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray30",
           fontface = "italic",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_graph(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Edge Bundling Charts:

Choose appropriate layouts - Circular dendrogram works best for edge bundling; ensure your data has hierarchical structure
Adjust tension carefully - The tension parameter (0-1) controls bundling tightness; 0.8-0.9 usually works well
Separate edge types - Use different styling for hierarchical vs. data edges to maintain clarity
Use transparency wisely - Set alpha 0.3-0.6 for bundled edges to show density without obscuring nodes
Color meaningfully - Use color gradients to show edge properties like weight or frequency
Size nodes by importance - Make higher-level nodes larger for visual hierarchy
Rotate labels appropriately - Use node_angle() to rotate labels following the circular layout
Consider audience - Edge bundling works best when viewers need to see overall patterns, not trace individual connections
Limit edge count - Edge bundling is most effective with 20-200 edges; too few doesn’t show benefit, too many becomes messy
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("bundling.png", width = 12, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

# Create interactive visualization (requires custom D3 script)

# Create simpler graph for force-directed

  directed = TRUE

ggraph(simple_graph, layout = "fr") +
  # Draw bundled edges
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = weight, alpha = weight),

  # Draw nodes

  ) +

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated histograms using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Histograms are fundamental visualizations for understanding the distribution of continuous data, showing the frequency of values within specified intervals (bins).
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, which contains eruption durations and waiting times for the Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone National Park.

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated histograms using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Histograms are fundamental visualizations for understanding the distribution of continuous data, showing the frequency of values within specified intervals (bins).
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, which contains eruption durations and waiting times for the Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone National Park.

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: use the faithful geyser dataset
data_faithful <- faithful %>%
  as_tibble() %>%                                  # Convert to tibble
  rename(
    eruption_time = eruptions,                     # Rename for clarity
    waiting_time = waiting
  )

# Preview the data
head(data_faithful)

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Histogram
Let’s start with a simple histogram showing the distribution of geyser eruption durations.

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_histogram()                                # Create histogram

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.










Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) - Initializes the plot with our geyser data, mapping eruption duration to the x-axis
Line 2: geom_histogram() - Adds histogram bars showing the count of eruptions within each time interval (bin)

What we have so far: A functional but basic histogram. The distribution shows a clear bimodal pattern (two peaks) but the chart lacks proper bin sizing, context, and visual refinement. You’ll also see a warning message about the default 30 bins.

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by optimizing bin width, adding color, statistical overlays, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Optimized bin width for better pattern visibility
Custom fill color with border definition
Density curve overlay showing the smoothed distribution
Mean line as a reference point
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Count labels on bars for precise reading



# Calculate mean for reference line
mean_eruption <- mean(data_faithful$eruption_time)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +
  # Histogram with specified bin width
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25,                      # 0.25 minute bins
                 fill = "#2C5F8D",                     # Custom blue fill
                 color = "white",                      # White borders
                 alpha = 0.8) +                        # Slight transparency
  # Add density curve overlay
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count) * 0.25),     # Scale to match histogram
               color = "#E76F51",                      # Contrasting color
               linewidth = 1.2) +                      # Thicker line
  # Add mean reference line
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_eruption,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray30",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Add mean label
  annotate("text", x = mean_eruption + 0.3, y = 35,
           label = paste0("Mean = ", round(mean_eruption, 2), " min"),
           color = "gray30", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Eruption Duration Shows Bimodal Distribution",
    subtitle = "272 eruptions recorded, grouped into 0.25-minute intervals",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Number of Eruptions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )









Code Explanation
Line 2: Calculates the mean eruption time for use as a reference line
Line 5: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) - Initializes the plot
Lines 7-10: geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25) - Creates histogram with 0.25-minute bins (rather than default 30 bins), custom blue fill, white borders for definition, and slight transparency
Lines 12-14: geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count) * 0.25)) - Adds a density curve scaled to match histogram counts by multiplying by bin width, using a contrasting orange color
Lines 16-19: geom_vline() - Adds a dashed vertical line at the mean eruption duration
Lines 21-23: annotate() - Adds text label showing the exact mean value
Lines 24-29: labs() - Adds descriptive title highlighting the bimodal pattern, subtitle with context, and clear axis labels
Line 30: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme
Lines 31-33: theme() - Customizes title formatting

What we have now: A much more informative chart with appropriate bin sizing revealing the bimodal pattern, a density overlay for smoothed context, and a mean reference line. The clean formatting and proper labeling make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with color-coded bins, statistical annotations, faceted comparison, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Color-coded bins by eruption type (short vs long)
Multiple statistical reference lines (mean, median, quartiles)
Bin count annotations on top of bars
Normal distribution overlay for comparison
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Summary statistics panel in the plot
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics
stats_summary <- data_faithful %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_time = mean(eruption_time),
    median_time = median(eruption_time),
    sd_time = sd(eruption_time),
    q25 = quantile(eruption_time, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(eruption_time, 0.75)
  )

# Create eruption category for color coding
data_faithful <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(
    eruption_type = case_when(
      eruption_time < 3 ~ "Short (< 3 min)",
      TRUE ~ "Long (≥ 3 min)"
    )
  )

# Calculate bin counts for annotations
bin_data <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(eruption_time, 
                   breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.25),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  count(bin) %>%
  mutate(midpoint = seq(1.625, 5.375, by = 0.25)[1:n()])

# Define custom colors
eruption_colors <- c(
  "Short (< 3 min)" = "#E76F51",    # Coral for short
  "Long (≥ 3 min)" = "#2C5F8D"      # Blue for long
)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +
  # Main histogram with color coding
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = eruption_type),
                 binwidth = 0.25,
                 color = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.3,
                 alpha = 0.85) +
  # Add statistical reference lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = stats_summary$mean_time,
             linetype = "solid",
             color = "gray20",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = stats_summary$median_time,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray40",
             linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(stats_summary$q25, stats_summary$q75),
             linetype = "dotted",
             color = "gray50",
             linewidth = 0.6) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = eruption_colors,
                    name = "Eruption Type") +
  # Format axes
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.5),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     breaks = seq(0, 40, by = 10)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Geyser Erupts in Two Distinct Patterns",
    subtitle = "Short eruptions (< 3 min) and long eruptions (≥ 3 min) form clear bimodal distribution",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Frequency (Number of Eruptions)",
    caption = "Data source: Azzalini & Bowman (1990) | 272 eruptions | Bin width = 0.25 minutes | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add statistics annotation box
  annotate("rect", 
           xmin = 4.5, xmax = 5.3, 
           ymin = 25, ymax = 38,
           fill = "white", color = "gray30", 
           alpha = 0.9, linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 36,
           label = "Summary Statistics",
           hjust = 0, fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.5, color = "gray20") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 34,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", round(stats_summary$mean_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 32.5,
           label = paste0("Median: ", round(stats_summary$median_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 31,
           label = paste0("SD: ", round(stats_summary$sd_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 29.5,
           label = paste0("n = ", stats_summary$n),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 27,
           label = "Lines: mean (solid),\nmedian (dashed),\nquartiles (dotted)",
           hjust = 0, size = 2.5, 
           color = "gray40", lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-11: Calculates comprehensive summary statistics including count, mean, median, standard deviation, and quartiles for annotations
Lines 14-20: Creates a categorical variable eruption_type to classify eruptions as short (< 3 minutes) or long (≥ 3 minutes) for color coding
Lines 23-29: Calculates the count of eruptions in each bin for potential annotations, including midpoints
Lines 32-35: Defines a custom color palette with meaningful colors (coral for short, blue for long eruptions)
Line 37: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 39-43: geom_histogram() creates color-coded bins with fill mapped to eruption type, white borders, and transparency
Lines 45-56: Multiple geom_vline() calls add reference lines for mean (solid), median (dashed), and quartiles (dotted) with different line styles and weights
Lines 58-59: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette with legend title
Lines 61-64: scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() format axes with appropriate breaks and expansion
Lines 66-72: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, descriptive subtitle explaining the pattern, and detailed caption with data source attribution
Lines 74-104: Multiple annotate() calls create a statistics summary box in the upper right corner containing: - White rectangle background - Title “Summary Statistics” - Mean, median, standard deviation, and sample size - Legend explaining the reference lines
Lines 105-129: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend positioned at top - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready histogram that clearly communicates the bimodal distribution of Old Faithful eruptions. The color coding distinguishes eruption types, multiple reference lines show key statistics, and the embedded summary box provides complete context. This chart is suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Histograms:

Choose bin width carefully - Use the Freedman-Diaconis rule: binwidth = 2 * IQR(x) / (length(x)^(1/3)) or experiment with different values to reveal patterns without over-smoothing
Always specify binwidth or bins - Never rely on ggplot2’s default 30 bins; choose based on your data characteristics and the story you want to tell
Add borders to bars - Use color = "white" or color = "gray30" to define bar boundaries, especially important when bars are adjacent
Consider density overlays - Adding geom_density() scaled appropriately helps show the smoothed distribution pattern
Show reference statistics - Add vertical lines for mean, median, or other important values to provide context
Use color meaningfully - Color-code bins when there are natural categories or thresholds in your data
Mind the y-axis - Label as “Frequency”, “Count”, or “Number of Observations” rather than just “count” for clarity
Handle skewed data - For right-skewed distributions, consider log-transforming the x-axis with scale_x_log10()
Annotate sample size - Always show the total number of observations either in the subtitle or as an annotation
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Want to create comparative histograms?
You can compare distributions across groups using facets or overlays:
# Faceted approach (recommended for many groups)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, fill = "#2C5F8D", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ cut, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  labs(title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Cut Quality",
       x = "Price (USD)",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()

# Overlay approach (best for 2-3 groups)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated lollipop charts using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Lollipop charts are excellent alternatives to bar charts when you want to emphasize individual data points while reducing visual clutter. They’re particularly effective for showing rankings, comparisons, or changes over categories.
We’ll use a dataset representing customer satisfaction scores across different service departments.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated lollipop charts using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Lollipop charts are excellent alternatives to bar charts when you want to emphasize individual data points while reducing visual clutter. They’re particularly effective for showing rankings, comparisons, or changes over categories.
We’ll use a dataset representing customer satisfaction scores across different service departments.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Create sample data: customer satisfaction scores by department
data_satisfaction <- tibble(
  department = c("Sales", "Support", "Billing", "Technical", 
                 "Shipping", "Returns", "Quality", "Management"),
  score = c(78, 85, 72, 88, 80, 68, 82, 75),
  target = 80  # Company target score
)

# Preview the data
head(data_satisfaction)

  department score target
  <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Sales         78     80

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Lollipop Chart
Let’s start with a simple lollipop chart showing satisfaction scores by department.

ggplot(data_satisfaction, aes(x = department, y = score)) +  # Set up with x and y
  geom_segment(aes(x = department, xend = department,        # Draw vertical lines
                   y = 0, yend = score)) +
  geom_point(size = 4)                                       # Add points at top









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_satisfaction, aes(x = department, y = score)) - Initializes the plot with department on x-axis and satisfaction score on y-axis
Lines 2-3: geom_segment() creates vertical lines from y=0 to the score value for each department
Line 4: geom_point() adds circular points at the top of each line, creating the “lollipop” appearance

What we have so far: A functional but basic lollipop chart. The data is visible but the chart lacks color, proper ordering, context, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by reordering, adding colors, including a target line, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Reordered departments by score for easier comparison
Color coding to distinguish above/below target
Horizontal orientation for better label readability
Target reference line showing company goal
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Larger points for better visibility



# Add column for above/below target
data_satisfaction <- data_satisfaction %>%
  mutate(
    performance = ifelse(score >= target, "Above Target", "Below Target"),
    performance = factor(performance, levels = c("Above Target", "Below Target"))
  )

ggplot(data_satisfaction, aes(x = reorder(department, score), y = score, 
                              color = performance)) +
  # Draw segments
  geom_segment(aes(x = reorder(department, score), 
                   xend = reorder(department, score),
                   y = 0, yend = score),
               linewidth = 1.5) +
  # Add points
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  # Add target reference line
  geom_hline(yintercept = 80, linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Flip coordinates for horizontal layout
  coord_flip() +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Above Target" = "#52A675", 
                                 "Below Target" = "#E76F51")) +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 20),
                     limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Satisfaction Scores by Department",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows company target (80 points)",
    x = "Department",
    y = "Satisfaction Score (0-100)",
    color = "Performance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "top"
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-6: Creates a new column performance categorizing departments as “Above Target” or “Below Target”
Lines 8-9: ggplot() with reorder(department, score) to sort departments by score, and color = performance for conditional coloring
Lines 11-15: geom_segment() creates vertical lines with increased thickness (linewidth = 1.5)
Line 17: geom_point() adds larger points (size = 5)
Lines 19-20: geom_hline() adds a dashed horizontal reference line at the target score (80)
Line 22: coord_flip() rotates the chart to horizontal orientation for better department name readability
Lines 24-25: scale_color_manual() applies green for above target and coral for below target
Lines 27-28: scale_y_continuous() sets axis breaks and limits
Lines 29-35: labs() adds descriptive title, subtitle explaining the target line, and clear axis labels
Line 36: theme_minimal() applies clean theme
Lines 37-40: theme() customizes title and legend position

What we have now: A much more informative chart with sorted departments, color-coded performance, and a clear target reference. The horizontal orientation and clean formatting make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, value labels, variance from target, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Variance indicators showing distance from target
Value labels on each point
Segment styling from target line instead of zero
Enhanced color palette with gradient effect
Department rankings in labels
Summary statistics annotation
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Data source caption for proper attribution



# Calculate variance from target and add rankings
target_value <- 80  # Store target as variable

data_satisfaction <- data_satisfaction %>%
  mutate(
    variance = score - target_value,
    rank = rank(-score, ties.method = "first"),
    dept_label = paste0("#", rank, " ", department)
  )

# Calculate summary statistics
avg_score <- round(mean(data_satisfaction$score), 1)
above_target_pct <- round(sum(data_satisfaction$score >= target_value) / 
                          nrow(data_satisfaction) * 100, 0)

# Define enhanced color palette
perf_colors <- c("Above Target" = "#2E7D32", "Below Target" = "#C62828")

ggplot(data_satisfaction, aes(x = reorder(dept_label, score), y = score)) +
  # Draw segments from target line to score
  geom_segment(aes(x = reorder(dept_label, score), 
                   xend = reorder(dept_label, score),
                   y = target_value, yend = score,
                   color = performance),
               linewidth = 2,
               alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add target reference line
  geom_hline(yintercept = target_value, 
             linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "gray30", 
             linewidth = 1) +
  # Add points with enhanced styling
  geom_point(aes(color = performance), 
             size = 6,
             alpha = 0.9) +
  # Add value labels
  geom_text(aes(label = score),
            hjust = -0.5,
            size = 3.5,
            fontface = "bold",
            color = "gray20") +
  # Add variance labels
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(variance >= 0, 
                                paste0("+", variance), 
                                as.character(variance))),
            hjust = 1.5,
            size = 3,
            color = "gray40") +
  # Flip coordinates
  coord_flip() +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_color_manual(values = perf_colors,
                     name = "vs Target (80)") +
  # Format x-axis (becomes y after flip)
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10),
                     limits = c(0, 95),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Customer Satisfaction Performance: 63% of Departments Meet Target",
    subtitle = "Technical leads with 88 points (+8 vs target) | Segments show variance from 80-point target",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Satisfaction Score (out of 100)",
    caption = "Data source: Q4 2024 Customer Satisfaction Survey | n = 1,247 responses | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add summary statistics as text annotation (no box, positioned at bottom right)
  annotate("text",
           x = 1, y = 90,
           label = paste0("Summary: Avg = ", avg_score, 
                         " | Above Target = ", above_target_pct, 
                         "% | Range = ", min(data_satisfaction$score), 
                         "-", max(data_satisfaction$score)),
           hjust = 0,
           size = 3.2,
           color = "gray30",
           fontface = "italic") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold",
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-7: Calculates variance from target, ranking, and creates department labels with rank numbers
Lines 10-12: Calculates summary statistics including average score and percentage above target
Line 15: Defines enhanced color palette with darker, more professional shades
Line 17: ggplot() with reordered department labels including rankings
Lines 19-26: geom_segment() creates segments that start at the target line (80) rather than zero, making variance immediately visible. Color coded by performance with increased thickness
Lines 28-31: geom_hline() adds prominent target reference line
Lines 33-35: geom_point() adds large colored points
Lines 37-41: geom_text() adds score value labels to the right of points
Lines 43-48: geom_text() adds variance labels (e.g., “+8” or “-12”) to the left of points
Line 50: coord_flip() for horizontal orientation
Lines 52-53: scale_color_manual() applies custom colors
Lines 55-57: scale_y_continuous() with expanded right margin for labels
Lines 59-65: labs() adds comprehensive labels including percentage meeting target in title, top performer in subtitle, and detailed caption
Lines 67-93: Multiple annotate() calls create a summary statistics box showing average, percentage above target, and score range
Lines 94-122: Comprehensive theme customization including enhanced typography, legend at top, grid customization, and proper margins

Final result: A publication-ready lollipop chart that clearly communicates satisfaction performance across departments. The segments starting from the target line, variance labels, ranking numbers, and summary statistics box create a comprehensive visualization suitable for executive presentations, reports, or dashboards.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Lollipop Charts:

Always reorder categories - Use reorder() to sort by value for easier visual comparison and pattern recognition
Use horizontal orientation for long labels - Apply coord_flip() when category names are lengthy or numerous
Start segments meaningfully - Instead of always starting at zero, consider starting from a baseline (like target or mean) to emphasize variance
Add reference lines - Use geom_hline() or geom_vline() to show targets, averages, or thresholds
Color with purpose - Use color to show categorical groups or highlight above/below threshold performance
Label directly - Add value labels with geom_text() to reduce need for axis reading, especially with many categories
Adjust segment thickness - Use linewidth = 1.5-2.5 for segments; too thin looks fragile, too thick looks heavy
Mind the point size - Points should be 4-6 size units; large enough to see but not overwhelming
Consider Cleveland dot plots - For comparing multiple groups, consider faceting or using geom_linerange() with two points
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

text:

Want to create grouped lollipop charts?
You can show multiple series with position dodging:
# Create data with two time periods
data_comparison <- data_satisfaction %>%
  select(department, score) %>%
  rename(current = score) %>%
  mutate(previous = current - sample(-5:8, n(), replace = TRUE)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(current, previous), 
               names_to = "period", 
               values_to = "score")

# Create grouped lollipop chart
ggplot(data_comparison, 
       aes(x = reorder(department, score), 
           y = score, 
           color = period)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, 
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = department, 
                   y = 0, yend = score),
               position = position_dodge(width = 0.5),
               linewidth = 1) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#2C5F8D", "#E76F51"),
                     labels = c("Current Quarter", "Previous Quarter")) +
  labs(title = "Satisfaction Score Comparison",
       x = "Department",
       y = "Score",
       color = "Period") +
  theme_minimal()
This creates side-by-side lollipops showing changes over time.

title: Creating Beautiful Lollipop Charts with ggplot2
text:
Alternative: Dumbbell Chart
Here’s a bonus approach showing change between two points:

# Create before/after data
data_dumbbell <- data_satisfaction %>%
  mutate(previous_score = score - sample(3:12, n(), replace = TRUE)) %>%
  select(department, previous_score, score, rank)

ggplot(data_dumbbell) +
  # Draw segments between points
  geom_segment(aes(x = previous_score, xend = score,
                   y = reorder(department, score), 
                   yend = reorder(department, score)),
               color = "gray70",
               linewidth = 2) +
  # Add previous period points
  geom_point(aes(x = previous_score, 
                 y = reorder(department, score)),
             color = "#E76F51",
             size = 5) +
  # Add current period points
  geom_point(aes(x = score, 
                 y = reorder(department, score)),
             color = "#52A675",
             size = 5) +
  # Add labels
  labs(
    title = "Customer Satisfaction Improvement by Department",
    subtitle = "All departments showed improvement from Q3 to Q4 2024",
    x = "Satisfaction Score",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # For data manipulation
library(sf)             # For spatial data handling
library(rnaturalearth)  # For geographic data
library(rnaturalearthdata) # Additional geographic data
library(ggspatial)      # For scale bars and north arrows
library(scales)         # For formatting

# Get UK map data at country level
uk_country <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", country = "United Kingdom", returnclass = "sf")

# Get UK regions (admin level 1)
uk_regions <- ne_states(country = "United Kingdom", returnclass = "sf")

# Create sample data: Average house price by region (fictional, in £1000s)
set.seed(42)
regional_data <- tibble(
  region = uk_regions$name,
  avg_house_price = round(rnorm(nrow(uk_regions), mean = 280, sd = 120)),
  unemployment_rate = round(rnorm(nrow(uk_regions), mean = 4.5, sd = 1.5), 1)
) %>%
  mutate(
    avg_house_price = pmax(avg_house_price, 150),  # Minimum value
    unemployment_rate = pmax(unemployment_rate, 2.0),  # Minimum value
    unemployment_rate = pmin(unemployment_rate, 8.0)   # Maximum value
  )

# Join spatial data with statistics
uk_map_data <- uk_regions %>%
  left_join(regional_data, by = c("name" = "region"))
