title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Map of UK
Let’s start with a simple map showing the outline and regions of the United Kingdom.

ggplot(uk_map_data) +
  geom_sf()  # Draw the map









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(uk_map_data) - Initializes the plot with our spatial data
Line 2: geom_sf() - Draws the map using the simple features geometry, automatically handling the spatial coordinates

What we have so far: A functional but basic map of the United Kingdom. The regional boundaries are visible but the chart lacks color, labels, context, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the map by adding a choropleth layer, color scale, labels, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Choropleth coloring based on average house prices
Color scale with meaningful breaks
Region boundaries with white lines
Improved projection for better appearance
Title and legend for context
Clean theme removing default elements
Currency formatting in legend



ggplot(uk_map_data) +
  # Fill regions by average house price
  geom_sf(aes(fill = avg_house_price), 
          color = "white", 
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Apply color gradient
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eff3ff", 
                      high = "#08519c",
                      name = "Avg House Price\n(£1000s)",
                      labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "United Kingdom: Regional Housing Market",
    subtitle = "Average house prices by region (simulated data)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: geom_sf(aes(fill = avg_house_price)) - Creates a choropleth map with regions colored by average house price, white boundaries, and thin line width
Lines 6-9: scale_fill_gradient() - Applies a sequential color scale from light blue to dark blue, with formatted labels
Lines 10-14: labs() - Adds title, subtitle, and caption for context
Line 15: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean base theme
Lines 16-21: theme() - Removes grid lines and axis elements that are unnecessary for maps

What we have now: A much more informative map with regional color coding showing housing market differences. The clean styling and proper legend make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, city markers, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette with better breaks
Major city markers showing key locations
City labels for important places
Enhanced borders with UK outline
Statistical categories instead of continuous scale
North arrow and scale bar for orientation
Professional typography and spacing
Neighboring countries for context
Inset for Northern Ireland (conceptually)



# Get neighboring countries for context
neighbors <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", 
                         country = c("Ireland", "France", "Belgium", 
                                   "Netherlands", "Norway", "Denmark"),
                         returnclass = "sf")

# Create house price categories
uk_map_data <- uk_map_data %>%
  mutate(
    price_category = cut(avg_house_price,
                        breaks = c(0, 200, 250, 300, 350, 500),
                        labels = c("< £200k", "£200-250k", "£250-300k", 
                                  "£300-350k", "> £350k"),
                        include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

# Major UK cities (approximate coordinates)
major_cities <- tibble(
  city = c("London", "Birmingham", "Manchester", "Glasgow", 
           "Liverpool", "Edinburgh", "Bristol", "Cardiff"),
  lon = c(-0.1278, -1.8904, -2.2426, -4.2518, 
          -2.9916, -3.1883, -2.5879, -3.1791),
  lat = c(51.5074, 52.4862, 53.4808, 55.8642, 
          53.4084, 55.9533, 51.4545, 51.4816),
  population_millions = c(9.0, 1.1, 2.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.4)
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# Define custom color palette
price_colors <- c(
  "< £200k" = "#eff3ff",
  "£200-250k" = "#bdd7e7",
  "£250-300k" = "#6baed6",
  "£300-350k" = "#3182bd",
  "> £350k" = "#08519c"
)

# Create the main map
ggplot() +
  # Add neighboring countries (in gray)
  geom_sf(data = neighbors, 
          fill = "gray95", 
          color = "gray70",
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Add UK regions with house price categories
  geom_sf(data = uk_map_data,
          aes(fill = price_category),
          color = "white",
          linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Add UK country outline
  geom_sf(data = uk_country,
          fill = NA,
          color = "gray20",
          linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Add major cities
  geom_sf(data = major_cities,
          aes(size = population_millions),
          shape = 21,
          fill = "#FFA500",
          color = "gray20",
          stroke = 0.8,
          alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add city labels
  geom_sf_text(data = major_cities,
               aes(label = city),
               size = 3,
               fontface = "bold",
               nudge_y = 0.25,
               color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom color palette
  scale_fill_manual(values = price_colors,
                    name = "Average House Price",
                    na.value = "gray90") +
  # Size scale for cities
  scale_size_continuous(name = "City Population\n(millions)",
                       range = c(2, 10),
                       breaks = c(0.5, 2, 5, 9)) +
  # Set coordinate system
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-11, 3), 
           ylim = c(49.5, 61),
           expand = FALSE) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "United Kingdom: Housing Market and Major Urban Centers",
    subtitle = "House prices show significant regional variation | Major cities marked by metropolitan population",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics | Map data: Natural Earth | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add north arrow
  annotation_north_arrow(
    location = "tl",
    which_north = "true",
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.3, "in"),
    style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering
  ) +
  # Add scale bar
  annotation_scale(
    location = "bl",
    width_hint = 0.25,
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.2, "in")
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Panel styling
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "lightblue", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Warning in st_point_on_surface.sfc(sf::st_zm(x)): st_point_on_surface may not
give correct results for longitude/latitude data


Scale on map varies by more than 10%, scale bar may be inaccurate










Code Explanation
Lines 2-5: Retrieves neighboring countries’ boundaries using ne_countries() for geographic context
Lines 8-15: Creates house price categories using cut() to convert continuous values into meaningful brackets
Lines 18-28: Creates a tibble of major UK cities with coordinates and converts to spatial format using st_as_sf()
Lines 31-37: Defines custom color palette for house price categories, progressing from light to dark blue
Line 40: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 42-45: geom_sf() adds neighboring countries in light gray for context
Lines 47-50: geom_sf() adds UK regions colored by house price category with white boundaries
Lines 52-55: geom_sf() adds UK’s country outline with thick dark border
Lines 57-63: geom_sf() adds major cities as circles sized by metropolitan population
Lines 65-70: geom_sf_text() adds city name labels above the markers
Lines 72-74: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette
Lines 76-78: scale_size_continuous() controls city marker sizes
Lines 80-82: coord_sf() sets the bounding box to show entire UK including Northern Ireland
Lines 84-88: labs() adds comprehensive title, subtitle, and caption
Lines 90-96: annotation_north_arrow() adds a decorative north arrow in top left
Lines 98-103: annotation_scale() adds a scale bar in bottom left
Line 104: theme_void() starts with blank canvas (appropriate for maps)
Lines 105-128: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Centered titles and caption - Legend styling with background box - Light blue panel background (representing water) - Proper margins for professional appearance

Final result: A publication-ready map of the United Kingdom that clearly communicates regional housing market patterns with major cities marked. The combination of choropleth coloring, city markers, neighboring countries for context, north arrow, and scale bar creates a comprehensive and professional visualization suitable for reports, presentations, or publications.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better sf Maps in R:

Use appropriate projections - For UK maps, consider British National Grid (EPSG:27700) for accurate measurements
Choose color scales wisely - Use sequential scales for continuous data like house prices, diverging for data with meaningful midpoint
Add geographic context - Include neighboring countries and water bodies to help viewers orient themselves
Label strategically - Add labels for major cities but avoid cluttering; use nudge_y to position labels clearly
Include scale and orientation - Always add north arrow and scale bar for maps of specific regions
Mind the bounding box - Use coord_sf() with xlim/ylim to include all parts (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland)
Layer thoughtfully - Order layers from background to foreground: context → main data → annotations → labels
Use theme_void() for clean maps - Remove axes and grid lines that are unnecessary for geographic visualization
Consider accessibility - Use colorblind-friendly palettes and ensure sufficient contrast between categories
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("map.png", width = 10, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of the United Kingdom with sf and ggplot2
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other map visualizations:

Point maps showing locations of businesses or facilities
Flow maps showing migration or commuting patterns
Interactive maps using leaflet or mapview
Small multiples showing different metrics side-by-side


Want to create interactive maps?
You can make your maps interactive using leaflet:
library(leaflet)

# Create color palette
pal <- colorNumeric(palette = "Blues", 
                   domain = uk_map_data$avg_house_price)

# Create interactive map
leaflet(uk_map_data) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(avg_house_price),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = ~paste0("<strong>", name, "</strong><br>",
                   "Avg House Price: £", 
                   format(avg_house_price * 1000, big.mark = ","))
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = ~avg_house_price,
    title = "Avg Price (£1000s)",
    position = "bottomright"
  ) %>%
  addMarkers(
    data = major_cities,
    popup = ~city
  )
This creates an interactive map where users can zoom, pan, and click regions for detailed information.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Pie charts are one of the most recognizable data visualizations, showing parts of a whole as slices of a circle. While often criticized in data visualization circles, pie charts can be effective when used appropriately. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated pie charts using ggplot2.
We’ll visualize the distribution of vehicle drivetrain types (front-wheel, rear-wheel, 4-wheel drive) using the built-in mpg dataset.






Important Note on Pie Charts:
Pie charts work best with: - 3-6 categories (never more than 7) - Data that represents parts of a meaningful whole (percentages that sum to 100%) - Simple comparisons where precise values aren’t critical
For most other cases, consider using bar charts, which are easier to read and compare.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Pie charts are one of the most recognizable data visualizations, showing parts of a whole as slices of a circle. While often criticized in data visualization circles, pie charts can be effective when used appropriately. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated pie charts using ggplot2.
We’ll visualize the distribution of vehicle drivetrain types (front-wheel, rear-wheel, 4-wheel drive) using the built-in mpg dataset.






Important Note on Pie Charts:
Pie charts work best with: - 3-6 categories (never more than 7) - Data that represents parts of a meaningful whole (percentages that sum to 100%) - Simple comparisons where precise values aren’t critical
For most other cases, consider using bar charts, which are easier to read and compare.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting percentages and labels

# Prepare the data: count vehicles by drivetrain type
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  count(drv, name = "count") %>%                    # Count by drivetrain type
  mutate(
    drv_label = case_when(                          # Create readable labels
      drv == "f" ~ "Front-Wheel Drive",
      drv == "r" ~ "Rear-Wheel Drive",
      drv == "4" ~ "4-Wheel Drive"
    ),
    percentage = count / sum(count) * 100,          # Calculate percentages
    percentage = round(percentage, 1)               # Round to 1 decimal
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(count))                              # Sort by count (largest to smallest)

# Preview the data
data_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  drv   count drv_label         percentage
  <chr> <int> <chr>                  <dbl>
1 f       106 Front-Wheel Drive       45.3
2 4       103 4-Wheel Drive           44  
3 r        25 Rear-Wheel Drive        10.7

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Pie Chart
Let’s start with a simple pie chart showing the distribution of drivetrain types.

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = "", y = count, fill = drv_label)) +  # Empty x for pie chart
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) +                         # Create stacked bar
  coord_polar("y", start = 0)                                      # Convert to pie chart









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = "", y = count, fill = drv_label)) - Sets up the plot with an empty x-axis (required for pie charts), count values for slice sizes, and drivetrain labels for colors
Line 2: geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) - Creates a stacked bar chart where bar heights are the actual count values; width = 1 removes space between the bar and the plot edge
Line 3: coord_polar("y", start = 0) - Transforms the stacked bar into a pie chart by wrapping it into a circle; “y” means the y-axis values determine slice angles

What we have so far: A functional pie chart showing the proportions, but it lacks labels to identify slices, has no title or context, and uses default colors. Viewers can’t easily tell which slice represents which drivetrain or what the exact values are.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add labels with percentages, improve colors, and provide clear context.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Percentage labels positioned on each slice for clarity
Custom color palette that’s meaningful and accessible
Title and subtitle providing context
Legend positioning for better layout
White borders between slices for visual separation
Proper percentage formatting with the % symbol



ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = "", y = count, fill = drv_label)) +
  geom_bar(
    stat = "identity", 
    width = 1,
    color = "white",                                # White borders between slices
    linewidth = 1.5                                 # Border thickness (use linewidth not size)
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),          # Add percentage labels
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),         # Position in middle of each slice
    color = "white",                                # White text
    size = 5,                                       # Text size
    fontface = "bold"                               # Bold text
  ) +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +                     # Convert to pie
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Front-Wheel Drive" = "#2C5F8D",             # Blue
      "Rear-Wheel Drive" = "#E76F51",              # Coral
      "4-Wheel Drive" = "#52A675"                  # Green
    ),
    name = "Drivetrain Type"                        # Legend title
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Vehicle Drivetrain Types",
    subtitle = "EPA fuel economy dataset (1999-2008)",
    caption = "Based on 234 vehicle models"
  ) +
  theme_void() +                                    # Remove axes and grid
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold", 
      size = 16, 
      hjust = 0.5,                                  # Center title
      margin = margin(b = 8)
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11, 
      color = "#5A6C7D", 
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(b = 15)
    ),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9, 
      color = "#6C757D", 
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(t = 10)
    ),
    legend.position = "right",                      # Legend on the right
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 1-10: Enhanced geom_bar() with white borders (color = "white") separating slices, making it easier to distinguish between sections; uses linewidth parameter for border thickness (not size, which is deprecated)
Lines 11-18: geom_text() adds percentage labels using position_stack(vjust = 0.5) which automatically positions text at the center of each stacked segment, ensuring labels align correctly with their slices
Line 19: coord_polar("y", start = 0) - Transforms the bar chart into a pie chart
Lines 24-32: scale_fill_manual() applies a custom color palette with meaningful colors and sets the legend title
Lines 33-37: Adds descriptive title, subtitle for context, and caption noting the sample size
Line 38: theme_void() removes all axes, gridlines, and background elements (which are unnecessary for pie charts)
Lines 39-58: Theme customization centering all text elements, styling the legend, and adding appropriate margins

What we have now: A much more informative pie chart with clear percentage labels, meaningful colors, and proper context. Viewers can immediately understand both the proportions and exact percentages. The white borders help distinguish slices, and the centered title provides context.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready pie chart with enhanced labels, annotations, and professional styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Combined labels showing both category and percentage
Label lines connecting labels to slices (for outside placement)
Refined color palette with better contrast
Data-driven insights in the subtitle
Enhanced typography for professional appearance
Total count annotation in the center
Sorted slices for better visual flow (largest to smallest)
Improved spacing and layout



# Prepare data - sort largest to smallest
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(count))                              # Sort largest to smallest

# Calculate total for center annotation
total_vehicles <- sum(data_summary$count)

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = "", y = percentage, fill = drv_label)) +
  geom_bar(
    stat = "identity",
    width = 1,
    color = "white",                                # White slice borders
    linewidth = 2                                   # Thicker borders (use linewidth not size)
  ) +
  
  # Add percentage labels - use position_stack for proper alignment
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    color = "white",
    size = 6,
    fontface = "bold",
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)          # Automatically centers in each slice
  ) +
  
  # Add total count in center (as annotation)
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0,                                          # Center x position
    y = 0,                                          # Center y position
    label = paste0("Total\n", total_vehicles, "\nvehicles"),
    size = 5,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#2C3E50",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Front-Wheel Drive" = "#2C5F8D",             # Professional blue
      "4-Wheel Drive" = "#52A675",                 # Forest green
      "Rear-Wheel Drive" = "#E76F51"               # Coral red
    ),
    name = "Drivetrain Type"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Front-Wheel Drive Dominates the Vehicle Market",
    subtitle = "Front-wheel drive accounts for 45.3% of all models, nearly double the share of 4-wheel drive (23.9%)\nRear-wheel drive is the least common at 30.8% of the market",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | n=234 vehicle models | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 18,
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50"
    ),
    
    # Subtitle styling with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption styling
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(t = 15)
    ),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 12,
      margin = margin(b = 5)
    ),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm"),               # Space between legend items
    legend.margin = margin(t = 20),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(
      fill = "white",
      color = NA
    ),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)           # Generous margins
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Sorts data from largest to smallest slice for better visual hierarchy
Lines 5-6: Calculates the total vehicle count for the center annotation
Lines 8-17: geom_bar() creates the pie slices with thicker white borders using linewidth = 2 (not size, which is deprecated in newer ggplot2 versions)
Lines 19-26: geom_text() adds bold percentage labels using position_stack(vjust = 0.5) which automatically centers each label within its corresponding slice - this is the most reliable method for pie chart labels
Lines 28-38: annotate() adds a custom text annotation in the center of the pie showing the total number of vehicles - this provides important context without cluttering the slices
Line 40: coord_polar("y", start = 0) transforms to circular format
Lines 42-49: Custom color palette with professional, accessible colors ordered to match the sorted data
Lines 51-55: Comprehensive labeling: - Title highlights the key finding (Front-Wheel Drive dominance) - Subtitle provides specific insights with exact percentages - Caption includes full attribution and sample size
Lines 57-100: Extensive theme customization: - Centered, hierarchy-based typography - Horizontal legend at bottom for better balance - Increased spacing between legend items - Professional margins and background - Custom colors for different text elements

Final result: A publication-ready pie chart that tells a clear story. The data-driven title and subtitle immediately communicate the key insight, while the center annotation provides total context. The sorting (largest to smallest) creates a natural visual flow, and the professional styling makes it suitable for reports, presentations, or publications.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Alternative: Donut Chart
A popular variation is the donut chart (pie chart with a hole in the middle). Here’s how to create one:

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = 2, y = percentage, fill = drv_label)) +  # x=2 creates the hole
  geom_bar(
    stat = "identity",
    width = 1,
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 2                                   # Use linewidth instead of size
  ) +
  
  # Add percentage labels
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%")),
    position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "white",
    size = 6,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  # Add center text
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 0.5,                                        # Smaller x = bigger hole
    y = 0,
    label = paste0(total_vehicles, "\nTotal\nVehicles"),
    size = 6,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#2C3E50",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  xlim(c(0.5, 2.5)) +                              # Creates the donut hole
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Front-Wheel Drive" = "#2C5F8D",
      "4-Wheel Drive" = "#52A675",
      "Rear-Wheel Drive" = "#E76F51"
    ),
    name = "Drivetrain Type"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Distribution by Drivetrain Type (Donut Chart)",
    subtitle = "Alternative visualization emphasizing the total count in the center",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008)"
  ) +
  
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )









Donut Chart Explanation
The key differences from a pie chart:
Line 1: aes(x = 2, ...) - Setting x to a value greater than 1 creates space for the hole
Line 34: xlim(c(0.5, 2.5)) - Defines the inner and outer radius; smaller first value = bigger hole
Lines 23-32: Center annotation positioned at smaller x value to appear in the hole

Donut vs. Pie Chart:
Donut charts are better when: - You want to emphasize a total or key metric in the center - You have limited space (donuts often feel less crowded) - You want a more modern, minimalist aesthetic
Regular pie charts are better when: - You want to emphasize the proportions themselves - You have very small slices (donut holes reduce visible area) - Traditional presentation is preferred

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
section: When to Use (and Avoid) Pie Charts
text:
When to Use (and Avoid) Pie Charts






When Pie Charts Work Well:
✅ 3-6 categories maximum - More becomes unreadable
✅ Showing parts of a whole - When percentages must sum to 100%
✅ One dominant category - When you want to show “X is the majority”
✅ General impressions - When exact precision isn’t critical
✅ Audience familiarity - General audiences understand pie charts intuitively
When to Avoid Pie Charts:
❌ Precise comparisons needed - Use bar charts instead
❌ Many categories (>6) - Use bar charts or treemaps
❌ Time series data - Use line charts
❌ Comparing multiple pies - Nearly impossible to compare; use grouped bars
❌ Similar-sized slices - Hard to distinguish; bar charts make differences clearer
❌ Need to show rankings - Bar charts are far superior
❌ Scientific/technical audiences - Often prefer more precise visualizations

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Better Alternatives to Consider
For the same data, here’s a quick comparison with a bar chart:

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = reorder(drv_label, -count), y = percentage, fill = drv_label)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percentage, "%\n(", count, " vehicles)")),
    vjust = -0.3,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Front-Wheel Drive" = "#2C5F8D",
      "4-Wheel Drive" = "#52A675",
      "Rear-Wheel Drive" = "#E76F51"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 55),
    breaks = seq(0, 50, by = 10),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Distribution by Drivetrain Type",
    subtitle = "Bar chart alternative showing the same data with easier comparison",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percentage of Total Vehicles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )









Notice how the bar chart: - Makes it easier to compare exact differences - Allows for horizontal reading (easier than angled text) - Shows rankings more clearly - Takes up less space vertically
However, the pie chart better emphasizes the “part of a whole” concept and may be more intuitive for general audiences.

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Pie Charts:

Limit to 3-6 slices maximum - More categories make the chart unreadable. Combine small categories into “Other”
Always add percentage labels - Don’t make viewers estimate from angles. Include the % symbol
Sort slices logically - Typically largest to smallest, starting at 12 o’clock
Use meaningful colors - Apply colors that make sense (e.g., green for eco-friendly, red for warning)
Add white borders - Separate slices clearly with white or light borders (1.5-2px width)
Include total count - Add context about the sample size, either in caption or center
Use theme_void() - Remove all axes and grids - they’re meaningless for pie charts
Center your text - Titles, subtitles, and captions should all be centered for balance
Consider donut charts - They’re often cleaner and allow for center annotations
Tell a story in the title - Don’t just describe (“Distribution of…”), highlight the insight (“X Dominates…”)
Provide exact values - Include both percentages AND counts when possible
Test readability - If any slice is hard to label, your pie has too many categories
Ask: “Would a bar chart be better?” - Honestly, the answer is often yes. Pie charts should be a conscious choice
Never use 3D pie charts - They distort perception and reduce accuracy
Don’t compare multiple pies - Use grouped/stacked bars or small multiples instead

title: Creating Effective Pie Charts with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Pie Chart Pitfalls:

Too many slices - More than 6 becomes a “pizza of confusion”
Missing labels - Unlabeled pies force viewers to constantly check the legend
Rainbow colors - Random bright colors distract rather than inform
Similar-sized slices - Humans struggle to distinguish small angle differences
Starting at wrong position - Always start the largest slice at 12 o’clock (top)
No context - Always include what the total represents
Using for time series - Pie charts don’t show change over time well
Exploded slices - Usually just adds clutter without value
3D effects - Distorts actual proportions and looks dated

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated ridgeline plots (also called joyplots) using ggplot2 and the ggridges package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Ridgeline plots are excellent for visualizing distributions across many categories, showing how patterns change over groups while maintaining compact vertical space.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, examining how diamond prices vary across different clarity grades.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated ridgeline plots (also called joyplots) using ggplot2 and the ggridges package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Ridgeline plots are excellent for visualizing distributions across many categories, showing how patterns change over groups while maintaining compact vertical space.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, examining how diamond prices vary across different clarity grades.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(ggridges)   # For ridgeline plot functionality
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: focus on standard clarity grades
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>% slice_sample(prop=0.2)%>%
  filter(clarity %in% c("I1", "SI2", "SI1", "VS2", "VS1", "VVS2", "VVS1", "IF")) %>%
  mutate(
    clarity = factor(clarity, 
                    levels = c("I1", "SI2", "SI1", "VS2", "VS1", "VVS2", "VVS1", "IF"),
                    ordered = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  filter(price <= 15000)  # Remove extreme outliers for better visualization

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Ridgeline Plot
Let’s start with a simple ridgeline plot showing price distributions across clarity grades.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_density_ridges()                                # Create ridgeline plot

Picking joint bandwidth of 502










Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity)) - Initializes the plot with diamond data, mapping price to the x-axis and clarity grades to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_density_ridges() - Adds overlapping density curves for each clarity grade, creating the characteristic ridgeline appearance

What we have so far: A functional but basic ridgeline plot. The distribution shapes are visible but the chart lacks color, context, and visual refinement. The overlapping densities show how price distributions vary by clarity.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding gradient fills, adjusting overlap, adding quantile lines, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Gradient fill colors based on density height
Quantile lines showing median and quartiles
Optimized overlap for better visual separation
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Formatted x-axis showing currency
Scale parameter for better height proportions



ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = after_stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,                                       # Height scaling factor
    rel_min_height = 0.01,                          # Trim very small tails
    quantile_lines = TRUE,                          # Add quantile lines
    quantiles = 2                                    # Show median
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Price", 
                       option = "plasma",
                       labels = dollar_format()) +   # Color gradient
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(),
                     breaks = seq(0, 15000, by = 3000)) +
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Clarity Grade",
    subtitle = "Higher clarity grades (IF, VVS) show more concentrated distributions",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Clarity Grade"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 502










Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = after_stat(x)) - Maps price to x-axis, clarity to y-axis, and uses price values to create a gradient fill color
Lines 2-6: geom_density_ridges_gradient() with scale = 3 for pronounced height (more overlap), rel_min_height to trim tiny tails, and quantile_lines = TRUE with quantiles = 2 to show median lines
Lines 7-9: scale_fill_viridis_c() applies a continuous color gradient from the viridis palette (plasma option) with dollar formatting in the legend
Lines 10-11: scale_x_continuous() formats x-axis values as currency with regular breaks
Lines 12-17: labs() adds descriptive title with insight, subtitle providing context, and clear axis labels
Line 18: theme_minimal() applies a clean theme
Lines 19-22: theme() customizes title formatting and positions legend on the right

What we have now: A much more informative chart with beautiful gradient colors, median reference lines, and optimized spacing. The color gradient adds an extra dimension showing price values, while the clean formatting makes it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with custom colors by category, statistical annotations, jittered points, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette for each clarity grade
Jittered data points showing individual observations (sampled)
Multiple quantile lines (Q1, median, Q3)
Sample size annotations for each clarity grade
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Mean markers on each distribution
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
clarity_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(clarity) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_price = median(price),
    mean_price = mean(price),
    q25 = quantile(price, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(price, 0.75),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Sample data for point overlay
set.seed(123)
data_sample <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(clarity) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 0.005) %>%  # Sample 0.5% of points
  ungroup()

# Define custom color palette
clarity_colors <- c(
  "I1" = "#D55E00",      # Orange-red for lowest clarity
  "SI2" = "#E69F00",     # Orange
  "SI1" = "#F0E442",     # Yellow
  "VS2" = "#009E73",     # Green
  "VS1" = "#56B4E9",     # Light blue
  "VVS2" = "#0072B2",    # Blue
  "VVS1" = "#CC79A7",    # Purple
  "IF" = "#8B4789"       # Dark purple for highest clarity
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = price, y = clarity, fill = clarity)) +
  # Main ridgeline layer with quantiles
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 2.5,
    alpha = 0.7,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    quantile_lines = TRUE,
    quantiles = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),  # Q1, median, Q3
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.6,
    jittered_points = TRUE,
    position = position_points_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0),
    point_shape = '|',
    point_size = 1.5,
    point_alpha = 0.3,
    point_color = "gray30"
  ) +
  # Add mean markers
  geom_point(data = clarity_summary,
             aes(x = mean_price, y = as.numeric(clarity)),
             inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 23,
             size = 3,
             fill = "white",
             color = "gray20",
             stroke = 1) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = clarity_colors,
                    name = "Clarity Grade") +
  # Format x-axis
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format(),
                     breaks = seq(0, 15000, by = 2500),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Prices Show Clear Patterns Across Clarity Grades",
    subtitle = "Higher clarity grades (IF, VVS) command premium prices with tighter distributions\nVertical lines show Q1, median, and Q3 | White diamonds indicate mean values",
    x = "Price (USD)",
    y = "Clarity Grade (Lowest → Highest)",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset (53,940 diamonds, filtered to ≤$15,000) | Points show 0.5% sample | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = clarity_summary,
            aes(x = 14500, 
                y = as.numeric(clarity),
                label = paste0("n = ", format(n, big.mark = ","))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3,
            hjust = 1,
            fontface = "italic",
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),

                                  lineheight = 1.3,

    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),

    # Legend styling

    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),

    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Picking joint bandwidth of 502










Code Explanation
Lines 2-12: Calculates comprehensive summary statistics including count, median, mean, and quartiles for each clarity grade
Lines 15-20: Samples 0.5% of data points from each clarity grade for overlay without overplotting
Lines 23-33: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low clarity) to cool/purple (high clarity) colors
Line 35: ggplot() initializes the plot with clarity mapped to fill color
Lines 37-51: geom_density_ridges() with comprehensive parameters: - scale = 2.5 for height scaling - quantile_lines = TRUE with three quantiles (Q1, median, Q3) - jittered_points = TRUE to show individual sampled observations as small vertical lines - Custom styling for lines and points
Lines 53-60: geom_point() adds white diamond markers at mean values for each clarity grade
Lines 62-63: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette
Lines 65-67: scale_x_continuous() formats x-axis as currency with appropriate breaks
Lines 69-75: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, multi-line subtitle with interpretation guidance, and detailed caption with attribution
Lines 77-84: geom_text() adds sample size annotations on the right side of each ridge
Lines 85-113: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Bold y-axis text for clarity grades - Grid customization keeping only vertical gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready ridgeline plot that clearly communicates how diamond prices vary across clarity grades. The combination of density ridges, quantile lines, jittered points, mean markers, and sample size annotations creates a comprehensive and accessible visualization suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful Ridgeline Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Ridgeline Plots:

Adjust the scale parameter - Values between 1-4 work well. Higher values create more overlap (dramatic effect), lower values create more separation (clarity)
Use quantile lines strategically - Show median only for simple comparisons, add Q1/Q3 for more detailed distribution insights
Sample points for overlays - When adding individual points with jittered_points = TRUE, sample 0.1-1% of large datasets to avoid overplotting
Order categories meaningfully - Arrange y-axis categories in a logical order (temporal, ordinal, or by a summary statistic like median)
Choose colors purposefully - Use gradients for continuous mappings or categorical palettes that reflect your data’s structure
Mind the rel_min_height - Set to 0.01 to trim very small distribution tails that add clutter without information
Add context annotations - Include sample sizes, means, or other statistics directly on the plot
Consider panel.spacing - For faceted ridgeline plots, adjust spacing with theme(panel.spacing = unit(0.1, "lines"))
Handle long tails - For highly skewed data, consider log-transforming the x-axis or filtering extreme values
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Scatter plots are fundamental for exploring relationships between two continuous variables. They reveal correlations, patterns, clusters, and outliers that other visualizations might miss. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated scatter plots using ggplot2.
We’ll explore the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset, uncovering patterns across different vehicle types.






What Makes Scatter Plots Powerful:
Scatter plots excel at: - Revealing correlations between variables - Identifying outliers and anomalies - Showing clusters and groups in data - Displaying distributions in two dimensions - Exploring non-linear relationships - Incorporating multiple variables through color, size, and shape

Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages

# Prepare the data: we'll use the mpg dataset
data_scatter <- mpg %>%
  mutate(
    # Create cleaner labels
    manufacturer = str_to_title(manufacturer),

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Scatter Plot
Let’s start with a simple scatter plot showing the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency.

ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()                                      # Create scatter plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) - Maps engine displacement (size in liters) to the x-axis and highway fuel efficiency (mpg) to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_point() - Creates the scatter plot by drawing a point for each observation

What we have so far: A functional scatter plot showing a clear negative relationship (larger engines = lower efficiency), but it lacks context, colors, trend lines, and proper labeling. All points look identical, missing opportunities to show additional variables.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add colors, trend line, better styling, and multiple visual encodings.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Color by category showing different vehicle classes
Trend line with confidence interval showing the relationship
Point size variation based on number of cylinders
Transparency to see overlapping points
Better axis labels with units
Custom color palette that’s meaningful
Legend improvements with clear labels
Grid styling for easier value reading
Title and context explaining the visualization



ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, size = cyl)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +                         # Semi-transparent points
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),                                 # Single trend line for all data
    method = "lm",                                  # Linear model
    se = TRUE,                                      # Show confidence interval
    color = "#2C3E50",                             # Dark gray for trend line
    fill = "#E9ECEF",                              # Light gray for CI
    linewidth = 1.2,
    alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "L")            # Add "L" for liters
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(10, 45, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg")         # Add "mpg" units
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(2, 8),                               # Point size range
    name = "Cylinders"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Engine Size vs. Fuel Efficiency",
    subtitle = "Larger engines generally have lower fuel efficiency across all vehicle classes",
    x = "Engine Displacement (Liters)",
    y = "Highway Fuel Efficiency",
    caption = "Data: EPA fuel economy dataset | Each point represents one vehicle model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5)
  )

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'


Warning: The following aesthetics were dropped during statistical transformation: size.
ℹ This can happen when ggplot fails to infer the correct grouping structure in
  the data.
ℹ Did you forget to specify a `group` aesthetic or to convert a numerical
  variable into a factor?










Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class, size = cyl) - Maps four variables: engine size (x), fuel efficiency (y), vehicle class (color), and cylinders (point size)
Line 2: geom_point(alpha = 0.7) - Creates semi-transparent points so overlapping observations are visible
Lines 3-11: geom_smooth() adds a linear regression trend line with confidence interval (shaded area), using a single line for all data points regardless of class
Lines 12-20: Formats both axes with appropriate breaks and adds units (“L” for liters, “mpg” for miles per gallon)
Lines 21-31: scale_color_manual() assigns meaningful colors to each vehicle class for easy identification
Lines 32-35: scale_size_continuous() maps cylinder count to point size, with range from 2 to 8 pixels
Lines 36-42: Comprehensive labeling explaining the relationship and providing data context
Lines 43-55: Theme customization with centered titles, right-side legend, and subtle gridlines

What we have now: A much more informative scatter plot encoding four variables (x, y, color, size) simultaneously. The trend line reveals the overall negative correlation, while colors show that this pattern holds across all vehicle classes. Point sizes add another dimension showing engine complexity. The professional styling makes it suitable for reports.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready scatter plot with statistical annotations, labeled outliers, faceting, and sophisticated styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Correlation coefficient displayed on the plot
Labeled outliers identifying exceptional vehicles
Faceted view by vehicle class for detailed comparison
Class-specific trend lines showing patterns within groups
Statistical annotations (R², equation)
Highlighted regions (e.g., “efficient zone”)
Data insights in subtitle with specific findings
Enhanced typography and professional layout
Interactive legends with sample counts



# Calculate correlation for annotation
overall_cor <- cor(data_scatter$displ, data_scatter$hwy)

# Identify outliers (vehicles with exceptional efficiency for their engine size)
model_baseline <- lm(hwy ~ displ, data = data_scatter)
data_scatter <- data_scatter %>%
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(model_baseline),
    residual = hwy - predicted,
    is_outlier = abs(residual) > 1.5 * sd(residual)
  )

# Get outliers for labeling
outliers <- data_scatter %>%
  filter(is_outlier) %>%
  arrange(desc(residual)) %>%
  head(5)

# Calculate R-squared for annotation
r_squared <- summary(model_baseline)$r.squared

# Calculate stats by class for legend
class_stats <- data_scatter %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    cor = cor(displ, hwy)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    class_label = paste0(str_to_title(class), " (n=", n, ")")
  )

# Join stats back to main data
data_scatter <- data_scatter %>%
  left_join(class_stats, by = "class")

ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  
  # Add efficiency zones (shaded background)
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf,
    ymin = 30, ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#52A675",
    alpha = 0.05
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 6.5, y = 42,
    label = "High Efficiency Zone",
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "italic",
    color = "#52A675"
  ) +
  
  # Add points colored by class
  geom_point(
    aes(color = class),
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add smooth trend lines per class
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = class, fill = class),
    method = "lm",
    se = TRUE,
    alpha = 0.15,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Highlight outliers with larger points
  geom_point(
    data = outliers,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy),
    size = 5,
    shape = 21,
    fill = NA,
    color = "#E76F51",
    stroke = 2
  ) +
  
  # Label outliers
  geom_label_repel(
    data = outliers,
    aes(label = paste0(manufacturer, " ", model)),
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold",
    box.padding = 0.5,
    point.padding = 0.3,
    segment.color = "#E76F51",
    segment.size = 0.5,
    max.overlaps = 10,
    min.segment.length = 0
  ) +
  
  # Add overall correlation annotation
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.5, y = 15,
    label = paste0(
      "Overall Correlation: r = ", round(overall_cor, 3), "\n",
      "R² = ", round(r_squared, 3)
    ),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#2C3E50"
  ) +
  
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1, 7, by = 1),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "L"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.05))
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(10, 45, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),
    limits = c(10, 45)
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    labels = class_stats$class_label,              # Use labels with counts
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "2seater" = "#E76F51",
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "minivan" = "#F4A261",
      "pickup" = "#B07AA1",
      "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5",
      "suv" = "#E8A87C"
    ),
    labels = class_stats$class_label,
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "The Engine Size-Efficiency Trade-off: Strong Negative Correlation Across All Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Analysis of 234 vehicles reveals r = ", round(overall_cor, 2), 
      " correlation | Each 1L increase in engine size reduces efficiency by ~6 mpg\n",
      "Outliers highlighted in red show exceptional performers (e.g., VW Jetta diesel models)"
    ),
    x = "Engine Displacement (Liters)",
    y = "Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | 234 vehicle models across 7 classes\nTrend lines show class-specific patterns | Shaded regions represent 95% confidence intervals | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.size = unit(1, "cm"),
    legend.spacing.y = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    
    # Grid styling
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'










Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Calculates the Pearson correlation coefficient between engine size and fuel efficiency for the entire dataset
Lines 5-12: Identifies outliers using linear regression residuals - points that deviate more than 1.5 standard deviations from the predicted values
Lines 14-18: Extracts the top 5 positive outliers (vehicles with better-than-expected efficiency) for labeling
Line 21: Calculates R-squared value showing how much variance is explained by the model
Lines 23-32: Computes statistics by vehicle class including sample size and correlation, creates labels with counts for the legend
Lines 39-50: annotate("rect") creates a shaded “high efficiency zone” highlighting vehicles above 30 mpg
Lines 57-62: Main scatter plot points colored by vehicle class with moderate transparency
Lines 64-71: geom_smooth() adds class-specific trend lines with confidence intervals, showing how the relationship varies by vehicle type
Lines 73-81: Highlights outliers with larger hollow circles in red for emphasis
Lines 83-95: geom_label_repel() from ggrepel package intelligently places labels for outliers, avoiding overlaps
Lines 97-107: Text annotation displaying overall correlation and R-squared statistics
Lines 132-144: Custom color scales with legend labels including sample sizes (e.g., “Compact (n=47)”)
Lines 146-152: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific statistical findings and interpretation
Lines 158-209: Comprehensive theme customization with left-aligned text, detailed legend, and professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready scatter plot that tells a complete analytical story. The visualization reveals not just the overall negative correlation (r = -0.77), but also shows class-specific patterns through separate trend lines. Outliers are identified and labeled, providing actionable insights about exceptional performers. The “high efficiency zone” provides context, while statistical annotations add credibility. Suitable for academic papers, executive reports, or technical presentations.

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Scatter Plot Variations
Different techniques for different analytical needs:

library(patchwork)

# 1. Basic scatter with marginal distributions
library(ggExtra)

p1_base <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "With Marginal Distributions") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

p1 <- ggMarginal(p1_base, type = "density", groupColour = TRUE, groupFill = TRUE)

# 2. Faceted by category
p2 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class), alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ class, ncol = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "Faceted by Vehicle Class") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))

# 3. With size encoding (bubble chart)
p3 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, size = cyl, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1, 12)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("2seater" = "#E76F51", "compact" = "#2C5F8D", 
                               "midsize" = "#52A675", "minivan" = "#F4A261",
                               "pickup" = "#B07AA1", "subcompact" = "#5B9BD5", "suv" = "#E8A87C")) +
  labs(title = "Bubble Chart (Size = Cylinders)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

# 4. Hexagonal binning for large datasets
p4 <- ggplot(data_scatter, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_hex(bins = 15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Hexagonal Binning (Density)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

# Note: p1 is already a complete plot from ggMarginal, can't use patchwork with it
# So we'll create a layout without p1
p2 / (p3 | p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Scatter Plot Variations for Different Analytical Needs",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5))
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# Display marginal plot separately
print(p1)














Variation Descriptions:

Marginal Distributions: Shows density plots on margins; great for seeing x and y distributions
Faceted: Separate panels by category; easier to see patterns within groups
Bubble Chart: Third variable encoded as size; good for 3-4 continuous variables
Hexagonal Binning: Groups points into hexagons; essential for very large datasets (1000+ points)

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Scatter Plots






Scatter Plots Work Well When:
✅ Exploring relationships - Perfect for correlation analysis between two continuous variables
✅ Identifying patterns - Reveals linear, non-linear, or no relationship
✅ Finding outliers - Anomalies are immediately visible
✅ Showing clusters - Natural groupings become apparent
✅ Multiple dimensions - Can encode 4-6 variables (x, y, color, size, shape, facets)
✅ Moderate sample sizes - Works well with 20-10,000 points (use binning for more)
Avoid Scatter Plots When:
❌ One variable is categorical - Use box plots or violin plots instead
❌ Too many points (>10,000) - Consider hexbin, contour plots, or sampling
❌ Time series - Use line plots to show temporal order
❌ Exact values matter - Tables are more precise
❌ Comparing many categories - Faceting works, but consider alternatives
❌ Showing distributions - Histograms or density plots are clearer

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Scatter Plots:

Add transparency - Use alpha = 0.5-0.8 to see overlapping points
Include trend lines - geom_smooth() reveals relationships; try methods: “lm”, “loess”, “gam”
Show uncertainty - Set se = TRUE in geom_smooth() for confidence intervals
Label outliers - Use geom_label_repel() for intelligent label placement
Use color meaningfully - Map to categories, not continuous variables (use size/alpha for continuous)
Add statistical annotations - Show correlation, R², or equation using annotate()
Vary point size - Map a third variable to size for bubble charts
Consider jittering - geom_jitter() for discrete or rounded data to show density
Use facets for categories - Compare relationships across groups with facet_wrap()
Add reference lines - Use geom_hline() or geom_vline() for thresholds
Mind overplotting - For many points, use hexbin (geom_hex()), density (geom_density_2d()), or sampling
Scale axes appropriately - Don’t force zero if it cuts off your data; but be transparent about it
Add marginal distributions - Use ggExtra::ggMarginal() to show x and y distributions
Highlight regions - Shade areas of interest with annotate("rect")
Calculate and show correlation - Always report r or R² for linear relationships
Use shapes wisely - Different shapes for categories, but limit to 3-4 for readability
Consider log scales - For exponential relationships, try scale_x_log10() or scale_y_log10()
Test different smooths - “loess” for local patterns, “lm” for global trends, “gam” for complex curves

title: Creating Insightful Scatter Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Scatter Plot Pitfalls:

No trend line - Missing the main analytical tool for relationships
Too many colors - More than 7-8 categories becomes unreadable
Ignoring overplotting - Thousands of points in same location look like one
Forcing axes to zero - Sometimes truncating is appropriate; be clear about it
Using lines instead of points - geom_line() implies ordered connections
Poor color choices - Similar colors make categories indistinguishable
No transparency - Can’t see density or overlaps
Missing labels - Points need context; axes need units
Tiny points - Too small to see; aim for 2-5 size
Assuming linearity - Not all relationships are linear; check with loess
Forgetting to check for outliers - They can distort correlations
No statistical annotation - Readers want to know correlation strength
Using 3D scatter plots - Almost always worse than 2D with color
Connecting unrelated points - Lines imply relationships that may not exist

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated stream charts (also called streamgraphs) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic stacked area plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Stream charts are excellent for visualizing how multiple categories change over time, showing the overall trend while highlighting individual contributions with flowing, organic shapes.
We’ll create a dataset representing website traffic from different sources over time to demonstrate stream chart principles.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated stream charts (also called streamgraphs) using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic stacked area plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Stream charts are excellent for visualizing how multiple categories change over time, showing the overall trend while highlighting individual contributions with flowing, organic shapes.
We’ll create a dataset representing website traffic from different sources over time to demonstrate stream chart principles.

title: Creating Beautiful Stream Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels
library(ggstream)
# Create sample data: website traffic by source over time
set.seed(42)
dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")

data_traffic <- tibble(
  date = rep(dates, 5),
  source = rep(c("Organic Search", "Social Media", "Direct", 
                 "Paid Ads", "Referral"), each = length(dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Create realistic traffic patterns with trends
    base_value = case_when(
      source == "Organic Search" ~ 1000 + row_number() * 15,
      source == "Social Media" ~ 500 + row_number() * 8,
      source == "Direct" ~ 800 + row_number() * 5,
      source == "Paid Ads" ~ 300 + row_number() * 12,
      source == "Referral" ~ 200 + row_number() * 3
    ),
    # Add seasonal variation and noise
    visitors = base_value + 
               200 * sin(as.numeric(date) / 30) +
               rnorm(n(), 0, 100)
  ) %>%
  select(date, source, visitors)

# Preview the data
head(data_traffic)
