title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Chord Diagrams:

Use circos.clear() religiously - Always call before and after creating chord diagrams to prevent parameter carryover issues
Order sectors meaningfully - Arrange regions by total flow, alphabetically, or by a meaningful metric using the order parameter
Add directional indicators - Use directional = 1 with arrows or height differences to show flow direction clearly
Adjust gaps strategically - Use gap.degree between 2-5 to balance compactness with readability
Color with purpose - Assign colors that match regional or categorical meanings, ensuring sufficient contrast
Show the data - Add annotations with actual flow values, totals, or percentages to provide concrete numbers
Mind the matrix diagonal - Self-loops (diagonal elements) can clutter the visualization; consider setting them to zero
Use transparency wisely - Set transparency between 0.3-0.6 to show overlapping flows without losing definition
Sort links for clarity - Use link.sort = TRUE and link.largest.ontop = TRUE to bring important flows forward
Export with care - Save as PDF or high-res PNG: pdf("chord.pdf", width = 10, height = 10) then run code, then dev.off()

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Next Steps

Sankey diagrams for linear flow representations
Network graphs for complex interconnections
Arc diagrams for simpler connection displays
Circular dendrograms for hierarchical relationships


Want to create interactive chord diagrams?
You can make your chord diagrams interactive using chorddiag:
# Install if needed
# install.packages("chorddiag")
library(chorddiag)

# Create interactive chord diagram
chorddiag(
  migration_matrix,
  groupColors = region_colors_adv,
  groupnamePadding = 20,
  groupThickness = 0.1,
  chordedgeColor = "gray30",
  showTicks = FALSE,
  margin = 120
)
This creates an interactive HTML widget where users can hover over chords to see exact values and highlight specific flows.

Here’s a bonus approach showing the same data as a heatmap:

# Convert to long format
migration_long <- migration_matrix %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("from") %>%
  pivot_longer(-from, names_to = "to", values_to = "students") %>%
  filter(from != to)  # Remove diagonal

# Create heatmap
ggplot(migration_long, aes(x = to, y = from, fill = students)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(students, big.mark = ",")),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#2C5F8D", high = "#E76F51",
                      name = "Students",
                      labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Student Migration Matrix: Origin to Destination",
    subtitle = "Cell values show number of students moving between regions",
    x = "Destination Region",
    y = "Origin Region"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated bar charts using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
We’ll use the built-in mpg dataset from ggplot2, which contains fuel economy data from 1999 to 2008 for 38 popular car models.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: calculate average highway mpg by car class
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%                           # Group data by vehicle class
  summarise(
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                        # Calculate mean highway mpg
    count = n()                                 # Count number of cars in each class
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_hwy))                        # Sort by mpg (highest to lowest)

# Preview the data
head(data_summary)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  class      avg_hwy count
  <chr>        <dbl> <int>
1 compact       28.3    47
2 subcompact    28.1    35
3 midsize       27.3    41
4 2seater       24.8     5
5 minivan       22.4    11
6 suv           18.1    62

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Bar Chart
Let’s start with a simple bar chart showing average highway fuel efficiency by vehicle class.

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = class, y = avg_hwy)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_col()                                          # Create bar chart (columns)









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = class, y = avg_hwy)) - Initializes the plot with our summarized data, mapping vehicle class to the x-axis and average highway mpg to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_col() - Adds bars to the plot where bar heights represent the actual values in the data

What we have so far: A functional but basic bar chart. The data is visible but the chart lacks context, proper ordering, and visual appeal.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by reordering bars, adding better labels, and applying a clean theme.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Reordered bars for better readability (highest to lowest)
Custom colors to make the chart more engaging
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Value labels on bars for precise data reading



ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy)) +  # Reorder bars by mpg
  geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") +                                          # Solid color fill
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_hwy, 1)),                           # Add value labels
            hjust = -0.2,                                              # Position labels to the right
            size = 3.5) +                                              # Set text size
  coord_flip() +                                                       # Flip to horizontal bars
  labs(
    title = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency by Vehicle Class",       # Main title
    subtitle = "Based on EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008)",           # Subtitle for context
    x = "Vehicle Class",                                               # X-axis label
    y = "Miles Per Gallon (Highway)"                                   # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                                    # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),              # Bold title
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()                               # Remove horizontal gridlines
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy) - Reorders the bars from highest to lowest fuel efficiency for easier comparison
Line 2: geom_col(fill = "#2C5F8D") - Creates bars with a custom blue color instead of default gray
Lines 3-5: geom_text() - Adds numeric labels to each bar, rounded to one decimal place and positioned slightly to the right
Line 6: coord_flip() - Flips the chart to horizontal orientation, making class names easier to read
Lines 7-12: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context
Line 13: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 14-17: theme() - Customizes specific theme elements like title formatting and removes horizontal gridlines for cleaner appearance

What we have now: A much more readable chart with proper ordering, context through labels, and a professional appearance. The horizontal orientation makes class names easier to read.

title: Creating Beautiful Bar Charts with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with color coding, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication or presentation.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Color-coded bars based on efficiency levels (high/medium/low)
Expanded y-axis to accommodate labels without overlap
Formatted axis labels with proper spacing
Custom color palette that’s colorblind-friendly
Enhanced typography for better readability
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Create efficiency categories for color coding
data_summary <- data_summary %>%
  mutate(
    efficiency_level = case_when(                    # Create categorical variable
      avg_hwy >= 28 ~ "High (≥28 mpg)",             # High efficiency
      avg_hwy >= 22 ~ "Medium (22-27 mpg)",         # Medium efficiency
      TRUE ~ "Low (<22 mpg)"                        # Low efficiency
    )
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
efficiency_colors <- c(
  "High (≥28 mpg)" = "#52A675",                     # Green for high efficiency
  "Medium (22-27 mpg)" = "#F4A261",                 # Orange for medium
  "Low (<22 mpg)" = "#E76F51"                       # Red for low efficiency
)

ggplot(data_summary, aes(x = reorder(class, avg_hwy), y = avg_hwy, fill = efficiency_level)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +                                              # Slightly narrower bars
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(avg_hwy, 1), " mpg")),          # Labels with units
            hjust = -0.1,                                              # Position outside bars
            size = 3.5,
            color = "#2C3E50",                                         # Dark gray text
            fontface = "bold") +                                       # Bold font
  scale_fill_manual(values = efficiency_colors,                        # Apply custom colors
                    name = "Efficiency Level") +                       # Legend title
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)),           # Expand right side for labels
                     breaks = seq(0, 35, by = 5)) +                    # Set axis breaks
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Highway Fuel Efficiency Varies Significantly Across Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = "Two-seaters and subcompact cars lead in fuel economy, while pickups lag behind",
    x = NULL,                                                          # Remove x-axis label (obvious)
    y = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +                                      # Base font size
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),                              # Remove horizontal grid
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),                                # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)                              # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Creates a new categorical variable efficiency_level using case_when() to classify vehicles into high/medium/low efficiency groups
Lines 11-15: Defines a colorblind-friendly color palette with meaningful colors (green for high, orange for medium, red for low efficiency)
Line 17: aes(..., fill = efficiency_level) - Maps the efficiency level to bar colors
Line 18: geom_col(width = 0.7) - Creates slightly narrower bars for a more refined appearance
Lines 19-23: Adds formatted labels with “mpg” units, positioned outside bars with bold dark gray text
Lines 24-25: scale_fill_manual() - Applies our custom color palette and sets the legend title
Lines 26-27: scale_y_continuous() - Expands the right side of the plot to prevent label cutoff and sets regular axis breaks
Lines 30-34: Enhanced labels with a descriptive title, informative subtitle, and proper data attribution in the caption
Lines 36-59: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Typography adjustments (sizes, weights, colors) - Legend positioning at the bottom - Refined gridlines (keeping only major x-gridlines) - Proper margins for breathing room

Final result: A publication-ready visualization with clear data communication, professional styling, and accessibility considerations. The color coding adds an extra layer of information, while the polished formatting makes the chart suitable for reports, presentations, or blog posts.

    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#5A6C7D"),

}

title: Creating Beautiful Box Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated box plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Box plots are excellent for comparing distributions across categories, showing median, quartiles, and outliers in a compact format.
We’ll use the built-in mtcars dataset from R, which contains specifications and performance data for 32 automobiles from 1973-74.

title: Creating Beautiful Box Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages

# Prepare the data: convert cylinders to factor and add car names
data_cars <- mtcars %>%

title: Creating Beautiful Box Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Box Plot
Let’s start with a simple box plot showing fuel efficiency (miles per gallon) by number of cylinders.

ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_boxplot()                             # Create box plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg)) - Initializes the plot with our car data, mapping cylinder count to the x-axis and miles per gallon to the y-axis
Line 2: geom_boxplot() - Adds box plots showing the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and outliers for each cylinder group

What we have so far: A functional but basic box plot. The statistical summaries are visible but the chart lacks context, visual appeal, and proper formatting.

title: Creating Beautiful Box Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding color, notches for confidence intervals, better labels, and applying a clean theme.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Color fill to distinguish each cylinder group
Notched boxes showing confidence intervals around medians
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
Individual data points overlaid for transparency



ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl)) +      # Add fill aesthetic
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.7) +                  # Notched boxes with transparency
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +          # Add jittered points
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                      # Apply color palette
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Decreases with More Cylinders",  # Main title
    subtitle = "Miles per gallon distribution for 32 automobiles (1973-74)",  # Subtitle
    x = "Number of Cylinders",                                # X-axis label
    y = "Miles Per Gallon"                                    # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                           # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),     # Bold title
    legend.position = "none"                                  # Remove redundant legend
  )

Notch went outside hinges

Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl) - Maps cylinder count to both x-axis position and fill color for visual distinction
Line 2: geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.7) - Creates box plots with notches (showing 95% confidence intervals around medians) and 70% opacity
Line 3: geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) - Adds individual data points with controlled horizontal spread to show the actual sample distribution
Line 4: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer
Lines 5-10: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context
Line 11: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 12-15: theme() - Customizes title formatting and removes the legend since cylinder count is already shown on x-axis

What we have now: A much more informative chart with color differentiation, confidence intervals via notches, and transparency showing all data points. The clean theme and proper labeling make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Box Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with custom styling, statistical annotations, summary statistics, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
Mean markers shown as diamonds overlaid on boxes
Sample size annotations showing number of cars in each category
Statistical comparison lines indicating significant differences
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Outlier highlighting with custom styling
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
cyl_summary <- data_cars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    median_mpg = median(mpg),                      # Median mpg
    mean_mpg = mean(mpg),                          # Mean mpg
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
cyl_colors <- c(
  "4" = "#52A675",                                 # Green for best efficiency
  "6" = "#F4A261",                                 # Orange for medium
  "8" = "#E76F51"                                  # Red for lowest efficiency
)

ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl)) +
  # Box plot layer with custom styling
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.6,
               outlier.shape = 21,                 # Hollow circles for outliers
               outlier.size = 3,
               outlier.fill = "white",
               outlier.color = "gray30",
               color = "gray30",
               linewidth = 0.6) +
  # Add jittered data points
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3, 
              size = 2, color = "gray20") +
  # Add mean markers
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 23, size = 4, 
               fill = "white", color = "gray30",
               stroke = 1.2) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cyl_colors,
                    name = "Cylinders") +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(10, 35, by = 5),
                     limits = c(10, 35)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Decreases Dramatically with Engine Size",
    subtitle = "4-cylinder cars average 26.7 MPG compared to 15.1 MPG for 8-cylinder vehicles",
    x = "Number of Cylinders",
    y = "Miles Per Gallon (Highway)",
    caption = "Data source: 1974 Motor Trend US magazine | White diamonds indicate mean values | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = cyl_summary,
            aes(x = cyl, y = 11, 
                label = paste0("n = ", n)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.5, fontface = "italic", 
            color = "gray30") +
  # Add mean value annotations
  geom_text(data = cyl_summary,
            aes(x = cyl, y = 34,
                label = paste0("μ = ", round(mean_mpg, 1))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.2, fontface = "bold",
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    # Legend removal
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )

Code Explanation
Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes, medians, and means for each cylinder group, used for annotations
Lines 12-17: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from green (efficient) to red (inefficient), optimized for colorblind accessibility
Line 19: ggplot() initializes the plot with cylinder count mapped to both x-position and fill color
Lines 21-28: geom_boxplot() creates notched box plots with custom outlier styling (hollow circles with gray borders), thicker box borders, and transparency
Lines 30-31: geom_jitter() adds individual data points with controlled horizontal spread and transparency to show the actual distribution
Lines 33-36: stat_summary() adds mean markers as white-filled diamonds, distinguishing them from the median line in the box plot
Lines 38-39: scale_fill_manual() applies our custom color palette
Lines 41-42: scale_y_continuous() sets regular y-axis breaks and limits for consistent display
Lines 44-49: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, a subtitle with specific numbers, and detailed caption with attribution
Lines 51-57: geom_text() adds sample size annotations at the bottom of the plot area
Lines 59-64: geom_text() adds mean value annotations (using Greek letter μ) at the top of the plot area
Lines 65-93: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend removal (since cylinder count is mapped to x-axis) - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that clearly communicates the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency. The combination of box plots (showing distribution), jittered points (showing raw data), mean markers (showing averages), and annotations (providing context) creates a comprehensive and accessible chart suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Box Plots:

Use notches for comparisons - Notched box plots show confidence intervals around medians; non-overlapping notches suggest statistically significant differences
Always show the data - For small to medium datasets (<100 points per group), overlay geom_jitter() or geom_point() to show individual observations
Distinguish mean from median - Use different markers for mean (stat_summary()) and median (box plot line) when both are informative
Style outliers meaningfully - Customize outlier appearance with outlier.shape, outlier.color, and outlier.size to make them visible but not distracting
Color with purpose - Use color gradients or categorical colors that match the ordering or meaning of your groups
Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per category so readers can assess reliability
Consider orientation - Use coord_flip() for horizontal box plots when category names are long
Add reference lines - Horizontal lines showing targets, thresholds, or overall means help viewers make comparisons
Mind the width - Adjust box width with the width parameter (default 0.75) to control visual density
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E76F51", "#52A675"),
                    name = "Transmission",
                    labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")) +

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated chord diagrams using the circlize package in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Chord diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows and connections between entities in a circular layout, making them ideal for migration patterns, trade relationships, or network connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing student migration patterns between different regions for university education.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)   # For data manipulation
library(circlize)    # For chord diagrams
library(scales)      # For formatting

# Create sample data: student migration between regions
regions <- c("Northeast", "Southeast", "Midwest", "Southwest", "West")

# Create a migration matrix
set.seed(42)
migration_matrix <- matrix(
  c(
    5000, 800, 600, 400, 1200,   # From Northeast
    900, 4500, 500, 800, 700,    # From Southeast
    700, 600, 3500, 500, 900,    # From Midwest
    500, 900, 400, 3000, 1100,   # From Southwest
    1300, 800, 1000, 1200, 4000  # From West
  ),
  nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(migration_matrix) <- regions
colnames(migration_matrix) <- regions

# Convert to data frame for easier viewing
migration_df <- as.data.frame(migration_matrix)
rownames(migration_df) <- regions

# Preview the data
head(migration_df)

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 1: Basic Chord Diagram
Let’s start with a simple chord diagram showing student migration flows between regions.

# Create basic chord diagram
chordDiagram(migration_matrix)  # Create chord diagram from matrix









Code Explanation
Line 2: chordDiagram(migration_matrix) - Creates a chord diagram from the migration matrix where rows represent origin regions and columns represent destination regions

What we have so far: A functional but basic chord diagram. The connections are visible but the chart lacks custom colors, clear labels, and visual refinement. The default settings make it difficult to interpret flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding custom colors, adjusting gaps, adding a title, and improving the visual hierarchy.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Custom color palette for each region
Adjusted gaps between sectors for clarity
Transparency on chord connections
Grid colors matching region colors
Directional emphasis with color coding
Better spacing and layout
Title and annotations for context



# Define color palette for regions
region_colors <- c(
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#52A675", 
  "Midwest" = "#E76F51",
  "Southwest" = "#F4A261",
  "West" = "#8B4789"
)

# Set circlize parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,              # Start at top
  gap.degree = 3                  # Gap between sectors
)

# Create chord diagram with custom colors
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  grid.col = region_colors,       # Sector colors
  transparency = 0.5,             # Make chords semi-transparent
  annotationTrack = "grid",
  preAllocateTracks = list(
    track.height = 0.3            # Height for labels
  )
)

# Add region labels
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    circos.text(
      CELL_META$xcenter, 
      CELL_META$ylim[1],
      CELL_META$sector.index,
      facing = "clockwise",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      adj = c(0, 0.5),
      cex = 1
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

# Add title with proper margins
par(mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))  # Increase top margin for title
title("Student Migration Between Regions\n(Origin → Destination)", 
      cex.main = 1.3, font.main = 2, line = -1)







# Clear the plot
circos.clear()


Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Defines a custom color palette assigning specific colors to each region
Line 11: circos.clear() - Clears any previous circular plots
Lines 12-15: circos.par() sets global parameters including starting position (90 degrees = top) and gaps between sectors
Lines 18-25: chordDiagram() creates the diagram with: - grid.col applying custom region colors - transparency = 0.5 for semi-transparent chords - preAllocateTracks reserving space for labels
Lines 28-42: circos.track() adds custom text labels with optimal positioning and rotation
Lines 45-46: Adds a descriptive title
Line 49: circos.clear() - Essential cleanup to reset parameters

What we have now: A much more readable chord diagram with custom colors, better spacing, and clear labels. The transparency and color coding make it easier to trace individual flows.

title: Creating Beautiful Chord Diagrams with circlize
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, directional indicators, flow highlights, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Gradient chord colors showing direction of flow
Link border styling for definition
Sector annotations showing total in/out flows
Highlighted major flows with emphasis
Enhanced labels with values
Legend explaining the visualization
Professional color scheme optimized for accessibility
Order optimization for better layout



# Calculate flow statistics
total_out <- rowSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
total_in <- colSums(migration_matrix) - diag(migration_matrix)
net_migration <- total_in - total_out

# Reorder regions by net migration
region_order <- names(sort(net_migration, decreasing = TRUE))

# Define enhanced color palette
region_colors_adv <- c(
  "West" = "#0072B2",
  "Northeast" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Southeast" = "#009E73",
  "Midwest" = "#E69F00",
  "Southwest" = "#D55E00"
)

# Clear and set parameters
circos.clear()
circos.par(
  start.degree = 90,
  gap.degree = 5,                          # Increase gap for clarity
  track.margin = c(0.01, 0.01),
  cell.padding = c(0.02, 1, 0.02, 1)
)

# Set plot margins for title and legend space
par(mar = c(6, 1, 4, 1))  # Increased bottom margin

# Create chord diagram with enhanced styling
chordDiagram(
  migration_matrix,
  order = region_order,                    # Order by net migration
  grid.col = region_colors_adv,
  transparency = 0.4,
  directional = 1,                         # Show direction
  direction.type = c("diffHeight", "arrows"),
  diffHeight = mm_h(2),                    # Height difference for direction
  link.arr.type = "big.arrow",             # Arrow style
  link.arr.length = 0.2,
  annotationTrack = "grid",                # Only grid track
  annotationTrackHeight = mm_h(8),         # Increased track height
  link.border = "gray30",                  # Border around chords
  link.lwd = 0.5,                          # Border width
  link.sort = TRUE,                        # Sort links
  link.largest.ontop = TRUE                # Put largest on top
)

# Add sector names and statistics in one track
circos.track(
  track.index = 1,
  panel.fun = function(x, y) {
    sector_name <- CELL_META$sector.index
    xcenter <- CELL_META$xcenter
    
    # Get inflow and outflow
    outflow <- format(round(total_out[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    inflow <- format(round(total_in[sector_name]), big.mark = ",")
    
    # Add region name
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(4),
      labels = sector_name,
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 1,
      font = 2,
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
    
    # Add statistics on same line, smaller
    circos.text(
      x = xcenter,
      y = CELL_META$cell.ylim[2] + mm_y(1),
      labels = paste0("↑", outflow, " ↓", inflow),
      facing = "bending.outside",
      niceFacing = TRUE,
      cex = 0.6,
      col = "gray40",
      adj = c(0.5, 0)
    )
  },
  bg.border = NA
)

  side = 3,
  line = 0.3,
  cex = 0.8,
  col = "gray40"
)

# Add summary statistics
mtext(
  paste0(
    "Total: ", 
    format(sum(migration_matrix) - sum(diag(migration_matrix)), big.mark = ","),
    " students | Largest: Northeast → West (",
    format(migration_matrix["Northeast", "West"], big.mark = ","),

text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Chord Diagrams:

Use circos.clear() religiously - Always call before and after creating chord diagrams to prevent parameter carryover issues
Order sectors meaningfully - Arrange regions by total flow, alphabetically, or by a meaningful metric using the order parameter
Add directional indicators - Use directional = 1 with arrows or height differences to show flow direction clearly
Adjust gaps strategically - Use gap.degree between 2-5 to balance compactness with readability
Color with purpose - Assign colors that match regional or categorical meanings, ensuring sufficient contrast
Show the data - Add annotations with actual flow values, totals, or percentages to provide concrete numbers
Mind the matrix diagonal - Self-loops (diagonal elements) can clutter the visualization; consider setting them to zero
Use transparency wisely - Set transparency between 0.3-0.6 to show overlapping flows without losing definition
Sort links for clarity - Use link.sort = TRUE and link.largest.ontop = TRUE to bring important flows forward
Export with care - Save as PDF or high-res PNG: pdf("chord.pdf", width = 10, height = 10) then run code, then dev.off()

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated density plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Density plots are excellent for visualizing the distribution of continuous variables, showing the probability density function and revealing patterns like skewness, modality, and concentration of values.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated density plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Density plots are excellent for visualizing the distribution of continuous variables, showing the probability density function and revealing patterns like skewness, modality, and concentration of values.
We’ll use the built-in diamonds dataset from ggplot2, which contains prices and attributes of nearly 54,000 diamonds.

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: focus on diamonds with standard cuts
data_diamonds <- diamonds %>%
  filter(cut %in% c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"),
         carat <= 3) %>%                           # Remove extreme outliers
  mutate(cut = factor(cut, levels = c("Fair", "Good", "Very Good", 
                                      "Premium", "Ideal")))  # Set factor order

# Preview the data
head(data_diamonds)

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Density Plot
Let’s start with a simple density plot showing the distribution of diamond carat weights.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_density()                          # Create density plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping carat weight to the x-axis
Line 2: geom_density() - Adds a density curve showing the smoothed probability distribution of carat values

What we have so far: A functional but basic density plot. The distribution shape is visible but the chart lacks context, comparative groups, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by comparing multiple groups, adding fill colors, adjusting transparency, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Multiple density curves comparing different cut qualities
Color fill with transparency to show overlapping distributions
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
Formatted x-axis for better readability



ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic by cut
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +                             # Density with transparency
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                   # Apply color palette
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) +      # Set x-axis breaks
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Diamond Carat Weight by Cut Quality",  # Main title
    subtitle = "Higher quality cuts tend toward smaller carat sizes",  # Subtitle
    x = "Carat Weight",                                   # X-axis label
    y = "Density",                                        # Y-axis label
    fill = "Cut Quality"                                  # Legend title
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), # Bold title
    legend.position = "top"                               # Move legend to top
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = carat, fill = cut) - Maps carat weight to x-axis and cut quality to fill color, enabling comparison across groups
Line 2: geom_density(alpha = 0.6) - Creates overlapping density curves with 60% opacity to show where distributions intersect
Line 3: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer
Line 4: scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) - Sets regular x-axis breaks every 0.5 carats for easier reading
Lines 5-11: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing insight, axis labels, and legend title for context
Line 12: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 13-16: theme() - Customizes title formatting and moves legend to top for better space utilization

What we have now: A much more informative chart showing how carat distributions differ across cut qualities. The transparent overlays and clean formatting make comparisons easy, revealing that ideal cuts concentrate in smaller carat ranges.

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with ridge-style presentation, statistical annotations, enhanced colors, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Stacked density presentation for clearer group comparison
Statistical reference lines showing means for each group
Sample size annotations in legend
Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Rug plot showing individual observations
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
cut_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    mean_carat = mean(carat),                      # Mean carat
    median_carat = median(carat),                  # Median carat
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly gradient)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#D55E00",                              # Orange-red for lowest
  "Good" = "#E69F00",                              # Orange
  "Very Good" = "#F0E442",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#009E73",                           # Green
  "Ideal" = "#0072B2"                              # Blue for highest
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut, color = cut)) +
  # Main density curves
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Add rug plot showing individual observations (sampled to avoid overplotting)
  geom_rug(data = data_diamonds %>% 
             group_by(cut) %>% 
             slice_sample(prop = 0.01),
           alpha = 0.3, length = unit(0.02, "npc")) +
  # Add mean reference lines
  geom_vline(data = cut_summary,
             aes(xintercept = mean_carat, color = cut),
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7,
             alpha = 0.8) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_colors,
                    name = "Cut Quality",
                    labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                   " (n = ", 
                                   format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                   ")")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cut_colors,
                     name = "Cut Quality",
                     labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                    " (n = ", 
                                    format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                    ")")) +
  # Format x-axis with better breaks and labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.25),
                     labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))) +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Carat Distribution Reveals Quality-Size Trade-offs",
    subtitle = "Ideal cut diamonds concentrate around 0.5-1.0 carats, while lower grades show broader distributions\nDashed lines indicate mean values for each cut quality",
    x = "Carat Weight",
    y = "Probability Density",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset (53,940 diamonds) | Sample of 1% shown in rug plot | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for interpretation
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 2.5,
           label = "Ideal cuts peak\nat lower carats",
           size = 3.5, fontface = "italic",
           color = "gray30", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("curve", x = 2.3, y = 2.4, 
           xend = 1.2, yend = 3.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = -0.3, color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes, means, and medians for each cut category, used for annotations and legend labels
Lines 12-19: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low quality) to cool (high quality) colors, optimized for colorblind accessibility
Line 21: ggplot() initializes the plot with carat mapped to x-axis and cut quality mapped to both fill and color (for consistency)
Lines 23-24: geom_density() creates density curves with transparency and thicker lines for better visibility
Lines 25-29: geom_rug() adds small tick marks at the bottom showing individual data points (sampled to 1% to avoid overplotting)
Lines 30-35: geom_vline() adds dashed vertical lines at the mean carat value for each cut quality, color-coded by group
Lines 37-48: scale_fill_manual() and scale_color_manual() apply our custom color palette and enhance legend labels with sample sizes in parentheses
Lines 50-52: scale_x_continuous() sets fine-grained breaks (every 0.25 carats) with proper decimal formatting
Line 54: scale_y_continuous() expands the top slightly to prevent clipping
Lines 56-62: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells a story, multi-line subtitle with interpretation guidance, and detailed caption with attribution and methodology notes
Lines 64-71: annotate() adds a text annotation with an arrow pointing to the Ideal cut peak, helping guide interpretation
Lines 72-99: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend positioned at bottom with custom sizing - Grid customization with lighter lines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that clearly communicates how diamond carat distributions vary by cut quality. The combination of overlapping density curves, mean reference lines, rug plot, and interpretive annotations creates a comprehensive and accessible chart suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Density Plots:

Adjust bandwidth carefully - Use the adjust parameter in geom_density() (default = 1) to control smoothness. Lower values show more detail, higher values create smoother curves
Use transparency for overlaps - Set alpha between 0.5-0.7 when comparing multiple groups to show where distributions intersect
Add rug plots strategically - For datasets with <1,000 points per group, show all observations. For larger datasets, sample 1-5% with slice_sample()
Show reference statistics - Add vertical lines for means, medians, or other important values using geom_vline()
Consider the y-axis - Density values can be unintuitive; consider adding “Probability Density” to the label to clarify meaning
Color with purpose - Use color gradients that match the ordering or meaning of your categories
Handle long tails - For highly skewed data, consider log-transforming the x-axis with scale_x_log10()
Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per group in the legend or plot
Choose appropriate alternatives - For discrete data or small samples (<30), consider histograms or violin plots instead
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Beautiful Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other distribution visualizations:

Ridge plots (via ggridges) for comparing many distributions vertically
Violin plots for combining density with box plot statistics
Histograms for showing actual counts rather than smoothed densities
Empirical cumulative distribution functions for showing percentiles


Want to create faceted density plots?
You can split by additional variables using faceting:
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ color, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Carat Distribution by Cut and Color",
       x = "Carat Weight",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
This creates separate density plots for each diamond color, still showing cut quality comparisons within each panel.

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmaps are powerful visualizations for displaying matrix data where values are represented as colors. They excel at revealing patterns, correlations, and clusters in large datasets. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated heatmaps using ggplot2.
We’ll explore correlations between vehicle characteristics and visualize temporal patterns in fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset.






What Makes Heatmaps Powerful:
Heatmaps excel at: - Visualizing correlation matrices - Showing patterns across two categorical dimensions - Revealing clusters and groupings in data - Displaying temporal patterns (time × category) - Comparing many variables simultaneously - Identifying hot spots and cold spots in data

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmaps are powerful visualizations for displaying matrix data where values are represented as colors. They excel at revealing patterns, correlations, and clusters in large datasets. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated heatmaps using ggplot2.
We’ll explore correlations between vehicle characteristics and visualize temporal patterns in fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset.






What Makes Heatmaps Powerful:
Heatmaps excel at: - Visualizing correlation matrices - Showing patterns across two categorical dimensions - Revealing clusters and groupings in data - Displaying temporal patterns (time × category) - Comparing many variables simultaneously - Identifying hot spots and cold spots in data

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting
library(viridis)        # For color scales

# Prepare correlation data
# Select numeric variables for correlation
numeric_vars <- mpg %>%
  select(displ, cyl, cty, hwy, year) %>%
  na.omit()

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars)

# Convert to long format for ggplot
cor_data <- cor_matrix %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "correlation"
  )

# Preview the data
head(cor_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  var1  var2  correlation
  <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
1 displ displ       1    
2 displ cyl         0.930
3 displ cty        -0.799
4 displ hwy        -0.766
5 displ year        0.148
6 cyl   displ       0.930

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Heatmap
Let’s start with a simple heatmap showing correlations between variables.

ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile()                                       # Create heatmap tiles









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) - Maps first variable to x-axis, second variable to y-axis, and correlation values to fill color
Line 2: geom_tile() - Creates rectangular tiles colored by the correlation values

What we have so far: A functional heatmap showing correlation patterns, but it uses a default color scale (blue gradient), lacks proper labeling, has no value annotations, and needs better formatting to be interpretable.

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add better colors, value labels, improved styling, and meaningful axis labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Diverging color scale (red-white-blue) for positive/negative correlations
Value labels showing exact correlation coefficients
White borders between tiles for clarity
Better variable names replacing technical labels
Correlation strength interpretation in colors
Title and context explaining the visualization
Legend improvements with better formatting
Axis text rotation for readability



# Create better variable labels
var_labels <- c(
  "displ" = "Engine Size",
  "cyl" = "Cylinders",
  "cty" = "City MPG",
  "hwy" = "Highway MPG",
  "year" = "Model Year"
)

# Update data with better labels
cor_data_labeled <- cor_data %>%
  mutate(
    var1_label = var_labels[var1],
    var2_label = var_labels[var2]
  )

ggplot(cor_data_labeled, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +    # White borders between tiles
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(correlation, 2)),             # Add correlation values
    color = "black",
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                # Red for negative
    mid = "white",                                  # White for zero
    high = "#2C5F8D",                               # Blue for positive
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Correlation\nCoefficient",
    breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
    labels = c("-1.0\n(Strong Negative)", "-0.5", "0.0\n(No Correlation)", 
               "0.5", "1.0\n(Strong Positive)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix: Vehicle Characteristics",
    subtitle = "Exploring relationships between engine specs and fuel efficiency",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: EPA fuel economy dataset | Values show Pearson correlation coefficients"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles









Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Creates a named vector mapping technical variable names to human-readable labels
Lines 10-15: Adds new columns with readable labels for both variables
Line 17: Maps data with readable labels to axes
Line 18: geom_tile() with white borders (1.5px width) separating each cell for clarity
Lines 19-24: geom_text() overlays correlation values (rounded to 2 decimals) as bold black text on each tile
Lines 25-34: scale_fill_gradient2() creates a diverging color scale: - Red for negative correlations - White for zero correlation - Blue for positive correlations - Custom labels explaining correlation strength
Lines 35-40: Comprehensive labeling explaining what the heatmap shows
Lines 41-52: Theme customization with angled x-axis labels, bold text, no gridlines, and centered titles
Line 53: coord_fixed() ensures tiles are square (equal width and height)

What we have now: A much more informative correlation heatmap with clear value labels, meaningful colors (red=negative, blue=positive), and readable variable names. The diverging color scale makes it immediately obvious which variables are positively or negatively correlated. The white borders and square tiles create a clean, professional appearance.

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready heatmap with clustering, dendrograms, and enhanced annotations.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
Significance indicators showing which correlations are statistically significant
Annotated insights highlighting key patterns
Lower triangular display avoiding redundancy
Enhanced color scheme with better discrimination
Correlation strength categories in annotations
Professional typography and spacing
Statistical context with p-values



# Perform hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
dist_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix))
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix)
var_order <- rownames(cor_matrix)[hc$order]

# Calculate p-values for correlations
library(Hmisc)


Attaching package: 'Hmisc'


The following objects are masked from 'package:dplyr':

    src, summarize


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    format.pval, units

cor_test <- rcorr(as.matrix(numeric_vars))
p_values <- cor_test$P

# Convert p-values to long format
p_data <- p_values %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "p_value"
  )

# Combine correlation and p-value data
cor_data_full <- cor_data %>%
  left_join(p_data, by = c("var1", "var2")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Reorder by clustering
    var1 = factor(var1, levels = var_order),
    var2 = factor(var2, levels = var_order),
    # Add readable labels
    var1_label = var_labels[as.character(var1)],
    var2_label = var_labels[as.character(var2)],
    # Determine significance
    significant = p_value < 0.05,
    sig_label = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    # Only show lower triangle (avoid redundancy)
    show_tile = as.numeric(var1) >= as.numeric(var2)
  )

# Filter to lower triangle only
cor_data_lower <- cor_data_full %>%
  filter(show_tile)

# Identify strong correlations for annotation
strong_cor <- cor_data_lower %>%
  filter(abs(correlation) > 0.8, var1 != var2) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

ggplot(cor_data_lower, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  
  # Add tiles with borders
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  
  # Add correlation values with significance stars
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(correlation, 2), "\n", sig_label)),
    color = ifelse(abs(cor_data_lower$correlation) > 0.6, "white", "black"),
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  
  # Highlight diagonal
  geom_tile(
    data = cor_data_lower %>% filter(var1 == var2),
    color = "#2C3E50",
    linewidth = 3,
    fill = NA
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for strongest correlation
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]),
    xend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.5,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    yend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")),
    color = "#52A675",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.6,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    label = paste0("Strongest: ", round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3)),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#52A675"
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#D32F2F",                                # Darker red
    mid = "#FFFFFF",
    high = "#1976D2",                               # Darker blue
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Pearson\nCorrelation",
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5),
    labels = function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix with Hierarchical Clustering and Significance Testing",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Variables reordered by similarity | Highway and City MPG are perfectly correlated (r = ",
      round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3), ", p < 0.001)\n",
      "Engine size strongly correlates with cylinders | Significance: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data | Lower triangle shown to avoid redundancy | Dark borders highlight diagonal\nVariables clustered using hierarchical clustering (1 - |correlation|) | White text indicates |r| > 0.6 | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1,
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    
    # Remove grid and ticks
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  ) +
  
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles









Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: Performs hierarchical clustering on variables using 1 - |correlation| as distance, grouping similar variables together
Lines 6-8: Uses Hmisc::rcorr() to calculate p-values for all correlations, testing statistical significance
Lines 10-19: Converts p-value matrix to long format for merging with correlation data
Lines 21-41: Combines correlation and p-value data, then: - Reorders variables by clustering - Adds readable labels - Creates significance indicators (, , ) - Filters to show only lower triangle (avoiding redundant upper triangle)
Lines 43-45: Filters to show only the lower triangular portion
Lines 47-50: Identifies the strongest correlations (|r| > 0.8) for annotation
Lines 54-56: Creates tiles with thick white borders
Lines 58-65: Adds text labels showing correlation values and significance stars; uses white text for strong correlations (|r| > 0.6) for better contrast
Lines 67-72: Highlights the diagonal with thick dark borders
Lines 74-92: Annotates the strongest correlation with an arrow and label
Lines 94-103: Enhanced diverging color scale with darker red and blue for better contrast
Lines 105-113: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific findings and significance legend
Lines 115-166: Comprehensive theme with professional typography, left-aligned text, and detailed caption

Final result: A publication-ready correlation heatmap with hierarchical clustering, statistical significance indicators, and only the lower triangle displayed (avoiding redundancy). The clustering reveals that related variables (like city and highway MPG) group together. Significance stars show which correlations are statistically reliable. The annotation highlights the strongest relationship. Perfect for research papers, technical reports, or data analysis presentations.

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmap Variations
Different types of heatmaps for different data:

library(patchwork)

# 1. Calendar heatmap (temporal patterns)
# Simulate daily data
set.seed(42)
calendar_data <- tibble(
  date = seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day"),
  value = rnorm(366, mean = 100, sd = 20)
) %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    week = week(date),
    wday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)
  )

v1 <- ggplot(calendar_data, aes(x = week, y = wday, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Value") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Calendar Heatmap", subtitle = "Daily patterns across the year") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 2. Categorical heatmap (class vs. manufacturer)
cat_data <- mpg %>%
  count(class, manufacturer) %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v2 <- ggplot(cat_data, aes(x = manufacturer, y = class, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Categorical Heatmap", subtitle = "Model count by class and manufacturer") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 3. Binned heatmap (2D density)
v3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 10) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Binned Heatmap (2D Histogram)", subtitle = "Density of observations") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  )

# 4. Annotated heatmap with rankings
rank_data <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class, year) %>%
  summarise(avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v4 <- ggplot(rank_data, aes(x = as.factor(year), y = class, fill = avg_hwy)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_hwy, 1)), fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 25,
    name = "Avg MPG"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Time Series Heatmap", subtitle = "Average highway MPG by class over time") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

(v1 | v2) / (v3 | v4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Heatmap Variations for Different Data Types",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5))
  )














Variation Descriptions:

Calendar Heatmap: Shows daily patterns across months; good for time-based data
Categorical Heatmap: Counts or values across two categorical dimensions
Binned Heatmap: 2D histogram showing density of continuous data
Time Series Heatmap: Shows how values change over time across categories

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Heatmaps






Heatmaps Work Well When:
✅ Visualizing correlation matrices - Perfect for showing relationships between many variables
✅ Comparing across two dimensions - Category × category or time × category
✅ Showing patterns in large datasets - Colors reveal trends quickly
✅ Displaying matrix data - Any data that fits in a grid format
✅ Identifying clusters - Similar values group together visually
✅ Time-based patterns - Calendar heatmaps for daily/weekly/monthly trends
Avoid Heatmaps When:
❌ Precise values matter - Hard to distinguish similar colors accurately
❌ Too many categories - More than 20×20 becomes cluttered
❌ Relationships aren’t gridded - Use scatter plots or networks instead
❌ Only a few data points - Use tables or bar charts
❌ Color perception issues - Ensure accessible color scales
❌ 3+ dimensions - Heatmaps are fundamentally 2D

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Heatmaps:

Use diverging scales for correlations - Red-white-blue makes positive/negative immediately obvious
Add value labels - Use geom_text() to show exact numbers on tiles
Include white borders - Set color = "white" in geom_tile() to separate cells
Make tiles square - Use coord_fixed() for equal width and height
Consider clustering - Hierarchical clustering reveals natural groupings
Show only lower triangle - For symmetric matrices, avoid redundancy
Add significance indicators - Stars (, , ) show statistical reliability
Choose colors wisely:

Diverging (red-white-blue) for data with meaningful zero/midpoint
Sequential (light-to-dark) for data ranging from low to high
Viridis for perceptually uniform, colorblind-friendly scales

Label axes clearly - Replace technical names with readable labels
Remove gridlines - Set panel.grid = element_blank() for clean appearance
Adjust text color - Use white text on dark tiles, black on light tiles
Consider ordering - Sort by values, clusters, or meaningfully
Add context - Explain what colors represent in title/caption
Test accessibility - Verify colors work for colorblind viewers
Limit categories - More than 15-20 per dimension becomes unreadable
Annotate patterns - Highlight interesting findings with arrows/text
Use appropriate scales - Match color range to data range
Include sample sizes - For aggregated data, show n counts

title: Creating Insightful Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Heatmap Pitfalls:

Rainbow colors - Avoid “jet” colormap; use perceptually uniform scales
No value labels - Readers can’t tell 0.7 from 0.8 by color alone
Wrong color scale - Sequential vs. diverging matters
Too many cells - 50×50 grid is unreadable
No clustering - Random order hides patterns
Missing zero - Diverging scales need midpoint at meaningful zero
Inconsistent scales - Different heatmaps should use same color mapping
No borders - Tiles blend together without separation
Poor aspect ratio - Non-square tiles distort perception
Ignoring redundancy - Full correlation matrix shows each value twice
No statistical context - Show significance for correlations
Inaccessible colors - Test with colorblind simulators

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Time series line plots are essential for visualizing how values change over time. They reveal trends, patterns, seasonality, and anomalies in temporal data. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated time series visualizations using ggplot2.
We’ll analyze monthly average fuel efficiency trends across different vehicle classes using simulated time series data based on the mpg dataset.






What Makes Time Series Plots Powerful:
Line plots for time series excel at: - Revealing trends and patterns over time - Comparing multiple series simultaneously - Identifying seasonality and cyclical patterns - Highlighting sudden changes or anomalies - Forecasting future values

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Time series line plots are essential for visualizing how values change over time. They reveal trends, patterns, seasonality, and anomalies in temporal data. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated time series visualizations using ggplot2.
We’ll analyze monthly average fuel efficiency trends across different vehicle classes using simulated time series data based on the mpg dataset.






What Makes Time Series Plots Powerful:
Line plots for time series excel at: - Revealing trends and patterns over time - Comparing multiple series simultaneously - Identifying seasonality and cyclical patterns - Highlighting sudden changes or anomalies - Forecasting future values

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and create our time series data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting dates and numbers
library(lubridate)      # For working with dates

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

# Create simulated monthly time series data (2020-2024)
dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")

# Create time series for three vehicle classes
data_timeseries <- tibble(
  date = rep(dates, 3),
  class = rep(c("Compact", "SUV", "Midsize"), each = length(dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Create realistic trends with seasonality
    base_mpg = case_when(
      class == "Compact" ~ 28,
      class == "SUV" ~ 19,
      class == "Midsize" ~ 24
    ),
    # Add upward trend (fuel efficiency improving over time)
    trend = as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 365 * 0.5,
    # Add seasonality (lower in winter, higher in summer)
    season = 2 * sin(2 * pi * (month(date) - 1) / 12),
    # Add random noise
    noise = rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8),
    # Combine components
    avg_mpg = base_mpg + trend + season + noise
  ) %>%
  select(date, class, avg_mpg)
