title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Line Plot
Let’s start with a simple line plot showing fuel efficiency over time.

ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) +
  geom_line()                                       # Create line plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) - Initializes the plot with date on x-axis, fuel efficiency on y-axis, and different colors for each vehicle class
Line 2: geom_line() - Draws connected lines through the data points in chronological order

What we have so far: A functional time series plot showing three lines, but it lacks context, proper date formatting, clear legends, and visual refinements. The trends are visible but not well-emphasized.

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add better formatting, smoother lines, point markers, and improved styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Formatted date axis with proper breaks and labels
Point markers to show actual data points
Thicker lines for better visibility
Custom color palette that’s meaningful and accessible
Title, subtitle, and labels for context
Legend improvements with better positioning
Grid styling for easier value reading
Y-axis formatting with clearer breaks



ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +                      # Thicker lines for visibility
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +             # Add points with transparency
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",                       # Break every 6 months
    date_labels = "%b %Y",                          # Format as "Jan 2020"
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.02)                 # Small padding on edges
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(15, 35, by = 5),                   # Y-axis breaks every 5 mpg
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg")          # Add "mpg" to labels
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",                        # Blue
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",                            # Coral
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"                         # Green
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Fuel Efficiency Trends Over Time",
    subtitle = "Monthly average highway MPG by vehicle class (2020-2024)",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Fuel Efficiency",
    caption = "Data: Simulated monthly averages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5)
  )









Code Explanation
Line 2: geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) - Creates thicker lines (1.2px) for better visibility and emphasis
Line 3: geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) - Adds semi-transparent points at each data observation, making it clear where actual measurements exist
Lines 4-8: scale_x_date() formats the date axis with breaks every 6 months, displays dates in “Month Year” format, and adds small padding at the edges
Lines 9-12: scale_y_continuous() sets y-axis breaks at regular 5 mpg intervals and adds “mpg” suffix to all labels
Lines 13-20: scale_color_manual() applies a custom colorblind-friendly palette with meaningful colors for each vehicle class
Lines 21-27: Comprehensive labeling with descriptive title, informative subtitle, clear axis labels, and data source attribution
Lines 28-41: Theme customization including centered titles, angled x-axis labels for readability, bottom legend, and subtle gridlines

What we have now: A much more readable time series plot with proper date formatting, visible data points, and clear context. The trends are easier to follow, and the professional styling makes it suitable for reports and presentations.

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready time series plot with trend highlights, annotations, and sophisticated styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Smoothed trend lines showing overall direction
Shaded confidence intervals around trends
Key event annotations marking important dates
Highlighted time periods (e.g., recent period)
Direct labels at the end of lines (no legend needed)
Enhanced gridlines with reference lines
Data-driven insights in subtitle
Professional color scheme with better contrast
Optimized layout for maximum clarity



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
summary_stats <- data_timeseries %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    start_mpg = first(avg_mpg),
    end_mpg = last(avg_mpg),
    change = end_mpg - start_mpg,
    pct_change = (change / start_mpg) * 100
  )

# Get the last date and values for direct labeling
last_values <- data_timeseries %>%
  filter(date == max(date))

ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class, fill = class)) +
  
  # Add shaded area for recent period (last year)
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = as.Date("2024-01-01"),
    xmax = as.Date("2024-12-01"),
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    alpha = 0.05,
    fill = "gray"
  ) +
  
  # Add horizontal reference line at 25 mpg (hypothetical target)
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 25,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#6C757D",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add smooth trend lines with confidence intervals
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = TRUE,                                      # Show confidence interval
    alpha = 0.15,                                   # Transparent shading
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Add actual data lines
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Add points at each observation
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  
  # Add direct labels at the end of each line
  geom_text(
    data = last_values,
    aes(label = class),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for reference line
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date("2020-06-01"),
    y = 25.5,
    label = "Target: 25 mpg",
    size = 3.5,
    color = "#6C757D",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for highlighted period
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date("2024-06-01"),
    y = 33,
    label = "2024 Performance",
    size = 3.5,
    color = "gray40",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",
    date_labels = "%b\n%Y",                         # Two-line date format
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))         # More space on right for labels
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(15, 35, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),
    limits = c(15, 35)
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"
    )
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"
    )
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Improving Across All Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = "Compact cars lead with 29.8 mpg in 2024, up 8.2% since 2020 | SUVs show strongest improvement at 10.5% gain\nSmoothed trend lines (dashed) show overall direction despite seasonal variation",
    x = NULL,                                       # Remove x-axis label (obvious it's time)
    y = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data: Simulated monthly averages (2020-2024) | Shaded areas show LOESS trend confidence intervals | Gray background highlights 2024 data\nVisualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 18,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50"
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.y = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 12,
      margin = margin(r = 10)
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.9),
    
    # Remove legend (using direct labels instead)
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid styling
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#F8F9FA", linewidth = 0.3),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'










Code Explanation
Lines 2-11: Calculates summary statistics including start/end values and percentage change for each class - used for creating data-driven insights in the subtitle
Lines 13-15: Extracts the final data points for each class to use in direct labeling at the end of lines
Lines 19-28: annotate("rect") creates a shaded gray background highlighting the most recent year (2024) for emphasis
Lines 30-37: geom_hline() adds a dashed horizontal reference line at 25 mpg (hypothetical efficiency target)
Lines 39-46: geom_smooth() adds smoothed trend lines using LOESS method with semi-transparent confidence intervals showing the uncertainty around the trend
Line 49: Main data lines with increased thickness (1.5px) and slight transparency
Line 52: Data points showing each monthly observation
Lines 54-62: geom_text() adds direct labels at the end of each line with class names, positioned to the right of the last point
Lines 64-72: Text annotation explaining the reference line
Lines 74-82: Text annotation labeling the highlighted 2024 period
Lines 84-88: Date axis with two-line format (“Jan”) and extra space on the right for direct labels
Lines 90-94: Y-axis with consistent breaks and formatted labels
Lines 96-114: Color and fill scales for both lines and confidence intervals
Lines 116-122: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific insights including actual numbers and percentage changes
Lines 124-175: Comprehensive theme customization with left-aligned text, no legend (replaced by direct labels), subtle gridlines, and professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready time series visualization that tells a complete story. The smoothed trend lines reveal the overall direction while preserving the detailed monthly data. Key features like the reference line, highlighted period, and direct labels make the chart self-explanatory. The data-driven subtitle provides immediate insights without requiring viewers to analyze the chart themselves. Suitable for executive presentations, reports, or publications.

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Time Series Patterns
Understanding what to look for in time series data:

# Create example patterns
pattern_dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-01"), by = "month")

pattern_data <- tibble(
  date = rep(pattern_dates, 4),
  pattern = rep(c("Upward Trend", "Seasonal Pattern", "Cyclical Pattern", "Random Walk"), 
                each = length(pattern_dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    value = case_when(
      pattern == "Upward Trend" ~ 
        10 + as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 365 * 5 + rnorm(n(), 0, 1),
      pattern == "Seasonal Pattern" ~ 
        20 + 5 * sin(2 * pi * (month(date) - 1) / 12) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5),
      pattern == "Cyclical Pattern" ~ 
        15 + 3 * sin(2 * pi * as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 730) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5),
      pattern == "Random Walk" ~ 
        cumsum(rnorm(n(), 0.05, 1))
    )
  )

ggplot(pattern_data, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2C5F8D", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2C5F8D", size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#E76F51", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ pattern, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "Common Time Series Patterns to Recognize",
    subtitle = "Blue line = actual data | Red dashed line = smoothed trend",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'















Pattern Descriptions:

Upward Trend: Consistent increase over time (e.g., revenue growth, temperature rise)
Seasonal Pattern: Regular fluctuations within a year (e.g., retail sales, weather)
Cyclical Pattern: Longer-term waves beyond seasonality (e.g., economic cycles)
Random Walk: No clear pattern, values drift up or down randomly (e.g., stock prices)

section: When to Use Time Series Line Plots
text:
When to Use Time Series Line Plots






Time Series Line Plots Work Well When:
✅ Showing trends over time - The primary use case for line charts
✅ Data is continuous - Works best with regularly spaced observations
✅ Temporal order matters - When the sequence of events is important
✅ Comparing multiple series - Up to 5-7 series can be overlaid effectively
✅ Identifying patterns - Seasonality, cycles, and anomalies become visible
✅ Forecasting - Trends can be extended to predict future values
Avoid Time Series Line Plots When:
❌ Data is categorical - Use bar charts instead
❌ Too many series (>10) - Consider small multiples (facets) or interactive plots
❌ Irregular time intervals - May need to interpolate or use scatter plots
❌ Part-to-whole is important - Use stacked area charts
❌ Exact values are critical - Consider adding tables or data labels
❌ Comparing distributions - Use box plots or violin plots over time

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Time Series Line Plots:

Format dates properly - Use scale_x_date() with appropriate breaks and labels (e.g., “%b %Y” for “Jan 2020”)
Add smoothed trends - Use geom_smooth() to show overall direction while keeping detailed data visible
Include data points - Especially for monthly/quarterly data, points show where actual observations exist
Use direct labels - When possible, label lines directly instead of relying only on legends
Highlight key periods - Use annotate("rect") to shade important time ranges
Add reference lines - Horizontal lines for targets, thresholds, or averages provide context
Choose appropriate line thickness - linewidth = 1.2-1.5 for main lines, thinner for trend lines
Mind the color count - Limit to 5-7 colors maximum; use facets for more series
Format axes clearly - Add units to labels (“mpg”, “$”, “%”) and use consistent breaks
Tell the story in text - Use title/subtitle to highlight insights viewers should notice
Consider seasonality - Note seasonal patterns in caption or add seasonal adjustment lines
Show uncertainty - When using smoothed trends, include confidence intervals (se = TRUE)
Optimize date labels - Angle x-axis text or use two-line format for better readability
Use meaningful baselines - Don’t always start y-axis at zero; choose range that shows variation clearly
Add annotations - Mark significant events, policy changes, or anomalies with text or arrows
Keep gridlines subtle - Light gray horizontal lines help reading; vertical ones are often unnecessary
Consider log scales - For exponential growth or data spanning orders of magnitude
Test different smoothing methods - Try “loess”, “lm”, or “gam” depending on your data

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Time Series Plot Pitfalls:

Inconsistent time intervals - Gaps in data can mislead; acknowledge or interpolate
Too many overlapping lines - More than 7 series becomes spaghetti; use facets
Poor date formatting - Default date labels are often crowded or unclear
Missing context - Always explain what the time period represents and any significant events
Ignoring outliers - Extreme values may indicate data errors or important events
Wrong smoothing method - Linear trends for cyclical data or vice versa
Misleading y-axis - Truncated axes can exaggerate or minimize trends
No uncertainty indication - Trends should show confidence when estimated
Overcrowded annotations - Too much text clutters the visualization
Forgetting axis labels - Always label axes with units

title: Creating Insightful Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Advanced: Adding Forecast Ribbon
Here’s how to extend your time series with a forecast:

# Example: Add forecast ribbon for next 6 months
library(forecast)

Registered S3 method overwritten by 'quantmod':
  method            from
  as.zoo.data.frame zoo 

# Filter one class for simpler example
compact_data <- data_timeseries %>%
  filter(class == "Compact")

# Create simple forecast (linear trend)
future_dates <- seq(max(compact_data$date) + months(1), 
                    max(compact_data$date) + months(6), 
                    by = "month")

# Simple linear model for forecast
model <- lm(avg_mpg ~ as.numeric(date), data = compact_data)
future_values <- predict(model, 
                         newdata = tibble(date = future_dates),
                         interval = "prediction")

forecast_data <- tibble(
  date = future_dates,
  forecast = future_values[,1],
  lower = future_values[,2],
  upper = future_values[,3]
)

ggplot() +
  # Historical data
  geom_line(data = compact_data, 
            aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg), 
            color = "#2C5F8D", 
            linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = compact_data, 
             aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg), 
             color = "#2C5F8D", 
             size = 1.5) +
  
  # Forecast
  geom_ribbon(data = forecast_data,
              aes(x = date, ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
              fill = "#E76F51",
              alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = forecast_data,
            aes(x = date, y = forecast),
            color = "#E76F51",
            linewidth = 1.2,
            linetype = "dashed") +
  
  # Vertical line separating historical from forecast
  geom_vline(xintercept = max(compact_data$date),
             linetype = "dotted",
             color = "#6C757D") +
  
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(
    title = "Compact Car Fuel Efficiency: Historical Data and 6-Month Forecast",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows predicted values | Shaded area represents 95% prediction interval",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Highway MPG"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated maps of Italy using the sf (simple features) package and ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic map and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Maps are excellent for visualizing spatial data, showing regional patterns, and communicating geographic information effectively.
We’ll use spatial data from the rnaturalearth package and create a choropleth map showing regional statistics across Italy.

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated maps of Italy using the sf (simple features) package and ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic map and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Maps are excellent for visualizing spatial data, showing regional patterns, and communicating geographic information effectively.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # For data manipulation
library(sf)             # For spatial data handling
library(rnaturalearth)  # For geographic data
library(rnaturalearthdata) # Additional geographic data
library(ggspatial)      # For scale bars and north arrows
library(scales)         # For formatting

# Get Italy map data at country level
italy_country <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", country = "Italy", returnclass = "sf")

# Get Italy regions (admin level 1)
italy_regions <- ne_states(country = "Italy", returnclass = "sf")

# Create sample data: GDP per capita by region (fictional)
set.seed(42)
regional_data <- tibble(
  region = italy_regions$name,
  gdp_per_capita = round(rnorm(nrow(italy_regions), mean = 32000, sd = 8000)),
  population = round(rnorm(nrow(italy_regions), mean = 3000000, sd = 2000000))
) %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_per_capita = pmax(gdp_per_capita, 20000),  # Minimum value
    population = pmax(population, 500000)           # Minimum value
  )

# Join spatial data with statistics
italy_map_data <- italy_regions %>%
  left_join(regional_data, by = c("name" = "region"))

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Map of Italy
Let’s start with a simple map showing the outline and regions of Italy.

ggplot(italy_map_data) +
  geom_sf()  # Draw the map









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(italy_map_data) - Initializes the plot with our spatial data
Line 2: geom_sf() - Draws the map using the simple features geometry, automatically handling the spatial coordinates

What we have so far: A functional but basic map of Italy. The regional boundaries are visible but the chart lacks color, labels, context, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the map by adding a choropleth layer, color scale, labels, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Choropleth coloring based on GDP per capita
Color scale with meaningful breaks
Region boundaries with white lines
Improved projection for better appearance
Title and legend for context
Clean theme removing default elements
Scale bar and north arrow for orientation



ggplot(italy_map_data) +
  # Fill regions by GDP per capita
  geom_sf(aes(fill = gdp_per_capita), 
          color = "white", 
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Apply color gradient
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fee5d9", 
                      high = "#a50f15",
                      name = "GDP per Capita\n(EUR)",
                      labels = comma_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Italy: Regional Economic Performance",
    subtitle = "GDP per capita by region (simulated data)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: geom_sf(aes(fill = gdp_per_capita)) - Creates a choropleth map with regions colored by GDP per capita, white boundaries, and thin line width
Lines 6-9: scale_fill_gradient() - Applies a sequential color scale from light orange to dark red, with formatted labels
Lines 10-14: labs() - Adds title, subtitle, and caption for context
Line 15: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean base theme
Lines 16-21: theme() - Removes grid lines and axis elements that are unnecessary for maps

What we have now: A much more informative map with regional color coding showing economic differences. The clean styling and proper legend make it presentation-ready.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, city markers, annotations, inset maps, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color palette with better breaks
Major city markers showing key locations
City labels for important places
Enhanced borders with Italy outline
Regional labels for largest regions
Statistical categories instead of continuous scale
North arrow and scale bar for orientation
Professional typography and spacing
Neighboring countries for context



# Get neighboring countries for context
neighbors <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", 
                         country = c("France", "Switzerland", "Austria", 
                                   "Slovenia", "Croatia"),
                         returnclass = "sf")

# Create GDP categories
italy_map_data <- italy_map_data %>%
  mutate(
    gdp_category = cut(gdp_per_capita,
                      breaks = c(0, 25000, 30000, 35000, 40000, 50000),
                      labels = c("< 25k", "25-30k", "30-35k", "35-40k", "> 40k"),
                      include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

# Major Italian cities (approximate coordinates)
major_cities <- tibble(
  city = c("Rome", "Milan", "Naples", "Turin", "Florence", "Venice", "Bologna"),
  lon = c(12.4964, 9.1900, 14.2681, 7.6869, 11.2558, 12.3155, 11.3426),
  lat = c(41.9028, 45.4642, 40.8518, 45.0703, 43.7696, 45.4408, 44.4949),
  population_millions = c(2.9, 3.1, 3.1, 1.7, 1.0, 0.9, 0.4)
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)

# Define custom color palette
gdp_colors <- c(
  "< 25k" = "#fee5d9",
  "25-30k" = "#fcae91",
  "30-35k" = "#fb6a4a",
  "35-40k" = "#de2d26",
  "> 40k" = "#a50f15"
)

# Create the main map
ggplot() +
  # Add neighboring countries (in gray)
  geom_sf(data = neighbors, 
          fill = "gray95", 
          color = "gray70",
          linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Add Italy regions with GDP categories
  geom_sf(data = italy_map_data,
          aes(fill = gdp_category),
          color = "white",
          linewidth = 0.5) +
  # Add Italy country outline
  geom_sf(data = italy_country,
          fill = NA,
          color = "gray20",
          linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Add major cities
  geom_sf(data = major_cities,
          aes(size = population_millions),
          shape = 21,
          fill = "yellow",
          color = "gray20",
          stroke = 0.8,
          alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add city labels
  geom_sf_text(data = major_cities,
               aes(label = city),
               size = 3,
               fontface = "bold",
               nudge_y = 0.3,
               color = "gray20") +
  # Apply custom color palette
  scale_fill_manual(values = gdp_colors,
                    name = "GDP per Capita (EUR)",
                    na.value = "gray90") +
  # Size scale for cities
  scale_size_continuous(name = "City Population\n(millions)",
                       range = c(2, 8),
                       breaks = c(1, 2, 3)) +
  # Set coordinate system
  coord_sf(xlim = c(6.5, 18.5), 
           ylim = c(36.5, 47.5),
           expand = FALSE) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Italy: Regional Economic Landscape and Major Urban Centers",
    subtitle = "GDP per capita varies significantly from north to south | Major cities marked by population size",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated regional statistics | Map data: Natural Earth | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add north arrow
  annotation_north_arrow(
    location = "tl",
    which_north = "true",
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.3, "in"),
    style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering
  ) +
  # Add scale bar
  annotation_scale(
    location = "bl",
    width_hint = 0.25,
    pad_x = unit(0.2, "in"),
    pad_y = unit(0.2, "in")
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Panel styling
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "aliceblue", color = NA),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

Warning in st_point_on_surface.sfc(sf::st_zm(x)): st_point_on_surface may not
give correct results for longitude/latitude data


Scale on map varies by more than 10%, scale bar may be inaccurate










Code Explanation
Lines 2-5: Retrieves neighboring countries’ boundaries using ne_countries() for geographic context
Lines 8-14: Creates GDP categories using cut() to convert continuous values into meaningful brackets
Lines 17-25: Creates a tibble of major Italian cities with coordinates and converts to spatial format using st_as_sf()
Lines 28-34: Defines custom color palette for GDP categories, progressing from light to dark
Line 37: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 39-42: geom_sf() adds neighboring countries in light gray for context
Lines 44-47: geom_sf() adds Italy regions colored by GDP category with white boundaries
Lines 49-52: geom_sf() adds Italy’s country outline with thick dark border
Lines 54-60: geom_sf() adds major cities as circles sized by population
Lines 62-67: geom_sf_text() adds city name labels above the markers
Lines 69-71: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette
Lines 73-75: scale_size_continuous() controls city marker sizes
Lines 77-79: coord_sf() sets the bounding box and removes padding
Lines 81-85: labs() adds comprehensive title, subtitle, and caption
Lines 87-93: annotation_north_arrow() adds a decorative north arrow in top left
Lines 95-100: annotation_scale() adds a scale bar in bottom left
Line 101: theme_void() starts with blank canvas (appropriate for maps)
Lines 102-125: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Centered titles and caption - Legend styling with background box - Light blue panel background (representing water) - Proper margins for professional appearance

Final result: A publication-ready map of Italy that clearly communicates regional economic patterns with major cities marked. The combination of choropleth coloring, city markers, neighboring countries for context, north arrow, and scale bar creates a comprehensive and professional visualization suitable for reports, presentations, or publications.

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better sf Maps in R:

Use appropriate projections - Consider using st_transform() to convert to appropriate coordinate systems (e.g., EPSG:3857 for web maps)
Choose color scales wisely - Use sequential scales for continuous data, diverging for data with meaningful midpoint, categorical for discrete groups
Add geographic context - Include neighboring regions, bodies of water, or landmarks to help viewers orient themselves
Label strategically - Add labels for major features but avoid cluttering; use geom_sf_text() or geom_sf_label()
Include scale and orientation - Always add north arrow and scale bar for maps showing unfamiliar areas
Mind the aspect ratio - Use coord_sf() with appropriate xlim/ylim to avoid distortion
Layer thoughtfully - Order layers from background to foreground: context → main data → annotations → labels
Use theme_void() for clean maps - Remove axes and grid lines that are unnecessary for geographic visualization
Consider accessibility - Use colorblind-friendly palettes and ensure sufficient contrast
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("map.png", width = 10, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Beautiful Maps of Italy with sf and ggplot2
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other map visualizations:

Point maps showing locations of events or facilities
Flow maps showing migration or trade patterns
Interactive maps using leaflet or mapview
Animated maps showing changes over time with gganimate


Want to create interactive maps?
You can make your maps interactive using leaflet:
library(leaflet)

# Create color palette
pal <- colorNumeric(palette = "YlOrRd", 
                   domain = italy_map_data$gdp_per_capita)

# Create interactive map
leaflet(italy_map_data) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal(gdp_per_capita),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "white",
    weight = 1,
    popup = ~paste0("<strong>", name, "</strong><br>",
                   "GDP per capita: €", 
                   format(gdp_per_capita, big.mark = ","))
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    pal = pal,
    values = ~gdp_per_capita,
    title = "GDP per Capita",

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated network charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Network charts (also called graph visualizations) are excellent for showing relationships, connections, and flows between entities. They’re useful for social networks, organizational structures, citation networks, and system dependencies.
We’ll create a dataset representing collaboration relationships between research departments in a university.

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated network charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Network charts (also called graph visualizations) are excellent for showing relationships, connections, and flows between entities. They’re useful for social networks, organizational structures, citation networks, and system dependencies.

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph

Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # For data manipulation
library(igraph)     # For network data structures
library(ggraph)     # For network visualization
library(ggforce)    # For geom_mark_hull
library(scales)     # For formatting

# Create nodes (departments)
nodes <- tibble(
  id = 1:10,
  name = c("Computer Science", "Mathematics", "Physics", "Chemistry",
           "Biology", "Engineering", "Statistics", "Medicine",
           "Psychology", "Economics"),
  type = c("STEM", "STEM", "STEM", "STEM",

)

# Create edges (collaborations)

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 1: Basic Network Chart
Let’s start with a simple network chart showing departments and their collaborations.

ggraph(network, layout = "fr") +  # Fruchterman-Reingold layout
  geom_edge_link() +                # Draw edges
  geom_node_point(size = 5)         # Draw nodes









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggraph(network, layout = "fr") - Initializes the network plot using the Fruchterman-Reingold force-directed layout algorithm
Line 2: geom_edge_link() - Draws lines representing connections between departments
Line 3: geom_node_point() - Draws circles representing each department

What we have so far: A functional but basic network chart. The connections are visible but the chart lacks labels, color coding, edge weights, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding labels, colors by department type, edge weights, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Node colors by department type
Node sizes based on publication counts
Edge transparency based on collaboration strength
Node labels showing department names
Improved layout algorithm
Legend for interpretation
Clean theme removing axes
Title and subtitle for context



ggraph(network, layout = "fr") +
  # Draw edges with transparency based on weight
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = collaborations),
                 color = "gray50",
                 show.legend = FALSE) +
  # Draw nodes colored by type, sized by publications
  geom_node_point(aes(color = type, size = publications),
                  alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 repel = TRUE,
                 size = 3.5,
                 fontface = "bold") +
  # Apply color palette
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2",
                     name = "Department Type") +
  # Scale sizes
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Publications",
                       range = c(5, 15)) +
  # Add labels
  labs(
    title = "University Research Collaboration Network",
    subtitle = "Departments connected by joint publications",
    caption = "Node size represents publication volume | Edge opacity shows collaboration strength"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, community detection, curved edges, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Community detection highlighting clusters
Curved edges for better aesthetics
Custom color palette by community
Network statistics annotations
Hub highlighting for most connected nodes
Enhanced typography and spacing
Background shading by community
Edge width and transparency based on strength



# Detect communities using Louvain method
communities <- cluster_louvain(network)
V(network)$community <- membership(communities)

# Calculate node degree (number of connections)
V(network)$degree <- degree(network)

# Identify hub nodes (degree > 4)
V(network)$is_hub <- V(network)$degree > 4

# Calculate network statistics
n_nodes <- vcount(network)
n_edges <- ecount(network)
density <- edge_density(network)
avg_degree <- mean(degree(network))

# Define custom color palette for communities
community_colors <- c(
  "1" = "#E76F51",
  "2" = "#2A9D8F",
  "3" = "#E9C46A",
  "4" = "#F4A261"
)

# Set layout for consistency
set.seed(42)
layout <- create_layout(network, layout = "fr")

ggraph(layout) +
  # Add community background shading
  geom_mark_hull(aes(x, y, group = community, fill = as.factor(community)),
                 alpha = 0.1,
                 expand = unit(3, "mm"),
                 radius = unit(3, "mm")) +
  # Draw edges with curved paths
  geom_edge_link(aes(alpha = collaborations, width = collaborations),
                 color = "gray40",
                 show.legend = FALSE,
                 end_cap = circle(3, 'mm'),
                 start_cap = circle(3, 'mm')) +
  # Draw nodes colored by community
  geom_node_point(aes(size = publications, 
                      color = as.factor(community),
                      shape = is_hub),
                  alpha = 0.9,
                  stroke = 1.5) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name, 
                     fontface = ifelse(is_hub, "bold", "plain")),
                 repel = TRUE,
                 size = 3.5,
                 max.overlaps = 20) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = community_colors,
                    name = "Community",
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = community_colors,
                     name = "Research\nCommunity") +
  # Scale edge properties
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.5, 3)) +
  scale_edge_alpha(range = c(0.3, 0.8)) +
  # Scale node sizes
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Annual\nPublications",
                       range = c(8, 20)) +
  # Shape scale for hubs
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 18),
                    name = "Node Type",
                    labels = c("Regular", "Hub (>4 connections)")) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "University Research Network: Community Structure and Collaboration Patterns",
    subtitle = "Four distinct research communities identified through collaboration patterns | Hub departments shown as diamonds",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated collaboration data | Layout: Fruchterman-Reingold | Community detection: Louvain algorithm | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add network statistics annotation
  annotate("text",
           x = max(layout$x) - 1,
           y = max(layout$y) - 0.5,
           label = paste0("Network Statistics:\n",
                         "Nodes: ", n_nodes, "\n",
                         "Edges: ", n_edges, "\n",
                         "Density: ", round(density, 3), "\n",
                         "Avg Degree: ", round(avg_degree, 1)),
           hjust = 1,
           vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray30",
           fontface = "italic",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_graph(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.box = "vertical",
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggraph Network Charts:

Choose appropriate layouts - Use “fr” (Fruchterman-Reingold) for general networks, “kk” (Kamada-Kawai) for smaller networks, “circle” for hierarchies, “tree” for trees
Scale node sizes meaningfully - Map size to importance metrics like degree, betweenness centrality, or domain-specific values
Use edge properties effectively - Map edge width/alpha to connection strength, use colors for different relationship types
Detect communities - Use algorithms like Louvain, Walktrap, or Edge Betweenness to identify natural groupings
Label strategically - Use repel = TRUE to avoid overlaps, bold important nodes, consider showing only hubs for large networks
Mind the layout seed - Set set.seed() for reproducible layouts, especially for presentations
Add context with annotations - Include network statistics like density, clustering coefficient, or path lengths
Use curved edges for clarity - Curved edges reduce visual clutter and make individual connections easier to trace
Highlight key nodes - Use different shapes or borders for important nodes (hubs, bridges, etc.)
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("network.png", width = 12, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Creating Beautiful Network Charts with ggraph
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other network visualizations:

Hierarchical networks using tree layouts
Bipartite networks showing two distinct node types
Temporal networks with animation showing evolution
Interactive networks using visNetwork or networkD3


Want to create interactive network charts?
You can make your networks interactive using visNetwork:
library(visNetwork)

# Prepare data for visNetwork
vis_nodes <- nodes %>%
  rename(label = name) %>%
  mutate(
    group = type,
    value = publications,
    title = paste0(name, "<br>Publications: ", publications)
  )

vis_edges <- edges %>%
  mutate(
    value = collaborations,
    title = paste0("Collaborations: ", collaborations)
  )

# Create interactive network
visNetwork(vis_nodes, vis_edges) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "STEM", color = "#E76F51") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Health", color = "#2A9D8F") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Social", color = "#E9C46A") %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = TRUE,
    nodesIdSelection = TRUE
  ) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)
This creates an interactive network where users can drag nodes, zoom, and click for details.

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Radar plots (also called spider charts or star plots) are excellent for visualizing multivariate data and comparing profiles across multiple dimensions. Each axis represents a different variable, and the data forms a polygon shape that makes patterns immediately visible.
In this tutorial, we’ll compare the performance profiles of different vehicle classes using the mpg dataset, analyzing them across multiple fuel efficiency and performance metrics.






What Makes Radar Plots Useful:
Radar plots excel at: - Comparing multiple entities across the same dimensions - Identifying strengths and weaknesses in profiles - Spotting patterns and outliers quickly - Showing balance (or lack thereof) across metrics

text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting and rescaling

# Prepare the data: compare vehicle classes across multiple metrics
data_summary <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_hwy = mean(hwy),                            # Highway fuel efficiency
    avg_cty = mean(cty),                            # City fuel efficiency
    avg_displ = mean(displ),                        # Engine displacement
    avg_cyl = mean(cyl),                            # Number of cylinders
    count = n()                                     # Number of models
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Select a few classes for comparison
data_radar <- data_summary %>%
  filter(class %in% c("compact", "suv", "midsize")) %>%
  select(class, avg_hwy, avg_cty, avg_displ, avg_cyl)

# Preview the data

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Radar Plot
Let’s start with a simple radar plot using base ggplot2 with coord_polar.

# Reshape data for ggplot (long format)
data_long <- data_radar %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -class,                                  # All columns except class
    names_to = "metric",                            # Metric names
    values_to = "value"                             # Values
  )

ggplot(data_long, aes(x = metric, y = value, group = class, color = class)) +
  geom_polygon(fill = NA) +                         # Draw the polygon outline
  geom_point(size = 3) +                            # Add points at each vertex
  coord_polar() +                                   # Convert to circular coordinates
  facet_wrap(~ class)                               # Separate plot for each class









Code Explanation
Lines 2-7: pivot_longer() reshapes the data from wide format (one row per class with multiple metric columns) to long format (one row per class-metric combination), which is required for ggplot2
Line 9: ggplot(aes(x = metric, y = value, group = class, color = class)) - Maps metrics to x-axis (which will become angles), values to y-axis (which will become distances from center), and groups/colors by vehicle class
Line 10: geom_polygon(fill = NA) - Creates the polygon shape connecting all points; fill = NA means no fill color, just the outline
Line 11: geom_point(size = 3) - Adds visible points at each metric position on the polygon
Line 12: coord_polar() - Transforms the Cartesian coordinates into polar coordinates, creating the circular radar chart
Line 13: facet_wrap(~ class) - Creates separate small radar plots for each vehicle class

What we have so far: Basic radar plots showing the shape of each vehicle class profile, but the scales are problematic (metrics have different ranges), there’s no context, and the visualization is hard to compare across classes.

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll normalize the data, overlay the plots for comparison, and add better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Normalized scales (0-1 range) so all metrics are comparable
Overlaid polygons instead of separate facets for direct comparison
Semi-transparent fills to see overlapping areas
Better axis labels with readable metric names
Custom color palette for distinguishing classes
Title and context to explain what we’re viewing
Grid reference lines at specific intervals



# Normalize data to 0-1 scale for fair comparison
data_radar_norm <- data_radar %>%
  mutate(across(
    .cols = -class,                                 # All columns except class
    .fns = ~rescale(.x, to = c(0, 1))              # Rescale to 0-1 range
  ))

# Reshape to long format
data_long_norm <- data_radar_norm %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -class,
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    metric_label = case_when(                       # Create readable labels
      metric == "avg_hwy" ~ "Highway MPG",
      metric == "avg_cty" ~ "City MPG",
      metric == "avg_displ" ~ "Engine Size",
      metric == "avg_cyl" ~ "Cylinders"
    )
  )

ggplot(data_long_norm, aes(x = metric_label, y = value, group = class, color = class, fill = class)) +
  geom_polygon(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1.2) +     # Semi-transparent fill with thicker lines
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +               # Points with slight transparency
  coord_polar() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),                               # Set limits from 0 to 1
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25),                  # Grid lines at 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1
    labels = percent                                # Show as percentages
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",                        # Blue
      "midsize" = "#52A675",                        # Green
      "suv" = "#E76F51"                             # Coral
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "suv" = "#E76F51"
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Class Performance Profiles",
    subtitle = "Normalized comparison across fuel efficiency and engine metrics",
    caption = "Note: All metrics scaled to 0-100% for fair comparison"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-7: mutate(across(...)) normalizes all numeric columns (except class) to a 0-1 scale using rescale() - this is crucial because metrics like MPG (10-40 range) and cylinders (4-8 range) would otherwise be incomparable
Lines 9-23: Reshapes data to long format and creates readable metric labels, replacing technical column names with user-friendly descriptions
Line 25: aes(..., fill = class) - Added fill aesthetic to enable semi-transparent polygon fills
Line 26: geom_polygon(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 1.2) - Creates filled polygons with 25% opacity (allows seeing overlaps) and thicker lines for visibility
Line 27: geom_point() with slight transparency to show all points even when overlapping
Lines 29-33: scale_y_continuous() sets the radial axis limits to 0-1, adds grid lines at quartiles, and formats labels as percentages
Lines 34-49: scale_color_manual() and scale_fill_manual() - Applies custom colors to distinguish vehicle classes, with both outline and fill colors defined
Lines 50-54: Comprehensive labels explaining the normalized comparison
Lines 55-68: Theme customization with centered titles, bold axis labels, bottom legend, and subtle gridlines

What we have now: A much more informative radar plot where all three vehicle classes are overlaid for direct comparison. The normalization ensures fair comparison, and the semi-transparent fills make it easy to see where profiles overlap. We can now clearly see that compacts excel in fuel efficiency while SUVs have larger engines.

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready radar plot with enhanced annotations, reference circles, and professional styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Reference grid circles at specific values for easier reading
Value labels at each data point showing actual values
Highlighted differences between best and worst performers
Color-coded legend with sample sizes
Enhanced gridlines for better readability
Data insights in the subtitle
Professional color scheme with better contrast
Optimized layout with improved spacing



# Prepare enhanced data with original values for labels
data_radar_enhanced <- data_radar %>%
  mutate(across(
    .cols = -class,
    .fns = ~rescale(.x, to = c(0, 1)),
    .names = "{.col}_norm"                          # Create normalized columns with _norm suffix
  ))

# Reshape for plotting
data_long_enhanced <- data_radar_enhanced %>%
  select(class, ends_with("_norm")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -class,
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    metric_clean = str_remove(metric, "_norm"),    # Remove _norm suffix
    metric_label = case_when(
      metric_clean == "avg_hwy" ~ "Highway\nMPG",
      metric_clean == "avg_cty" ~ "City\nMPG",
      metric_clean == "avg_displ" ~ "Engine\nSize (L)",
      metric_clean == "avg_cyl" ~ "Number of\nCylinders"
    )
  )

# Add original values for labeling
data_original_long <- data_radar %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -class,
    names_to = "metric_clean",
    values_to = "original_value"
  )

data_long_final <- data_long_enhanced %>%
  left_join(data_original_long, by = c("class", "metric_clean"))

# Create reference circles data
reference_circles <- data.frame(
  y = rep(c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75), each = 100),
  x = rep(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 100), 3)
)

ggplot(data_long_final, aes(x = metric_label, y = value, group = class)) +
  
  # Add subtle reference circles
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75),
    color = "#E9ECEF",
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Add filled polygons
  geom_polygon(
    aes(fill = class, color = class),
    alpha = 0.2,
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  
  # Add points
  geom_point(
    aes(color = class),
    size = 4,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  
  # Add value labels (original values, not normalized)
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(original_value, 1), color = class),
    size = 3,
    fontface = "bold",
    vjust = -1.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  
  coord_polar() +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1.15),                            # Extended limit to fit labels
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x * 100, "%")
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "suv" = "#E76F51"
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class",
    labels = c(
      "compact" = "Compact Cars",
      "midsize" = "Midsize Cars",
      "suv" = "SUVs"
    )
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "midsize" = "#52A675",
      "suv" = "#E76F51"
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class",
    labels = c(
      "compact" = "Compact Cars",
      "midsize" = "Midsize Cars",
      "suv" = "SUVs"
    )
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Vehicle Performance Profiles: Compacts Excel in Efficiency, SUVs Lead in Power",
    subtitle = "Compact cars achieve 37% higher highway MPG than SUVs (28.3 vs 18.8 mpg)\nwhile SUVs have 65% larger engines (4.4L vs 2.7L displacement)",
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data (1999-2008) | Metrics normalized to 0-100% scale for comparison\nActual values shown at each point | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 16,
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 11,
      color = "#2C3E50",
      margin = margin(t = 5)
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D"),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.spacing.x = unit(1, "cm"),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 20),
    legend.key.size = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    
    # Grid styling
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-10: Creates normalized columns while preserving original values - uses .names = "{.col}_norm" to create new columns with _norm suffix, keeping both normalized (for plotting) and original (for labels) values
Lines 12-28: Reshapes normalized data and creates clean, multi-line metric labels for better readability in the circular layout
Lines 30-36: Reshapes original data separately to preserve actual values for display
Lines 38-39: Joins normalized and original data so we can plot normalized values but label with actual values
Lines 41-45: Creates reference circle data (though not used in final plot, kept for reference)
Lines 49-54: geom_hline() adds dashed reference circles at 25%, 50%, and 75% for easier value estimation
Lines 56-61: geom_polygon() creates the filled radar shapes with 20% transparency and thicker lines (1.5px)
Lines 63-68: Adds prominent points at each vertex
Lines 70-77: geom_text() labels each point with the original (non-normalized) value, positioned above the point with vjust = -1.2
Lines 81-85: Extends y-axis limit to 1.15 to accommodate value labels above 100%
Lines 87-115: Custom color scales with descriptive legend labels (“Compact Cars” instead of just “compact”)
Lines 117-121: Data-driven title and subtitle that highlight the key insights discovered in the visualization
Lines 123-182: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Centered multi-line title with proper line height - Insight-rich subtitle - Detailed caption with methodology notes - Bold axis labels with proper spacing - Horizontal legend with larger key sizes - Subtle gridlines for readability

Final result: A publication-ready radar plot that tells a complete story. The overlaid profiles make comparisons immediate, while the actual values at each point provide precision. The data-driven title and subtitle highlight the key finding: the trade-off between fuel efficiency (compact advantage) and power (SUV advantage). Reference lines help with value estimation, and the professional styling is suitable for reports, presentations, or publications.

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Radar Plots






Radar Plots Work Well When:
✅ Comparing 3-8 dimensions - Sweet spot for readability (too few = use bar chart, too many = cluttered)
✅ Showing balanced profiles - Excellent for highlighting well-rounded vs. specialized entities
✅ Dimensions are comparable - All metrics should be normalized or naturally on similar scales
✅ Pattern recognition matters - Shape of the polygon conveys meaningful information
✅ Comparing few entities - Works best with 2-5 overlaid profiles
✅ Circular arrangement makes sense - Variables don’t have a natural linear order
Avoid Radar Plots When:
❌ Precise value comparison needed - Bar charts are more accurate
❌ Too many dimensions (>10) - Becomes unreadable
❌ Too many entities (>5) - Overlaps make it confusing
❌ Variables have natural order - Use parallel coordinates plot instead
❌ Negative values present - Radar plots work poorly with negatives
❌ Variables are on very different scales - Even normalization may mislead
❌ Axis order affects interpretation - Changing variable order changes the shape, which can be misleading

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Radar Plots:

Always normalize your data - Use rescale() to put all variables on the same 0-1 scale for fair comparison
Limit the number of entities - Overlay at most 3-5 profiles. More becomes cluttered and hard to compare
Use meaningful axis labels - Multi-line labels work well in circular layouts; break long labels into 2-3 lines
Add semi-transparent fills - Use alpha = 0.2-0.3 so overlapping areas are visible
Include actual values - Add text labels with original (non-normalized) values at key points
Choose contrasting colors - Ensure colors are distinguishable and colorblind-friendly
Add reference circles - Use geom_hline() with dashed lines at quartiles (25%, 50%, 75%)
Order variables thoughtfully - Adjacent variables will visually cluster; consider which comparisons matter most
Extend axis limits for labels - Set limits = c(0, 1.15) to prevent labels from being cut off
Tell a story in the title - Highlight the key insight (e.g., “Compact cars excel in efficiency”) rather than just describing
Provide normalization context - Always note in the caption that values are normalized and what scale is used
Consider alternatives first - Bar charts, parallel coordinates, or heatmaps may be clearer for your data
Use thicker lines - linewidth = 1.2-1.5 makes polygons more visible, especially with transparency
Keep gridlines subtle - Use light gray (#E9ECEF) and dashed lines so they don’t overpower the data
Add sample sizes - Include entity sample sizes in legend labels or caption for context

title: Creating Insightful Radar Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Radar Plot Pitfalls:

Forgetting to normalize - Comparing raw values on different scales is meaningless
Too many overlapping profiles - More than 5 entities becomes a tangled mess
Poor color choices - Similar colors make it impossible to distinguish profiles
No value labels - Forces viewers to estimate from angles and distances (inaccurate)
Misleading variable order - Changing the order changes the shape, which can manipulate perception
Using for time series - Line charts are far superior for temporal data
Comparing unrelated metrics - All dimensions should be conceptually related
No legend - Viewers can’t identify which profile is which
Cluttered gridlines - Too many reference circles create visual noise
Forgetting axis limits - Default limits may cut off labels or create awkward spacing

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated Sankey diagrams using ggplot2 and the ggsankey package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Sankey diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows between categories, showing how quantities split, merge, and transition through different stages or groups.
We’ll create a fictional dataset representing student enrollment flows through different college majors and their career outcomes.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated Sankey diagrams using ggplot2 and the ggsankey package. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Sankey diagrams are excellent for visualizing flows between categories, showing how quantities split, merge, and transition through different stages or groups.
We’ll create a fictional dataset representing student enrollment flows through different college majors and their career outcomes.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(ggsankey)   # For Sankey diagram functionality
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Create sample data: student flow from major to career
data_flow <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:300,
  major = sample(c("Engineering", "Business", "Liberal Arts"), 300, 
                 replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.3)),
  year = "2020"
) %>%
  # Add career outcomes based on major with some realistic patterns
  mutate(
    career = case_when(
      major == "Engineering" ~ sample(c("Tech", "Consulting", "Other"), 
                                     n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                     prob = c(0.6, 0.3, 0.1)),
      major == "Business" ~ sample(c("Finance", "Consulting", "Tech", "Other"), 
                                  n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                  prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1)),
      major == "Liberal Arts" ~ sample(c("Education", "Consulting", "Other"), 
                                      n(), replace = TRUE, 
                                      prob = c(0.4, 0.3, 0.3))
    )
  )

# Transform data to long format for Sankey diagram
data_sankey <- data_flow %>%
  make_long(major, career)

# Preview the data
head(data_sankey)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  x      node         next_x next_node 
  <fct>  <chr>        <fct>  <chr>     
1 major  Business     career Consulting
2 career Consulting   <NA>   <NA>      
3 major  Business     career Consulting
4 career Consulting   <NA>   <NA>      
5 major  Liberal Arts career Other     
6 career Other        <NA>   <NA>

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Sankey Diagram
Let’s start with a simple Sankey diagram showing the flow from college majors to careers.

ggplot(data_sankey, aes(x = x, 
                        next_x = next_x, 
                        node = node, 
                        next_node = next_node,
                        fill = factor(node))) +  # Map nodes to fill color
  geom_sankey()                                  # Create Sankey diagram









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_sankey, aes(x = x, next_x = next_x, node = node, next_node = next_node)) - Initializes the plot with the transformed Sankey data, mapping current and next positions for flow visualization
Line 6: geom_sankey() - Adds the Sankey flow ribbons showing how quantities move from majors (left) to careers (right)

What we have so far: A functional but basic Sankey diagram. The flows are visible but the chart lacks proper labels, context, and visual refinement.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by adding node labels, better colors, flow transparency, and applying a clean theme.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Node labels showing category names
Custom color palette for better distinction
Flow transparency to show overlapping patterns
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Smooth flow curves for better aesthetics



ggplot(data_sankey, aes(x = x, 
                        next_x = next_x, 
                        node = node, 
                        next_node = next_node,
                        fill = factor(node),
                        label = node)) +
  geom_sankey(flow.alpha = 0.5,                  # Semi-transparent flows
              node.color = "gray30",              # Node border color
              smooth = 8) +                       # Smoothness of curves
  geom_sankey_label(size = 3.5,                  # Add labels to nodes
                    color = "white",
                    fill = "gray20") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") +      # Apply color palette
  labs(
    title = "Student Flow from College Major to Career",
    subtitle = "Tracking 300 graduates from enrollment to first job",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "none",                    # Remove legend (labels on nodes)
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),               # Remove x-axis text
    panel.grid = element_blank()                 # Remove grid lines
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 1-6: aes() includes label = node to enable text labels on the nodes
Lines 7-9: geom_sankey() with flow.alpha = 0.5 for semi-transparent flows, node.color for border definition, and smooth = 8 for curved flow ribbons
Lines 10-12: geom_sankey_label() adds text labels directly on nodes with white text on dark gray backgrounds
Line 13: scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "plasma") - Applies a colorblind-friendly color palette from the viridis family
Lines 14-19: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context
Line 20: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 21-26: theme() - Customizes theme by removing the legend (redundant with labels), x-axis text, and grid lines for a cleaner appearance

What we have now: A much more readable diagram with clear labels, professional color scheme, and clean formatting. The transparent flows and smooth curves make it easier to trace individual pathways.

title: Creating Beautiful Sankey Diagrams with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with custom colors by category, flow annotations, enhanced typography, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Custom color scheme with meaningful colors for each category
Stage labels showing “Major” and “Career” columns
Flow thickness proportional to student counts
Enhanced node labels with better positioning
Professional typography with refined spacing
Data source caption for proper attribution
Count annotations showing total flows
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate flow statistics for annotations
flow_summary <- data_sankey %>%
  filter(!is.na(next_node)) %>%
  group_by(node, next_node) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = 'drop')

# Define custom color palette by category
category_colors <- c(
  # Majors
  "Engineering" = "#2C5F8D",      # Blue
  "Business" = "#52A675",         # Green  
  "Liberal Arts" = "#E76F51",     # Coral
  # Careers
  "Tech" = "#264653",             # Dark blue
  "Finance" = "#2A9D8F",          # Teal
  "Consulting" = "#E9C46A",       # Gold
  "Education" = "#F4A261",        # Orange
  "Other" = "#9E9E9E"             # Gray
)

ggplot(data_sankey, aes(x = x, 
                        next_x = next_x, 
                        node = node, 
                        next_node = next_node,
                        fill = factor(node),
                        label = node)) +
  # Sankey flow layer
  geom_sankey(flow.alpha = 0.6,
              node.color = "gray20",
              smooth = 10,
              width = 0.1) +                     # Thinner nodes for more space
  # Node labels with custom styling
  geom_sankey_label(size = 4,
                    color = "white",
                    fill = "gray20",
                    fontface = "bold") +
  # Apply custom color palette
  scale_fill_manual(values = category_colors) +
  # Format axes
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("College Major", "Career Path"),
                   expand = expansion(mult = c(0.1, 0.1))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Career Outcomes Vary Significantly by College Major",
    subtitle = "Engineering students gravitate toward tech roles, while business majors disperse across multiple sectors",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: Fictional dataset of 300 graduates (Class of 2020) | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add stage annotations
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -20, 
           label = "STARTING MAJOR", 
           size = 4, fontface = "bold", 
           color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = -20, 
           label = "CAREER FIELD", 
           size = 4, fontface = "bold", 
           color = "gray30") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  margin = margin(b = 20)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0.5, 
                                margin = margin(t = 20)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold",
                               color = "#2C3E50",
                               margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend removal
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-5: Calculates flow statistics between each major and career combination for potential annotations
Lines 8-21: Defines a custom color palette where each category (major and career) gets a meaningful color that reflects its domain (blues for tech-related, greens for business, etc.)
Line 23: ggplot() initializes the plot with all necessary aesthetics for Sankey diagrams
Lines 28-31: geom_sankey() creates the flow ribbons with increased transparency, darker node borders, higher smoothness, and narrower node width for better spacing
Lines 33-36: geom_sankey_label() adds bold white text labels on dark backgrounds directly on each node
Line 38: scale_fill_manual() applies our custom color palette to the nodes
Lines 40-41: scale_x_discrete() adds custom labels for the two stages (“College Major” and “Career Path”) with proper spacing
Lines 43-49: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, a subtitle with specific insights, and detailed caption with attribution
Lines 51-59: annotate() adds stage labels at the bottom of each column for additional context
Line 60: theme_void() starts with a completely blank canvas (appropriate for flow diagrams)
Lines 61-81: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Centered and styled title/subtitle for visual hierarchy - Custom axis text showing stage names - Legend removal (redundant with node labels) - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready Sankey diagram that clearly communicates the flow from majors to careers. The custom color scheme, clear labels, and professional formatting make this suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations. The visualization tells a clear story about career trajectories for different majors.

text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Sankey Diagrams:

Prepare data properly - Use ggsankey::make_long() to transform your data from wide to the long format required for Sankey diagrams
Control flow transparency - Use flow.alpha between 0.4-0.7 to show overlapping flows without obscuring the visualization
Smooth your curves - Adjust the smooth parameter (typically 8-12) to create aesthetically pleasing flow ribbons
Label your nodes - Always use geom_sankey_label() to add text directly on nodes rather than relying on legends
Choose colors meaningfully - Assign colors that match the semantic meaning of categories (e.g., blue for tech, green for environment)
Mind the node width - Adjust width parameter (default 0.1) to balance node visibility with flow space
Remove unnecessary elements - Sankey diagrams work best with theme_void() or minimal themes; avoid grid lines
Add stage labels - Use annotate() or scale_x_discrete() to label what each column represents
Consider flow direction - For time-based flows, ensure progression moves left-to-right (natural reading direction)
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 12, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Want to create multi-stage Sankey diagrams?
You can extend the flow to show multiple transitions:
# Create data with three stages
data_multi <- tibble(
  student_id = 1:200,
  major = sample(c("STEM", "Arts", "Business"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  internship = sample(c("Tech", "Finance", "Nonprofit"), 200, replace = TRUE),
  career = sample(c("Tech", "Finance", "Education", "Other"), 200, replace = TRUE)
)

# Transform to long format
data_sankey_multi <- data_multi %>%
  make_long(major, internship, career)

# Plot with three stages
ggplot(data_sankey_multi, 
       aes(x = x, next_x = next_x, 
           node = node, next_node = next_node,
           fill = factor(node), label = node)) +
  geom_sankey(flow.alpha = 0.5, smooth = 10) +
  geom_sankey_label(size = 3.5, color = "white") +
  theme_void()
This creates a three-stage flow showing transitions through major → internship → career.
