title: Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Density Plot
Let’s start with a simple density plot showing the distribution of diamond carat weights.

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_density()                          # Create density plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat)) - Initializes the plot with our diamond data, mapping carat weight to the x-axis
Line 2: geom_density() - Adds a density curve showing the smoothed probability distribution of carat values

What we have so far: A functional but basic density plot. The distribution shape is visible but the chart lacks context, comparative groups, and visual refinement.

title: Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by comparing multiple groups, adding fill colors, adjusting transparency, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Multiple density curves comparing different cut qualities
Color fill with transparency to show overlapping distributions
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
Formatted x-axis for better readability



ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut)) +      # Add fill aesthetic by cut
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +                             # Density with transparency
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                   # Apply color palette
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) +      # Set x-axis breaks
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Diamond Carat Weight by Cut Quality",  # Main title
    subtitle = "Higher quality cuts tend toward smaller carat sizes",  # Subtitle
    x = "Carat Weight",                                   # X-axis label
    y = "Density",                                        # Y-axis label
    fill = "Cut Quality"                                  # Legend title
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                       # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), # Bold title
    legend.position = "top"                               # Move legend to top
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: aes(x = carat, fill = cut) - Maps carat weight to x-axis and cut quality to fill color, enabling comparison across groups
Line 2: geom_density(alpha = 0.6) - Creates overlapping density curves with 60% opacity to show where distributions intersect
Line 3: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer
Line 4: scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.5)) - Sets regular x-axis breaks every 0.5 carats for easier reading
Lines 5-11: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle providing insight, axis labels, and legend title for context
Line 12: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements
Lines 13-16: theme() - Customizes title formatting and moves legend to top for better space utilization

What we have now: A much more informative chart showing how carat distributions differ across cut qualities. The transparent overlays and clean formatting make comparisons easy, revealing that ideal cuts concentrate in smaller carat ranges.

title: Density Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with ridge-style presentation, statistical annotations, enhanced colors, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Stacked density presentation for clearer group comparison
Statistical reference lines showing means for each group
Sample size annotations in legend
Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Rug plot showing individual observations
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
cut_summary <- data_diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    mean_carat = mean(carat),                      # Mean carat
    median_carat = median(carat),                  # Median carat
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly gradient)
cut_colors <- c(
  "Fair" = "#D55E00",                              # Orange-red for lowest
  "Good" = "#E69F00",                              # Orange
  "Very Good" = "#F0E442",                         # Yellow
  "Premium" = "#009E73",                           # Green
  "Ideal" = "#0072B2"                              # Blue for highest
)

ggplot(data_diamonds, aes(x = carat, fill = cut, color = cut)) +
  # Main density curves
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Add rug plot showing individual observations (sampled to avoid overplotting)
  geom_rug(data = data_diamonds %>% 
             group_by(cut) %>% 
             slice_sample(prop = 0.01),
           alpha = 0.3, length = unit(0.02, "npc")) +
  # Add mean reference lines
  geom_vline(data = cut_summary,
             aes(xintercept = mean_carat, color = cut),
             linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7,
             alpha = 0.8) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cut_colors,
                    name = "Cut Quality",
                    labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                   " (n = ", 
                                   format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                   ")")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = cut_colors,
                     name = "Cut Quality",
                     labels = paste0(levels(data_diamonds$cut), 
                                    " (n = ", 
                                    format(cut_summary$n, big.mark = ","), 
                                    ")")) +
  # Format x-axis with better breaks and labels
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, by = 0.25),
                     labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))) +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Diamond Carat Distribution Reveals Quality-Size Trade-offs",
    subtitle = "Ideal cut diamonds concentrate around 0.5-1.0 carats, while lower grades show broader distributions\nDashed lines indicate mean values for each cut quality",
    x = "Carat Weight",
    y = "Probability Density",
    caption = "Data source: ggplot2 diamonds dataset (53,940 diamonds) | Sample of 1% shown in rug plot | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for interpretation
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 2.5,
           label = "Ideal cuts peak\nat lower carats",
           size = 3.5, fontface = "italic",
           color = "gray30", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("curve", x = 2.3, y = 2.4, 
           xend = 1.2, yend = 3.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"), type = "closed"),
           curvature = -0.3, color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.4),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes, means, and medians for each cut category, used for annotations and legend labels
Lines 12-19: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from warm (low quality) to cool (high quality) colors, optimized for colorblind accessibility
Line 21: ggplot() initializes the plot with carat mapped to x-axis and cut quality mapped to both fill and color (for consistency)
Lines 23-24: geom_density() creates density curves with transparency and thicker lines for better visibility
Lines 25-29: geom_rug() adds small tick marks at the bottom showing individual data points (sampled to 1% to avoid overplotting)
Lines 30-35: geom_vline() adds dashed vertical lines at the mean carat value for each cut quality, color-coded by group
Lines 37-48: scale_fill_manual() and scale_color_manual() apply our custom color palette and enhance legend labels with sample sizes in parentheses
Lines 50-52: scale_x_continuous() sets fine-grained breaks (every 0.25 carats) with proper decimal formatting
Line 54: scale_y_continuous() expands the top slightly to prevent clipping
Lines 56-62: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells a story, multi-line subtitle with interpretation guidance, and detailed caption with attribution and methodology notes
Lines 64-71: annotate() adds a text annotation with an arrow pointing to the Ideal cut peak, helping guide interpretation
Lines 72-99: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Multi-line subtitle with adjusted line height - Legend positioned at bottom with custom sizing - Grid customization with lighter lines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that clearly communicates how diamond carat distributions vary by cut quality. The combination of overlapping density curves, mean reference lines, rug plot, and interpretive annotations creates a comprehensive and accessible chart suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Density Plots:

Adjust bandwidth carefully - Use the adjust parameter in geom_density() (default = 1) to control smoothness. Lower values show more detail, higher values create smoother curves
Use transparency for overlaps - Set alpha between 0.5-0.7 when comparing multiple groups to show where distributions intersect
Add rug plots strategically - For datasets with <1,000 points per group, show all observations. For larger datasets, sample 1-5% with slice_sample()
Show reference statistics - Add vertical lines for means, medians, or other important values using geom_vline()
Consider the y-axis - Density values can be unintuitive; consider adding “Probability Density” to the label to clarify meaning
Color with purpose - Use color gradients that match the ordering or meaning of your categories
Handle long tails - For highly skewed data, consider log-transforming the x-axis with scale_x_log10()
Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per group in the legend or plot
Choose appropriate alternatives - For discrete data or small samples (<30), consider histograms or violin plots instead
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

       x = "Carat Weight",

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated edge bundling charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic hierarchical plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Edge bundling is an excellent technique for reducing visual clutter in network visualizations by bundling edges that follow similar paths. This creates a cleaner, more organized appearance especially useful for hierarchical data or networks with many connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing organizational relationships and communication patterns within a company.

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated edge bundling charts using ggraph and igraph packages in R. We’ll start with a basic hierarchical plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Edge bundling is an excellent technique for reducing visual clutter in network visualizations by bundling edges that follow similar paths. This creates a cleaner, more organized appearance especially useful for hierarchical data or networks with many connections.
We’ll create a dataset representing organizational relationships and communication patterns within a company.

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # For data manipulation
library(igraph)     # For network data structures
library(ggraph)     # For network visualization
library(scales)     # For formatting

# Create hierarchical structure (organizational chart)
hierarchy <- data.frame(
  from = c("CEO", "CEO", "CEO",
           "VP Sales", "VP Sales", "VP Sales",
           "VP Tech", "VP Tech", "VP Tech", "VP Tech",
           "VP Ops", "VP Ops"),
  to = c("VP Sales", "VP Tech", "VP Ops",
         "Sales East", "Sales West", "Sales Int'l",
         "Dev Team", "QA Team", "Design", "Data Science",
         "Logistics", "Customer Service")
)

# Create edges for cross-department communication
communications <- data.frame(
  from = c("Sales East", "Sales West", "Dev Team", "QA Team", 
           "Design", "Data Science", "Logistics", "Customer Service",
           "Sales Int'l", "Dev Team", "Sales East"),
  to = c("Dev Team", "Design", "QA Team", "Dev Team",
         "Dev Team", "Dev Team", "Sales East", "Sales West",
         "Data Science", "Data Science", "Logistics"),
  weight = c(15, 12, 25, 30, 18, 22, 10, 14, 16, 20, 8)
)

# Combine hierarchy and communications
all_edges <- bind_rows(
  hierarchy %>% mutate(type = "hierarchy", weight = 1),
  communications %>% mutate(type = "communication")
)

# Get all unique nodes
all_nodes <- data.frame(
  name = unique(c(all_edges$from, all_edges$to))
) %>%
  mutate(
    level = case_when(
      name == "CEO" ~ 1,
      name %in% c("VP Sales", "VP Tech", "VP Ops") ~ 2,
      TRUE ~ 3
    ),
    department = case_when(
      name == "CEO" ~ "Executive",
      grepl("Sales|Sales East|Sales West|Sales Int'l", name) ~ "Sales",
      grepl("Tech|Dev|QA|Design|Data", name) ~ "Technology",
      grepl("Ops|Logistics|Customer", name) ~ "Operations",
      TRUE ~ "Executive"
    )
  )

# Create graph from HIERARCHY ONLY for proper tree structure
hierarchy_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(d = hierarchy, vertices = all_nodes, directed = TRUE)

# Add all edges as attributes for later use
E(hierarchy_graph)$type <- "hierarchy"
V(hierarchy_graph)$dept <- all_nodes$department[match(V(hierarchy_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]

# Preview the data
head(all_edges)

      from          to      type weight
1      CEO    VP Sales hierarchy      1
2      CEO     VP Tech hierarchy      1
3      CEO      VP Ops hierarchy      1
4 VP Sales  Sales East hierarchy      1
5 VP Sales  Sales West hierarchy      1
6 VP Sales Sales Int'l hierarchy      1

head(all_nodes)

        name level department
1        CEO     1  Executive
2   VP Sales     2      Sales
3    VP Tech     2 Technology
4     VP Ops     2 Operations
5 Sales East     3      Sales
6 Sales West     3      Sales

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 1: Basic Hierarchical Layout
Let’s start with a simple hierarchical tree showing the organizational structure.

ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "tree") +
  geom_edge_link() +                    # Draw edges
  geom_node_point(size = 5) +           # Draw nodes
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),     # Add labels
                 repel = TRUE, 
                 size = 3)









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "tree") - Initializes the plot using a tree layout which arranges nodes hierarchically
Line 2: geom_edge_link() - Draws straight lines representing connections
Line 3: geom_node_point() - Draws circles for each node
Lines 4-6: geom_node_text() - Adds labels with repel to avoid overlaps

What we have so far: A functional but basic tree layout. The hierarchy is visible but with many cross-connections, the chart becomes cluttered and hard to read.

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
section: Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement with Edge Bundling
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement with Edge Bundling
Now we’ll improve the chart by applying edge bundling, adding colors, and better styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Dendrogram layout for hierarchical display
Color coding by department
Node sizes by hierarchical level
Diagonal edges for tree structure
Improved labels with better positioning
Clean theme removing axes
Title and legend for context



# Use linear dendrogram layout first
ggraph(hierarchy_graph, layout = "dendrogram", circular = FALSE) +
  # Draw edges
  geom_edge_diagonal(alpha = 0.4, color = "gray50") +
  # Draw nodes colored by department
  geom_node_point(aes(size = (4 - level) * 3, color = dept),
                  alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name),
                 hjust = 1.1,
                 size = 3) +
  # Apply color palette
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2",
                     name = "Department") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Organizational Hierarchy (Dendrogram Layout)",
    subtitle = "Hierarchical structure showing reporting relationships",
    caption = "Dendrogram layout organizes nodes by hierarchical level"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggraph() with dendrogram layout and circular = TRUE creates a radial hierarchical layout
Line 1: ggraph() with dendrogram layout (horizontal tree structure)
Line 3: geom_edge_diagonal() creates curved diagonal edges connecting parent to child nodes
Lines 5-6: geom_node_point() draws nodes sized by level and colored by department
Lines 8-11: geom_node_text() adds labels positioned to the left of nodes
Lines 13-14: scale_color_brewer() applies colorblind-friendly palette
Line 15: scale_size_identity() uses calculated sizes directly
Line 16: coord_flip() rotates to vertical orientation
Lines 17-21: labs() adds comprehensive labels
Line 31: theme_graph() removes axes and grid
Lines 32-36: Custom theme adjustments

What we have now: A much cleaner visualization with edge bundling reducing clutter. The circular layout and color coding make it easier to see both hierarchy and cross-department communications.

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with enhanced styling, edge filtering, annotations, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Separate hierarchy and communication edges with different styling
Edge width based on communication volume
Custom color palette with better contrast
Sector labels showing departments
Communication statistics annotations
Enhanced node styling with borders
Gradient edge coloring by weight
Professional typography and spacing



# Create full graph with all edges for visualization
full_graph <- graph_from_data_frame(d = all_edges, vertices = all_nodes, directed = TRUE)

# Add edge attributes
E(full_graph)$edge_type <- all_edges$type
E(full_graph)$edge_weight <- all_edges$weight

# Add node attributes
V(full_graph)$dept <- all_nodes$department[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]
V(full_graph)$node_level <- all_nodes$level[match(V(full_graph)$name, all_nodes$name)]

# Define custom color palette
dept_colors <- c(
  "Executive" = "#8B4789",
  "Sales" = "#E76F51",
  "Technology" = "#2C5F8D",
  "Operations" = "#52A675"
)

# Create layout
set.seed(42)

ggraph(full_graph, layout = "fr") +
  # Draw edges with different styles by type
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = edge_type, 
                     alpha = edge_type,
                     width = ifelse(edge_type == "communication", edge_weight/10, 0.5)),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, 'mm')),
                 end_cap = circle(3, 'mm')) +
  # Color edges by type
  scale_edge_colour_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = "gray70", 
                                      "communication" = "#a50f15"),
                          name = "Connection Type") +
  scale_edge_alpha_manual(values = c("hierarchy" = 0.3,
                                     "communication" = 0.7),
                         guide = "none") +
  scale_edge_width_identity() +
  # Draw nodes with enhanced styling
  geom_node_point(aes(size = (4 - node_level) * 4, 
                      fill = dept),
                  shape = 21,
                  color = "gray20",
                  stroke = 1,
                  alpha = 0.9) +
  # Add node labels
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name,
                     fontface = ifelse(node_level == 1, "bold", "plain")),
                 repel = TRUE,
                 size = 3.5,
                 max.overlaps = 20) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = dept_colors,
                    name = "Department") +
  scale_size_identity() +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Organizational Network: Hierarchical Structure and Cross-Department Communications",
    subtitle = "Force-directed layout showing both reporting lines (gray) and communication flows (red)",
    caption = "Data source: Simulated organizational data | Edge width indicates communication volume | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add annotation for communication stats
  annotate("text",
           x = -2, 
           y = 2,
           label = paste0("Communication Flows:\n",
                         "Total Links: ", sum(all_edges$type == "communication"), "\n",
                         "Departments: ", n_distinct(all_nodes$department) - 1, "\n",
                         "Avg Weight: ", round(mean(communications$weight), 1)),
           hjust = 0,
           vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5,
           color = "gray30",
           fontface = "italic",
           lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_graph(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16,
                              hjust = 0.5,
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "#5A6C7D",
                                  hjust = 0.5,
                                  lineheight = 1.3,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D",
                                hjust = 0.5,
                                margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = "gray80"),
    legend.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    
    # Background
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-3: Assigns edge type and weight attributes to the graph edges
Lines 6-7: Calculates in-degree and out-degree for each node
Lines 10-15: Defines custom color palette for the four departments
Lines 18-19: Creates layout with set seed for reproducibility
Line 21: ggraph() initializes plot with pre-calculated layout
Lines 23-30: First geom_conn_bundle() draws hierarchy edges (reporting structure) as light gray with lower opacity
Lines 32-39: Second geom_conn_bundle() draws communication edges with color gradient and variable width
Lines 41-46: Scale functions for edge color and width
Lines 48-53: geom_node_point() draws nodes as circles with borders, sized inversely by level (CEO largest)
Lines 55-62: geom_node_text() adds labels with automatic rotation following circular layout, bold for top level
Lines 64-66: scale_fill_manual() applies custom department colors
Lines 68-72: labs() adds comprehensive title, subtitle, and detailed caption
Lines 74-86: annotate() adds communication statistics in top left corner
Lines 87-115: Comprehensive theme customization including enhanced typography, legend styling, and proper margins

Final result: A publication-ready edge bundling visualization that clearly separates hierarchical structure from communication patterns. The bundled edges reduce clutter while making it easy to see which departments communicate most frequently. The combination of size coding, color coding, and dual edge types creates a comprehensive visualization suitable for executive presentations, reports, or publications.

title: Edge Bundling Charts with ggraph
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better Edge Bundling Charts:

Choose appropriate layouts - Circular dendrogram works best for edge bundling; ensure your data has hierarchical structure
Adjust tension carefully - The tension parameter (0-1) controls bundling tightness; 0.8-0.9 usually works well
Separate edge types - Use different styling for hierarchical vs. data edges to maintain clarity
Use transparency wisely - Set alpha 0.3-0.6 for bundled edges to show density without obscuring nodes
Color meaningfully - Use color gradients to show edge properties like weight or frequency
Size nodes by importance - Make higher-level nodes larger for visual hierarchy
Rotate labels appropriately - Use node_angle() to rotate labels following the circular layout
Consider audience - Edge bundling works best when viewers need to see overall patterns, not trace individual connections
Limit edge count - Edge bundling is most effective with 20-200 edges; too few doesn’t show benefit, too many becomes messy
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("bundling.png", width = 12, height = 12, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

)

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmaps are powerful visualizations for displaying matrix data where values are represented as colors. They excel at revealing patterns, correlations, and clusters in large datasets. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated heatmaps using ggplot2.
We’ll explore correlations between vehicle characteristics and visualize temporal patterns in fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset.






What Makes Heatmaps Powerful:
Heatmaps excel at: - Visualizing correlation matrices - Showing patterns across two categorical dimensions - Revealing clusters and groupings in data - Displaying temporal patterns (time × category) - Comparing many variables simultaneously - Identifying hot spots and cold spots in data

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmaps are powerful visualizations for displaying matrix data where values are represented as colors. They excel at revealing patterns, correlations, and clusters in large datasets. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated heatmaps using ggplot2.
We’ll explore correlations between vehicle characteristics and visualize temporal patterns in fuel efficiency using the mpg dataset.






What Makes Heatmaps Powerful:
Heatmaps excel at: - Visualizing correlation matrices - Showing patterns across two categorical dimensions - Revealing clusters and groupings in data - Displaying temporal patterns (time × category) - Comparing many variables simultaneously - Identifying hot spots and cold spots in data

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting
library(viridis)        # For color scales

# Prepare correlation data
# Select numeric variables for correlation
numeric_vars <- mpg %>%
  select(displ, cyl, cty, hwy, year) %>%
  na.omit()

# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars)

# Convert to long format for ggplot
cor_data <- cor_matrix %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "correlation"
  )

# Preview the data
head(cor_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 3
  var1  var2  correlation
  <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
1 displ displ       1    
2 displ cyl         0.930
3 displ cty        -0.799
4 displ hwy        -0.766
5 displ year        0.148
6 cyl   displ       0.930

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Heatmap
Let’s start with a simple heatmap showing correlations between variables.

ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile()                                       # Create heatmap tiles









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(cor_data, aes(x = var1, y = var2, fill = correlation)) - Maps first variable to x-axis, second variable to y-axis, and correlation values to fill color
Line 2: geom_tile() - Creates rectangular tiles colored by the correlation values

What we have so far: A functional heatmap showing correlation patterns, but it uses a default color scale (blue gradient), lacks proper labeling, has no value annotations, and needs better formatting to be interpretable.

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add better colors, value labels, improved styling, and meaningful axis labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Diverging color scale (red-white-blue) for positive/negative correlations
Value labels showing exact correlation coefficients
White borders between tiles for clarity
Better variable names replacing technical labels
Correlation strength interpretation in colors
Title and context explaining the visualization
Legend improvements with better formatting
Axis text rotation for readability



# Create better variable labels
var_labels <- c(
  "displ" = "Engine Size",
  "cyl" = "Cylinders",
  "cty" = "City MPG",
  "hwy" = "Highway MPG",
  "year" = "Model Year"
)

# Update data with better labels
cor_data_labeled <- cor_data %>%
  mutate(
    var1_label = var_labels[var1],
    var2_label = var_labels[var2]
  )

ggplot(cor_data_labeled, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +    # White borders between tiles
  geom_text(
    aes(label = round(correlation, 2)),             # Add correlation values
    color = "black",
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",                                # Red for negative
    mid = "white",                                  # White for zero
    high = "#2C5F8D",                               # Blue for positive
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Correlation\nCoefficient",
    breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
    labels = c("-1.0\n(Strong Negative)", "-0.5", "0.0\n(No Correlation)", 
               "0.5", "1.0\n(Strong Positive)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix: Vehicle Characteristics",
    subtitle = "Exploring relationships between engine specs and fuel efficiency",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: EPA fuel economy dataset | Values show Pearson correlation coefficients"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles









Code Explanation
Lines 2-8: Creates a named vector mapping technical variable names to human-readable labels
Lines 10-15: Adds new columns with readable labels for both variables
Line 17: Maps data with readable labels to axes
Line 18: geom_tile() with white borders (1.5px width) separating each cell for clarity
Lines 19-24: geom_text() overlays correlation values (rounded to 2 decimals) as bold black text on each tile
Lines 25-34: scale_fill_gradient2() creates a diverging color scale: - Red for negative correlations - White for zero correlation - Blue for positive correlations - Custom labels explaining correlation strength
Lines 35-40: Comprehensive labeling explaining what the heatmap shows
Lines 41-52: Theme customization with angled x-axis labels, bold text, no gridlines, and centered titles
Line 53: coord_fixed() ensures tiles are square (equal width and height)

What we have now: A much more informative correlation heatmap with clear value labels, meaningful colors (red=negative, blue=positive), and readable variable names. The diverging color scale makes it immediately obvious which variables are positively or negatively correlated. The white borders and square tiles create a clean, professional appearance.

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready heatmap with clustering, dendrograms, and enhanced annotations.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
Significance indicators showing which correlations are statistically significant
Annotated insights highlighting key patterns
Lower triangular display avoiding redundancy
Enhanced color scheme with better discrimination
Correlation strength categories in annotations
Professional typography and spacing
Statistical context with p-values



# Perform hierarchical clustering to reorder variables
dist_matrix <- as.dist(1 - abs(cor_matrix))
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix)
var_order <- rownames(cor_matrix)[hc$order]

# Calculate p-values for correlations
library(Hmisc)
cor_test <- rcorr(as.matrix(numeric_vars))
p_values <- cor_test$P

# Convert p-values to long format
p_data <- p_values %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("var1") %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -var1,
    names_to = "var2",
    values_to = "p_value"
  )

# Combine correlation and p-value data
cor_data_full <- cor_data %>%
  left_join(p_data, by = c("var1", "var2")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Reorder by clustering
    var1 = factor(var1, levels = var_order),
    var2 = factor(var2, levels = var_order),
    # Add readable labels
    var1_label = var_labels[as.character(var1)],
    var2_label = var_labels[as.character(var2)],
    # Determine significance
    significant = p_value < 0.05,
    sig_label = case_when(
      p_value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p_value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p_value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    ),
    # Only show lower triangle (avoid redundancy)
    show_tile = as.numeric(var1) >= as.numeric(var2)
  )

# Filter to lower triangle only
cor_data_lower <- cor_data_full %>%
  filter(show_tile)

# Identify strong correlations for annotation
strong_cor <- cor_data_lower %>%
  filter(abs(correlation) > 0.8, var1 != var2) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

ggplot(cor_data_lower, aes(x = var1_label, y = var2_label, fill = correlation)) +
  
  # Add tiles with borders
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  
  # Add correlation values with significance stars
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(correlation, 2), "\n", sig_label)),
    color = ifelse(abs(cor_data_lower$correlation) > 0.6, "white", "black"),
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  
  # Highlight diagonal
  geom_tile(
    data = cor_data_lower %>% filter(var1 == var2),
    color = "#2C3E50",
    linewidth = 3,
    fill = NA
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for strongest correlation
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]),
    xend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.5,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    yend = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")),
    color = "#52A675",
    linewidth = 1.5
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = which(var_order == strong_cor$var1[1]) + 0.6,
    y = which(var_order == strong_cor$var2[1]),
    label = paste0("Strongest: ", round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3)),
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#52A675"
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#D32F2F",                                # Darker red
    mid = "#FFFFFF",
    high = "#1976D2",                               # Darker blue
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    name = "Pearson\nCorrelation",
    breaks = seq(-1, 1, by = 0.5),
    labels = function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Correlation Matrix with Hierarchical Clustering and Significance Testing",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Variables reordered by similarity | Highway and City MPG are perfectly correlated (r = ",
      round(strong_cor$correlation[1], 3), ", p < 0.001)\n",
      "Engine size strongly correlates with cylinders | Significance: *** p < 0.001, ** p < 0.01, * p < 0.05"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data source: EPA fuel economy data | Lower triangle shown to avoid redundancy | Dark borders highlight diagonal\nVariables clustered using hierarchical clustering (1 - |correlation|) | White text indicates |r| > 0.6 | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 15,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50",
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1,
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    
    # Remove grid and ticks
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  ) +
  
  coord_fixed()                                     # Square tiles









Code Explanation
Lines 2-4: Performs hierarchical clustering on variables using 1 - |correlation| as distance, grouping similar variables together
Lines 6-8: Uses Hmisc::rcorr() to calculate p-values for all correlations, testing statistical significance
Lines 10-19: Converts p-value matrix to long format for merging with correlation data
Lines 21-41: Combines correlation and p-value data, then: - Reorders variables by clustering - Adds readable labels - Creates significance indicators (, , ) - Filters to show only lower triangle (avoiding redundant upper triangle)
Lines 43-45: Filters to show only the lower triangular portion
Lines 47-50: Identifies the strongest correlations (|r| > 0.8) for annotation
Lines 54-56: Creates tiles with thick white borders
Lines 58-65: Adds text labels showing correlation values and significance stars; uses white text for strong correlations (|r| > 0.6) for better contrast
Lines 67-72: Highlights the diagonal with thick dark borders
Lines 74-92: Annotates the strongest correlation with an arrow and label
Lines 94-103: Enhanced diverging color scale with darker red and blue for better contrast
Lines 105-113: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific findings and significance legend
Lines 115-166: Comprehensive theme with professional typography, left-aligned text, and detailed caption

Final result: A publication-ready correlation heatmap with hierarchical clustering, statistical significance indicators, and only the lower triangle displayed (avoiding redundancy). The clustering reveals that related variables (like city and highway MPG) group together. Significance stars show which correlations are statistically reliable. The annotation highlights the strongest relationship. Perfect for research papers, technical reports, or data analysis presentations.

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Heatmap Variations
Different types of heatmaps for different data:

library(patchwork)

# 1. Calendar heatmap (temporal patterns)
# Simulate daily data
set.seed(42)
calendar_data <- tibble(
  date = seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-31"), by = "day"),
  value = rnorm(366, mean = 100, sd = 20)
) %>%
  mutate(
    month = month(date, label = TRUE),
    week = week(date),
    wday = wday(date, label = TRUE, week_start = 1)
  )

v1 <- ggplot(calendar_data, aes(x = week, y = wday, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Value") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 4) +
  labs(title = "Calendar Heatmap", subtitle = "Daily patterns across the year") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 2. Categorical heatmap (class vs. manufacturer)
cat_data <- mpg %>%
  count(class, manufacturer) %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v2 <- ggplot(cat_data, aes(x = manufacturer, y = class, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Categorical Heatmap", subtitle = "Model count by class and manufacturer") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# 3. Binned heatmap (2D density)
v3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 10) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Binned Heatmap (2D Histogram)", subtitle = "Density of observations") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  )

# 4. Annotated heatmap with rankings
rank_data <- mpg %>%
  group_by(class, year) %>%
  summarise(avg_hwy = mean(hwy), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(class = str_to_title(class))

v4 <- ggplot(rank_data, aes(x = as.factor(year), y = class, fill = avg_hwy)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_hwy, 1)), fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#E76F51",
    mid = "#F4A261",
    high = "#52A675",
    midpoint = 25,
    name = "Avg MPG"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Time Series Heatmap", subtitle = "Average highway MPG by class over time") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

(v1 | v2) / (v3 | v4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Heatmap Variations for Different Data Types",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5))
  )














Variation Descriptions:

Calendar Heatmap: Shows daily patterns across months; good for time-based data
Categorical Heatmap: Counts or values across two categorical dimensions
Binned Heatmap: 2D histogram showing density of continuous data
Time Series Heatmap: Shows how values change over time across categories

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
When to Use Heatmaps






Heatmaps Work Well When:
✅ Visualizing correlation matrices - Perfect for showing relationships between many variables
✅ Comparing across two dimensions - Category × category or time × category
✅ Showing patterns in large datasets - Colors reveal trends quickly
✅ Displaying matrix data - Any data that fits in a grid format
✅ Identifying clusters - Similar values group together visually
✅ Time-based patterns - Calendar heatmaps for daily/weekly/monthly trends
Avoid Heatmaps When:
❌ Precise values matter - Hard to distinguish similar colors accurately
❌ Too many categories - More than 20×20 becomes cluttered
❌ Relationships aren’t gridded - Use scatter plots or networks instead
❌ Only a few data points - Use tables or bar charts
❌ Color perception issues - Ensure accessible color scales
❌ 3+ dimensions - Heatmaps are fundamentally 2D

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tips for Creating Better Heatmaps:

Use diverging scales for correlations - Red-white-blue makes positive/negative immediately obvious
Add value labels - Use geom_text() to show exact numbers on tiles
Include white borders - Set color = "white" in geom_tile() to separate cells
Make tiles square - Use coord_fixed() for equal width and height
Consider clustering - Hierarchical clustering reveals natural groupings
Show only lower triangle - For symmetric matrices, avoid redundancy
Add significance indicators - Stars (, , ) show statistical reliability
Choose colors wisely:

Diverging (red-white-blue) for data with meaningful zero/midpoint
Sequential (light-to-dark) for data ranging from low to high
Viridis for perceptually uniform, colorblind-friendly scales

Label axes clearly - Replace technical names with readable labels
Remove gridlines - Set panel.grid = element_blank() for clean appearance
Adjust text color - Use white text on dark tiles, black on light tiles
Consider ordering - Sort by values, clusters, or meaningfully
Add context - Explain what colors represent in title/caption
Test accessibility - Verify colors work for colorblind viewers
Limit categories - More than 15-20 per dimension becomes unreadable
Annotate patterns - Highlight interesting findings with arrows/text
Use appropriate scales - Match color range to data range
Include sample sizes - For aggregated data, show n counts

title: Heatmaps with ggplot2
text:
Common Mistakes to Avoid






Heatmap Pitfalls:

Rainbow colors - Avoid “jet” colormap; use perceptually uniform scales
No value labels - Readers can’t tell 0.7 from 0.8 by color alone
Wrong color scale - Sequential vs. diverging matters
Too many cells - 50×50 grid is unreadable
No clustering - Random order hides patterns
Missing zero - Diverging scales need midpoint at meaningful zero
Inconsistent scales - Different heatmaps should use same color mapping
No borders - Tiles blend together without separation
Poor aspect ratio - Non-square tiles distort perception
Ignoring redundancy - Full correlation matrix shows each value twice
No statistical context - Show significance for correlations
Inaccessible colors - Test with colorblind simulators

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated histograms using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Histograms are fundamental visualizations for understanding the distribution of continuous data, showing the frequency of values within specified intervals (bins).
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, which contains eruption durations and waiting times for the Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone National Park.

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated histograms using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.
Histograms are fundamental visualizations for understanding the distribution of continuous data, showing the frequency of values within specified intervals (bins).
We’ll use the built-in faithful dataset from R, which contains eruption durations and waiting times for the Old Faithful geyser in Yellowstone National Park.

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: use the faithful geyser dataset
data_faithful <- faithful %>%
  as_tibble() %>%                                  # Convert to tibble
  rename(
    eruption_time = eruptions,                     # Rename for clarity
    waiting_time = waiting
  )

# Preview the data

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Histogram
Let’s start with a simple histogram showing the distribution of geyser eruption durations.

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +  # Set up the plot with x variable
  geom_histogram()                                # Create histogram









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) - Initializes the plot with our geyser data, mapping eruption duration to the x-axis
Line 2: geom_histogram() - Adds histogram bars showing the count of eruptions within each time interval (bin)

What we have so far: A functional but basic histogram. The distribution shows a clear bimodal pattern (two peaks) but the chart lacks proper bin sizing, context, and visual refinement. You’ll also see a warning message about the default 30 bins.

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll improve the chart by optimizing bin width, adding color, statistical overlays, and applying a clean theme with better labels.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Optimized bin width for better pattern visibility
Custom fill color with border definition
Density curve overlay showing the smoothed distribution
Mean line as a reference point
Improved axis labels and title for clarity
Clean theme to remove visual clutter
Count labels on bars for precise reading



# Calculate mean for reference line
mean_eruption <- mean(data_faithful$eruption_time)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +
  # Histogram with specified bin width
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25,                      # 0.25 minute bins
                 fill = "#2C5F8D",                     # Custom blue fill
                 color = "white",                      # White borders
                 alpha = 0.8) +                        # Slight transparency
  # Add density curve overlay
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count) * 0.25),     # Scale to match histogram
               color = "#E76F51",                      # Contrasting color
               linewidth = 1.2) +                      # Thicker line
  # Add mean reference line
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_eruption,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray30",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  # Add mean label
  annotate("text", x = mean_eruption + 0.3, y = 35,
           label = paste0("Mean = ", round(mean_eruption, 2), " min"),
           color = "gray30", size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Eruption Duration Shows Bimodal Distribution",
    subtitle = "272 eruptions recorded, grouped into 0.25-minute intervals",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Number of Eruptions"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )









Code Explanation
Line 2: Calculates the mean eruption time for use as a reference line
Line 5: ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) - Initializes the plot
Lines 7-10: geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25) - Creates histogram with 0.25-minute bins (rather than default 30 bins), custom blue fill, white borders for definition, and slight transparency
Lines 12-14: geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(count) * 0.25)) - Adds a density curve scaled to match histogram counts by multiplying by bin width, using a contrasting orange color
Lines 16-19: geom_vline() - Adds a dashed vertical line at the mean eruption duration
Lines 21-23: annotate() - Adds text label showing the exact mean value
Lines 24-29: labs() - Adds descriptive title highlighting the bimodal pattern, subtitle with context, and clear axis labels
Line 30: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme
Lines 31-33: theme() - Customizes title formatting

What we have now: A much more informative chart with appropriate bin sizing revealing the bimodal pattern, a density overlay for smoothed context, and a mean reference line. The clean formatting and proper labeling make it presentation-ready.

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s take it to the next level with color-coded bins, statistical annotations, faceted comparison, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Color-coded bins by eruption type (short vs long)
Multiple statistical reference lines (mean, median, quartiles)
Bin count annotations on top of bars
Normal distribution overlay for comparison
Enhanced typography with refined spacing
Summary statistics panel in the plot
Data source caption for proper attribution
Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance



# Calculate summary statistics
stats_summary <- data_faithful %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_time = mean(eruption_time),
    median_time = median(eruption_time),
    sd_time = sd(eruption_time),
    q25 = quantile(eruption_time, 0.25),
    q75 = quantile(eruption_time, 0.75)
  )

# Create eruption category for color coding
data_faithful <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(
    eruption_type = case_when(
      eruption_time < 3 ~ "Short (< 3 min)",
      TRUE ~ "Long (≥ 3 min)"
    )
  )

# Calculate bin counts for annotations
bin_data <- data_faithful %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(eruption_time, 
                   breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.25),
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  count(bin) %>%
  mutate(midpoint = seq(1.625, 5.375, by = 0.25)[1:n()])

# Define custom colors
eruption_colors <- c(
  "Short (< 3 min)" = "#E76F51",    # Coral for short
  "Long (≥ 3 min)" = "#2C5F8D"      # Blue for long
)

ggplot(data_faithful, aes(x = eruption_time)) +
  # Main histogram with color coding
  geom_histogram(aes(fill = eruption_type),
                 binwidth = 0.25,
                 color = "white",
                 linewidth = 0.3,
                 alpha = 0.85) +
  # Add statistical reference lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = stats_summary$mean_time,
             linetype = "solid",
             color = "gray20",
             linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = stats_summary$median_time,
             linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray40",
             linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(stats_summary$q25, stats_summary$q75),
             linetype = "dotted",
             color = "gray50",
             linewidth = 0.6) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = eruption_colors,
                    name = "Eruption Type") +
  # Format axes
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1.5, 5.5, by = 0.5),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     breaks = seq(0, 40, by = 10)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Geyser Erupts in Two Distinct Patterns",
    subtitle = "Short eruptions (< 3 min) and long eruptions (≥ 3 min) form clear bimodal distribution",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Frequency (Number of Eruptions)",
    caption = "Data source: Azzalini & Bowman (1990) | 272 eruptions | Bin width = 0.25 minutes | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add statistics annotation box
  annotate("rect", 
           xmin = 4.5, xmax = 5.3, 
           ymin = 25, ymax = 38,
           fill = "white", color = "gray30", 
           alpha = 0.9, linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 36,
           label = "Summary Statistics",
           hjust = 0, fontface = "bold",
           size = 3.5, color = "gray20") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 34,
           label = paste0("Mean: ", round(stats_summary$mean_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 32.5,
           label = paste0("Median: ", round(stats_summary$median_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 31,
           label = paste0("SD: ", round(stats_summary$sd_time, 2), " min"),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 29.5,
           label = paste0("n = ", stats_summary$n),
           hjust = 0, size = 3, color = "gray30") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.55, y = 27,
           label = "Lines: mean (solid),\nmedian (dashed),\nquartiles (dotted)",
           hjust = 0, size = 2.5, 
           color = "gray40", lineheight = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    
    # Legend styling
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-11: Calculates comprehensive summary statistics including count, mean, median, standard deviation, and quartiles for annotations
Lines 14-20: Creates a categorical variable eruption_type to classify eruptions as short (< 3 minutes) or long (≥ 3 minutes) for color coding
Lines 23-29: Calculates the count of eruptions in each bin for potential annotations, including midpoints
Lines 32-35: Defines a custom color palette with meaningful colors (coral for short, blue for long eruptions)
Line 37: ggplot() initializes the plot
Lines 39-43: geom_histogram() creates color-coded bins with fill mapped to eruption type, white borders, and transparency
Lines 45-56: Multiple geom_vline() calls add reference lines for mean (solid), median (dashed), and quartiles (dotted) with different line styles and weights
Lines 58-59: scale_fill_manual() applies custom color palette with legend title
Lines 61-64: scale_x_continuous() and scale_y_continuous() format axes with appropriate breaks and expansion
Lines 66-72: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, descriptive subtitle explaining the pattern, and detailed caption with data source attribution
Lines 74-104: Multiple annotate() calls create a statistics summary box in the upper right corner containing: - White rectangle background - Title “Summary Statistics” - Mean, median, standard deviation, and sample size - Legend explaining the reference lines
Lines 105-129: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend positioned at top - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready histogram that clearly communicates the bimodal distribution of Old Faithful eruptions. The color coding distinguishes eruption types, multiple reference lines show key statistics, and the embedded summary box provides complete context. This chart is suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Key Takeaways






Tip



Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Histograms:

Choose bin width carefully - Use the Freedman-Diaconis rule: binwidth = 2 * IQR(x) / (length(x)^(1/3)) or experiment with different values to reveal patterns without over-smoothing
Always specify binwidth or bins - Never rely on ggplot2’s default 30 bins; choose based on your data characteristics and the story you want to tell
Add borders to bars - Use color = "white" or color = "gray30" to define bar boundaries, especially important when bars are adjacent
Consider density overlays - Adding geom_density() scaled appropriately helps show the smoothed distribution pattern
Show reference statistics - Add vertical lines for mean, median, or other important values to provide context
Use color meaningfully - Color-code bins when there are natural categories or thresholds in your data
Mind the y-axis - Label as “Frequency”, “Count”, or “Number of Observations” rather than just “count” for clarity
Handle skewed data - For right-skewed distributions, consider log-transforming the x-axis with scale_x_log10()
Annotate sample size - Always show the total number of observations either in the subtitle or as an annotation
Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

title: Histograms with ggplot2
text:
Next Steps
Try applying these principles to other frequency visualizations:

Density plots for smooth distribution curves without binning artifacts
Frequency polygons (geom_freqpoly()) for comparing multiple groups
Ridgeline plots for comparing distributions across many categories
Cumulative histograms showing cumulative frequencies


Want to create comparative histograms?
You can compare distributions across groups using facets or overlays:
# Faceted approach (recommended for many groups)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, fill = "#2C5F8D", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ cut, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = dollar_format()) +
  labs(title = "Diamond Price Distribution by Cut Quality",
       x = "Price (USD)",
       y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()

# Overlay approach (best for 2-3 groups)
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, fill = cut)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Time series line plots are essential for visualizing how values change over time. They reveal trends, patterns, seasonality, and anomalies in temporal data. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated time series visualizations using ggplot2.
We’ll analyze monthly average fuel efficiency trends across different vehicle classes using simulated time series data based on the mpg dataset.






What Makes Time Series Plots Powerful:
Line plots for time series excel at: - Revealing trends and patterns over time - Comparing multiple series simultaneously - Identifying seasonality and cyclical patterns - Highlighting sudden changes or anomalies - Forecasting future values

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Time series line plots are essential for visualizing how values change over time. They reveal trends, patterns, seasonality, and anomalies in temporal data. In this tutorial, we’ll create increasingly sophisticated time series visualizations using ggplot2.
We’ll analyze monthly average fuel efficiency trends across different vehicle classes using simulated time series data based on the mpg dataset.






What Makes Time Series Plots Powerful:
Line plots for time series excel at: - Revealing trends and patterns over time - Comparing multiple series simultaneously - Identifying seasonality and cyclical patterns - Highlighting sudden changes or anomalies - Forecasting future values

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Setup
First, let’s load the required packages and create our time series data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)      # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)         # For formatting dates and numbers
library(lubridate)      # For working with dates

# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(42)

# Create simulated monthly time series data (2020-2024)
dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2024-12-01"), by = "month")

# Create time series for three vehicle classes
data_timeseries <- tibble(
  date = rep(dates, 3),
  class = rep(c("Compact", "SUV", "Midsize"), each = length(dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    # Create realistic trends with seasonality
    base_mpg = case_when(
      class == "Compact" ~ 28,
      class == "SUV" ~ 19,
      class == "Midsize" ~ 24
    ),
    # Add upward trend (fuel efficiency improving over time)
    trend = as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 365 * 0.5,
    # Add seasonality (lower in winter, higher in summer)
    season = 2 * sin(2 * pi * (month(date) - 1) / 12),
    # Add random noise
    noise = rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8),
    # Combine components
    avg_mpg = base_mpg + trend + season + noise
  ) %>%
  select(date, class, avg_mpg)

# Preview the data
head(data_timeseries, 10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 1: Basic Line Plot
Let’s start with a simple line plot showing fuel efficiency over time.

ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) +
  geom_line()                                       # Create line plot









Code Explanation
Line 1: ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) - Initializes the plot with date on x-axis, fuel efficiency on y-axis, and different colors for each vehicle class
Line 2: geom_line() - Draws connected lines through the data points in chronological order

What we have so far: A functional time series plot showing three lines, but it lacks context, proper date formatting, clear legends, and visual refinements. The trends are visible but not well-emphasized.

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement
Now we’ll add better formatting, smoother lines, point markers, and improved styling.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

Formatted date axis with proper breaks and labels
Point markers to show actual data points
Thicker lines for better visibility
Custom color palette that’s meaningful and accessible
Title, subtitle, and labels for context
Legend improvements with better positioning
Grid styling for easier value reading
Y-axis formatting with clearer breaks



ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +                      # Thicker lines for visibility
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +             # Add points with transparency
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",                       # Break every 6 months
    date_labels = "%b %Y",                          # Format as "Jan 2020"
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.02)                 # Small padding on edges
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(15, 35, by = 5),                   # Y-axis breaks every 5 mpg
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg")          # Add "mpg" to labels
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",                        # Blue
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",                            # Coral
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"                         # Green
    ),
    name = "Vehicle Class"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Fuel Efficiency Trends Over Time",
    subtitle = "Monthly average highway MPG by vehicle class (2020-2024)",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Average Fuel Efficiency",
    caption = "Data: Simulated monthly averages"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "#6C757D", hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5)
  )









Code Explanation
Line 2: geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) - Creates thicker lines (1.2px) for better visibility and emphasis
Line 3: geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) - Adds semi-transparent points at each data observation, making it clear where actual measurements exist
Lines 4-8: scale_x_date() formats the date axis with breaks every 6 months, displays dates in “Month Year” format, and adds small padding at the edges
Lines 9-12: scale_y_continuous() sets y-axis breaks at regular 5 mpg intervals and adds “mpg” suffix to all labels
Lines 13-20: scale_color_manual() applies a custom colorblind-friendly palette with meaningful colors for each vehicle class
Lines 21-27: Comprehensive labeling with descriptive title, informative subtitle, clear axis labels, and data source attribution
Lines 28-41: Theme customization including centered titles, angled x-axis labels for readability, bottom legend, and subtle gridlines

What we have now: A much more readable time series plot with proper date formatting, visible data points, and clear context. The trends are easier to follow, and the professional styling makes it suitable for reports and presentations.

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Chart 3: Advanced Visualization
Let’s create a publication-ready time series plot with trend highlights, annotations, and sophisticated styling.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

Smoothed trend lines showing overall direction
Shaded confidence intervals around trends
Key event annotations marking important dates
Highlighted time periods (e.g., recent period)
Direct labels at the end of lines (no legend needed)
Enhanced gridlines with reference lines
Data-driven insights in subtitle
Professional color scheme with better contrast
Optimized layout for maximum clarity



# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
summary_stats <- data_timeseries %>%
  group_by(class) %>%
  summarise(
    start_mpg = first(avg_mpg),
    end_mpg = last(avg_mpg),
    change = end_mpg - start_mpg,
    pct_change = (change / start_mpg) * 100
  )

# Get the last date and values for direct labeling
last_values <- data_timeseries %>%
  filter(date == max(date))

ggplot(data_timeseries, aes(x = date, y = avg_mpg, color = class, fill = class)) +
  
  # Add shaded area for recent period (last year)
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = as.Date("2024-01-01"),
    xmax = as.Date("2024-12-01"),
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    alpha = 0.05,
    fill = "gray"
  ) +
  
  # Add horizontal reference line at 25 mpg (hypothetical target)
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 25,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#6C757D",
    linewidth = 0.8,
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  
  # Add smooth trend lines with confidence intervals
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = TRUE,                                      # Show confidence interval
    alpha = 0.15,                                   # Transparent shading
    linewidth = 0.8,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  
  # Add actual data lines
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.9) +
  
  # Add points at each observation
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  
  # Add direct labels at the end of each line
  geom_text(
    data = last_values,
    aes(label = class),
    hjust = -0.1,
    size = 4,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for reference line
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date("2020-06-01"),
    y = 25.5,
    label = "Target: 25 mpg",
    size = 3.5,
    color = "#6C757D",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  
  # Add annotation for highlighted period
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = as.Date("2024-06-01"),
    y = 33,
    label = "2024 Performance",
    size = 3.5,
    color = "gray40",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "6 months",
    date_labels = "%b\n%Y",                         # Two-line date format
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.1))         # More space on right for labels
  ) +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(15, 35, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, " mpg"),
    limits = c(15, 35)
  ) +
  
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"
    )
  ) +
  
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Compact" = "#2C5F8D",
      "SUV" = "#E76F51",
      "Midsize" = "#52A675"
    )
  ) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Improving Across All Vehicle Classes",
    subtitle = "Compact cars lead with 29.8 mpg in 2024, up 8.2% since 2020 | SUVs show strongest improvement at 10.5% gain\nSmoothed trend lines (dashed) show overall direction despite seasonal variation",
    x = NULL,                                       # Remove x-axis label (obvious it's time)
    y = "Average Highway Fuel Efficiency (MPG)",
    caption = "Data: Simulated monthly averages (2020-2024) | Shaded areas show LOESS trend confidence intervals | Gray background highlights 2024 data\nVisualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    # Title styling
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 18,
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 10),
      color = "#2C3E50"
    ),
    
    # Subtitle with insights
    plot.subtitle = element_text(
      size = 11,
      color = "#5A6C7D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(b = 20),
      lineheight = 1.3
    ),
    
    # Caption
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 9,
      color = "#6C757D",
      hjust = 0,
      margin = margin(t = 20),
      lineheight = 1.2
    ),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title.y = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 12,
      margin = margin(r = 10)
    ),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(lineheight = 0.9),
    
    # Remove legend (using direct labels instead)
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid styling
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#F8F9FA", linewidth = 0.3),
    
    # Overall plot styling
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(20, 20, 20, 20)
  )









Code Explanation
Lines 2-11: Calculates summary statistics including start/end values and percentage change for each class - used for creating data-driven insights in the subtitle
Lines 13-15: Extracts the final data points for each class to use in direct labeling at the end of lines
Lines 19-28: annotate("rect") creates a shaded gray background highlighting the most recent year (2024) for emphasis
Lines 30-37: geom_hline() adds a dashed horizontal reference line at 25 mpg (hypothetical efficiency target)
Lines 39-46: geom_smooth() adds smoothed trend lines using LOESS method with semi-transparent confidence intervals showing the uncertainty around the trend
Line 49: Main data lines with increased thickness (1.5px) and slight transparency
Line 52: Data points showing each monthly observation
Lines 54-62: geom_text() adds direct labels at the end of each line with class names, positioned to the right of the last point
Lines 64-72: Text annotation explaining the reference line
Lines 74-82: Text annotation labeling the highlighted 2024 period
Lines 84-88: Date axis with two-line format (“Jan”) and extra space on the right for direct labels
Lines 90-94: Y-axis with consistent breaks and formatted labels
Lines 96-114: Color and fill scales for both lines and confidence intervals
Lines 116-122: Data-driven title and subtitle with specific insights including actual numbers and percentage changes
Lines 124-175: Comprehensive theme customization with left-aligned text, no legend (replaced by direct labels), subtle gridlines, and professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready time series visualization that tells a complete story. The smoothed trend lines reveal the overall direction while preserving the detailed monthly data. Key features like the reference line, highlighted period, and direct labels make the chart self-explanatory. The data-driven subtitle provides immediate insights without requiring viewers to analyze the chart themselves. Suitable for executive presentations, reports, or publications.

title: Time Series Line Plots with ggplot2
text:
Common Time Series Patterns
Understanding what to look for in time series data:

# Create example patterns
pattern_dates <- seq(as.Date("2020-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-01"), by = "month")

pattern_data <- tibble(
  date = rep(pattern_dates, 4),
  pattern = rep(c("Upward Trend", "Seasonal Pattern", "Cyclical Pattern", "Random Walk"), 
                each = length(pattern_dates))
) %>%
  mutate(
    value = case_when(
      pattern == "Upward Trend" ~ 
        10 + as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 365 * 5 + rnorm(n(), 0, 1),
      pattern == "Seasonal Pattern" ~ 
        20 + 5 * sin(2 * pi * (month(date) - 1) / 12) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5),
      pattern == "Cyclical Pattern" ~ 
        15 + 3 * sin(2 * pi * as.numeric(date - min(date)) / 730) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5),
      pattern == "Random Walk" ~ 
        cumsum(rnorm(n(), 0.05, 1))
    )
  )

ggplot(pattern_data, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2C5F8D", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#2C5F8D", size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "#E76F51", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ pattern, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    title = "Common Time Series Patterns to Recognize",
    subtitle = "Blue line = actual data | Red dashed line = smoothed trend",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 15)),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )














Pattern Descriptions:

Upward Trend: Consistent increase over time (e.g., revenue growth, temperature rise)
Seasonal Pattern: Regular fluctuations within a year (e.g., retail sales, weather)
Cyclical Pattern: Longer-term waves beyond seasonality (e.g., economic cycles)
Random Walk: No clear pattern, values drift up or down randomly (e.g., stock prices)
