title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and COBIT
COBIT provides governance objectives, control orientation, and assurance structure for enterprise governance of information and technology. MoR complements COBIT by giving a practical risk management method that can be used to support governance decisions, control prioritisation, and risk reporting.

title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and TOGAF
TOGAF supports architecture governance, target-state design, and transition planning. MoR helps identify architecture, transformation, dependency, technology obsolescence, and migration risks that affect architecture roadmaps.

title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and ITIL 4
ITIL 4 includes risk considerations within service management, continuity, change enablement, supplier management, and continual improvement. MoR provides a broader enterprise risk structure that can strengthen service, operational, and resilience decision-making.

title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and PRINCE2
PRINCE2 includes project-level risk management as part of controlled delivery. MoR provides the wider organisational approach and can be used as the parent risk method for all PRINCE2 projects.

title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and MSP / MoP / P3O
MoR strengthens portfolio, programme, and office governance by standardising risk language, escalation routes, tolerances, and reporting across the full change landscape.

title: MoR - Management of Risk
text:
MoR and ISO / Regulatory Frameworks
MoR can be aligned with ISO 31000, ISO 27001, ISO 22301, DORA, NIS2, internal control models, and sector regulations. It is particularly useful where organisations need a practical management method that sits between high-level policy and day-to-day risk decisions.

Specialist Systems - Methodologies
text:
Yes, many specialist systems have distinct implementation methodologies.
In practice, these methodologies usually come from one of four sources:

vendor-branded methodologies
systems integrator or partner delivery frameworks
industry-specific engineering or validation lifecycles
generic project delivery models tailored to the platform, such as agile, waterfall, hybrid, or phased rollout

Some products have a very explicit named methodology, while others rely on a delivery pattern shaped by the operational and regulatory context.



The implementation approach usually depends less on the software brand alone and more on the type of system being deployed.
For example:

a large ERP platform is usually implemented through a fit-to-standard, configuration-led method
an industrial control system is usually implemented through an engineering lifecycle with testing and commissioning
a healthcare or laboratory platform often requires a validation-heavy rollout
a multi-site retail or operational platform often uses a template-and-wave rollout






SAP historically used ASAP, while its current implementation method is SAP Activate.
SAP describes SAP Activate as a structured implementation framework combining best practices, implementation methodology, and guided configuration tools. SAP also describes six phases in the framework and positions it around fit-to-standard and clean core principles.[@sap_activate]



Oracle has long used the Oracle Unified Method (OUM) as its formal delivery method framework. Oracle continues to maintain OUM learning and training content, including structure, principles, and delivery readiness material.[@oracle_oum]
In practice, Oracle projects may also use cloud-specific implementation approaches layered on top of OUM or aligned with product-specific delivery guidance.[@oracle_oum_training]



Guidewire refers to SurePath as a guided, proven implementation approach intended to support faster and more predictable delivery. This is especially relevant in InsuranceSuite and cloud-oriented implementations, often alongside agile delivery and partner-led execution.[@guidewire_surepath; @guidewire_training]




Not every specialist platform has a widely publicised branded method.
Many sectors instead rely on a delivery model shaped by operational realities:

industrial and OT platforms tend to use detailed engineering, FAT, SAT, commissioning, and handover
clinical and regulated systems tend to use controlled deployment, traceability, validation, and strong change management
transport, hospitality, retail, and logistics systems often use site templates and deployment waves
core banking and insurance systems often combine vendor guidance, systems integrator methods, and programme-level governance

Choosing the wrong implementation methodology creates major delivery risk.
A methodology should match:

the criticality of the platform
the degree of regulation
the level of standardisation versus customisation
the number of deployment sites
the data migration complexity
the integration footprint
the need for operational rehearsal, commissioning, or validation

For example, a SCADA deployment should not be run exactly like a SaaS HR implementation, and a hospital EHR rollout should not be treated as a simple packaged software installation.

architecture governance
cyber security and resilience
data migration governance
test management
operational readiness
training and change management
service transition and support model design

This means implementation methodology is not just a project method; it is also a governance and assurance mechanism.



Yes, there are specific methodologies for implementing specialist systems.

Guidewire SurePath

Others are not branded in the same way, but still follow recognisable industry-specific patterns such as:

engineering and commissioning lifecycles
validation-heavy regulated deployment
template-and-wave rollouts
package-led transformation methods

The most useful way to analyse them is not only by vendor, but by system class, risk profile, regulatory burden, and deployment model.

title: ITIL
text:
ITIL 4 is a service management framework used to design, deliver, operate, and continually improve services. It moves beyond a narrow process view and frames service management as a system for co-creating value with customers, users, suppliers, and internal stakeholders.
ITIL 4 is centred on the Service Value System (SVS), the Service Value Chain, the Four Dimensions of Service Management, and a set of practices that help organisations translate strategy into reliable and improving service outcomes.
It is useful not only in traditional IT operations but also in digital product management, platform teams, cloud operations, enterprise support functions, and cross-functional service organisations.



The purpose of ITIL 4 is to help organisations:

align services with business outcomes and customer value;
establish a common operating model for design, transition, support, and improvement;
improve reliability, responsiveness, and service experience;
create consistent governance and accountability across service teams;
support digital transformation through adaptable practices rather than rigid process bureaucracy; and
embed continual improvement into daily operations and strategic change.




ITIL 4 is especially useful when an organisation needs a coherent service management model across operations, support, delivery, and supplier ecosystems. Common situations include:

establishing or improving IT service management;
modernising service desk, incident, problem, and change practices;
introducing service ownership and service catalogue management;
improving end-to-end service design and transition controls;
integrating Agile, DevOps, product, and operations ways of working;
improving customer experience and service-level performance; and
strengthening governance over outsourced or multi-supplier environments.

ITIL 4 is a service management framework used to design, deliver, operate, and continually improve services. It moves beyond a narrow process view and frames service management as a system for co-creating value with customers, users, suppliers, and internal stakeholders.
ITIL 4 is centred on the Service Value System (SVS), the Service Value Chain, the Four Dimensions of Service Management, and a set of practices that help organisations translate strategy into reliable and improving service outcomes.
It is useful not only in traditional IT operations but also in digital product management, platform teams, cloud operations, enterprise support functions, and cross-functional service organisations.

Service Value Chain Activities







Activity
Description




Plan
Shared understanding of vision, current state, improvement priorities, and direction.


Improve
Continual improvement of products, services, practices, and all value chain activities.


Engage
Understanding stakeholder needs, maintaining relationships, and ensuring transparency.


Design & Transition
Ensuring new or changed services meet stakeholder expectations for quality, cost, and time to market.

Acquiring, developing, and implementing service components.

title: ITIL
text:
Four Dimensions of Service Management







Dimension
Description




Organisations and People
Roles, culture, structure, competencies, and workforce capacity needed to deliver services.


Information and Technology
Data, knowledge, applications, infrastructure, automation, and supporting tools.


Partners and Suppliers
External providers, contracts, sourcing models, and ecosystem dependencies.


Value Streams and Processes
End-to-end workflows, controls, activities, and measurement paths that produce outcomes.



The four dimensions help prevent service design from being too narrow. A change that looks good from a tooling perspective may still fail because of skills, supplier, process, or governance gaps.

Purpose

title: ITIL
text:
Service Management Practices







Practice
Purpose




Availability Management
Ensure services meet agreed availability targets.


Business Analysis
Translate stakeholder needs into requirements and improvement opportunities.


Capacity and Performance Management
Ensure services and resources perform to current and future needs.


Change Enablement
Maximise successful changes while controlling risk.


Incident Management
Restore normal service as quickly as possible after disruption.


IT Asset Management
Manage lifecycle, control, and value of IT assets.


Monitoring and Event Management
Observe services, components, and events to support stability and response.


Problem Management
Reduce the likelihood and impact of incidents by managing root causes and workarounds.


Release Management
Make new and changed services or features available for use.


Service Catalogue Management
Provide accurate information about available services and offers.


Service Configuration Management
Maintain trusted information about configuration items and their relationships.


Service Continuity Management
Ensure the organisation can continue or recover services after disruption.


Service Design
Design products and services fit for purpose and use.


Service Desk
Provide the primary point of contact for users and many operational workflows.


Service Level Management
Set, monitor, and improve service targets and service experience.


Service Request Management
Fulfil pre-defined user requests efficiently and consistently.


Service Validation and Testing
Confirm that services meet design and business requirements.

title: ITIL
text:
Technical Management Practices







Practice
Purpose




Deployment Management
Move new or changed components into live or test environments.


Infrastructure and Platform Management
Oversee infrastructure and platform components supporting services.


Software Development and Management
Develop, maintain, and control software throughout its lifecycle.



In practice, organisations rarely implement all practices at the same level of maturity from the start. A phased adoption approach often begins with service desk, incident, request, change enablement, problem, service level, monitoring, and configuration-related capabilities, then expands into broader governance, portfolio, supplier, and improvement disciplines.

title: ISO/IEC 27001
text:
ISO/IEC 27001 provides the requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an information security management system (ISMS). It enables organisations to manage information security risks systematically and to demonstrate that information security is governed through a structured management system.
This document provides a practical template for defining the organisation’s ISO/IEC 27001 governance model, ISMS scope, risk management approach, control structure, implementation roadmap, and assurance model. It can be used to document how the organisation aligns information security governance, risk treatment, controls, and continual improvement into a coherent operating model.

title: ISO/IEC 27001
text:
Purpose
This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring an information security management system aligned to ISO/IEC 27001.

title: ISO/IEC 27001
text:
Objectives
The main objectives of applying ISO/IEC 27001 are to:

establish a formal and auditable information security management system
protect confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information
align information security with business objectives and enterprise risk
apply systematic risk assessment and risk treatment
define and maintain appropriate information security controls
provide evidence of governance, monitoring, and continual improvement
support internal assurance and external certification where required

title: ISO/IEC 27001
text:

security governance, risk treatment, and control monitoring activities
incident management, resilience, and continual improvement activities within the ISMS scope



Out of scope
Document justified exclusions, if any.

ISO/IEC 27001 is the world’s best-known standard for information security management systems and specifies the requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an ISMS. It is designed to support a risk-based approach that can be scaled to organisations of different sizes and sectors. :contentReferenceoaicite:1

title: ISO/IEC 27001
section: Relationship to ISO/IEC 27002 and Annex A
text:
Relationship to ISO/IEC 27002 and Annex A
Describe how the organisation uses:

ISO/IEC 27001 for management system requirements
Annex A as the information security controls reference
ISO/IEC 27002:2022 for guidance on information security controls

ISO states that ISO/IEC 27001 contains the ISMS requirements, while ISO/IEC 27002 provides detailed control guidance. ISO material and SC 27 guidance also explain that Annex A is a normative reference set of controls that must be considered as part of risk treatment and comparison for completeness. :contentReferenceoaicite:2

title: ISO/IEC 27001
text:
Suggested Maturity Levels

Level 1: Initial
Security activities are reactive, fragmented, and poorly governed.


Level 2: Repeatable
Basic ISMS components exist but are inconsistently applied and weakly evidenced.


Level 3: Defined
The ISMS scope, policies, risk treatment, and controls are documented and broadly implemented.


Level 4: Managed
The ISMS is measured, reviewed, audited, and actively improved through leadership oversight.


Level 5: Optimised
Information security is fully integrated into enterprise governance, architecture, operations, and supplier management with strong evidence and continual improvement.

title: GDPR
text:
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is a foundational privacy and data protection framework governing the processing of personal data in the European Union and the European Economic Area, with extra-territorial reach where organisations process the data of EU data subjects. This document provides a structured governance and implementation template to support compliance, assurance, and continuous improvement.
This template can be used to document the organisation’s GDPR operating model, control environment, compliance roadmap, and integration with wider governance, cybersecurity, risk, and data management frameworks.

title: GDPR
text:
Purpose
This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring GDPR compliance across the enterprise.

title: GDPR
text:
Objectives
The main objectives of GDPR compliance are to:

protect the rights and freedoms of natural persons
ensure lawful, fair, and transparent processing of personal data
establish accountability for personal data governance
reduce legal, financial, operational, and reputational risks
embed privacy by design and by default into business and technology processes

DAMA International is the professional association that promotes the discipline of data management.
DMBOK is the body of knowledge published by DAMA and used as the main reference model for enterprise data management.
For consistency with the wider enterprise governance book, this chapter treats DMBOK as the framework and DAMA as the organisational and professional context around it.



DMBOK provides a structured view of the disciplines required to manage data across its lifecycle. It helps organisations treat data as a strategic asset by establishing governance, architecture, quality, security, metadata, master data, and analytics capabilities.



DMBOK is particularly valuable where organisations need to:

establish enterprise data governance
improve trust in data
reduce duplication and inconsistency
strengthen compliance and control
support analytics, reporting, and AI
align business, technology, and risk perspectives around data

title: COBIT
text:
COBIT is a framework from ISACA for the governance and management of enterprise information and technology. It helps organisations ensure that information and technology support business goals, deliver value, optimise risk, and use resources responsibly.
COBIT is not just an IT operations model. It is an enterprise governance framework that connects board priorities, executive decision-making, control requirements, architecture, service delivery, security, assurance, and performance measurement into one coherent system.



The purpose of COBIT is to help enterprises:

create value from information and technology;
balance benefits realisation, risk optimisation, and resource optimisation;
align technology decisions with stakeholder needs and enterprise strategy;
establish clear governance accountabilities;
define management objectives, controls, and performance measures; and
provide a common language between the board, executives, auditors, risk, architecture, security, and operational teams.




COBIT is especially useful when an organisation needs a structured governance model across multiple technology and business functions. Typical situations include:

enterprise-wide IT governance transformation;
strengthening board oversight of digital and technology investment;
integrating risk, compliance, security, architecture, and service management;
improving auditability and control maturity;
rationalising overlapping frameworks and standards;
creating a governance layer above delivery frameworks such as PRINCE2, MSP, Agile, DevOps, or ITIL; and
supporting regulated or high-dependability environments.

title: COBIT
text:
Governance vs Management
COBIT makes a deliberate distinction between governance and management:

Governance ensures stakeholder needs, conditions, and options are evaluated to determine balanced, agreed enterprise objectives; direction is set through prioritisation and decision-making; and performance and compliance are monitored.
Management plans, builds, runs, and monitors activities to achieve the direction set by the governing body.

This distinction is valuable because many organisations mix strategic oversight with operational delivery. COBIT helps clarify which decisions belong to the board or executive governing body and which belong to management functions.

title: COBIT
text:
Common Implementation Tips

Start with the pain points, not the framework vocabulary.
Use COBIT to unify what already exists instead of replacing every method.
Keep governance forums clear and decision-oriented.
Design concise artefacts that support decisions and evidence controls.
Integrate governance metrics with portfolio, operational, security, and audit dashboards.
Build strong ownership for APO02, APO05, APO12, APO13, DSS02, DSS04, and MEA02/03 in most enterprises.

title: COBIT
text:
Metric Design Guidance
Good COBIT metrics should balance:

value: are we delivering the intended outcomes?
risk: are exposures within appetite?
resources: are people, money, data, and services used effectively?
conformance: are controls and obligations being met?
improvement: are capability and governance maturity advancing?

title: COBIT
text:
Scenario: Mid-Sized Financial Services Organisation
A regulated financial services organisation has grown through acquisitions. It has duplicated systems, inconsistent architecture decisions, unclear ownership of technology investment, increasing audit findings, weak visibility of risk, and recurring service incidents.

How COBIT Helps

EDM establishes board-level oversight of benefits, risk, resources, and stakeholder transparency.
APO02 creates a single I&T strategy aligned to enterprise priorities.
APO03 defines architecture principles and review controls.
APO05 improves portfolio governance and prioritisation.
APO12 and APO13 strengthen risk and security governance.
BAI01 and BAI11 structure change through programme and project governance.
DSS02, DSS03, and DSS04 improve operational reliability, problem management, and continuity.
MEA02 and MEA03 support control monitoring and regulatory compliance.



Key Artefacts Produced

governance charter and decision rights matrix;
integrated I&T strategy and target operating model;
enterprise architecture principles and review board terms of reference;
portfolio prioritisation model and benefits reporting pack;
risk and control catalogue linked to regulatory requirements;
service dashboards for incidents, changes, availability, and continuity;
assurance plan and audit action tracker.



Expected Outcomes
Within 12 to 18 months, the organisation should expect better governance visibility, fewer duplicate initiatives, clearer accountability, improved audit closure rates, stronger change control, and more reliable critical services.

title: AI Act(EU)
text:
The European Union Artificial Intelligence Act establishes a harmonised legal framework for artificial intelligence across the Union. It is designed to support trustworthy, human-centric AI while protecting health, safety, and fundamental rights. The regulation applies a risk-based approach and introduces different obligations depending on whether an AI system is prohibited, high-risk, subject to transparency requirements, or outside the main mandatory obligations. It also introduces a distinct governance and compliance framework for general-purpose AI models.
This document provides a practical template for defining the organisation’s AI Act governance model, AI risk management approach, control structure, implementation roadmap, and assurance model. It can be used to document how the organisation aligns AI governance, legal compliance, risk management, technical controls, oversight, and assurance into a coherent operating model.

title: AI Act(EU)
text:
Purpose
This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring compliance with the EU AI Act across the enterprise.

title: AI Act(EU)
text:
Objectives
The main objectives of applying the AI Act are to:

ensure AI systems are lawful, safe, and trustworthy
protect health, safety, and fundamental rights
establish clear accountability for providers, deployers, and other operators
identify and manage AI risks proportionately
strengthen transparency, human oversight, and technical robustness
support evidence-based governance, assurance, and regulatory readiness
integrate AI governance with cybersecurity, privacy, architecture, risk, and compliance practices

text:

governance, documentation, monitoring, and incident escalation arrangements

title: DORA
text:
The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) establishes a harmonised European Union framework for managing digital operational resilience across the financial sector. It strengthens the ability of financial entities to withstand, respond to, and recover from ICT-related disruptions, cyber incidents, and third-party service failures.
This document provides a practical template for defining the organisation’s DORA governance model, ICT risk management approach, control structure, implementation roadmap, and assurance model. It can be used to document how the organisation aligns resilience, cybersecurity, third-party risk, and regulatory compliance into a coherent operating model.

title: DORA
text:
Purpose
This document provides a practical template for defining, implementing, operating, and assuring compliance with DORA across the enterprise.

title: DORA
text:
Objectives
The main objectives of applying DORA are to:

strengthen digital operational resilience across regulated financial services
establish clear accountability for ICT risk and resilience
improve prevention, detection, response, and recovery capabilities
ensure consistent handling and reporting of ICT-related incidents
strengthen oversight of ICT third-party dependencies and concentration risk
support resilience testing and continuous improvement
integrate operational resilience with enterprise governance, risk, compliance, and assurance

title: DORA
text:
Scope
Describe the scope of DORA applicability in the organisation.

In scope

applications, infrastructure, cloud services, and networks

ICT third-party service providers and contractual arrangements
digital operational resilience testing activities
incident management and regulatory reporting processes



Out of scope
Document justified exclusions, if any.

title: DORA
text:
Background
DORA provides a unified regulatory framework for digital operational resilience in the financial sector. It addresses the management of ICT risk, resilience testing, ICT incident handling and reporting, ICT third-party risk, and supervisory oversight of critical ICT third-party providers.

title: IT Engineering
text:
IT engineering is the discipline of designing, building, integrating, operating, securing, and improving the technology systems that organisations rely on. It is where business intent is translated into working digital capability.
In practice, IT engineering is not limited to software development or infrastructure support. It spans the full lifecycle of digital systems, from understanding business needs and defining requirements to architecture, implementation, deployment, operations, resilience, and continual improvement.
A helpful way to view IT engineering is as applied engineering for digital systems. It combines technical depth with systems thinking, governance, operational discipline, and business alignment.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Software Engineering
Software engineering focuses on designing and building applications, APIs, automation, and user-facing or internal digital services.
Typical concerns include:

requirements and acceptance criteria
software design and modularity
maintainability and technical debt
testing and quality assurance
version control and release management
security in code
performance and scalability

Common tools and practices include Git, CI/CD pipelines, automated testing, containerisation, code review, and structured development methods.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Infrastructure Engineering
Infrastructure engineering is concerned with the compute, storage, virtualisation, hosting, and operating environments that support digital services.
This includes:

physical and virtual servers
operating systems
storage platforms
backup and restore capability
high availability design
cloud services
infrastructure as code
patching and lifecycle management

A mature infrastructure engineering capability ensures that platforms are stable, efficient, recoverable, and aligned to architecture standards.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Network Engineering
Network engineering enables secure and reliable communication between systems, users, sites, and external services.
Typical areas include:

routing and switching
LAN, WAN, and Wi-Fi
DNS and DHCP
firewalls and segmentation
VPN and remote access
load balancing
bandwidth, throughput, and latency management

Without sound network engineering, even well-built applications can fail due to poor connectivity, instability, or weak security boundaries.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Security Engineering
Security engineering ensures that protection is built into systems from the start rather than added as an afterthought.
This includes:

identity and access management
privileged access controls
encryption
secure configuration baselines
vulnerability management
endpoint and server hardening
logging and detection
incident response integration
zero trust principles
secure design and threat modelling

In modern organisations, security engineering is a core discipline of IT engineering rather than a separate final gate.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Platform Engineering
Platform engineering focuses on creating internal platforms that make delivery easier, faster, and more consistent for engineering teams.
Examples include:

standard cloud landing zones
reusable deployment patterns
internal developer platforms
shared Kubernetes environments
common observability tooling
self-service infrastructure templates

Its goal is to reduce friction and improve consistency across teams.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Data Engineering
Data engineering designs and builds the data pipelines and platforms that support reporting, analytics, operational decision-making, and AI use cases.
Typical responsibilities include:

data ingestion
ETL and ELT pipelines
warehousing and lakehouse platforms
data quality controls
metadata and lineage
schema design
streaming pipelines
governance and retention

Data engineering is increasingly central to enterprise IT engineering because many business capabilities now depend on trustworthy and timely data.

title: IT Engineering
text:
DevOps and Site Reliability Engineering
DevOps and SRE practices connect development and operations to improve delivery speed, service reliability, and recovery capability.
Important ideas include:

automation of builds and deployments
continuous integration and continuous delivery
monitoring and alerting
incident response
post-incident review
service level objectives
reliability engineering
error budgets and resilience thinking

These practices help engineering teams move from fragmented handovers to integrated service ownership.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Architecture and Solution Engineering
Architecture and solution engineering ensure that technology choices are coherent, scalable, secure, and aligned with enterprise direction.
This includes:

solution design
integration patterns
target-state thinking
standards and guardrails
technology rationalisation
cost and risk trade-offs
alignment with business capabilities

Architecture provides the structural logic that prevents engineering from becoming a collection of disconnected technical decisions.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Discover
This stage clarifies the problem, the users, the business goals, and the constraints. It may include process analysis, stakeholder engagement, current-state assessment, and identification of risks or dependencies.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Design
This stage defines the solution. It includes architecture, data flows, security controls, operational model, resilience patterns, integration mechanisms, and design documentation.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Build
This stage turns the design into working reality through code, configuration, scripting, cloud resources, network changes, integrations, and automation.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Test
This stage validates that the service works as intended and is fit for purpose. Testing may include:

functional testing
integration testing
performance testing
security testing
failover and recovery testing
user acceptance testing

title: IT Engineering
text:
Deploy
This stage puts the solution into a live or production environment through managed release processes, deployment pipelines, environment promotion, and change controls.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Operate
This stage ensures the service is run properly. It includes monitoring, support, patching, backup, incident response, problem management, capacity management, and operational reporting.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Improve
This stage learns from performance, incidents, user feedback, audit findings, and technical debt, then uses those lessons to strengthen the service or engineering approach.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Requirements
Strong engineering starts with clarity about what problem is being solved and what success looks like.
Requirements often include:

functional requirements
non-functional requirements
constraints
assumptions
dependencies
acceptance criteria

Non-functional requirements are especially important because they shape how well a system performs in the real world. These typically cover:

availability
performance
security
scalability
maintainability
resilience
recoverability

title: IT Engineering
text:
Architecture
Architecture determines the structure of the solution and the logic that connects its parts. It is often considered across multiple layers:

business architecture
application architecture
data architecture
technology architecture
security architecture

Architecture is not abstract decoration; it is what gives engineering coherence and sustainability.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Integration
Most enterprise systems do not stand alone. They connect to other systems, users, and data sources.
Common integration patterns include:

APIs
events and message queues
batch interfaces
file exchanges
service buses
data pipelines

Integration is often where complexity and failure risk accumulate, so it deserves deliberate engineering attention.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Data
Data is a core asset in nearly all modern services. Engineering must address:

data quality
ownership
lifecycle
privacy
security
retention
access control
traceability

Poor data engineering can undermine reporting, decision-making, compliance, automation, and AI usage.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Security
Security applies at every layer, including:

user identity
device and endpoint
network
application
platform
data
monitoring and detection
backup and recovery

Secure-by-design thinking is now a hallmark of modern IT engineering.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Operations
Engineering is incomplete if the solution cannot be run, supported, monitored, restored, or improved.
Operational readiness usually includes:

monitoring and alerting
runbooks and support procedures
ownership and escalation paths
service metrics
patching schedules
backup validation
recovery testing

title: IT Engineering
text:
Reliability
A reliable system performs consistently and recovers effectively when faults occur.
Key considerations include:

redundancy
failover
dependency mapping
recovery procedures
recovery time objectives
recovery point objectives
graceful degradation

title: IT Engineering
text:
Scalability
Scalability is the ability of a service to handle increased load without unacceptable degradation.
Approaches include:

vertical scaling
horizontal scaling
caching
queue-based workloads
distributed architectures
database tuning

title: IT Engineering
text:
Performance
Performance concerns how quickly and efficiently a service responds. It is affected by code, database design, infrastructure, networks, integration patterns, and concurrency.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Maintainability
Maintainability is the ease with which a system can be understood, supported, fixed, and enhanced. It is improved by modular design, coding standards, documentation, testing, and clear ownership.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Observability
Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system by using logs, metrics, traces, dashboards, and alerts. It is essential for troubleshooting and operational improvement.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Resilience
Resilience is the capacity to continue operating or recover quickly when disruptions occur, whether caused by component failure, cyber incidents, demand spikes, or external outages.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Automation
Automation reduces manual effort, variation, and operational risk. Typical candidates for automation include:

builds
testing
deployments
infrastructure provisioning
compliance checks
account provisioning
patching
reporting

title: IT Engineering
text:
ITIL

title: IT Engineering
text:

title: IT Engineering
text:

title: IT Engineering
text:
ISO/IEC 27001
This supports information security management, policy frameworks, controls, and assurance.

title: IT Engineering
text:
NIST Cybersecurity Framework
This supports practical cybersecurity structuring across identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover perspectives.

title: IT Engineering
text:
DevOps and SRE Practices
These support engineering flow, automation, reliability, observability, and integrated service ownership.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Delivery Frameworks
Frameworks such as Agile, Scrum, PRINCE2, MSP, and similar methods can help structure change delivery around engineering work.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Technical Depth
A strong grounding in at least one or two technical domains is essential.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Systems Thinking
Good engineers understand dependencies, trade-offs, interfaces, bottlenecks, and second-order effects.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Problem Solving
Engineering often involves diagnosing issues, structuring ambiguity, and making sound design choices under constraints.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Communication
Engineers must explain technical matters clearly to colleagues, managers, business leaders, auditors, suppliers, and support teams.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Documentation
Good documentation enables support, transfer of knowledge, auditability, and maintainability.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Risk Awareness
Every technical decision has implications for cost, complexity, security, resilience, and supportability.

title: IT Engineering
text:
Business Literacy
Understanding processes, value, cost, and organisational objectives helps engineers make better decisions.

title: IT Engineering
text:
“It is just coding”
Coding is important, but IT engineering is much broader and includes architecture, infrastructure, security, operations, integration, and governance.

title: IT Engineering
text:
“Infrastructure alone is enough”
Infrastructure provides a platform, but without applications, integrations, data, and operational controls it does not deliver business value on its own.

title: IT Engineering
text:
“Security can be added later”
Late-stage security usually creates rework, cost, and residual risk. It is far better to design it in from the outset.

title: IT Engineering
section: “If it works, it is well engineered”
text:
“If it works, it is well engineered”
A service may function today but still be fragile, undocumented, insecure, or difficult to support. Good engineering is about more than short-term functionality.

title: IT Engineering
text:
“Operations is separate from engineering”
A service that cannot be monitored, restored, patched, or supported has not been fully engineered.

title: IT Engineering
text:
1. Business Layer
Why the service exists and what business capability it enables.

title: IT Engineering
text:
2. Process Layer
How work flows through the organisation and where technology supports or automates it.

title: IT Engineering
text:
3. Application Layer
What software, services, and interfaces provide the required functionality.

title: IT Engineering
text:
4. Data Layer
What information is created, stored, transformed, exchanged, and protected.

title: IT Engineering
text:
5. Technology Layer
What infrastructure, platforms, cloud services, and networks run the solution.

title: IT Engineering
text:
6. Control Layer
How governance, security, operations, compliance, and risk management keep the service safe and reliable.
This model is especially useful because it helps connect executive concerns with engineering realities.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
A modern IT enterprise should be understood as a whole system, not as a collection of disconnected technical teams. Its purpose is to align technology with business strategy, deliver change in a controlled way, run reliable services, and maintain trust through risk management, security, compliance, and assurance.
This chapter presents a practical mental model for understanding how a modern IT enterprise works. It is designed to help executives, architects, PMOs, service leaders, risk professionals, and auditors think about the enterprise using a common structure.
The core idea is simple:

A modern IT enterprise is a governed system that aligns strategy, architecture, investment, delivery, operations, and assurance to create business value with controlled risk.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
Conceptual view





flowchart LR
    A[Why\nStrategy and Value] --> B[What\nCapabilities, Policies, Architecture]
    B --> C[How\nChange, Delivery, Operations]
    C --> D[Who\nOrganisation and Accountability]
    D --> E[Control\nRisk, Security, Compliance, Audit]

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
Why: Strategy and Value
The enterprise starts with purpose. IT exists to support business outcomes, improve performance, enable innovation, and protect the organisation.
Typical questions at this level include:

What is the organisation trying to achieve?
What value should technology create?
Which risks are acceptable?
Where should investment be concentrated?

Typical outputs include:

business strategy
digital strategy
IT strategy
investment priorities
risk appetite
target outcomes and measures

Mental point: IT starts with purpose, not technology.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
What: Enterprise Design
Once strategic intent is clear, the enterprise must define what it needs in order to operate and evolve successfully.
This includes:

business capabilities
services
products
data
applications
platforms
standards
policies
control objectives

Typical outputs include:

capability maps
enterprise architecture blueprints
service catalogue
data models
technology standards
policies and control frameworks

Mental point: architecture is the bridge between ambition and implementation.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
How: Change and Run
A modern IT enterprise has two main operating engines:

the change engine, which transforms the organisation
the run engine, which operates services and technology day to day


Change engine
The change engine includes:

portfolio management
programme management
project management
product development
business transformation



Run engine
The run engine includes:

service management
user support
infrastructure and cloud operations
application support
monitoring and reliability
continuity and resilience

Mental point: the enterprise must be able to change and run at the same time.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
Who: Organisation and Accountability
The enterprise requires clear roles, decision rights, ownership, and reporting lines.
Typical accountability layers include:

Board
CEO
CIO
CTO
CISO
CDO
PMO or Portfolio Office
Operations leadership
Risk, Compliance, and Audit functions

Typical questions include:

Who decides?
Who owns?
Who delivers?
Who approves?
Who assures?

Mental point: governance is accountability made visible.

title: Modern IT Enterprise
text:
Control: Assurance and Trust
Control functions create confidence that the enterprise is secure, compliant, financially responsible, and properly governed.
These controls cut across all enterprise layers:

risk management
information security
regulatory compliance
internal control
procurement control
internal audit
external assurance

Typical questions include:

Are we secure?
Are we compliant?
Are risks understood?
Are controls operating effectively?
Can we demonstrate evidence?

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Management of Portfolios (MoP) is a portfolio management framework originally developed by the UK Cabinet Office and now positioned within the wider PRINCE2 / PeopleCert portfolio. It provides a structured approach to selecting, prioritising, governing, balancing, and controlling an organisation’s portfolio of change initiatives so that investment decisions remain aligned with strategy, capacity, risk appetite, and expected benefits.
MoP is concerned with doing the right change, not merely delivering change correctly. Where project and programme methods focus on execution, MoP focuses on whether the organisation is investing in the right mix of initiatives and whether those initiatives continue to deserve funding and executive attention.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP provides a governance model for turning strategic intent into a managed portfolio of investments. It usually operates through two interacting management cycles:

a portfolio definition cycle, which decides what should enter, remain in, or leave the portfolio; and
a portfolio delivery cycle, which monitors progress, performance, risk, dependency, and benefits across the approved portfolio.

Together, these cycles help the organisation continuously answer five core questions:

Are we investing in the right things?
Are we investing at the right level?
Do we have the capacity and capability to deliver?
Are we obtaining the expected benefits and value?
Should we continue, stop, defer, or rebalance current investments?

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Senior Management Commitment
Portfolio management requires visible executive sponsorship. Without sustained support from the board or executive committee, prioritisation decisions are often bypassed by local interests or political pressures.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Governance Alignment
Portfolio management must fit the wider corporate governance model. Investment decisions, controls, reporting, escalation, and assurance should align with finance, risk, audit, and strategy structures.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Strategy Alignment
Every portfolio decision should be traceable to business strategy, policy direction, regulatory obligations, or target operating model outcomes. MoP helps ensure the portfolio remains strategically coherent.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Portfolio Office Support
A capable portfolio office is needed to coordinate information, maintain standards, support prioritisation, consolidate reporting, and enable evidence-based decision-making.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Prioritised and Categorised Investment
Work should be grouped and compared using clear categories such as mandatory change, growth, operational resilience, compliance, technical debt, or innovation. Prioritisation becomes stronger when investment categories are explicit.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Effective Controls
The portfolio requires clear entry criteria, stage controls, tolerance thresholds, exception escalation, review points, and closure rules. Good controls improve transparency and reduce waste.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Benefits Realisation Focus
MoP does not stop at approving investment. It also requires ongoing attention to whether expected benefits remain credible, measurable, and likely to be realised.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
What MoP Governs
MoP governs the aggregate portfolio of change investments rather than any single project or programme. It provides the decision framework for selecting, funding, balancing, monitoring, and adapting the overall change landscape.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Understand
This area focuses on understanding the organisation’s strategic objectives, current change landscape, constraints, risk appetite, and stakeholder priorities.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Categorise
Candidate initiatives are grouped into meaningful categories so that comparisons can be made fairly and transparently. Categories may include mandatory, run-the-business improvement, strategic growth, innovation, resilience, and compliance.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Prioritise
Initiatives are assessed using agreed criteria such as strategic alignment, cost, benefit, urgency, risk, regulatory necessity, dependency impact, and resource demand.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Balance
Portfolio balancing ensures the mix of investments is realistic and aligned to organisational capacity, affordability, and strategic timing. This often involves trade-offs across horizons, business units, and risk profiles.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Plan
Once decisions are made, the approved portfolio is sequenced and reflected in roadmaps, funding plans, dependency views, and delivery expectations.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Manage and Control
The live portfolio is monitored through reporting, governance reviews, exception handling, benefit tracking, dependency management, and ongoing re-prioritisation.

text:
How to Read the MoP Process Model
Unlike project methods that follow a delivery lifecycle for one initiative, MoP is cyclical and continuous. The organisation repeatedly reviews strategy, capacity, performance, and change demand to refine the portfolio over time.

text:
MoP and COBIT
COBIT provides governance objectives, control structures, performance oversight, and enterprise governance language. MoP can act as the portfolio decision mechanism that turns governance priorities into an investment portfolio.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP and TOGAF
TOGAF provides target architecture, roadmaps, and architecture governance. MoP helps decide which architecture-led initiatives should be funded, sequenced, and balanced in the wider portfolio.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP and ITIL 4
ITIL 4 supports service strategy, value delivery, and continual improvement. MoP helps prioritise service-improvement investments and balance them against resilience, compliance, and innovation initiatives.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP and PRINCE2
PRINCE2 governs individual projects. MoP operates above projects, helping decide which projects should exist, how they are prioritised, and when they should be stopped or accelerated.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP and MSP
MSP governs programmes and transformational change. MoP determines which programmes should be launched or sustained, while MSP manages the coordinated delivery of each approved programme.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
MoP and P3O
P3O provides the office structures and support services that can enable MoP in practice. A portfolio office is often the operational backbone for portfolio reporting, governance support, standards, and decision-pack preparation.

title: MoP - Management of Portfolios
text:
Common Implementation Tips

Start with a clear executive mandate and decision model.
Define a simple portfolio taxonomy and prioritisation approach first.
Build one trusted portfolio register before expanding tooling.
Introduce consistent reporting, benefits tracking, and dependency views.
Review portfolio affordability and change capacity regularly.
Use stop / defer / accelerate decisions as normal governance behaviour.
Improve maturity iteratively rather than trying to design a perfect model upfront.

MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP (Managing Successful Programmes) is a programme management framework used for coordinating related projects and change activities so that organisations can deliver strategic outcomes and realise benefits. It is designed for complex change that cannot be managed effectively through isolated projects alone.
MSP sits above project management. It helps leaders shape a programme vision, organise governance, control delivery tranches, manage stakeholders, and ensure that change is embedded into business operations so expected benefits are actually achieved.



The purpose of MSP is to help organisations:

translate strategy into coordinated transformational change;
organise programmes around outcomes, capabilities, and benefits;
align projects and business change activity under one governance structure;
manage uncertainty, interdependencies, and stakeholder complexity;
control progress through tranches and decision points;
embed new ways of working into operational areas; and
sustain benefits after delivery is complete.




MSP is especially useful when change is broad, strategic, and cross-functional. Typical situations include:

enterprise transformation programmes;
digital modernisation across several business units;
mergers, restructuring, or operating model redesign;
large public sector reform or policy implementation;
regulatory transformation requiring multiple coordinated initiatives;
capability-building programmes such as ERP, CRM, cloud, cyber, or data transformation; and
change portfolios where benefits realisation is as important as technical delivery.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
Governance vs Management in MSP
MSP distinguishes between strategic sponsorship, programme governance, and programme management.

Governance provides direction, decision authority, investment control, and assurance.
Programme management coordinates the programme environment, plans the tranches, manages interdependencies, controls risks and issues, and supports benefit delivery.
Business leadership and operational management ensure the organisation adopts new capabilities and changes behaviour so benefits can be realised.

This distinction matters because many programmes fail not from weak projects, but from poor sponsorship, weak business ownership, or failure to embed change.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP and COBIT
COBIT provides the enterprise governance layer. MSP can be used as the transformation execution model for large change initiatives authorised by COBIT governance structures. COBIT defines value, control, and oversight; MSP organises coordinated delivery of strategic change.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP and TOGAF
TOGAF helps define the target architecture and roadmap. MSP provides the programme governance, change coordination, and benefits management to implement that architecture across the enterprise.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP and ITIL 4
ITIL 4 supports service design, transition, operation, and value co-creation. MSP can govern major service transformation programmes, while ITIL practices support operational readiness and live service management.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP and PRINCE2
This is one of the strongest natural pairings. MSP governs the programme, benefits, and business change. PRINCE2 manages the component projects delivering specific outputs within each tranche.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
text:
MSP and MoP / P3O
MoP helps decide which programmes and projects should be prioritised across the enterprise. P3O defines the office structures and support services that can underpin MSP governance and control.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes

Formally close the programme when governance objectives are met, while ensuring remaining benefit ownership is handed over to the business.

title: MSP - Managing Successful Programmes
P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O stands for Portfolio, Programme and Project Offices. It is a framework for designing, implementing, and operating a coordinated office model that supports strategic change across the enterprise. Rather than defining a single PMO shape, P3O explains how different support offices can be organised and linked so that portfolio decisions, programme coordination, and project control work as one governance system.
P3O helps organisations move beyond isolated project administration. It creates an operating model in which decision support, assurance, standards, reporting, resource coordination, benefits tracking, and delivery enablement are aligned across change initiatives.
In current official positioning, P3O remains part of the wider PeopleCert / AXELOS family of portfolio, programme, and project management guidance. The current certification path is presented as P3O Foundation and P3O Practitioner.



The purpose of P3O is to help organisations:

create a coherent office model for change governance;
define how portfolio, programme, and project support functions should fit together;
improve visibility, consistency, standards, and decision support;
strengthen prioritisation, dependency management, and reporting;
provide executive information for investment and assurance decisions; and
make PMOs more strategic, value-adding, and scalable.




P3O is especially useful when an organisation has many concurrent initiatives and needs more than a single local PMO. Typical situations include:

enterprise transformation with multiple programmes and projects;
organisations building or redesigning a PMO operating model;
environments with weak visibility across the change portfolio;
delivery landscapes with inconsistent methods, templates, and reporting;
organisations needing clearer assurance, governance, and escalation routes;
complex change involving shared resources and cross-project dependencies; and
public sector, regulated, or board-driven environments where structured reporting and control matter.

Permanent and Temporary Offices
P3O distinguishes between permanent offices and temporary offices.

Permanent offices provide enduring organisational capability, standards, governance support, and enterprise memory.
Temporary offices are created for a programme or major project for the duration of that initiative.

A mature enterprise often uses a hybrid design: a permanent portfolio office and centre of excellence, with temporary or semi-permanent programme/project support offices created as needed.

This balances consistency and proximity to delivery teams.

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and COBIT
COBIT provides governance objectives and control expectations. P3O provides the organisational support model that helps operationalise governance across the change portfolio.

COBIT defines governance requirements.
P3O helps create the office structure and reporting model to support them.

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and MoP
MoP helps govern what the portfolio is and how investment choices are made. P3O helps define which office capability supports that portfolio.

MoP = portfolio decision framework
P3O = portfolio support operating model

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and MSP
MSP provides programme governance and benefits-led transformation. P3O provides programme office design and support services for those programmes.

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and PRINCE2
PRINCE2 defines project governance and control. P3O helps structure the PMO / project office capability that supports PRINCE2 projects consistently.

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and ITIL 4
ITIL 4 helps with service management and value delivery. P3O helps manage the change governance and office support needed to deliver transformation into live services.

title: P3O - Project Ofice
text:
P3O and TOGAF
TOGAF defines architecture direction and change roadmaps. P3O helps provide the reporting, coordination, and office support structure around the related programmes and projects.

Vendor case studies sometimes refer to implementations in three to six months. These are usually associated with one or more of the following conditions:

narrow scope
minimal customisation
strong template reuse
lower migration complexity
limited site count
low regulatory burden
experienced implementation partner
strong executive sponsorship and business availability

By contrast, the longest programmes usually involve:

large legacy estates
many interfaces
poor master data quality
high customisation
multiple geographies
difficult cutover windows
major operating model change
extensive validation or assurance obligations




A practical early-stage formula is:

Estimated Duration = Base Duration x Complexity Factors



Assume a WMS starts with a base of 6 months.
Add complexity:

three warehouses: +30%
ERP and carrier integrations: +25%
handheld device rollout: +10%
large inventory migration: +20%

Result:

6 months x 1.85 = approximately 11 months

This is not mathematically exact, but it is a useful planning approach for portfolio discussions.

When estimating implementation time, it is useful to create at least three scenarios:

optimistic
most likely
high complexity

A robust planning model should also separate:

design and mobilisation
build and configuration
migration and integration
testing
training and readiness
cutover
hypercare and stabilisation

This makes it easier to communicate which part of the timeline is technical effort and which part is operational readiness.



Implementation time for specialist systems should always be estimated as a range, not a single number.
The best predictor is not only the product itself, but also:

system class
delivery method
number of sites
migration complexity
integration footprint
operational criticality
regulatory burden
business readiness

As a result, a relatively small package implementation may take only a few months, while a large operational transformation programme may run for several years.



Oracle describes ERP implementation as a substantial, multi-step process including configuration, migration, testing, training, and go-live planning.[@oracle_erp_impl] SAP positions SAP Activate as a structured implementation framework for SAP transformations.[@sap_activate] Guidewire describes accelerated implementations and cloud transformation approaches that can shorten delivery where scope is controlled.[@guidewire_bolt] Engineering-led industrial implementations commonly include testing and commissioning patterns such as factory acceptance testing and site acceptance testing.[@siemens_commissioning]

text:
Vendor case studies sometimes refer to implementations in three to six months. These are usually associated with one or more of the following conditions:

narrow scope

title: Specialist Systems - Implementation time
text:
A practical early-stage formula is:

Estimated Duration = Base Duration x Complexity Factors



Assume a WMS starts with a base of 6 months.
Add complexity:

three warehouses: +30%
ERP and carrier integrations: +25%
handheld device rollout: +10%
large inventory migration: +20%

Result:

6 months x 1.85 = approximately 11 months

This is not mathematically exact, but it is a useful planning approach for portfolio discussions.

title: TOGAF
text:
TOGAF is an enterprise architecture standard from The Open Group. It provides a structured method, content framework, and governance approach for designing, planning, implementing, and governing enterprise architecture.
TOGAF is not only a way to draw architecture diagrams. It is a complete approach for moving from business strategy to target architecture, transition roadmaps, implementation governance, and architecture capability development. It helps organisations align business, data, application, and technology change in a controlled and repeatable way.



The purpose of TOGAF is to help enterprises:

translate business strategy into architecture direction;
design current-state and target-state enterprise architecture;
govern change through a repeatable architecture development method;
create transition roadmaps from baseline to target states;
establish architecture principles, standards, and decision rights; and
improve alignment across strategy, delivery, operations, risk, and technology platforms.




TOGAF is especially useful when an organisation needs a disciplined architecture method across business and technology change. Typical situations include:

enterprise transformation and operating model redesign;
modernisation of applications, data platforms, or infrastructure;
digital strategy execution and capability-based planning;
mergers, acquisitions, or organisational restructuring;
cloud migration and platform rationalisation;
development of enterprise standards and architecture governance; and
integration of multiple delivery programmes under one target-state design.

title: TOGAF
text:
Architecture Governance vs Delivery Governance
TOGAF distinguishes architecture governance from general project or operational governance:

Architecture governance ensures that architecture principles, standards, target states, and design decisions are defined, reviewed, approved, and followed.
Delivery governance ensures that projects and programmes are managed well, on time, and within scope.

This distinction is important because a project can be well-managed yet still produce a solution that increases technical debt, duplicates platforms, or conflicts with enterprise direction. TOGAF adds the architecture control layer.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
This file consolidates the project documentation related to FIRO and The Human Element into a single knowledge-base chapter in Quarto format.

Note on terminology: the request referred to “FIFO and Human Element”. In this context, the intended term is almost certainly FIRO, which is the interpersonal theory developed by Will Schutz and later extended into The Human Element.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Will Schutz
Will Schutz was a psychologist whose work began with research into group compatibility and interpersonal behaviour. His early work developed into FIRO, and later into The Human Element, which integrated interpersonal theory with a broader developmental and experiential methodology.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
section: From FIRO to The Human Element
text:
From FIRO to The Human Element
A useful way to understand the evolution is:

FIRO began as a theory of interpersonal behaviour
FIRO-B became a behavioural instrument to assess interpersonal preferences and patterns
The Human Element expanded the model into a fuller developmental system involving self-awareness, emotional honesty, choice, self-esteem, and group effectiveness

This progression matters because it shows that The Human Element is not merely a personality questionnaire. It is an approach to human effectiveness that combines:

theory
self-inquiry
reflection
emotional awareness
experiential learning
group process work
application to leadership and organisations

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
The three dimensions

Inclusion
Inclusion relates to contact, visibility, participation, recognition, belonging, and whether a person feels “in” or “out”.
Common questions beneath inclusion include:

Do I belong here?
Am I seen?
Am I accepted?
Do I matter to this group?
How much contact do I want with others?

Typical team expressions:

joining or withdrawing
speaking up or staying silent
seeking attention or avoiding exposure
wanting frequent interaction or preferring distance
feeling excluded, overlooked, or unnecessary

At work, inclusion often appears in:

onboarding
team meetings
participation in decisions
stakeholder engagement
social integration
workshop dynamics
cross-functional collaboration



Control
Control relates to influence, responsibility, structure, power, authority, competence, and decision rights.
Common questions beneath control include:

Am I competent?
Who decides?
How much influence do I have?
Can I trust others to lead or deliver?
Do I need structure or freedom?

Typical team expressions:

directing vs following
organising vs resisting direction
ambiguity tolerance
conflict over ownership
micro-management
struggle over accountability
preference for clear governance vs flexible autonomy

At work, control often appears in:

decision-making forums
governance structures
delegation
accountability
role clarity
escalation paths
programme and project leadership



Openness / Affection
In classic FIRO language this dimension was often called Affection. In later Human Element and related interpretations it is frequently rendered as Openness, emphasising authenticity, emotional transparency, closeness, warmth, and trust.
Common questions beneath openness include:

Can I be real here?
Am I liked?
Can I trust this person?
Is it safe to tell the truth?
How much emotional closeness do I want?

Typical team expressions:

honesty vs guardedness
warmth vs distance
trust vs suspicion
empathy vs detachment
emotional disclosure vs emotional control
direct feedback vs polite avoidance

At work, openness often appears in:

feedback conversations
conflict resolution
mentoring
leadership presence
one-to-ones
trust building
collaboration under pressure

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Expressed and wanted behaviour
A very practical element in FIRO-based work is the difference between what a person expresses toward others and what the person wants from others.
Examples:

Someone may express high inclusion by inviting others in, yet want low inclusion and still feel crowded.
Someone may express low control but want high control, creating frustration.
Someone may express warmth but want little openness in return, or the reverse.

This distinction is useful because many interpersonal tensions arise not from one trait alone, but from the mismatch between:

what I do
what I want
what others do
what others want

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Awareness
Awareness means noticing what is happening in oneself and in the group:

feelings
assumptions
bodily signals
reactions
defensiveness
stories we are telling ourselves
the impact we have on others

Without awareness, people act automatically and often defensively.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Choice
One of the strongest Human Element ideas is that people often feel they “have no choice” when in fact they do have choice, even if the available choices are difficult.
Growth comes from recognising:

what I am doing
why I am doing it
what alternatives I have
what consequences follow from each option

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Truthfulness
Truthfulness does not mean brutal honesty or emotional dumping. It means reducing distortion and becoming more real, more congruent, and less defended.
In practice this can mean:

naming what is happening
acknowledging discomfort
speaking clearly about needs and boundaries
giving feedback honestly and respectfully
reducing pretence

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Self-esteem
A defining Human Element view is that many performance and relationship problems are rooted in impaired self-esteem.
Low self-esteem may show up as:

defensiveness
control behaviour
perfectionism
withdrawal
blame
avoidance
over-compliance
status anxiety
inability to receive feedback

Healthy self-esteem supports:

openness
accountability
curiosity
resilience
confidence without domination
connection without dependency

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Congruence
Congruence is alignment between:

what I feel
what I think
what I say
what I do

The more congruent a person is, the more trustworthy and effective they tend to be.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Group effectiveness
The Human Element suggests that group performance depends not only on technical capability, but also on the quality of interpersonal relations.
A technically strong team may still underperform because of:

hidden agendas
fear of embarrassment
lack of trust
superficial agreement
dependence on hierarchy
unresolved authority issues
silence around conflict
low willingness to say what is true

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Leadership
For leaders, the model is particularly useful because it highlights the hidden emotional and relational layers under everyday management problems.
Examples:

Inclusion-related leadership issues

people not speaking in meetings
stakeholders feeling left out
cliques within teams
remote staff becoming invisible
new joiners struggling to integrate



Control-related leadership issues

unclear authority
duplication of decisions
micro-management
passive resistance
confusion over ownership
weak escalation discipline



Openness-related leadership issues

lack of trust
conflict avoidance
performative agreement
guarded communication
poor quality feedback
inability to discuss difficult topics

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Change and transformation
During change, Human Element work helps explain why resistance is often emotional and relational rather than purely rational.
People may resist because they fear:

exclusion
loss of competence
loss of control
loss of identity
loss of status
loss of relationship security

That makes the framework useful in:

organisation design
programme leadership
transformation offices
mergers
leadership transitions
team reset workshops
post-conflict repair

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Inclusion in practice
Healthy inclusion tends to look like:

balanced participation
clear welcome
people feeling seen
appropriate involvement
respectful visibility

Dysfunctional inclusion patterns can include:

isolation
attention-seeking
social over-dependence
disengagement
chronic exclusion
token involvement

Questions for reflection:

Who feels included in this team?
Who is consistently left out?
Who dominates airtime?
Who never volunteers?
Where are people seeking recognition indirectly?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Control in practice
Healthy control tends to look like:

clear accountability
proportionate authority
good delegation
confidence with boundaries
structured freedom

Dysfunctional control patterns can include:

power struggle
over-control
abdication
dependency
ambiguity
hidden vetoes
passive resistance

Questions for reflection:

Who really decides here?
Is accountability explicit?
Are people over-directed or under-led?
Where does ownership break down?
Where is authority assumed but not agreed?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Openness in practice
Healthy openness tends to look like:

honesty
warmth
trust
empathy
appropriate vulnerability
respectful candour

Dysfunctional openness patterns can include:

guardedness
emotional distance
pseudo-harmony
gossip
avoidance
overexposure without containment

Questions for reflection:

Can people tell the truth here?
What remains unsaid?
Is feedback safe?
Are relationships real or performative?
Is conflict handled directly?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Stakeholder engagement
FIRO provides a useful lens for stakeholder behaviour:

some stakeholders want high inclusion and regular contact
some want high control and strong decision rights
some value openness and trust before they commit
some become disruptive when their core needs are frustrated

Questions to ask:

Does this stakeholder need visibility, influence, reassurance, trust, or autonomy?
Are they reacting to the content of the work, or to how they are being engaged?
Is their resistance really about the proposal, or about belonging, power, or safety?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Project governance
Many governance issues that appear procedural are partly interpersonal:

steering committees that do not make decisions
sponsors who overrule informally
teams that hide bad news
workstreams that compete for authority
delivery teams that feel excluded from decisions

Human Element interpretation:

Inclusion: who is invited into the conversation?
Control: who believes they have the right to decide?
Openness: who feels safe enough to tell the truth?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
PMO leadership
A PMO can use the Human Element in:

workshop design
stakeholder analysis
conflict repair
escalation coaching
retrospectives
leadership diagnostics
team reset interventions
role and governance clarity work

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Strengths

practical and human-centred
useful for teams, leadership, and relationships
explains recurring interpersonal tension clearly
integrates behaviour with deeper self-awareness
applicable in coaching, facilitation, and organisational development
helps connect performance problems with relational dynamics
highly relevant where trust and candour matter

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Typical value

improved communication
better conflict handling
stronger trust
more honest feedback
reduced defensiveness
clearer leadership behaviour
stronger team cohesion
better decision quality

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Cautions

It is not a substitute for clinical or therapeutic treatment.
It should not be used to label or trap people.
Assessment scores should be interpreted with care.
Deep emotional work requires skilled facilitation.
Cultural context matters.
Organisational problems are not only interpersonal; structure, incentives, workload, and strategy also matter.

A weak application turns the model into simplistic typing. A strong application uses it as a lens for dialogue, awareness, and responsible choice.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Individual reflection

When do I feel most included?
When do I feel ignored or marginalised?
How do I react when I lack control?
How do I behave when I feel incompetent?
What makes it hard for me to be open?
What truths do I avoid saying?
What defensive pattern do I return to under stress?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Team reflection

What do we avoid talking about?
Where is trust high and low?
Who is not really included?
How clear are decision rights?
What happens when conflict appears?
Do people feel safe enough to say bad news early?
What would more truthfulness look like in this team?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Leadership reflection

Do I create inclusion or dependency?
Do I provide clarity or over-control?
Do I invite candour or shut it down?
Can people disagree with me safely?
What human need is driving the resistance I see?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Core works and source lineage

Schutz, W. C. FIRO: A Three-Dimensional Theory of Interpersonal Behavior.
Schutz, W. C. The Human Element: Productivity, Self-Esteem, and the Bottom Line.
Later FIRO-related developments include FIRO-B, Element B, and associated organisational applications.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Notes for this project file
