Where prior project chats discussed related behavioural and interpersonal frameworks, this file normalises them into a single, reusable knowledge-base chapter.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
The Human Element is a personal and interpersonal development framework created by Will Schutz. It focuses on how awareness, choice, truthfulness, self-esteem, and behavioural flexibility affect performance, relationships, leadership, trust, and team effectiveness.
A central intellectual foundation beneath The Human Element is FIRO:

Fundamental
Interpersonal
Relations
Orientation

FIRO explains interpersonal behaviour through recurring human needs and concerns that appear in relationships, teams, and organisations. In its widely used form, it focuses on three dimensions:

Inclusion
Control
Openness / Affection

Within the broader Human Element tradition, these dimensions are often interpreted not only as behavioural patterns, but also as gateways to deeper issues of belonging, competence, authenticity, trust, and self-regard.

Inclusion relates to contact, visibility, participation, recognition, belonging, and whether a person feels “in” or “out”.
Common questions beneath inclusion include:

Do I belong here?
Am I seen?
Am I accepted?
Do I matter to this group?
How much contact do I want with others?

Typical team expressions:

joining or withdrawing
speaking up or staying silent
seeking attention or avoiding exposure
wanting frequent interaction or preferring distance
feeling excluded, overlooked, or unnecessary

At work, inclusion often appears in:

onboarding
team meetings
participation in decisions
stakeholder engagement
social integration
workshop dynamics
cross-functional collaboration



Control
Control relates to influence, responsibility, structure, power, authority, competence, and decision rights.
Common questions beneath control include:

Am I competent?
Who decides?
How much influence do I have?
Can I trust others to lead or deliver?
Do I need structure or freedom?

Typical team expressions:

directing vs following
organising vs resisting direction
ambiguity tolerance
conflict over ownership
micro-management
struggle over accountability
preference for clear governance vs flexible autonomy

At work, control often appears in:

decision-making forums
governance structures
delegation
accountability
role clarity
escalation paths
programme and project leadership



Openness / Affection
In classic FIRO language this dimension was often called Affection. In later Human Element and related interpretations it is frequently rendered as Openness, emphasising authenticity, emotional transparency, closeness, warmth, and trust.
Common questions beneath openness include:

Can I be real here?
Am I liked?
Can I trust this person?
Is it safe to tell the truth?
How much emotional closeness do I want?

Typical team expressions:

honesty vs guardedness
warmth vs distance
trust vs suspicion
empathy vs detachment
emotional disclosure vs emotional control
direct feedback vs polite avoidance

At work, openness often appears in:

feedback conversations
conflict resolution
mentoring
leadership presence
one-to-ones
trust building
collaboration under pressure

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Expressed and wanted behaviour
A very practical element in FIRO-based work is the difference between what a person expresses toward others and what the person wants from others.
Examples:

Someone may express high inclusion by inviting others in, yet want low inclusion and still feel crowded.
Someone may express low control but want high control, creating frustration.
Someone may express warmth but want little openness in return, or the reverse.

This distinction is useful because many interpersonal tensions arise not from one trait alone, but from the mismatch between:

what I do
what I want
what others do
what others want

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Awareness
Awareness means noticing what is happening in oneself and in the group:

feelings
assumptions
bodily signals
reactions
defensiveness
stories we are telling ourselves
the impact we have on others

Without awareness, people act automatically and often defensively.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Choice
One of the strongest Human Element ideas is that people often feel they “have no choice” when in fact they do have choice, even if the available choices are difficult.
Growth comes from recognising:

what I am doing
why I am doing it
what alternatives I have
what consequences follow from each option

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Truthfulness
Truthfulness does not mean brutal honesty or emotional dumping. It means reducing distortion and becoming more real, more congruent, and less defended.
In practice this can mean:

naming what is happening
acknowledging discomfort
speaking clearly about needs and boundaries
giving feedback honestly and respectfully
reducing pretence

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Self-esteem
A defining Human Element view is that many performance and relationship problems are rooted in impaired self-esteem.
Low self-esteem may show up as:

defensiveness
control behaviour
perfectionism
withdrawal
blame
avoidance
over-compliance
status anxiety
inability to receive feedback

Healthy self-esteem supports:

openness
accountability
curiosity
resilience
confidence without domination
connection without dependency

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Congruence
Congruence is alignment between:

what I feel
what I think
what I say
what I do

The more congruent a person is, the more trustworthy and effective they tend to be.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Group effectiveness
The Human Element suggests that group performance depends not only on technical capability, but also on the quality of interpersonal relations.
A technically strong team may still underperform because of:

hidden agendas
fear of embarrassment
lack of trust
superficial agreement
dependence on hierarchy
unresolved authority issues
silence around conflict
low willingness to say what is true

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Leadership
For leaders, the model is particularly useful because it highlights the hidden emotional and relational layers under everyday management problems.
Examples:

Inclusion-related leadership issues

people not speaking in meetings
stakeholders feeling left out
cliques within teams
remote staff becoming invisible
new joiners struggling to integrate



Control-related leadership issues

unclear authority
duplication of decisions
micro-management
passive resistance
confusion over ownership
weak escalation discipline



Openness-related leadership issues

lack of trust
conflict avoidance
performative agreement
guarded communication
poor quality feedback
inability to discuss difficult topics

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Change and transformation
During change, Human Element work helps explain why resistance is often emotional and relational rather than purely rational.
People may resist because they fear:

exclusion
loss of competence
loss of control
loss of identity
loss of status
loss of relationship security

That makes the framework useful in:

organisation design
programme leadership
transformation offices
mergers
leadership transitions
team reset workshops
post-conflict repair

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Inclusion in practice
Healthy inclusion tends to look like:

balanced participation
clear welcome
people feeling seen
appropriate involvement
respectful visibility

Dysfunctional inclusion patterns can include:

isolation
attention-seeking
social over-dependence
disengagement
chronic exclusion
token involvement

Questions for reflection:

Who feels included in this team?
Who is consistently left out?
Who dominates airtime?
Who never volunteers?
Where are people seeking recognition indirectly?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Control in practice
Healthy control tends to look like:

clear accountability
proportionate authority
good delegation
confidence with boundaries
structured freedom

Dysfunctional control patterns can include:

power struggle
over-control
abdication
dependency
ambiguity
hidden vetoes
passive resistance

Questions for reflection:

Who really decides here?
Is accountability explicit?
Are people over-directed or under-led?
Where does ownership break down?
Where is authority assumed but not agreed?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Openness in practice
Healthy openness tends to look like:

honesty
warmth
trust
empathy
appropriate vulnerability
respectful candour

Dysfunctional openness patterns can include:

guardedness
emotional distance
pseudo-harmony
gossip
avoidance
overexposure without containment

Questions for reflection:

Can people tell the truth here?
What remains unsaid?
Is feedback safe?
Are relationships real or performative?
Is conflict handled directly?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Stakeholder engagement
FIRO provides a useful lens for stakeholder behaviour:

some stakeholders want high inclusion and regular contact
some want high control and strong decision rights
some value openness and trust before they commit
some become disruptive when their core needs are frustrated

Questions to ask:

Does this stakeholder need visibility, influence, reassurance, trust, or autonomy?
Are they reacting to the content of the work, or to how they are being engaged?
Is their resistance really about the proposal, or about belonging, power, or safety?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Project governance
Many governance issues that appear procedural are partly interpersonal:

steering committees that do not make decisions
sponsors who overrule informally
teams that hide bad news
workstreams that compete for authority
delivery teams that feel excluded from decisions

Human Element interpretation:

Inclusion: who is invited into the conversation?
Control: who believes they have the right to decide?
Openness: who feels safe enough to tell the truth?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
PMO leadership
A PMO can use the Human Element in:

workshop design
stakeholder analysis
conflict repair
escalation coaching
retrospectives
leadership diagnostics
team reset interventions
role and governance clarity work

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Strengths

practical and human-centred
useful for teams, leadership, and relationships
explains recurring interpersonal tension clearly
integrates behaviour with deeper self-awareness
applicable in coaching, facilitation, and organisational development
helps connect performance problems with relational dynamics
highly relevant where trust and candour matter

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Typical value

improved communication
better conflict handling
stronger trust
more honest feedback
reduced defensiveness
clearer leadership behaviour
stronger team cohesion
better decision quality

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Cautions

It is not a substitute for clinical or therapeutic treatment.
It should not be used to label or trap people.
Assessment scores should be interpreted with care.
Deep emotional work requires skilled facilitation.
Cultural context matters.
Organisational problems are not only interpersonal; structure, incentives, workload, and strategy also matter.

A weak application turns the model into simplistic typing. A strong application uses it as a lens for dialogue, awareness, and responsible choice.

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Individual reflection

When do I feel most included?
When do I feel ignored or marginalised?
How do I react when I lack control?
How do I behave when I feel incompetent?
What makes it hard for me to be open?
What truths do I avoid saying?
What defensive pattern do I return to under stress?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Team reflection

What do we avoid talking about?
Where is trust high and low?
Who is not really included?
How clear are decision rights?
What happens when conflict appears?
Do people feel safe enough to say bad news early?
What would more truthfulness look like in this team?

title: FIRO and The Human Element
text:
Leadership reflection

Do I create inclusion or dependency?
Do I provide clarity or over-control?
Do I invite candour or shut it down?
Can people disagree with me safely?
What human need is driving the resistance I see?

text:

Vendor case studies sometimes refer to implementations in three to six months. These are usually associated with one or more of the following conditions:

narrow scope
minimal customisation
strong template reuse
lower migration complexity
limited site count
low regulatory burden
experienced implementation partner
strong executive sponsorship and business availability

By contrast, the longest programmes usually involve:

large legacy estates
many interfaces
poor master data quality
high customisation
multiple geographies
difficult cutover windows
major operating model change
extensive validation or assurance obligations




A practical early-stage formula is:

Estimated Duration = Base Duration x Complexity Factors



Assume a WMS starts with a base of 6 months.
Add complexity:

three warehouses: +30%
ERP and carrier integrations: +25%
handheld device rollout: +10%
large inventory migration: +20%

Result:

6 months x 1.85 = approximately 11 months

This is not mathematically exact, but it is a useful planning approach for portfolio discussions.

When estimating implementation time, it is useful to create at least three scenarios:

optimistic

A robust planning model should also separate:

design and mobilisation
build and configuration
migration and integration
testing
training and readiness
cutover
hypercare and stabilisation

This makes it easier to communicate which part of the timeline is technical effort and which part is operational readiness.



Implementation time for specialist systems should always be estimated as a range, not a single number.
The best predictor is not only the product itself, but also:

system class
delivery method
number of sites
migration complexity
integration footprint
operational criticality
regulatory burden
business readiness

As a result, a relatively small package implementation may take only a few months, while a large operational transformation programme may run for several years.



Oracle describes ERP implementation as a substantial, multi-step process including configuration, migration, testing, training, and go-live planning.[@oracle_erp_impl] SAP positions SAP Activate as a structured implementation framework for SAP transformations.[@sap_activate] Guidewire describes accelerated implementations and cloud transformation approaches that can shorten delivery where scope is controlled.[@guidewire_bolt] Engineering-led industrial implementations commonly include testing and commissioning patterns such as factory acceptance testing and site acceptance testing.[@siemens_commissioning]

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
section: People respond to their map of reality, not reality itself
text:
People respond to their map of reality, not reality itself
A central NLP idea is that people do not respond directly to the world in a pure or objective way. Instead, they respond to their internal representation of events.
That representation is shaped by:

attention
memory
beliefs
values
language
prior experiences
emotional state
interpretation

This is often summarised informally as:

The map is not the territory.

In practice, this means that changing interpretation can change response.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Experience has structure
NLP assumes that subjective experience is not random. It has patterns and structure. If that structure can be noticed, it can sometimes be changed.
Examples include:

what a person says to themselves internally
what images they mentally create
where their attention goes
what bodily sensations they notice
how they sequence memory and imagination
what meaning they assign to events

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
section: If a pattern was learned, it may be changed
text:
If a pattern was learned, it may be changed
NLP often works from the assumption that unhelpful habits, responses, and emotional associations are not fixed identities. They are patterns, and patterns can be interrupted, redesigned, or replaced.
This is one reason NLP became attractive in coaching and self-development.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Modelling excellence
A distinctive NLP principle is that excellence can be modelled. The question becomes:

What exactly does an effective person do?
How do they frame the situation?
What language do they use?
What do they pay attention to?
What sequence of internal and external actions produces the result?

This modelling mindset makes NLP attractive for leadership, sales, facilitation, presentation skills, negotiation, and coaching.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Sensory awareness
NLP places strong emphasis on observing fine details in communication and behaviour, such as:

facial expression
breathing changes
posture
voice tone
rhythm of speech
eye movement patterns
energy shifts
tension and relaxation

The intent is to become more attentive to what is happening in oneself and in others.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Representational systems
A common NLP idea is that people often prefer certain sensory modes when processing experience. These are usually described as:

Visual
Auditory
Kinesthetic
sometimes Olfactory
sometimes Gustatory

In practical NLP teaching, this often appears as attention to whether someone talks in terms of:

images
sounds
feelings
movement
sensory memory

A cautious interpretation is best here. The practical value often lies in increasing communication flexibility, rather than rigidly typing people.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Submodalities
Submodalities are the finer qualities within internal sensory experience.
Examples:

Visual submodalities

bright or dim
near or far
colour or black-and-white
still or moving
large or small
clear or blurred



Auditory submodalities

loud or quiet
fast or slow
near or far
harsh or soft
internal or external



Kinesthetic submodalities

warm or cool
heavy or light
tense or relaxed
moving or still
located in one place or spread through the body

NLP often proposes that changing these qualities can change the emotional impact of a memory or imagined event.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
State
An NLP state is a temporary pattern of thoughts, feelings, physiology, focus, and behaviour.
Examples:

confidence
anxiety
curiosity
calm
motivation
frustration
determination

Much NLP practice is about learning how to recognise, shift, access, or stabilise states.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Physiology
NLP often teaches that body use and mental state are linked. Posture, breathing, muscle tone, facial expression, and movement can influence how a person feels and thinks.
This is one reason many NLP exercises involve:

standing differently
breathing differently
shifting eye focus
changing voice tone
changing movement patterns

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Language patterns
Language is central in NLP because words do not just describe experience; they can also shape it.
NLP pays close attention to:

deletions
distortions
generalisations
vagueness
assumptions
emotionally loaded phrasing
self-talk
question structure

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Rapport
Rapport is one of the most widely used NLP ideas. It refers to establishing a sense of connection, trust, ease, and mutual understanding.
Practical elements may include:

matching pace of conversation
tuning to the other person’s language
listening closely
respecting their frame of reference
showing genuine presence
reducing unnecessary friction

A healthy interpretation of rapport is not manipulation. It is relational attunement.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Anchoring
Anchoring is the process of linking a specific internal state to a trigger, so that the state becomes easier to access later.
Examples of anchors:

a word or phrase
a gesture
a touch point
a breath pattern
a visual cue
a posture

A practical use might be:

recall a strong confident experience
intensify the state
apply a chosen trigger at the peak
repeat
use the trigger later to evoke the state

This is one of the better-known NLP techniques for performance preparation.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Reframing
Reframing means changing the meaning assigned to an experience so that new responses become possible.
Examples:

a mistake becomes feedback
resistance becomes a sign of concern or investment
nervousness becomes activation for performance
criticism becomes information

Reframing can be very useful in coaching, negotiation, emotional regulation, and stakeholder communication.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Swish pattern
The swish pattern is an NLP technique commonly used to shift an unwanted habitual response by replacing it with a more desired mental image and response pattern.
Typical use cases:

self-doubt before speaking
unwanted habits
hesitation
performance nerves
unhelpful impulse loops

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Visualisation and future pacing
NLP often uses guided mental rehearsal.
Future pacing means imagining a future situation while mentally and emotionally rehearsing a more effective response.
This can support:

presentations
difficult conversations
interviews
negotiations
confidence building
behaviour change

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Meta Model
The Meta Model is a questioning framework designed to challenge vague, distorted, or limiting language.
It is used to clarify statements such as:

“They never listen to me.”
“I always fail.”
“Nobody supports this.”
“I have no choice.”
“This will be a disaster.”

A Meta Model style response asks for precision:

Who specifically?
Always?
Compared to what?
How do you know?
What stops you?
What would happen if you did?

This is useful in coaching, analysis, conflict resolution, and critical thinking.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Milton Model
The Milton Model is often described as the opposite complement to the Meta Model.
Where the Meta Model seeks precision, the Milton Model uses artful vagueness, permissive language, metaphor, suggestion, and indirect influence. It is associated with hypnotic or trance-oriented communication and with language designed to bypass resistance.
This makes it relevant in:

guided relaxation
permissive suggestion
storytelling
soft persuasion
therapeutic language patterns
confidence or focus scripts

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Parts work
Some NLP approaches describe internal conflict as if different “parts” of the self are pulling in different directions.
Examples:

one part wants safety, another wants growth
one part wants discipline, another wants relief
one part wants to speak up, another fears rejection

Parts work attempts to surface the positive intention behind each side and reduce internal conflict.

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Stakeholder engagement
NLP-style questioning can help reveal:

what the stakeholder really values
what language they respond to
what emotional concern is driving resistance
whether the issue is uncertainty, control, trust, visibility, or risk

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Difficult conversations
NLP can support difficult conversations by helping a person:

regulate their state first
notice assumptions
choose language carefully
listen for distortions and generalisations
reframe the situation without denying reality

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Presentations and public speaking
NLP techniques are commonly used for:

calming anxiety
anchoring confidence
mentally rehearsing success
shifting self-talk
connecting with audience states
improving vocal and non-verbal delivery

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Practical strengths

highly action-oriented
accessible language
strong focus on communication
encourages behavioural flexibility
offers tools for confidence and preparation
useful for coaching and facilitation
often helpful for reframing and state work

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Why people find it attractive

it feels usable immediately
it gives language for subjective experience
it often improves observation skills
it supports more intentional communication
it can help people feel less trapped by their habitual patterns

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Main criticisms

inconsistent definitions across schools and practitioners
broad claims that exceed evidence
weak or mixed empirical support for many claims
some techniques are presented too confidently
risk of oversimplifying complex psychological issues
possibility of using rapport or influence techniques manipulatively

Mainstream summaries note that NLP became popular in self-help and commercial settings, but that definitions vary and empirical support is limited. citeturn329171search0

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Practical caution
NLP may be useful as a communication and coaching toolkit, but it should not be treated as a complete, scientifically validated model of human psychology.
It is also not a substitute for:

evidence-based mental health treatment
formal clinical care
rigorous behavioural science
sound organisational analysis

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Individual reflection

What outcome do I actually want?
What pattern keeps repeating?
What state do I enter before the problem appears?
What do I say to myself internally?
What meaning am I assigning to the event?
What would a more useful frame be?
What would I do differently if I already felt confident?

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Communication reflection

What language is the other person using?
What assumptions are hidden in their words?
What are they leaving out?
What emotional state are they in?
Am I listening to content only, or also to pattern and state?
What question would create more clarity?

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Performance reflection

What helps me access confidence reliably?
What visualisation strengthens rather than weakens me?
What anchor could I build for focus or calm?
How do I want to show up in the next important moment?

text:

title: Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP)
text:
Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) is a framework and collection of techniques intended to help people understand how subjective experience, language, behaviour, and internal mental patterns interact.
In practical use, NLP is often presented as a way to improve:

communication
self-awareness
emotional state management
confidence
behaviour change
goal focus
influence and rapport
personal effectiveness

NLP became popular in coaching, self-help, sales, training, facilitation, and communication development. It is often valued for its practical techniques and structured conversational methods.
At the same time, NLP is controversial. Many of its claims are broader than the available empirical support. For that reason, it is best approached as a pragmatic toolkit and model of change rather than as a scientifically established theory of mind.

title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288
text:
ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 provides the overarching framework for system life cycle processes across the full life of a system, from conception through development, production, utilisation, support, and retirement. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 provides the corresponding framework for software life cycle processes, and is typically used either on its own for software-centric work or together with 15288 when software forms part of a broader system.
Taken together, the two standards provide a disciplined engineering lifecycle model that helps organisations structure and govern how they define, design, build, integrate, verify, validate, transition, operate, maintain, and retire systems and software.
These standards do not prescribe a single delivery method such as waterfall, V-model, agile, DevOps, or spiral. Instead, they define a process architecture that can be tailored and applied iteratively, concurrently, and recursively.



The value of 12207 and 15288 is that they create a common language for engineering and lifecycle governance across:

business stakeholders
acquirers and suppliers
architects and engineers
project and programme managers
quality and assurance functions
operations and support teams

They help answer core questions such as:

What lifecycle processes should exist?
How do system engineering and software engineering fit together?
How do governance, project control, and engineering execution connect?
How do we maintain traceability from business need to retirement?

This makes the standards particularly useful in large IT and engineering programmes, regulated environments, critical systems, systems integration, product engineering, and enterprise transformation.



A practical way to understand the two standards is:

title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288
text:
ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288 provides the overarching framework for system life cycle processes across the full life of a system, from conception through development, production, utilisation, support, and retirement. ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 provides the corresponding framework for software life cycle processes, and is typically used either on its own for software-centric work or together with 15288 when software forms part of a broader system.
Taken together, the two standards provide a disciplined engineering lifecycle model that helps organisations structure and govern how they define, design, build, integrate, verify, validate, transition, operate, maintain, and retire systems and software.
These standards do not prescribe a single delivery method such as waterfall, V-model, agile, DevOps, or spiral. Instead, they define a process architecture that can be tailored and applied iteratively, concurrently, and recursively.

title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207 and 15288
text:

operations and support teams

What lifecycle processes should exist?
How do system engineering and software engineering fit together?
How do governance, project control, and engineering execution connect?
How do we maintain traceability from business need to retirement?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
This note explains how risk acts throughout the main IT, governance, architecture, delivery, service, and cyber frameworks. It is designed as a reusable reference for a knowledge base and can support governance design, PMO/ITSM integration, architecture reviews, audit mapping, and executive communication.
The core idea is simple:

Risk is the thread that connects strategy, architecture, delivery, operations, security, resilience, assurance, and improvement.

Different frameworks emphasise different parts of the same risk chain.

Service, continuity, supplier, security, change, and operational risk
Embeds risk into live service management and continual improvement
Service risk logs, change assessments, continuity plans, service metrics


TOGAF
Enterprise architecture
Architecture, transition, standards, and technology risk
Influences principles, standards, target states, and transition roadmaps
Architecture principles, standards, roadmaps, design decisions


PRINCE2
Project governance and control
Scope, schedule, cost, quality, dependency, delivery risk
Manages uncertainty through stages, controls, escalation, and decisions
Risk register, exception reports, stage decisions


MSP
Programme governance
Transformation, benefits, stakeholder, dependency risk
Manages risk across multiple projects, outcomes, and change tranches
Programme risk register, dependency views, tranche decisions


NIST RMF
Security and privacy life cycle
Security and privacy risk
Formalises risk through categorisation, control selection, implementation, assessment, authorisation, and monitoring
Security categorisation, control baselines, assessment results


NIST CSF
Cybersecurity governance and operations
Enterprise cyber risk
Connects executive governance to protect, detect, respond, and recover capabilities
Risk profiles, metrics, target state actions


DORA
Regulatory resilience and ICT risk
ICT risk, resilience, third-party ICT risk
Makes operational resilience, testing, incident reporting, and third-party oversight mandatory in regulated finance
ICT risk framework, resilience evidence, incident reporting records

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
ISO 31000
ISO 31000 is the umbrella discipline. It is not limited to IT. It provides a common language and structure for risk management across the enterprise. It is most useful when an organisation wants one coherent approach to risk across governance, projects, operations, architecture, security, and compliance.

Risk role in ISO 31000

Integrates risk into governance and decision-making
Provides principles and a management framework
Encourages consistent identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment, monitoring, and communication
Supports a shared taxonomy and scoring model across disciplines

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
COBIT
COBIT treats risk as a matter of governance first, management second. It is strong where the organisation needs a structured connection between board oversight, executive accountability, control design, and assurance.

Risk role in COBIT

Board and executive focus on risk optimisation
Management translates risk direction into practices and controls
Risk is linked to security, continuity, suppliers, change, information, and assurance
Useful for integrating CIO, CISO, PMO, audit, and architecture views



Practical interpretation
COBIT is especially effective when you want to answer questions such as:

Are we governing IT risk properly?
Are accountabilities clear?
Are we balancing value, risk, and resources?
Is our assurance model coherent?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
ITIL
ITIL treats risk as part of value delivery through services. It does not approach risk mainly as board theory; it approaches it as a practical concern in operating and improving digital services.

Risk role in ITIL

Embedded in service design, transition, support, and improvement
Present in incident, problem, change enablement, supplier, security, monitoring, and continuity practices
Focuses on service stability, quality, resilience, and operational visibility



Practical interpretation
ITIL is most useful when the question is:

How do we keep risk under control while running live services?
How do we reduce service disruption and change failure?
How do we improve resilience, supportability, and customer value?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
TOGAF
TOGAF acts on risk before delivery starts in earnest by improving structure. It reduces risk through architecture principles, standards, target-state thinking, transition architecture, and roadmap choices.

Risk role in TOGAF

Reduces structural risk through better design
Addresses complexity, integration, obsolescence, standards, and technology alignment
Strengthens security and resilience by embedding them into architecture decisions



Practical interpretation
TOGAF helps answer:

Are we designing avoidable risk into the estate?
Are our standards increasing or reducing exposure?
Are transition plans realistic and controlled?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
PRINCE2
PRINCE2 handles risk in a controlled project environment. It is concerned with uncertainty that could affect scope, cost, schedule, quality, and continued business justification.

Risk role in PRINCE2

Identifies and assesses project-level risks
Defines owners, actions, responses, and escalation paths
Uses stage control and exception-based management
Links risk to decision points and business case viability



Practical interpretation
PRINCE2 is useful when the question is:

Will this project still deliver what it promised?
What threatens schedule, scope, cost, or quality?
When should the issue be escalated or re-planned?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
MSP
MSP treats risk at transformation scale rather than single-project scale. It is concerned with whether a programme will land successfully, coordinate its dependencies, achieve desired outcomes, and realise benefits.

Risk role in MSP

Manages uncertainty across multiple projects and workstreams
Focuses on dependency risk, benefit risk, organisational change risk, stakeholder risk, and governance risk
Supports tranche-based decisions and transformation control



Practical interpretation
MSP is valuable when the question becomes:

Will the programme achieve strategic outcomes, not just outputs?
Are the interdependencies being managed effectively?
Is change adoption or benefits realisation at risk?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
NIST RMF
NIST RMF formalises risk in a structured security and privacy life cycle. It is control-oriented and evidence-driven.

Risk role in NIST RMF

Categorises information systems and data sensitivity
Selects and tailors controls
Implements and assesses those controls
Supports authorisation decisions and ongoing monitoring



Practical interpretation
NIST RMF is strong when the organisation asks:

What controls are required for this system?
Are those controls operating effectively?
Can this system be authorised or remain in service?

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
NIST CSF
NIST CSF provides an outcome-based cybersecurity structure. It is particularly helpful for executive communication because it links governance to operational cyber capabilities.

Risk role in NIST CSF

Frames cyber risk through Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Supports target-state design and maturity improvement
Connects cyber operations with leadership communication and prioritisation

title: How Risk Acts Throughout IT Frameworks
text:
DORA
DORA makes ICT risk and operational resilience a matter of regulatory discipline in the financial sector.

Risk role in DORA

Requires structured ICT risk management
Emphasises digital operational resilience
Requires incident reporting, resilience testing, and third-party oversight
Pushes resilience from good practice into formal compliance obligations

title: Strategic Alignment of IT
text:
Strategic Alignment of IT
This is a top-down view of how IT work is typically organized and governed in mature organizations (drawing on common practices from strategic planning, IT portfolio management, programme/project frameworks such as PRINCE2/MSP, software delivery (waterfall/Agile/hybrid), ITIL-style transition, and architecture frameworks such as TOGAF). Layers interact and iterate; documents are living artefacts that cascade and are refined downward.

1. Strategic Alignment to the Business
Purpose: Ensure IT investments and capabilities support business goals, strategy, risk appetite, and value creation.
Key activities:
- Business strategy review and IT strategy formulation.
- Identification of business capabilities, value streams, and pain points.
- Prioritization of IT opportunities against business outcomes.
- Definition of high-level principles, policies, and constraints.
- Stakeholder engagement and governance setup (e.g., IT steering committee).
Typical documents:
- Business Strategy / Corporate Strategy.
- IT Strategy / Digital Strategy / Technology Roadmap.
- Business Case (high-level or enterprise).
- Strategic Objectives & KPIs / OKRs.
- IT Principles, Policies, and Standards.
- Capability Map / Value Stream maps.
- Risk Appetite / Compliance statements.
- Governance Framework / RACI for strategic decisions.


2. Portfolio Management
Purpose: Select, balance, and govern the set of programmes, projects, and operational investments that deliver the strategy. Optimize value, risk, and capacity.
Key activities:
- Demand management and intake.
- Portfolio prioritization and ranking (value, cost, risk, strategic fit).
- Resource and capacity planning across the portfolio.
- Benefits management and tracking at portfolio level.
- Portfolio-level risk, dependency, and financial oversight.
- Continuous review and rebalancing (kill, pause, accelerate).
Typical documents:
- Portfolio Strategy / Investment Thesis.
- Portfolio Roadmap / Pipeline view.
- Demand / Intake Register.
- Prioritization criteria and scoring model.
- Portfolio Business Case / Financial model.
- Resource / Capacity Plan.
- Benefits Realization Plan (portfolio-level).
- Portfolio Risk & Dependency Register.
- Portfolio Dashboard / Status reports.
- Portfolio Governance Charter.


3. Delivery – Programmes and Projects
Purpose: Translate selected portfolio items into coordinated change initiatives (programmes for multi-project transformational change; projects for discrete deliverables).
Key activities:
- Programme/project initiation and definition.
- Scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, and stakeholder management.
- Dependency and benefits management.
- Stage/gate or iterative governance and reporting.
- Change control and issue resolution.
- Closure and lessons learned.
Typical documents:
- Programme/Project Brief or Mandate.
- Business Case (detailed).
- Programme Definition Document / Project Initiation Document (PID) or equivalent (charter, scope statement).
- Benefits Realization Plan / Benefits Map.
- Programme/Project Plan (schedule, WBS, milestones).
- Risk, Issue, Assumption, Dependency (RAID) Log.
- Stakeholder Engagement / Communication Plan.
- Resource Plan / Budget.
- Quality Plan / Acceptance Criteria.
- Stage/Gate reviews, Progress/Status reports, Change Requests.
- Closure Report / Lessons Learned / Post-Implementation Review.


4. Software Development
Purpose: Design, build, test, and prepare the software (or product increments) that deliver the required functionality and non-functional requirements.
Key activities (can be waterfall, Agile/Scrum/Kanban, or hybrid):
- Requirements elicitation and analysis.
- Solution design (high-level and detailed).
- Architecture & technical design (application level).
- Coding / configuration / low-code development.
- Unit, integration, system, and acceptance testing.
- Continuous integration, security scanning, code quality.
- Documentation of the solution.
Typical documents / artefacts:
- Requirements (Business Requirements Document – BRD, Functional Requirements Specification – FRS, User Stories / Product Backlog, Non-Functional Requirements).
- Use Cases / Process models / Wireframes / Prototypes.
- Solution Architecture Document / High-Level Design (HLD).
- Detailed Design / Technical Design Document (TDD) / API specifications.
- Data Model / Interface Control Documents.
- Test Strategy, Test Plans, Test Cases, Test Reports / Defect logs.
- Source code, build scripts, CI/CD pipeline definitions.
- User/Admin guides, Release notes.
- Definition of Done / Acceptance criteria evidence.


5. Transition to Production
Purpose: Safely move the developed solution into the live environment with minimal disruption, ensuring readiness of people, process, and technology.
Key activities:
- Release and deployment planning.
- Environment preparation and data migration.
- Operational readiness (support models, runbooks, monitoring).
- Training and knowledge transfer.
- Cutover / go-live execution and hypercare.
- Handover to service operations (ITIL-style).
- Post-implementation review and benefits confirmation.
Typical documents:
- Release / Deployment Plan / Runbook.
- Transition Plan / Cutover Plan.
- Operational Readiness Checklist / Assessment.
- Support Model / Service Level Agreements (SLAs) / Operational Level Agreements.
- Training materials and knowledge transfer records.
- Data Migration Plan and validation reports.
- Go-Live Checklist / Rollback Plan.
- Change Request / Release notes for production.
- Hypercare Plan and Post-Go-Live Review / Lessons Learned.
- Service Acceptance / Handover Certificate.


6. Infrastructure
Purpose: Provide, configure, secure, and operate the underlying compute, storage, network, cloud, and platform services that host applications and data.
Key activities:
- Infrastructure design and capacity planning.
- Provisioning (on-prem, cloud, hybrid).
- Configuration management and automation (IaC).
- Security hardening, monitoring, backup/DR.
- Ongoing operations, patching, scaling, and cost optimization.
- Alignment with application non-functional requirements.
Typical documents:
- Infrastructure Architecture / Design Document.
- Capacity Plan / Performance requirements.
- Network / Security / Cloud architecture diagrams.
- Infrastructure as Code (Terraform/CloudFormation/etc.) and configuration baselines.
- Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs).
- Monitoring, Alerting, and Logging design.
- Backup, Recovery, and Disaster Recovery Plans / DR test reports.
- Security & Compliance assessments / Hardening standards.
- Cost / FinOps reports.
- Change records for infrastructure.


7. Architecture (Enterprise / Solution / Technical)
Purpose: Provide coherent structure, standards, and guidance across business, data, application, and technology domains so that solutions are consistent, interoperable, secure, and future-proof. Architecture work spans all layers above.
Key activities:
- Enterprise Architecture (EA) development and governance.
- Solution Architecture for specific initiatives.
- Technical/Reference Architecture and patterns.
- Standards, principles, and roadmaps.
- Architecture reviews and compliance.
- Technology radar / innovation tracking.
Typical documents:
- Enterprise Architecture Framework / Metamodel.
- Architecture Principles and Standards.
- Business / Data / Application / Technology Architecture views (e.g., TOGAF ADM artefacts).
- Current-State and Target-State Architecture.
- Architecture Roadmap / Transition Architectures.
- Solution Architecture Document (SAD).
- Reference Architectures / Patterns / Building Blocks.
- Technology Standards Catalogue / Approved products list.
- Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).
- Architecture Review Board decisions and compliance reports.
- Integration / API / Security architecture artefacts.


How the layers connect

Strategy sets the “why” and high-level “what.”

Portfolio decides “which” initiatives and sequences them.

Programmes/Projects manage the “how and when” of change delivery.

Software Development produces the application artefacts.

Transition moves them safely into production.

Infrastructure provides the runtime platform.

Architecture supplies the guardrails, standards, and coherence across everything.

Documents cascade and are refined: a strategic objective becomes a portfolio item, which becomes a programme/project business case and PID, which drives requirements and designs, which feed release and operational artefacts. Governance (steering committees, architecture boards, change advisory boards, etc.) operates at each level with appropriate decision rights.
This structure can be adapted to pure Agile product models (where portfolio becomes product portfolio, programmes/projects become value streams or product teams, and many documents become living backlogs and ADRs) or to highly regulated waterfall environments. The core flow and artefact types remain recognisable.
